Uniform Title: Sādhanamālā, Volume 2 Author: Benoytosh Bhattacharya

Description: This text is a compendium of *sādhanas*, that is, ritual procedures for the worship of Buddhist Tantric deities, particularly those of the Anuttarayoga Tantra. Each *sādhana* provides a description of the deity—including its form, color, vehicle (*vāhana*), and so forth—along with the corresponding visualization (*bhāvanā*), its mantra, and its applications in worship and yogic practice. These were composed by a wide range of eminent Buddhist masters. The earliest author is the Siddha Saraha, who is dated to approximately 630 CE. Along with him are numerous other great Buddhist Siddhas, such as Nāgārjuna, Kukkurīpa, Indrabhūti, Kṛṣṇapāda, Śabara, and others, who flourished during the seventh and eighth centuries. The latest contributors belong to the twelfth century, which establishes the terminus ad quem for the compilation of this collection.

Sādhanamālā | Second Part.
Homage to Kurukullā, who arises from Tārā! First of all, the mantra-practitioner, seated comfortably on a soft cushion or similar seat in some pleasing location,
having brought down the Blessed Lady depicted on a cloth or other support and performed the external worship, [should contemplate] the stainless [deity] within his own heart.
Having visualized the moon, which has the luster of the full moon and arises from the primordial vowel (A), one should place the seed-syllable upon it; specifically,
the fourth of the sibilants (Ha) situated above the color of fire.
It is joined with the letter *ī* (or *i*) and adorned by two spaces (*ākāśa*).
Having made the world stainless with his variegated rays,
and having purified the Sahā world-system and the other realms, he went to Mount Kurukulla.
Having thus exhorted Tārā and caused her to come before him,
the wise one should emanate clouds of great worship from that seed-syllable.
With collections of flowers, incense, lamps, perfumes, and food offerings,
as well as with the worship of graceful gestures, garlands, dance, song, and instrumental music.
The Three Jewels are my refuge; I confess all my misdeeds;
I rejoice in the merit of the world; I set my mind upon the enlightenment of a Buddha.
Thus the mantra should be recited three times, and then "It should be forgiven" should also be said.
In this regard, there is this verse:
"Whatever slight misdeed has been committed by me, of dull intellect,
that must be forgiven by you, O Goddess, for you are the savior of embodied beings."
Then, one's mind should again be established in the dwelling of loving-kindness;
having generated a mind of compassion, one should bring forth a mind of sympathetic joy.
Afterwards, one remains equanimous toward everything by means of the established principle of mind-only;
thereafter, one should make the mind empty in order to abandon the appearance of intrinsic nature.
The five aggregates, which are the basis for rebirth, are burned by the fire of emptiness;
having recited: "Oṃ, I am of the nature of the vajra of the wisdom of emptiness."
For a moment, one should practice the yoga of emptiness to allow the mind to rest;
then, recollecting the previous vow, one should again contemplate the seed-syllable alone.
I have deceived these beings who are destined for final nirvana;
how shall I rescue them from this bottomless ocean of existence?
Thus, filled with compassion for sentient beings, he should abandon the motionless emptiness and,
by means of his mind, generate the mind that consists of the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu).
Having perceived the seed-syllable called "blue lotus" (utpala) from its locus,
therefrom arises the lunar disc within the lotus, produced from the vowel *a*.
Within that moon, moreover, is the seed-syllable; from it, rays of light have gone forth.
By these rays, all world-systems without exception are purified as the object of meditation.

One should meditate on all that is to be purified and all that is to be realized as entering those lotuses by means of rays of light from ten million Buddhas; thereafter, the arising of the Tārā-mantra occurs.
Four-armed, red in color, seated upon a red lotus throne,
adorned with a pair of red garments, auspicious, and wearing red earrings and a crown.
Furthermore, she holds the gesture of fearlessness (abhaya) and an arrow with her two right hands,
while holding a blue lotus and a red lotus with her two left hands.
She dwells within a cave on Mount Kurukullā, adorned with a crown of Arolika;
beneath her red lotus seat stands Rāhu.
Kāmadeva, together with his wife, should be meditated upon as being extremely overwhelmed.
Above Rāhu is Kāmadeva with his wife, seated upon a throne;
there, she sits in the vajra-paryaṅka posture, possessing every artistic skill.
Having correctly meditated upon the Blessed Lady, adorned with all ornaments,
and having attained the form of the commitment (samaya-mūrti), one should summon the wheel of gnosis (jñāna-cakra).
The wisdom-wheel (jñānacakra), instantly perfected in form, stands before one;
having drawn it in with "jaḥ," caused it to enter with "hūṃ," bound it with "vaṃ," and gratified it with "hoḥ."
One should enter the path of bliss through the application of the *samayamudrā*;
when one has formed the *añjali* with both hands, they are bent and made fleshy.
A needle is formed by two long [fingers]; the ring fingers are placed in the middle of the needle.
The two middle fingers are joined like creepers, and the two thumbs are directed downwards.
With this, one should bind [the disciple] with the *samayā* [mudrā] and cause him to enter the *jñānacakra*.
Then, the adept, reciting the verse "I pray to the Buddhas for initiation," should request the empowerment.
Just as the great festival was bestowed upon the Buddhas by Bodhivajra, so too,
for the sake of my protection, grant me today the first [empowerment] of Khavajra.
Those great beings bestow what is known as the royal consecration;
the wise one [is consecrated] like a flower-consecration by means of the five [faces], Locanā and the others.
I bestow the great vajra consecration, honored by the three realms,
which arises from the abode of the three secrets of all the Buddhas.
From the consecration by the Buddhas, Tārā becomes the Dharmacūḍāmaṇi,
illuminating the three worlds with the radiance of her red-colored mind.
Having obtained the jewel of consecration, one should accomplish all siddhis for half a year through firm possession, according to the prescribed procedure before [the deity].
Having offered the bali-oblation at the three junctions of the day, preceded by the sequence of meditative cultivation,
one should recite the mantra with a concentrated mind using this Heart of Tārā.

Oṃ kurukulle hrīḥ hūṃ svāhā. Then, having performed the preliminary service by reciting one hundred thousand syllables, one should subsequently undertake the ritual activity. By one part, wisdom increases; by the other part, it brings about subjugation.
By means of just a third part, a man becomes a remover of poison.
He would be worshipful to the entire world, even to women who are arrogant with pride; the excellent mantra-holder, the all-pervading lord, enjoys [them] according to his will.
Through the practice of yoga with the beautiful celestial maidens.
The syllable *hrīḥ*, placed upon the parasol of passion, becomes the secret of women; that same syllable on the tongue generates the Buddha, and it is likewise in the center of the heart.

Those endowed with compassion should know that the heart-mantra of Tārā— the syllables of Dharma which are well-articulated, which neutralize poison for those who have been bitten, and which conquers the three worlds— is truly effective.
Having visualized oneself as Kurukullā, arisen from the syllable *tāra*, within a lotus—
having placed the object of practice inside— that one should meditate upon her as overwhelmed by passion.
The adept should contemplate [the goddess] holding the nectar of the lotus of the wisdom-being (jñānasattva) upon his head;
thus, he should meditate for seven days at the three junctions of the day.
Having achieved the minor accomplishments through gradual practice, the wise one shall achieve the great accomplishment; there is no doubt about this in any way.
The sādhana of Kurukullā arising from the Tārā described in the Kalpa is completed.
Homage to Kurukullā, who arises from Tārā;
by the mere recollection of whom gods, asuras, and humans alike [are subdued].
They certainly become her servants; I bow to that Tāriṇī.

First of all, the mantra-practitioner, seated comfortably in some place conducive to the mind— free from contact with women and the like— should [visualize], within his own heart, upon a moon disc transformed from the first vowel (A),...
Having first illuminated the world with masses of red rays of light emanating from the seed-syllable *hrīḥ* together with its radiance,
one should visualize Kurukullā residing on Mount Kurukulla.
Having exhorted the Blessed Lady and brought her before him,
he visualized her in the expanse of the sky.
One should worship with various offerings of flowers, incense, and so forth, emanated by the rays of light from the seed-syllable in the heart. Following that, there is prostration,
confession of misdeeds, rejoicing in merit, dedication, and taking refuge in the Three Jewels, preceded by the generation of the mind of enlightenment (*bodhicitta*).
The Triple Gem is my refuge; I confess all my misdeeds; I rejoice in the merit of the world; I set my mind upon the enlightenment of a Buddha.

Thus one should recite three times. Then, preceded by the cultivation of the four divine abodes (*brahmavihāra*), having meditated upon the emptiness of all phenomena (*sarvadharma-śūnyatā*), one should recite the empowerment mantra: *oṃ śūnyatājñānavajrasvabhāvātmako ’ham*. Thereafter, [one should contemplate] the entire world as suffering.

Sustaining one's own mind with compassion and visualizing it in the form of a seed-syllable, one should contemplate its transformation: upon a red water-lily, there is a moon disc transformed from the first vowel (A), upon which the seed-syllable resides. From the rays of light of that seed-syllable, as before, one illuminates the world, summons infinite millions of Tathāgatas, and causes them to enter within. One should then contemplate [the deity] transformed from that lotus and so forth.

She is red in color, seated upon a red lotus and moon, with a red silk garment as her upper robe, surrounded by a red halo of light, and adorned with a red earring and crown; she has four arms: the right hands bestow fearlessness and hold an arrow drawn to the full, while the left hands hold a jewel-bow and a red utpala lotus.
She wears a crown of the Tathāgata Amitābha;
she dwells within a cave on Mount Kurukulla, positioned above Kāmadeva together with his consort, who rests upon the head of Rāhu;
she is endowed with the erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra-rasa) and possesses the prime of youth.
One should meditate on Kurukullā. Thus, having generated the *samayasattva*, one should instantly summon the *jñānasattva* before oneself.
Having worshipped with the *samayamudrā*, one should dissolve [the deity] into the interior by way of the path of bliss (*sukhamārga*).
In this regard, the *samayamudrā* is as follows:

having inserted the two ring fingers into the middle of the needle-like tips of the two middle fingers of the hollowed palms joined together (*sampuṭāñjali*), there should be two creepers on the backs of the middle fingers.
Having inserted two thumbs downward while they remain joined, that is the Utpala mudrā, which has that shape. Following that:
"Just as the great festival was bestowed upon the Buddhas by Bodhivajra..."
For the sake of my protection as well, grant me the Space-Vajra and the others.
Having thus prayed:
"I bestow the consecration of the Great Vajra, which is venerated by the three realms and arises from the source of the three secrets of all Buddhas."

One should meditate on the consecration being bestowed by Locanā and the other goddesses, who recite these words at the command of the Buddha. Amitābha is established upon the crown. Having performed such meditation, one should perform the recitation (japa), neither too fast nor too slow, neither indistinct nor lacking the proper measure of syllables, and free from improper thoughts: *Oṃ Kurukulle hrīḥ*.
*Hrīṃ svāhā*, *Ḍhaḥ hrīḥ huḥ svāhā*, *Hūṃ svāhā*. Thus, following the sequence of the three junctions (*trisandhya*),
preceded by the offering of oblations (*bali*) such as flour and sugar,
with constant, firm, and respectful immersion, [may it be] requested by me.

One should practice for six months with the [protective] enclosures; then the signs of accomplishment appear. Following that, in the first month, the pacification of diseases and other afflictions occurs; in the second month, one obtains excellent food unasked for; in the third, the acquisition of various kinds of clothing; in the fourth, one receives various kinds of betel-leaf incessantly; and in the fifth...

In the sixth month, there is union with women endowed with the qualities of various forms and so forth; there is union with divine women belonging to the gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, kinnaras, and others.

Generally, for one who meditates upon the Bhagavatī, trouble comes from women themselves. Therefore, by abandoning these works of Māra and meditating, there occurs either in a dream or directly the manifestation of the Bhagavatī, as well as the accomplishments of the sword, collyrium, foot-ointment, invisibility, mercury, elixirs, and mastery over those who move through the air, on the earth, and in the netherworld (pātāla).

One should accomplish the *siddhis*. If there is no response, then having bound the previously mentioned mudrā and performed worship, the offering of oblations (*bali*), and so forth, one should recite the mantra throughout the entire night on the full moon at the end of six months. Thereupon, it blazes and one becomes a perfected being (*siddha*). By means of that mudrā, [even] Brahmā, Indra, Rudra, Nārāyaṇa, and the rest...

[The syllables] ḍha, ga, kha, and a: drawn forth by Brahmā and Upendra, they arrive and, having entered into the state of servants, accomplish whatever is desired by the practitioner. From that time forward, free from birth, old age, and death, the Siddha [traverses] the world-realms.
Having gone to the realm, one beholds the Tathāgatas and attains the *bhūmi*, the *dhāraṇīs*, and so forth.
The independent *sādhana* of Kurukullā arising from Tārā— [according to K, it is the Kurukullā following the sequence of the *Āryatārākalpa*]— is completed.
Homage to Kurukullā!

First, the practitioner, seated on a comfortable seat, should visualize the Blessed Lady, the Buddhas, and the Bodhisattvas before him by means of the rays of light from the seed-syllable in his own heart; having worshipped them, he should perform the taking of the three refuges and so forth.
One should perform [this]. Then, having resolved upon emptiness and empowered it with the mantra,
one should visualize a syllable *tāṃ*— garlanded with rays of light— within a moon disc arisen from the syllable *a*.

One should visualize the Blessed Lady Kurukullā as the transformation of that [syllable], red in color, seated in the vajra-paryaṅka posture upon a sun disc on a red eight-petaled lotus, with six arms,
holding the Trailokyavijaya mudrā with her first pair of right and left hands.
Holding a goad and a red utpala lotus with her second right and left hands,
and with her remaining two hands drawing a bow and arrow drawn back to her ear, wearing red garments,
crowned with the five Tathāgatas, and red-colored, [she is situated] upon a moon mandala on the pericarp of a red utpala at the heart of the sādhya.

Having visualized the syllable *tām* (or *am*) mounted upon a wind mandala, one should pierce it with the goad at the heart, draw it in, and sit within its heart; then, repeatedly piercing the object of practice (*sādhya*) with an arrow consisting of a red lotus bud, one should recite the mantra. There, this is the mantra: *oṃ kurukulle hrīḥ*.
"Bring so-and-so under my control! Hoḥ! Svāhā! Then, seeing him agitated, brought under control, and fallen at one's feet, one should dispatch him. In this way, one brings even Śakra under control.
Thus ends the *Ṣaḍbhujakurukullāsādhana*.
Homage to Kurukullā!

Having meditated as before up to the point of emptiness, upon a sun disk produced from the syllable *repha* [or *sūryamaṇḍala*], one should visualize the syllable *hrīḥ*, whose form consists of emanation and reabsorption.
Having meditated on the emanation and reabsorption [of light], and through its instantaneous transformation, one should visualize the Blessed Lady Kurukullā, eight-armed and red in color,
seated in the vajra-paryaṅka posture upon a sun disk on a red eight-petaled lotus, dwelling in the center of a peaked pavilion (kūṭāgāra).
(Holding the Trailokyavijaya mudrā with the first two hands; with the remaining right hands, [holding] a hook...)

One should visualize [the central deity] holding an arrow drawn back to the ear and displaying the boon-granting gesture (*varadamudrā*), while with her remaining left hands she holds a noose, a bow, and a blue lotus; she is adorned with all ornaments. On the eastern petal is Prasannatārā, on the southern petal Niṣpannatārā, on the western petal Jayatārā, on the northern petal Karṇatārā, and on the northeastern petal Cundā.
One should meditate on Cundā in the southeast petal, Aparājitā in the southwest petal, Pradīpatārā in the northwest petal, and Gaurītārā in the northwest [petal]. All of these are red in color,
wear the crowns of the five Tathāgatas, and sit in the vajra-paryanka posture.

With her two right hands she displays the *varada* mudrā and holds an arrow drawn to the ear; with her two left hands she holds a blue lotus and a bow. At the eastern gate is Vajravetālī, pot-bellied, with a distorted face, red in color, crowned by Akṣobhya, and holding a raised index finger and a goad in her two right hands.

Holding a vajra, a bell, and a noose with her two left hands, [one should visualize] Aparājitā at the southern gate, yellow in color, wearing a crown of Ratnasambhava, holding a staff and a goad with her two right hands,
and holding a bell and a noose with her two left hands; and at the western gate, Ekajaṭā, black in color, with hair standing upright.
Lambodara, with her lips pressed by her teeth, Amitābha upon her crown,
holding a vajra and a goad in her two right hands and a bell and a noose in her two left hands; at the northern gate is Vajragāndhārī,
golden-yellow in color, with Amoghasiddhi upon her crown.

One should visualize her with a distorted face and a protruding belly, holding a sword and a goad in her two right hands, and a bell and a noose in her two left hands. These four goddesses stand in the *ālīḍha* posture. In this regard, the Trailokyavijaya mudrā is as follows: the two palms are joined back-to-back.
Having formed a knot with the two ring fingers, one should press the little fingers and the middle fingers with the thumbs, and [hold] the two index fingers.
One should gracefully hold [the hand] in the shape of a hook at the forehead. When weary from meditation, one should recite the mantra:

*oṃ kurukulle hrīḥ svāhā*. By ten thousand recitations (*ayuta*), all people become submissive; by a hundred thousand (*niyuta*), ministers; by a million (*lakṣa*), kings. [The offering of] an *utpala*...

One should offer oblations of *aśvattha* fuel-sticks smeared with clarified butter and honey; one attains the desired state. Having kindled the fire with *śrīphala* wood, one should offer one hundred thousand oblations of *śrīphala* fruits smeared with clarified butter and honey.

[One should] recite [the mantra]; thus the royal ministers become submissive. One should offer a thousand blue lotuses and present a thousand lamps of ghee before the Goddess; all kings will become submissive.
The *Sādhana* of Eight-Armed Kurukullā is completed.
This is the work of Indrabhūtipāda.

Now, if the practitioner (mantrin) desires to bring a woman or a man under his control, he should begin on the first day of the bright fortnight and recite [the mantra] ten thousand times daily at the three junctions of the day, relying upon the Blessed Lady, wearing red garments and covering his body.
The procedure for this is as follows: in one's own heart, there is a red eight-petaled lotus born from the syllable Hrīḥ, which is red and situated within a sun disk.
Having visualized the stalk reaching as far as the vulva, one should contemplate eight bees upon its eight petals,
which are the transformations of the eight vowels: ā, ī, ū, ṛ, ḷ, ai, au, and aḥ.
Having seen [the winds] situated in their respective order— exceedingly joyful, nourished, enraged, and red-colored— and impelled by the wind from one's own nose,
they emerge through the opening of one's own ring finger while meditating upon the person to be acted upon (*sādhya*).
Having meditated upon those [syllables] transformed into the eight short vowels— *a, i, u, ṛ, ḷ, e, o, aṃ*— which have entered the right nostril and been offered as they were cut and shattered,
[one should strike] the victim with a multitude of arrows consisting of red lotus buds drawn back to the ear.
Having pierced the *kiñjalka* (the filaments) of the *sādhyā* and taken those transformed arrows,
the yogin, having emerged through the opening of her left nostril,
should contemplate them entering his own heart through his right nostril; thereafter, having bound them with a lotus-stalk at the throat and pierced the *yoni*.
Having pressed [her] with the goad and brought her under one's control with the flame of the reins, one should mount her and joyfully recite the mantra:
*oṃ kurukulle hrīḥ amukīṃ me vaśamānaya svāhā*. It is said that she is accomplished within seven days. *The Sādhana of Kurukullā through the Bhramarī-yoga.*
Having prostrated before the Mother Kurukullā, the bestower of accomplishments,
her instruction— which grants all attainments— is now written down. One engaged in the yoga of Kurukullā should meditate upon this instruction.
From the syllable *hrīḥ* situated upon the filaments of a red utpala lotus in the heart-sun, there emerge a noose, a goad, and an utpala lotus.

Having bound the body of gnosis—which is red in color—with the noose at the throat and pierced it in the heart with the goad, one causes it to emerge through the nostril, mounted upon a wind-mandala transformed from the syllable *yaṃ*. [In manuscript Ḍh, it is *paṃ*.]
Having struck him in the heart or the *bhaga* with a blue lotus,
and having brought him forth, one should place him on his left side supine; then, by means of the syllable *hrīḥ*, one should withdraw the rays into one's own heart.
At the syllable *ḍha*, one should cause it to enter through the right nostril. Afterwards, once again,

having emerged from within the line of light rays in the form of a red lotus arisen from the seed-syllable in the heart, it reaches the space between the eyebrows, touches the left ear, encircles the head, exits through the opening of the right ear, and by that [same path]—

Having inserted the shaft of the lotus-bud’s stalk— drawn back to the ear— into the hollow of the ray-line of the *kalikāra* (the "bud-maker"), and having slightly opened the mouth of the bud, one should pierce repeatedly, by means of the method of devouring, the *liṅga* or the *bhaga* of the person to be acted upon (*sādhya*), using the seed-syllable.
Some say: one should visualize the target as being pervaded in all limbs by rays that have entered through the impact of the arrow, bleeding, agitated, and without refuge.

If the target has risen up, one should strike it; then, visualizing the target fallen at the soles of one's own feet, one should perform the piercing (vedha) once again in the same manner. However, when one becomes incapable of piercing, then [at the aperture of the seed-syllable in the heart]...

Having raised the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*) through the ray that has entered the aperture, and having placed them supine upon the navel-lotus with their head resting on the left side, one should visualize them pervaded by the seed-syllable’s rays like a mass of snowflakes, rendered agitated; then one should recite the mantra: *oṃ kurukulle hrīḥ*.
Svāhā! This is another instruction on the sequence of the Svādhiṣṭhāna [cakra]; it is also the sequence of the instruction on Kurukullā.
p.
356) Oṃ, homage to Kurukullā!
First, having sat upon a comfortable seat and assumed the form of Kurukullā, [one should contemplate] all sentient beings... [k: omits]
One should begin to bring [all beings] under control. In one’s own heart, visualize a sun disk;
upon it, the syllable *TĀṂ* of red color. From that, five rays of light emanate, making offerings to the Tathāgatas.
Having performed the confession of misdeeds and so forth with the words “The Three Jewels are my refuge,” and so on, one should contemplate emptiness. Afterward—

Upon that is a red utpala lotus; above that is a sun mandala; and above that is the syllable *tāṃ*, red in color. Having transformed all of this, one should meditate upon oneself as the noble lady Kurukullā, red in color, with four arms: in her right hands she holds an arrow and a gesture of fearlessness, while in her left she holds a bow and an utpala lotus;
she stands in the vajra-paryaṅka posture, wearing a red bodice and upper garment.
One should visualize Kāmadeva together with his consort below. Then, endowed with meditative visualization, one should recite the mantra: Oṃ Kurukulle hrīḥ svāhā.
This is the *Kurukullā-sādhana*.
Having meditated upon a red utpala lotus born from the syllable *hrīḥ* within the moon-maṇḍala at one’s own heart (*svahṛd*), its center occupied by the syllable *hrīḥ*,
and having visualized the Noble Kurukullā as its transformation— she who is red in color and seated upon a red lotus and moon-disc—
She has a halo of red light, wears various red garments and an upper robe, and bears Amitābha on her crown; she has four arms,
and with her two principal hands she holds a flowery bow and an arrow adorned with the bud of a red utpala flower drawn back to the ear,
while with her left—

Having seen her holding a *sakanda* and a blooming red lotus in her [right] hand, granting boons with her right [hand], and radiant with the great sentiment of passion (*śṛṅgāra-rasa*), [she is visualized]. (The term *mahā* is omitted in manuscripts k, g, and kh.)
Having seen them, one should unify them with the Jñānasattva and,

beholding hundreds of thousands of hosts of gods, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, mahoragas, yakṣas, men, and women in the ten directions— whose bodies are bowed in prostration, who are filled with extreme devotion, and who are under the power of another— one should recite *oṃ*.

One should recite the mantra "Kurukulle hrīḥ svāhā," beginning from one hundred thousand recitations until one has directly beheld the Blessed Lady. Then, someone desiring to bring another under their control, having completed the hundred-thousand recitation, should perform the yoga as described.

Having prostrated with devotion and established the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*)— drawn forward by the hook-like rays of light from his own body which stand amidst the gods and asuras— in front of him,
he should visualize a sixteen-petaled red lotus in his own heart, and within that [lotus], in the heart [of the *sādhya*].
Having reflected upon her steadfastness as before, according to the sequence taught by the noble Vajrānaṅga,
one should firmly seize the syllable of her name within one's own heart with the mantra through the meditation on the bee and the hook;
likewise, having pierced her heart with the arrow, she becomes faint from great passion.
Having bound him by the feet with a bow and by the neck with a noose of blue lotuses, and having drawn him near and cast him down at one's own feet—
one should pierce a man in the heart with a goad,
or a woman in the *dharmodaya*— with the mantra: *Oṃ kurukulle amukaṃ amukīṃ vā*.

One should recite the mantra *ākarṣaya hrīḥ svāhā*. Once the target (*sādhya*) has been drawn in, one should recite that same mantra, interlacing it with the words "bring under control" (*vaśamānaya*). By a hundred recitations in general, a multitude of men and women [is brought under control].
By ten thousand [recitations], the royal minister becomes submissive; by one hundred thousand, the people of the realm;
by seven hundred thousand, the king; and by ten million, the maidens of the gods and asuras.
By means of infinite recitation performed with devotion, continuity, and over a long period of time— whether involving divine animals such as Garuḍa and Airāvata, or ordinary animals—
one may bring even the three worlds under one's control.
The Sadhana of Noble and Glorious Kurukullā.

First, at the beginning of the meditation, having sat upon a soft seat on a patch of ground smeared with five kinds of fragrant substances, the practitioner— joyful in mind, observant of vows, and composed— should then visualize within his heart a sun disk transformed from the syllable *repha*, formidable with garlands of flames, and in its center, the red syllable *hrīḥ*. Then, [light] issues forth from the syllable *hrīḥ*.
Having illuminated the realms of sentient beings situated in the ten directions with networks of light rays,

and having established them in the form of the illustrious Kurukullā, one should visualize those light rays returning and re-entering that very [deity]. Thereafter, in the sky before one, [one should visualize her] appearing as a sixteen-year-old girl...

Kh, A: In front [of her], one should visualize [the goddess] with eight blazing, tawny, upward-pointing hair-tufts, having a head adorned with five skulls, seated upon a corpse, her necklace decorated with a garland of severed heads, standing in the dancing posture of half-lotus (ardhaparyaṅka),
with a face made terrifying by slightly bared fangs and a protruding tongue.
Adorned with ornaments consisting of bracelets, earrings, necklaces, armlets, girdles, and anklets; clothed in a tiger skin;
with three eyes fixed upon a moving, red, circular bow;
crowned by Lord Amitābha; and possessing four arms.
One should visualize her holding a red lotus bud as an arrow drawn back to the ear and a red flower-bow;
with her remaining two arms, she holds a goad made of red flowers and a red lotus.
This is for the purpose of worshipping her.
One should worship with the fivefold offerings arising from the syllable *hrīḥ* situated within the solar disc at one’s own heart—
namely, flowers, incense, lamps, perfumes, food offerings, and so forth. Having thus worshipped, the yogi, possessed of supreme compassion, [proceeds].
With devotion, one bows by means of the body and so forth— that is, through the prostration of the body and so on. Then, whatever sin has been committed by me,
caused to be committed, or even rejoiced in, that [is confessed] before the Bhagavatī.
He teaches directly. Thereafter, he maintains the bodhicitta, which consists in the rescue of the realm of sentient beings fallen into the ocean of saṃsāra.
Then, one should cultivate the four divine abidings (brahmavihāras). Following that is the meditation on emptiness.
In that regard, one should establish the mind as "mind-only" with this mantra: *oṃ śūnyatājñānavajrasvabhāvātmako ’ham*.

Thus is the empowerment of the mind (*cittādhiṣṭhāna*). Following that, one should visualize in the space before oneself a solar disc transformed from the syllable *repha* (ra), formidable with its blazing flames. Above that, one should visualize a crossed-vajra (*viśvavajra*) transformed from a black syllable *hūṃ*, as well as a protective fence, a canopy, and a ground consisting of vajras; this is the protection wheel (*rakṣācakra*). Then—
In the center, one should visualize the divine *dharmodaya*-wisdom in the form of the letter *e*, white in color. In its center is a red eight-petaled lotus arising from the syllable *hrīḥ* in red;
upon its filaments is a sun disk transformed from the letter *ra*.

[One visualizes] the sun, transformed from the red syllable *hrīḥ*, and repeats "thus the protection wheel" (*iti rakṣācakraṃ*). Above that [is] *kh*; [one] also repeats the same for *a*. Above that is an arrow; again, above that is a full moon white as snow, consisting of the thirty-two major marks (*dvātriṃśallakṣaṇa*); and again above that is a solar disc (*sūryamaṇḍala*) in the form of the eighty-four consonants.

Between those two, one should visualize a red syllable *hrīḥ* transformed into a red utpala bud and arrows, which have entered one’s own mind. Afterwards, having become one with the moon, sun, and arrows, one should visualize oneself as liquefied and, as before, in the form of Kurukullā. Having visualized this, in one’s own heart...
With the letter *ra* situated in the heart,
one should again visualize a solar disc at its navel and the syllable *hrīḥ*.

Having drawn in the Lord Amitābha by means of the rays of light arising from that [deity], and having brought him forth, one should worship him with both secret and ordinary offerings and request the empowerment (*abhiṣeka*). In this regard, the request is as follows: "May the Lord Amitābha empower me. (Or: *mām*...)

"O Lord! Then, by that Amitanātha, one should visualize five vases filled with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) pulsating forth from one's own heart. Then, having bathed [the deity] with those vases completely filled with the five nectars...

One should cause the vases to enter one's own heart. Having caused them to enter there, the yogi should visualize Lord Amitābha upon his head; having thus meditated during the three junctions of the day, he should recite the mantra. Then the mantra is: *oṃ kurukulle hrīḥ svāhā*.
Recitation performed specifically with red sandalwood is especially effective. One should perform the consecration of the mouth with *oṃ āḥ hūṃ*.

Then, the practitioner, desiring to bring a woman or a man under his control, should begin on the first day of the bright fortnight and recite the mantra ten thousand times daily at the three junctions of the day. Visualizing the form of the Blessed Lady, wearing red garments and covering his body with them, he should then [visualize] in his own heart an eight-petaled red lotus, which has arisen from the transformation of the red syllable *hrīḥ* situated within the sun located in his heart.
One should visualize the stalk reaching as far as the vulva. Upon its petals are eight bees,
transformed from the eight internal vowels, which are extremely joyful, nourished, and have faces red with anger, arranged in their sequential order.
[Having been] thoroughly cultivated, impelled by the wind from one's own nose,
they fly up, emerge through the left nostril, enter the right nostril of the person to be acted upon,
and— due to being violently mown down and shattered— the first eight vowels [are extracted].
One should visualize some slightly red petals as being joined together. (p. 361) *Vistīrṇa* (k, g: *vibhāva*; kh, a: *vibhūṣa*).

The yogi should look; then, with an arrow consisting of the bud of a red lotus drawn back to the ear, the mantra-practitioner, joined with a fixed fist, should pierce the filaments. Then those bees, impelled by their own convention, emerge through the opening of the left nostril, [each taking] one vowel.

Having grasped her, one should cause her to enter through the right nostril of the yogin; thus, by means of the knowledge of oneself and the other, one should effect their unification within one's own heart. Afterwards, having bound her by the neck with a lotus, and having pressed her yoni with a goad, one should bring her under control while visualizing her as being pierced by a shower of arrows.
The practitioner should bring the target, mounted upon a whirling firebrand,
by means of the mantra-form;
always joyful and well-resolved, he should recite the mantra according to the oral instruction.

Oṃ kurukulle hrīḥ smukīṃ me vaśamānaya svāhā! One should perform this entire rite day and night. Then, impelled by the mantra, she comes, becoming agitated—her hair disheveled or naked, rendered helpless and tormented by the god of love.
Having attained that [state], one should worship the Buddha-maṇḍala through one's own preferred yoga.
Vast accomplishment is not obstructed by anyone.
Thus ends the *Sādhana* of Kurukullā as emerged from Oḍḍiyāna. [Kh, A: Oḍi; Kh: adds *oṃ siddhiḥ* after the colophon.]
Having paid homage to Kurukullā for the sake of increasing the intelligence of beginners,
the stages of meditative cultivation (bhāvanākrama) are here described through the grace of the Guru’s feet.
First, the practitioner— desiring to liberate all sentient beings and himself from all sufferings—
should rise at the dawn twilight, perform the washing of the face and other preliminary rites,
sit upon a comfortable seat in a place conducive to the mind, and, turning away from all other thoughts, [recite] the mantra of the three principles (tritattva).
Having performed the protection of the place, oneself, and the yoga, one should visualize a bright lunar disc in one’s own heart.

Above that, one should contemplate one’s own seed-syllable emitting rays of light; with those rays, having drawn the Blessed Lady from the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu) and established her in front, one should worship her with various kinds of diverse and fragrant offerings, and perform prostrations and so forth.
Having asked for forgiveness and dedicated the merit, one should make an aspiration.
Then, having meditated upon emptiness with this mantra: *oṃ śūnyatājñānavajrasvabhāvātmako ’ham*.

Having empowered oneself once more with the three principles (*tritattva*), one should contemplate oneself in the sky as having a luminous form, like a painting. Immediately thereafter, one should visualize a white moon disc in one's own heart, upon which is a blue lotus born from the seed-syllable *hrīḥ*, and above that—
Having performed the radiation and reabsorption [of light] from the seed-syllable situated above the mandala-circle marked by nectar,

one should empower oneself with the mantra of the three principles; and [one should visualize] the Goddess, who holds a rosary, a lotus, and a vessel of nectar in her right and left hands, who has three eyes, and who is surrounded by all the Tathāgatas, headed by Padmadhṛk.

She is consecrated by the sixteen goddesses beginning with Vīṇā; her matted hair is adorned with a crown and various flowers resplendent with Amitābha; she is endowed with the erotic and other aesthetic sentiments (rasas); she gazes at the rosary held slightly in her right sprout-like hand;
and she stands upon a white lotus from the Ocean of Milk, atop the lap of Amṛta.
Seated upon a sattvaparyaṅka throne,
she is adorned with bracelets, armlets, earrings, anklets, pearl necklaces, divine garments, and other ornaments.
Her hair is bound by the blue Ananta; she wears a necklace made of the milk-white Vāsuki;
her fierce earrings are made of the red Takṣaka;
her sacred thread is made of the dūrvā-green Karkoṭaka; and she wears a necklace made of the white Padma, the lord of nāgas.
She has anklets made of great lotuses the color of lotus stalks,
bracelets made of yellow Śaṅkhapāla, and armlets made of Kulika like smoke-colored clouds; she is of brilliant white complexion.
One should meditate on her whose form drips nectar and whose mind is moist with compassion.

Immediately thereafter, having visualized the primordial seed-syllable upon a lunar disc in one’s own heart, radiating rays of light, and having brought all sentient beings—having produced them in the form of the Blessed Lady—by means of those rays, [one should do so] with this: *oṃ jaḥ hūṃ vaṃ hoḥ*.

Having unified them like milk and water through the mantra and caused them to enter one's own body, one should satisfy and stabilize the previously worshipped Bhagavatī by means of the three principles (tritattva)—white, red, and black—and seal her at the head, throat, and heart with the mudrās.
Thereafter, by the rays expanded from the seed-syllable of the heart, [one should contemplate those residing] in the world-realms such as Sukhāvatī and Mahā... etc.

One should recite the verses preceded by the recitation of the following, while visualizing all the Tathāgatas headed by Amitanātha, accompanied by the sixteen goddesses beginning with Vīṇā, and [the vessel] filled with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta), camphor, saffron, musk, and fragrant scents, which are of the nature of the five Tathāgatas: In this regard, the verse is as follows:
Verse:
Just as the Great Festival was bestowed upon the Buddhas by Bodhivajra—[Note: In manuscript *kha*, instead of this verse, *a* reads: "Having awakened by means of Bodhivajra," and so forth].
For the sake of my protection as well, grant me the Space-Vajra and the others.
The great vajra consecration, honored by the three realms, is divided into three types.
I take hold of that which arises from the abode of the three secrets of all the Buddhas.
Just as all the Tathāgatas were bathed immediately upon birth,
so shall I bathe you with pure, divine water.
"May all the Tathāgatas, headed by Amitanātha and accompanied by the sixteen goddesses beginning with Vīṇā, consecrate me!
With the mantra "Oṃ sarvatathāgatābhiṣeka-samaya-śriye Āḥ Hūṃ," they likewise consecrate him and enter into his crown, and Amitābha remains upon his head as the leader.

The reception of the consecration: thereupon, from one’s own navel, having caused to emerge through the gate of bliss the letter *sa*— situated upon the moon within a lotus, mounted upon the seed-syllable of fire (*ra*), joined with the nasal bindu, the *nāda*, and the fourth vowel (*au*), radiant with the vowels and consonants, consisting of nectar, white, and shining intensely like a lamp lit from another lamp— [End of sentence fragment]
Having instantly seized the power of all jewels, mantras, and medicinal herbs, one should cause them to enter the *nāda* through the gateway of the navel.

Again and again, the yogi— endowed with the recollection of his own true nature (*svarūpa*)— having made a ninefold string from thread spun by a virgin, and having fashioned a rosary of fifty-one crystal beads, [should perform the practice] with *patrañjīva*.
Or, having grasped [the substance] with the thumb and middle finger of the *prabhu* (lord) [mudrā], one should perform the rite for pacification (*śāntika*) one hundred and one times;
or, using the thumbs of the wrathful [mudrā], one should contemplate it for a long time at three or four sessions of the day.

Through the yoga of attracting knowledge, one should mutter that very same mantra-syllable with a firm mind and an absorbed consciousness. Having performed the preliminary service (*pūrvasevā*) for one hundred thousand recitations, by muttering it ten thousand times every day for two and a half months, one becomes a poet and effects the destruction of poison.
Even one of little merit, by muttering it twenty-one hundred thousand times, [should use] water consecrated twenty-one times...
If a stylus or the hand is empowered with the mantra twenty-one times and placed in someone's hand or upon their head, even if that person is a fool,
they will become a poet; they will become a debater whom no assembly can overcome, and they will possess a radiance equal to Mañjuśrī.

One contemplates all the scriptures even if they have not been heard. Or, for the increase of wisdom, this mantra should be recited according to the teacher’s instruction: *oṃ kurukulle hrīḥ vada vada vāgvādini svāhā*. By the recitation of one hundred thousand repetitions of this seven-syllable mantra, [wisdom is attained].
By performing eighty thousand oblations of white flowers anointed with the three sweets, conjoined with the previously described ritual procedure and the mantra, one obtains even a Nāga maiden,
as well as a divine or human woman who has not been sought; this is no wonder.

This is established: the Blessed Buddha is inconceivable, the Buddha-dharmas are also inconceivable, and the accomplishments of the Buddhas are inconceivable; for the power of jewels, mantras, and medicinal herbs is indeed inconceivable. As before, with a thread spun by a young maiden...

Having prepared a cloth-painting by a weaver who has observed the Poṣadha vows, and having placed it before him at the three times of day, worshipping it with fragrant flowers, the mantra should be recited with pride and a mind of loving-kindness (*maitracitta*).
He says that for one whose mind is characterized by lethargy, agitation, doubt, indolence, or hesitation, or whose mind is distracted or dull, [the practice] is in vain.
Because of the statement "known by all," these states such as *styāna* (sloth) and so forth must be diligently avoided with effort for the sake of quickly restraining the mind. Furthermore,

the ten-syllable mantra of Tārā should be recited through this Kurukullā-yoga for the pacification of all obstacles (*vighna*) and for the subjugation (*vaśa*) of sentient beings, since there is no difference between Tārā and Kurukullā.
The procedure for wisdom:
One should consume the leaves called *gṛha*, as well as *śaṭī*,
*yaṣṭimadhu*, *brāhmī*, and *māgadhī*, together with honey.
The one who has accomplished his task.

The instruction for this is as follows: having consecrated the medicine seven times with the seven-syllable mantra, one should produce it as consisting of nectar, and then assume the form of the Blessed Lady oneself.

Having brought down the Blessed Lady depicted on a cloth or similar medium and having worshipped her, one should consume it at dawn. At the time of sleep, one should make a small packet, place it in the mouth, and go to bed. By this means, one becomes possessed of great wisdom. *Oṃ kurukulle svāhā*.
The ritual procedure for the Prajñā-tantra:
Ghee and the root of *tagara*, likewise marked with a wheel;
by means of an ointment applied to the site of the fang-bite, or by drinking it, one removes poison.

The Tantra of Poison: Having visualized the Blessed Lady, who has arisen from the transformation of the previously mentioned signs, seed-syllable, and red color, with her mind entirely moistened by compassion;
and having visualized within one's own heart, upon a red moon, the syllable *oṃ* situated on a six-pointed wheel, [as it appears in k and g], followed by *kurukulle*.

Saying "svāhā," one should summon the Blessed Lady, who is the nature of the Knowledge Being (jñānasattva), by means of the radiating rays of light from the seven seed-syllables; having caused her to enter through the gate of bliss (sukhadvāra) by means of the previously mentioned mantra as before, one should merge her into oneness and perform all the rites beginning with the three principles (tritattva).
Having drawn forth the person to be subdued with rays from the seed-syllable in the heart, bound him with the noose of the rosary, and cast him down at one's own feet—
seeing him with disheveled hair, overwhelmed, as if dead, and having turned that very rosary-noose into a goad—

Having drawn out the consciousness of the victim through the door of great bliss— that is, through the aperture of the *avadhūtī*— by means of the noose of the rosary, using either red sandalwood or coral, at the door of the victim's private parts.
With a rosary of twenty-six beads held between the ring finger and the thumb, and with a mind full of passion,
one should recite the seven-syllable mantra. As before, the red syllable *hrīḥ* should again be visualized upon the pericarp of the lotus filaments.
The rite for subjugation (*vaśyavidhi*).
Furthermore, by one desiring to bring a woman under control, on the eighth day of the month of Aśoka, beneath an *aśoka* tree— [kh, a: p. 367] —
Having gone to Menamāṣṭa and donned red garments, with a one-pointed mind and an exceedingly longing disposition,
having performed the yoga of Kurukullā and consumed *madanaphala* (love-fruit), one should apply a *tilaka* (forehead mark) with the juice of *kārmācikā*.
Having dressed her, with a mind that is submissive and devoted, one should recite the mantra.
In this regard, the mantra is: *oṃ hrīḥ amukīṃ me vaśamānaya svāhā*. Or else, by means of the seven-syllable mantra.

Or, having interlaced the name ending with "svāhā," one should recite the mantra. It brings even the deities under one's control, let alone insignificant humans. Even Mahākāla was brought under control by Hārītī, the great yakṣiṇī, by means of this Kurukullā mantra.
The rite for subjugation (*vaśyavidhi*):
*jārī*, *caṇḍālikā*, *snehamallī*, one's own semen,
dead people, and intestinal worms bring about subjugation when consumed.
Having taken the eye and the restless heart of a dead man, as well as the flesh of his forehead and likewise his nose,
one should grind them, cook them in oil under the Puṣya asterism, and it becomes a means of subjugation.
Of the people.
The ritual procedure for subjugation (*vaśya-tantra-vidhi*):
Oṃ Kurukulle, destroy, destroy all evil ones; pin them down, pin them down; shatter, shatter; crush, crush;
annihilate, annihilate; drive away, drive away; accomplish what is desired for me; grant me peace!
Grant me nourishment; make all sentient beings subject to my will, svāhā! Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ krauṃ hūṃ.
With this mantra—haṃ [ḍh, g: heṃ], hāṃ [ḍh: hāḥ], hāḥ [k:

hoḥ]—one should visualize the food and other offerings as consisting of nectar, resembling mercury, within a lotus vessel situated upon the mandalas of wind and fire [ḍh: three mandalas]; then, one should consecrate it with the three-syllable mantra.

[The syllables] *k, ḍh, g, kh, a* [represent] the Lord of the Eye (*dyakṣa*). They are offered to the Blessed Lady and to all beings. With the mantra *oṃ muḥ*, one should dismiss all the worship and other rites. By this, the pacification of great obstacles occurs.
This is the procedure for the *bali* offering.
Now I shall explain the ritual procedure for the fire-pit (homakuṇḍa):
with a peaceful mind during pacification (śāntika), with a nourishing mind during enrichment (puṣṭika),
with an eager mind during subjugation (vaśya), and with an agitated mind during killing (māraṇa).
In rites for pacification, the shape is circular; in rites for enrichment, it is the shape of a wind-wheel;
in rites for subjugation, it is called the half-moon; and in rites for killing, it is like the element of space.
For the rite of pacification, it should be one cubit; for nourishment, two cubits from that point;
as it is for subjugation, so it is for attraction; and for killing, it should be twenty finger-breadths.
In rites for pacification, it should be half a cubit; in rites for nourishment, one cubit;
in rites for killing, two fingers; and likewise in rites for attraction and subjugation, five fingers.
One should perform the *śāntika* fire-offering on the auspicious lunar days (*pratipad*), the *pauṣṭika* on the full moon,
the *abhicāra* on the fourteenth day, and the rite of subjugation (*vaśyakarman*) on the eighth day.
Thus it is said. Others [state]:

"Then one should inscribe the mantra according to the dimensions of the fire-pit (homakuṇḍa). For pacification (śāntika), it should be made circular; one should mark it as being one cubit (hasta) in measure."
One should dig half a cubit into the ground and have it colored white; then,
having drawn circular shapes all around on both sides.
For the rite of nourishment (*pauṣṭika*), one should dig a pit two cubits deep, or then one cubit;
it should be square and level, and marked with lines.
With yellow ochre.
For an act of sorcery (abhicāra), one should dig a triangular pit twenty finger-breadths in width and fifteen finger-breadths deep, and draw it filled with garlands of flames.
A half-moon should be drawn for the rites of subjugation and attraction;
thus the sacrificial pit (homakuṇḍa) is prescribed, and one should designate the directions and their respective portions.
Facing north, the mantra-practitioner should begin the rite of pacification;
for enrichment, always in the east; and for malevolent magic, in the south.
In the west, however, it is always said that [rites such as] summoning and eradication are performed;
malevolent magic (abhicāra) is always black, while for subjugation (vaśya), it is five-colored.
With sesame, rice, milk, ghee, and honey—
combined with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta)— the rites for pacification (śāntika) and nourishment (pauṣṭika) are considered effective.
One should offer all kinds of fuel from milky trees and fragrant woods,
as well as various types of edible food, or the bali offering for all beings (sārvabhautika).
The practitioner should perform pacifying rites during the autumn, nourishing rites during the winter,
and all rites of sorcery during the summer.
It is taught that the rite for pacification (śāntika) should be performed at dusk, and likewise the rite for nourishment (pauṣṭika) at dawn;
one should perform the rite of malevolent magic (abhicāraka) at midday or at midnight.
Indeed, those teachers who do not speak of a fixed number for the fire-offering ritual,
and who are greatly peaceful, are honored within the Buddha's teaching.
Others who possess minds of passion, those who are hateful, those who revile others,
those who are arrogant, and those possessed by delusion— these are excluded from the teaching of the Buddha.
Thus ends the procedure for the fire-offering pit (*homakuṇḍa*).
Furthermore, one who has been bitten by Time (*kāladaṣṭa*)—
through desire (*kāma*) or by means of the body (*kāya*), according to the teacher’s instruction— having recognized the time, [should place] himself...
Having meditated on the form of Śeṣanāga, white in color, situated upon an eight-petaled lotus in one’s own heart,

one should visualize the seed-syllable of Prajñā located within the mandala of Prajñā, drinking the nectar of great bliss; then, having projected it from the eyes, [one should visualize it] reaching the person to be accomplished (sādhya) from the head, eyes, face, hands, private parts, down to the feet.

One should meditate upon it as it floats with a one-pointed and firm mind. Otherwise, having properly prepared the ring finger—joined with the *poṣadha* [vow], bearing the seed-syllable previously mentioned for the maṇḍala—at the base of the bell joined with the seed-syllable, one should touch it; likewise the staff.

Having given it, one should cover it with the index finger or with a cloth containing the life-force (*jīva*); otherwise, one should touch the previously mentioned locations with an unbleached cloth. The preliminary *poṣadha* vow should be administered; otherwise, one should meditate upon [the deity] floating within the lunar disc.
Now, a drink of *suraghoṣa* and *ṭaṅkana* should be given.

The ritual placement of the limbs (*aṅganyāsa*) must always be performed with the hand. One who has been bitten by [the snake] through the three principles (*tritattva*) should be liberated; by this, he shall rise up, of this there is no doubt. Furthermore, one who has been bitten by the Lord of Serpents while bound at the throat, or one being carried into the sky by the King of Birds while squeezed by his beak, or one who has entered the sky—such a person shall become free from poison. It flowed away.
If one meditates upon the moon together with its stars as being like a skull-cup overflowing with water, the poison of those who are dancing becomes neutralized; it is not otherwise.
If one sees the bitten person as if he were Govinda, sleeping upon the coils of Ananta, and bathed in the waters of the Ocean of Milk, the poison becomes neutralized; it is not otherwise.
The western direction is known as the past; it brings about supreme pacification and exhilaration. White is to be known as the remover of poison, while yellow, moreover, causes immobilization.
Transference is performed with red [pigment], and movement is considered to be done with black;
endowed with four arms as appropriate and possessed of the four seed-syllables,
it certainly effects immobilization, eradication, ritual placement, and paralyzing.
One should apply the "Parastambha-Meru" [technique], but one must perform the *stobhana* (paralysis) and *cālana* (movement) accompanied by focused concentration (*praṇidhāna*).

He who blocks the mouth, eyes, ears, and nose with his own hands destroys poison by means of the utterance of the *Haṃsa*, according to the Guru’s instruction. Having drawn up the poison with his fist, he transfers it; of this there is no doubt.
Through the application of its own purgative, the poison is destroyed by the consumption of *vyoṣa*.

And by the application of drinking *sauvīra* produced from the ocean, poison is killed. Furthermore, a white-hooded snake marked with a discus is carried by men without hesitation; such a serpent is cherished.
Guha, Siṃha, Candra, and Sūrya—those who have but one [enemy], their armor is secure; even if Kāla becomes enraged, what can he do? They are armored.
[Shadow: A cave, a lion, the moon, the sun, and a single serpent have come together for them;
what can that wretched, enraged Time do?]
The *Sādhana* of White Kurukullā is completed.
Homage to Kurukullā!
Her eyes resemble blooming lotuses stirred by the wind; all her limbs captivate the fresh beauty of the forest.
Prostrate before Kurukullā, who wields a clearly manifest ring-shaped bow and a shimmering goad marked with the syllable *iṣṭa*,
and who destroys the serpent of desire.
First, at the beginning of the meditation, having sat upon a soft seat with a joyful mind on a secluded patch of ground smeared with the five perfumes, the practitioner should then, in his heart,
visualize a sun disk marked by a red letter *ra*, formidable with garlands of flames; then, from that, [he should visualize] the first vowel in his own heart.

Then, [visualize] a moon disc, upon which is the supreme seed-syllable adorned below with fire and differentiated by the fourth vowel; then, having emerged from that seed-syllable as networks of light rays, illuminating all the world-systems situated in the ten directions,
and having established them in the form of Śrī Kurukullā, they return again and enter back into that very same seed-syllable as networks of light rays.
One should visualize her. Then, subsequently, in the space before one, one should visualize her having the appearance of a sixteen-year-old,
with blazing tawny hair standing upright, a head adorned with five skulls, seated upon Garuḍa in the vajra-paryaṅka posture, endowed with a white halo, and possessing six arms.
She holds the *trailokyavijaya* mudrā with her first pair of hands, right and left;

with her second pair of left and right hands, she holds the gestures of fearlessness (*abhaya*) and a white *kundakalikā* bud; and with her remaining two arms, she holds a rosary and a water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*), possessing the sentiment of erotic passion (*śṛṅgāra-rasa*).
Visualizing her bearing horns, her creeper-like arms adorned with golden bracelets, proud of her fresh youth,

clad in white garments with a white bodice and upper robe, decorated with all ornaments, and wearing a crown of the five Tathāgatas; having placed that seed-syllable upon the moon disc at the center of a white utpala lotus in the heart.

Having thus meditated upon the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*), one should cultivate the thought: "I myself am the Noble Lady Kurukullā. Then, in one's own heart, there is the eighth [vowel], situated upon a moon-maṇḍala produced from the first vowel.
The seed-syllable of that [deity], accompanied by the fivefold offerings of arising, one should worship the various goddesses with the spreading clouds of the net of offerings;
this is "worship. Having worshipped, the supremely compassionate yogi, bowing with devotion, should pay homage with body, speech, and mind; this is "homage.
And having paid homage, [one should perform] the confession of sins, the rejoicing in merit, and so forth.

He performs the rejoicing in merit (*puṇyānumodanā*), thinking: "Whatever evil karma has been committed, caused to be done, or approved by me, all of that is today confessed in the presence of the Blessed Lady. Thereafter, he maintains the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*) in order to rescue those sentient beings who have fallen into the ocean of existence.

"I shall make the mind-vajra supreme"—this is the generation of the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*). Thereafter, one should cultivate those four sublime abodes (*brahmavihāra*). Following that, having investigated all phenomena, in order to abandon the ordinary body, one brings to presence the mantra of intrinsic purity and [realizes] emptiness.

Having meditated upon [the self] as consisting of the three worlds, one should consecrate one’s own mind with this mantra: *oṃ śūnyatājñānavajrasvabhāvātmako ’ham* (I am of the nature of the vajra of the wisdom of emptiness). Thereafter, out of the power of the previously made aspiration (*praṇidhāna*), the mantra-practitioner, beholding the welfare of sentient beings, should generate a divine body by means of the sequence of mantra-deployment (*mantranyāsa*).

The indication of the divine body: subsequently, in the space above, is the eighth seed-syllable; from it arises a blossoming white lotus, upon which is the eighth seed-syllable, adorned with a half-moon and a bindu, and modified below by the sixth vowel.

One should contemplate that [seed-syllable] transformed into a universal vajra, and by means of that, a ground made of vajras, a vajra canopy, and a vajra enclosure. Then, in the center, one should visualize the divine, white gnosis of the source of phenomena (dharmodaya) in the form of the syllable *E*. In its center is the eighth white seed-syllable, situated below [the *E*].
Adorned with fire (the letter *ra*) upon the head, modified by the fourth vowel (*ī*), and accompanied by the visarga (*ḥ*);
from that arises a white eight-petalled lotus; above that, in the pericarp, is the seventh seed-syllable, which arises from that.
Above that, one should visualize the sun arising from the first vowel (A), and above that, the moon and sun adorned with the eighty minor marks;

the moon is of the nature of a mirror and is embellished with the thirty-two major marks. Between these two, one should contemplate one's own mind having entered into the bud of a white utpala flower produced from the transformation of its white seed-syllable. Afterwards—
Having visualized oneself as having become one with the moon, the seat, the sun, and the mind— as if a liquid—

thereafter one should visualize oneself in the form of Kurukullā as previously described. Then, having visualized that, one should visualize a sun at one's own heart by means of the syllable *repha* (ra), and again visualize the seed-syllable at its navel.

Having drawn in Amitābha from the realm of Akaniṣṭha by means of the rays of light arising therefrom, and having worshipped him with both secret and non-secret offerings, one should request the empowerment. In this regard, the request is as follows: "May the Lord Amitābha empower me.
Then, by that Lord Amitābha, [one visualizes] vases filled with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) emanated from his own heart.

One should visualize this. Then, one should bathe the Blessed One with those vases filled with the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*). Then, one should contemplate those vases as having entered into one's own heart. Then, having performed the placement (*vinyāsa*), one should contemplate Lord Amitābha upon the crown of the head.
Then, having practiced the meditation at the three junctions of the day and performed the placement, one should recite the mantra.

The extraction of the Nyāsa-mantra: One should place the third seed-syllable of the sixth [vowel], adorned with a half-moon and a bindu, differentiated below by the fifth vowel, extending from the breast up to the peak of the head;
one should place the white [syllable] born from the first vowel, adorned with a half-moon, at the throat; and the red [syllable] of the third [vowel].

One should place the third seed-syllable, adorned with a half-moon and embellished below by the letter *ra*, differentiated by the fourth vowel (*ū*), extending from the navel down to the bladder; it is yellow. One should place the second seed-syllable of the first [group], adorned with a half-moon, extending as far as the two feet; it is green. These represent earth, water, fire, wind, and space.
Having placed the fifth [syllable]—kṣiṃ jaṃ khaṃ gaṃ skaṃ saṃ jaḥ hūṃ vaṃ hoḥ khaṃ raṃ—at the head, heart, crown, navel, and throat;

The ritual placement (*nyāsa*) removes poison arising from *kālakūṭa* and other sources. Now, therefore, follows the extraction of the root mantra: having first placed the Lord of Letters (*varṇeśvara*), then the fifth of the fifth, and the fifth of the seventh at the end—[this is repeated in k and g]—adorned with two dots (*bindu*s), and then the first seed-syllable of the first.
The second seed-syllable of the sixth [consonant], modified by the fifth vowel; again, the first seed-syllable of the first [consonant], modified by the fifth vowel;
the third seed-syllable of the sixth [consonant]; again, that third seed-syllable of the sixth [consonant] joined with the first of the eleventh [vowels].
One should take the fourth seed-syllable of the seventh [vowel], adorned below with fire (the letter *ra*) and modified at the head by the fourth vowel (*ī*), and place a visarga at its end; then,
having added "namaḥ" at the end once more, one should join it with the ending "vauṣaṭ".
And likewise "svāhā" at the end; in this manner, one should perform it everywhere.

With these fifteen seed-syllables, one should recite the mantra a hundred thousand times according to the number of its syllables, and perform a fire-oblation with flowers and other offerings consisting of one-tenth of that amount.
By the entry of the vital breath into the right [nostril], there is a binding by means of the sun and moon;
having performed this binding of the vital breath in both the right and the left, the mantra-practitioner should always perform the recitation.
One should string the beads of the rosary, consisting of one hundred and eight [beads], made of crystal or pearl, onto threads. One should not move the bead at the time of the exhalation of breath;
rather, when the breath has entered, one should recite the mantra if one desires success for oneself.

Oṃ kṣaḥ kurukulle hrīḥ namo vauṣaṭ svāhā—this is the heart mantra (*hṛdayamantra*) of the Goddess. Oṃ śvete hūṃ phaṭ—this is for the head (*śiraḥ*). Oṃ śvetajaṭini svāhā—this is for the crest-lock (*śikhā*). Oṃ ratnāmitābhapadmasambhavāya—this is the armor (*kavaca*). Oṃ cakṣusamantacakṣuviśodhane svāhā—this is for the eyes (*netra*). Oṃ bhayanāśani—this is for the destruction of fear.

*Bhati taṭi vaitaḍi [k; vairaṭi] śvete śvetajaṭini hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ [one *phaṭ* is omitted in k, g] svāhā.* This is the weapon mantra (*astramantra*). The recitation of the mantra is performed with a rosary of pearl beads. Having purified the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*), they are consecrated with the mantra *oṃ āḥ hūṃ*.
By means of the three syllables and the three principles (*tritattva*), there is that consecration (*adhiṣṭhāna*); from consecration comes the accomplishment of mantra (*mantrasiddhi*).
Having meditated on the primordial vowel (*ādisvara*) in one's own heart, [one visualizes] a lotus-vessel upon three skull-cups; in its center are the five seed-syllables (*bīja*).
Then, emerging from those seeds, one goes to Pullīramalaya and further to Jālandhara; then, having reached Jālandhara...
One should awaken the Tathāgatas. Having seen all of them as one, one should quickly perceive them in the form of a lunar disc.

The nectar flowing through the path of the aperture of the uvula (*ghaṇṭikā*) shall satisfy the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases. Having satisfied them, it remains in that vessel; there, above the uvula—

One should visualize the syllable Oṃ suspended above the syllable Hūṃ in the center of the mouth. Then, from the vessel of the lotus in one's own heart, there arises the pure nectar of gnosis (jñānāmṛta). From that, the wind mandala, transformed from the syllable Yaṃ, appears blue, shaped like a bow and marked with a banner. Above that, by means of the syllable Ra, there is the fire mandala, triangular in shape.

One should visualize above that [linga], which is marked by flames and blazing with the splendor of light rays, a white eight-petaled lotus at the navel, complete with a pericarp and a stalk, extending as far as the penis. In its center is the syllable *Hrīḥ*, surrounded by garlands of flames and intensely radiant; from its transformation, one should contemplate the Blessed Lady Kurukullā.

One should satisfy [the deity] with the nectar of gnosis (*jñānāmṛta*). One should visualize her as being empowered by the five Tathāgatas. Having meditated upon her as raining down this nectar of gnosis, the knower of mantras should always apply it at all times for those overcome by poison.
Then, the practitioner, desiring to destroy poison, beginning from the first day of the bright fortnight,
at each of the three junctions of the day, should recite ten thousand times daily; thus, while maintaining the form of the Blessed Lady, wearing white garments and covering his body, thereafter—

One should visualize within one's own heart an eight-petalled lotus, white in color, transformed from the syllable *hrīḥ* situated upon a moon, with its stalk reaching down to the *yoni*. Upon its petals, one should visualize eight bees, transformed from the eight vowels, which are joyful, contented, nourished, and have faces that are black and red, recited in their proper sequence.

Having recited [the mantra], one should visualize the eight vowels— slightly white and joined with leaves— as being impelled by the wind from one's own nose; having flown up and emerged through the nostril on the side opposite one's own right, they enter the right nostril of the victim afflicted by poison, and having rapidly torn and shattered it, they render it free of poison, which should then be inhaled.

Having reflected thus, the yogi, imagining that [the poison] has emerged through the opening of the right nostril of the one afflicted by poison, subsequently causes the victim to rise by striking him with a rosary and sprinkling him with water from a water-pot.
The practitioner, himself becoming the crest-jewel of Tārkṣya, should manifest the three times;
with the form of a whirling firebrand and the form of the mantra,
the yogi, possessing the oral instruction and being ever-blissful, should perform the recitation with firm resolve.
One should install the Nāgas, beginning with Ananta and ending with Kulika, in all the locations—
first the installation of the consonants, and especially that of the vowels; after that, Ananta and Kulika are situated at the binding of the hair-knots.
Takṣaka, with the luster of gold, is poised as an ornament for the ear;
Mahāpadma, with the brilliance of molten gold, is at the wrist.
Karkoṭaka, white in color, stands [there] performing the act of wearing the sacred thread;
Vāsuki, however, possessing the pure luster of a red lotus, is upon the girdle.
The knower of mantras should always be adorned with such formidable ornaments as lotuses and conchs resembling the *kundabandhūka* flower on his feet.
Assuming the form of Kurukullā and seated upon Garuḍa, one should thus accomplish the moving and the unmoving through this sequence;
the practitioner whose self is thus cultivated shall himself become Tārkṣyacūḍāmaṇi.
And remaining there, the practitioner of mantra, well-composed, should recite the mantra at the three junctions of the day.

By means of this very mantra, the practitioner, having prepared a meal of curd-rice with arka leaves, shall cause those afflicted by poison to eat it and thereby remove them from the oceans of poison. Or, having consecrated a full water-pot or a right-spiraling conch shell twenty-one times with the mantra, he should have the water drunk by those suffering from poison.
White meditation, in the form of a drop (*bindu*) on the forehead, neutralizes poison. Yellow meditation effects immobilization (*stambhana*).

Red meditation, in the form of a serpent, causes the paralysis of poison. Red meditation also effects the transference of poison. Green meditation effects revival. Thus the specific varieties of meditation have been explained.
Thus concludes the *Ākṛṣṭakurukullāsādhana*, extracted from the *Śrīmanmāyājālamahāyogatantra* in sixteen thousand verses.
This is the work of the venerable teacher Śrī Kṛṣṇapāda (the author’s name is given only in the Ḍh manuscript).
379) Having briefly visualized oneself as the form of Kurukullā born from the *tāra* syllable, and having beheld the object of accomplishment (*sādhya*) within the *dharmodaya*,...

Having consecrated him with the ray of gnosis residing in one’s own heart, one should meditate upon him as completely purified, with palms joined in the *sampuṭa* gesture, brought under control, and reddish in color; this is the procedure for subjugation (*vaśya*).
Now, I shall describe the sādhana of the Blessed Lady Kurukullā. First, the practitioner of mantra—

Seated on a comfortable cushion, having visualized Kurukullā, along with the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, upon a cloth painting or similar support before him, and having performed a mental offering, he should prostrate and undertake the going for refuge and so forth with this [verse]:
"The Three Jewels are my refuge; I confess all my misdeeds."
Without hesitation, I set my mind upon the awakening of a Buddha, which is the merit of the entire world.
I generate the supreme mind of awakening; I invite all sentient beings in their great multitude.
I shall practice the desired, sublime conduct of awakening so that I may become a Buddha for the benefit of the world.
With these and other words, one should generate the mind of awakening (*bodhicitta*).
Immediately thereafter, having recited three times "Oṃ, all phenomena are pure by nature; I am pure by nature," and having resolved upon natural purity, one should contemplate emptiness.
Having visualized the syllable *tāṃ*, garlanded with rays of light, upon a moon disc arising from the first vowel (*a*) within one’s own heart,
and having illuminated the world-systems of the ten directions with the mass of rays emerging from it and brought all sentient beings under control,
one should perceive oneself in the form of Kurukullā by entering that seed-syllable as her very body.
She is red in color, seated in the vajra-paryaṅka posture upon a lotus and sun disk, possessing a beautiful halo, and has six arms;
with her first pair of right and left hands— (p. 380)

She wears the Trailokyavijaya mudrā with her second right and left hands, holding a hook (aṅkuśa) and a red lotus respectively; with her remaining two hands, she holds a bow drawn to her ear and an arrow. She is radiant with the grace of the erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra-rasa), her vine-like arms are adorned with golden bracelets, and she exudes the pride of fresh youth.
[She is] youthful, wearing red garments, with a red bodice and upper robe, adorned with all ornaments,

and crowned with the five Tathāgatas. Having placed the syllable *Tāṃ*— resembling a bandhūka or javā flower— upon a moon disc at the center of a red utpala lotus in her heart, and having meditated thus, one should cultivate the divine pride (*ahaṃkāra*).
"I am indeed the Noble Lady Kurukullā. Then, having seen herself worshipped and praised by various deities through the emanation of clouds of offerings and so forth,
she mounts the wind-maṇḍala, pierces with a hook the heart of the one to be accomplished, and sits down upon his heart.

One should utter it with pride (*sāṭopa*). With an arrow resembling the bud of a red lotus, one should repeatedly bind the object of the rite (*sādhya*). Herein is the mantra: *oṃ kurukulle hrīḥ amukaṃ vaśamānaya hoḥ svāhā*. Then, seeing the object of the rite rendered distraught and fallen at one's feet...
One should send [the messenger]. For one who meditates thus constantly at the three junctions of the day, even Śakra is brought under control. As for the preliminary service (*pūrvasevā*) for this:

on an auspicious day, after the hair and other [defects] have been removed from a new cloth, the painting should be commissioned by an artist observing the *poṣadha* vows in a secluded place. When the painting has been completed and consecrated, in front of it—

Having smeared a mandala with white sandalwood paste, having lit a lamp of clarified butter, and having worshipped the Bhagavatī with the fivefold offerings, one should recite the mantra ten thousand times. Herein is the mantra: Oṃ Kurukulle hrīḥ svāhā. Thereafter, one becomes capable of performing all rites.
The Sadhana of the Noble Six-Armed Kurukullā is completed.
Having bowed to Kurukullā, who is connected to the *Hevajratantra* and who brings the three worlds under her control, I shall clearly explain her sādhana.

In this tantra, the mantra-practitioner authorized for cultivation, having risen from bed in the morning, visualizes within his heart a red syllable *hrīḥ* upon a solar disc transformed from the syllable *raṃ*. Seeing the Blessed Lady Kurukullā, who will be described hereafter, before him by means of its rays, he [worships her] with clouds of the fivefold offerings.

Having performed worship, one should recite three times before her the verse beginning with "The Three Jewels are my refuge," and so forth. Then, taking sentient beings who are afflicted by the three types of suffering as the object of one's mind, one should cultivate great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), characterized by the removal of their suffering. Thereafter—

Having meditated upon emptiness—which has the characteristic of non-dual representation (vijñapti) and the nature of the non-existence of both phenomena and persons, who possess the natures of the grasped and the grasper—one should consecrate it with this mantra: "Oṃ, I am of the nature of the vajra of the wisdom of emptiness. Then, that very non-dual mind [is placed] in space.

Having visualized a solar disc, in its center, upon a sun situated on the pericarp of a red utpala flower produced from the syllable *hrīḥ* in red, one should see that very seed-syllable; then, having performed its radiation and reabsorption, and having caused all that to enter back into it and transform,
one should perceive oneself in the form of the illustrious Kurukullā.
In the center of a red eight-petaled lotus, she stands in the *tāṇḍava* dance upon a corpse and a sun disk in the half-lotus posture (*ardhaparyaṅka*).

She possesses a solar halo, is surrounded by the eight cremation grounds in the cardinal and intermediate directions, is red in color, sixteen years of age, with tawny hair standing erect, and bears five skulls on her head representing the five Buddhas.
She is adorned with a necklace of freshly severed heads, her face terrifying with bared fangs and a lolling tongue;
her three eyes are fixed upon a red orb on her left shoulder; she embodies the sentiments of wrath and passion;
and she is decorated with ornaments fashioned from three bones: a discus, earrings, a necklace, a breast-ornament, a girdle, armlets, and anklets.
