One should visualize her holding, with her two primary arms, a red flower-bow drawn to the ear with arrows consisting of red lotus buds; and with her remaining two arms, she holds a noose and a goad made of red lotuses.
One should visualize the syllables Oṃ, Āḥ, and Hūṃ at his head, throat, and heart. Then,

having seen the red syllable Hrīḥ upon the sun at the center of the red utpala lotus situated on the sun of one’s own heart, and having summoned all the Tathāgatas by means of its rays and made requests to them, he is consecrated with vases filled with the five nectars.

As she is being consecrated, the Blessed One Amitābha arises upon her crown. Then, having emanated the eight goddesses from the seed-syllable at one's own heart and worshipped them with their respective substances of bodhicitta and so forth,
one should dissolve them back into that very same seed-syllable.
He is not devoid of the mantra of the Self, nor is he without wealth;
he possesses supreme great bliss, yet he is neither removed from it nor distracted by it.
The shadow [text]:
It is devoid of syllables and ends, yet it is neither a dot nor a circle;
this bestows supreme great bliss, yet it is neither cast away nor thrown up.

With this, one should offer praise. Then, having prepared the lamp of the five nectars according to the procedure for tasting nectar, and having made the tongue consist of a vajra born from a white syllable *HŪṂ*, one should empower it with the three syllables and thereby satisfy oneself in the form of Kurukullā. When weary from meditation, the practitioner should recite the mantra; in that same manner.
Having mentally inscribed the eight-syllable mantra garland— *oṃ kurukulle hrīḥ svāhā*— blazing like a row of lamps, encircling the syllable *hrīḥ*,
one should recite it with a rosary of red sandalwood, free from defects such as haste or delay.
By ten million recitations (p.
383), one brings under control those sentient beings fallen into the wheel of the six realms of existence; however, during the intervals between the junctions (sandhyāntara).
Having visualized oneself as the form of Kurukullā, instantaneously perfected, one should perform the worship, praise, and other rites.

While performing all activities such as listening to and explaining the teachings, one should do so with the very pride of being the Blessed Lady. Then, one should make aspirations according to one's inclination.
And here, the oral instruction transmitted through the lineage of gurus is written down: the seed-syllable of one's own heart, dripping with liquid nectar, rises from the heart,
encircles the head by way of a counter-clockwise rotation,
exits through the cavity of the right ear, and enters through the cavity at the nock of the arrow situated upon the bowstring in the right hand.

Having caused them to enter the pericarp of that bud, having opened them by means of its rays, and having caused them to enter the hearts of sentient beings throughout the universe through their radiance, one should impel those lotuses, bring them back, and cause them to re-enter that very same place; then, having formed them into a bud, [one draws them out] from the arrow through the opening of the ear.

Having turned the head clockwise and stationed it between the eyebrows, one should enter— according to the oral instruction— the locations of great bliss at the throat, heart, and navel via the path of the *avadhūtī*. Then, as if filled with the true bliss born from the stainless samādhi of wisdom and means, [one remains].
One should perceive one's own body as the three worlds; at that very moment, one should recollect this verse:
"Neither beginning, nor end, nor middle; neither existence nor nirvāṇa.
This is that supreme great bliss—neither other, nor self."
It has no beginning, no end, and no middle; it is neither existence nor nirvāṇa.
This is that which bestows supreme great bliss; it is neither another nor one's own.
In this manner, by repeatedly subduing sentient beings until he becomes capable of directly enjoining them toward great enlightenment (*mahābodhi*),
[the practitioner] should likewise [visualize] the seed-syllable of the male or female object of accomplishment (*sādhya*)— who has been meditated upon in the form of Kurukullā—
from the chest of the practitioner.
When the arrow-shaft situated in the right hand has been awakened by its rays, having entered through the right ear in that same manner,
having gone in that same manner, having stayed in that same manner, and having entered again in that same manner, one reaches that place.

Having gone there, one should likewise remain in the form of Śrī Kurukullā; it is stated that the syllable *hrīḥ* is placed upon the parasol of passion (*madanātapatra*), and so forth. Consequently, her heart necessarily becomes subject to the power of the practitioner and the person to be acted upon, and she becomes eager to accomplish all tasks.
By the merit acquired through performing this sādhana known as Kurukullā,
may all people be brought under control for the purpose of being established in awakening.
The *Svādhiṣṭhāna-kurukullā-sādhana* according to the sequence of the *Śrī-hevajra-tantra* is completed.
This work is the composition of Sahajavilāsa.
Homage to Kurukullā! [This sādhana is found only in K and G; see fol. 34].

According to the previously mentioned procedure, however, one should meditate upon her as arisen from the seed-syllable *hrīḥ* on a moon-disc at one’s own heart—red in color, with a hand raised holding an arrow in the right, and holding a red lotus and a bow in the left. Then...
Having visualized the object to be accomplished before oneself, one should pierce the heart with an arrow resembling a red lotus bud, drawn from an ear-to-ear bow.

Having applied [the mantras] to the heart, the *ūrṇā* (between the eyebrows), the throat, and the crown of the head using the previously mentioned mudrā, one then performs the recitation: *oṃ kurukulle hrīḥ devadattaṃ vaśamānaya svāhā*.
The Concise Sadhana of Kurukullā is completed.
Homage to Śuklakurukullā. [This sādhana is found only in ḍ, dh, and kh; see fol. 92.]
I pay homage to Kurukullā, who is white in color and has four arms;
with two hands she holds an arrow and a bow, and with the other two she offers a white lotus and the gesture of fearlessness.
Seated in the lotus posture, divine, with red earrings and a crown,
her fangs bared, three-eyed, and with tawny hair rising upward from her head.
Then, seated in a comfortable posture, having visualized a moon disc in his own heart and upon it the syllable *hrīḥ*,
which is white in color like crystal and radiating pure rays of light,
he should worship the white Buddhas and Bodhisattvas drawn by those rays before him and prostrate with his head.
In their presence, one should perform the confession of misdeeds, the rejoicing in merit, and then the dedication [of that merit];
having performed the going for refuge and the generation of the bodhicitta, one should cultivate the four divine abodes:

loving-kindness (*maitrī*), which is the thought of the welfare of others; compassion (*karuṇā*), which is the act of destroying the suffering of others; and sympathetic joy (*muditā*), which is delight in the happiness of others.

One should cultivate equanimity toward the neglect of faults. Then, one should recite the mantra of emptiness: *oṃ śūnyatājñānavajrasvabhāvātmako ’ham*. Then, having performed the radiation and reabsorption by means of the previously mentioned syllable *hrīḥ*, one should meditate on oneself as Kurukullā, white in color, according to the initial sequence, within one’s own heart.
Upon a white-colored eight-petaled lotus, there is a sun mandala; therein is the Goddess, born from the syllable Hrīṃ, possessing a variegated form, white in color, with four arms—
holding a bow in her left hand and an arrow drawn back to the ear with her right, a white utpala lotus in her [other] left, and a hand in the gesture of fearlessness (abhaya) in her [other] right.

Seated in the lotus posture, adorned with divine garments, wearing an upper robe of white silk, possessing formidable fangs and three eyes, with tawny hair standing erect, crowned by Amitābha, seated upon a solar disc with solar radiance,
decorated with various ornaments, her hair bound by the blue Ananta serpent, and her earrings made of the red Takṣaka serpent.
She has a yellow necklace of Śaṅkhapāla, armlets of multi-colored Kulika,
a green Karkoṭaka as her sacred thread, and a white Vāsuki as her girdle.

Adorned with a great necklace of white lotuses as pale as lotus stalks, her anklets on the feet are formed by the white Nanda and Upananda, the kings of serpents; furthermore, the eight Kurukulla serpents, having joined their palms in reverence, dwell upon the soles of her feet. Thus...

Having generated the *samayasattva* and unified it with the *jñānasattva*, one should worship while meditating upon them. In the directions starting from the east are Akṣobhya, Vairocana, Ratnasambhava, and Amoghasiddhi. In the corners starting from the southeast are Locanā, Māmakī, Pāṇḍarā, and Tārā.
Having performed these meditations, one should perform worship according to the sequential method.
Having performed the worship and made it firm, one should recollect the mantra of recitation;
by the mere recitation of which one brings the three worlds under control.

Oṃ kurukulle hrīḥ svāhā. By the mere recitation of this, one becomes a conqueror of the three worlds. Through a white-colored [mantra], one effects the removal of poison; through crystal, one obtains wisdom; through gold, one gains power over others; and through a lotus, destruction [of enemies].
Now, I shall further explain the mantra for the agitation of cities, by which [all things] are accomplished.

The Tridaśas: Oṃ kurukulle amuka ca ṭa ta pa ya śa hrīṃ phaṭ svāhā. This is the mantra named Aṣṭasiddhi. One should meditate upon the eight bestowers of examination and the state of the eight sovereign powers (*aṣṭaiśvarya*). One is honored even by the Tridaśas. Now I shall describe another meditation:
The recitation, more secret than the secret, has been taught for the sake of attaining accomplishment;
it is performed at the head, palate, throat, heart, and the pair of breasts.

One should place the mantra upon the hips, the chest, and the two feet. For the sake of accomplishing one's purpose, it agitates the nāgas of the world and draws in even the asuras and deities, including gods such as Brahmā and Rudra; how much more so, then, insignificant human beings? Indeed, when these mantras are uttered...

(387) One should recite ten thousand [times] that which is unuttered; utterance is devoid of non-utterance—one should recite ten million times. By such mere recitation, the yogin, pervading the three worlds, shall go to the fourteen worlds. He grants the vision of his own will. Thus it has been told.
In the accomplishment of mantras:
by one hundred thousand recitations, one becomes a king of gods; by ten thousand, a human being;
by ten million, animals such as beasts and birds; and by seven hundred thousand, an asura.
By reciting the mantra one hundred thousand times, one attains the state of awakening of Vajragarbha. Herein is the instruction:
"One should indeed assume the form of Kurukullā at the foremost [time] of day and night; give the foremost [attainment] at the end.
Firmly holding the Guru’s command, honor it; speak, and subdue all enemies; destroy [the obstacles]."
Having assumed that form of Kurukullā, those who indeed place the seed-syllable *hrīḥ* before them day and night,
and having established firm respect for the words of the Guru, Śabarapāda says that they bring about the destruction of poisons.
This is the auspicious *sādhana* of Viṣadanta, which accomplishes all rites, concerning the White Kurukullā, the most supreme among the supreme vidyās of the three worlds.
The *Sādhana* of White Kurukullā is completed.
This work is the composition of the venerable Siddha Śabara.

First, having visualized a red moon disc in one’s own heart, one should behold the syllable *hrīḥ* of red color. Then, one should perform the confession of misdeeds and so forth. Afterward, one should meditate on emptiness. Within that emptiness—

The wise yogin, remaining steady, should visualize the sun before him by means of the syllable *repha* (ra), and above that, he should visualize a blue-colored syllable *hūṃ*. From its transformation arises a double vajra (*viśvavajra*), from which arises a vajra-ground, a vajra-fence, and the binding of a vajra-canopy. *Oṃ rakṣa rakṣa hūṃ hūṃ*.

*hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ phaṭ svāhā*. Afterwards, the yogin [visualizes] a red lotus; above that, a moon mandala; above that, a red utpala flower transformed from the syllable *hrīḥ* with red petals; and above that, again a moon mandala, transformed from which [arises the deity].

One should visualize oneself as Kurukullā, standing in a dancing posture with one leg half-bent (ardhaparyaṅka), her waist draped in a tiger skin— specifically a fresh tiger skin— and adorned with the five mudrās;
her hair is tied upward, her locks are tawny, and her crown is graced by Lord Amitābha.

[Visualize her] with a bow, arrow, blue lotus, and goad in her hands. In this practice, there is no restriction regarding place, nor is there any restriction regarding food. Furthermore, the recitation of the mantra should be performed in such a way that no one perceives it. Oṃ Kurukulle hrīḥ svāhā.
A king is brought under control by one hundred thousand [recitations], the common people by ten thousand;
animals, birds, and the like by one million, and the asuras by seven hundred thousand.
The *Hevajra-krama-kurukullā-sādhana* is completed.
Homage to Kurukullā!
To her whose eyes possess a luster like the rising sun at dawn, a soft radiance of unceasing Lakṣmī, and who shines with the brilliance of the passion-vajra—

We pay homage to her, the accomplishment of the medicine that subdues the world unequaled, by contemplating whom with one-pointed mind, the vine-like arms of the women of the city of the Thirty-three are obtained as bonds.
Seated in a cremation ground, in a dense mountain cave or a deep abyss, at a crossroads, under a tree, in one's own home, or in some other place free from disturbances,
one should meditate according to the sequence of the glorious Hevajra on the form that is the outflow of the gnosis transformed from the three worlds.
[She is] the illusory power that brings about the extinction of the duality of the world, shattered by the radiance of the weapons such as the red lotus.

First, having contemplated loving-kindness (*maitrī*) toward sentient beings in the form of affection felt for one's own children, and then, through the realization that even one’s sole child can wither away, cultivating compassion (*karuṇā*) for all sentient beings;
and seeing the abundance of their mass of happiness and prosperity, rejoicing greatly— this is sympathetic joy (*muditā*).
One should meditate on him as the singular embodiment of the welfare of others, whose mind toward all beings is devoid of indifference— whether harmful or beneficial— and having completed all this,
[one should visualize] those disciples of the Sugata and the Guru, joined with the rays of the syllable *hrīḥ*, red in color, situated upon a radiant sun within one's own heart.
Having drawn forth the Buddhas together with a radiant vibration,

one should reveal whatever wholesome karma— whether performed, caused to be done, or approved— in previous births throughout successive lives, even if it has become faded; and likewise, one should rejoice in their virtue.

Having understood that all [phenomena] have transcended time solely through the command of the Blessed One, the True Guru, one should meditate upon that supreme, incomparable, and innate nature of reality (dharmarūpa) of the Victors.

That omniscience is itself the entire threefold world; it is that very essence of beauty, the supreme perfection of all the perfections (pāramitās), appearing in the form of their respective manifestations.
The yogin, immersed therein through the application of his vow, becomes of the nature of the *dharmakāya*;
from it arises the wheel of the single sun, expanding with rays produced by the form of the *saṃbhogakāya*.
Therein, the syllable *HŪṂ*, blue in luster, then generates the universal vajra (*viśvavajra*).
That self-enclosure and cage is impenetrable even by the most powerful and eminent heroes among the great Māras.
Thereafter, upon the sun— which is like a grain of dust shining on the lover of the red lotus (the sky)—

there is a red lotus arisen from the syllable *hrīḥ*, above which the solar disc blazes forth. Within that [disc] is the goddess Hrīḥ, fierce and intensely radiant with the great, glowing, reddish light of the all-pervading [universe].
It may possess the splendor of a fierce and unrestrained fire, intense from the conflagration of the onset of passion.
She possesses a radiance like that of the eastern sun, her pride manifest through unsurpassed and great youth;
she has brilliant, tawny hair standing erect, and she is burdened by the weight of her breasts and hips, being the very essence of tender erotic grace.
Her fangs are formidable, touched by the rays of the three eyes of the one who rests upon her left;
from the interior of her quivering mouth, the unrestrained luster of the tip of her long tongue is emitted as it whirls about.
With the tip of her left foot placed upward upon the shoulder of a corpse from which the pervasive radiance of the blazing fire of the universe streams forth,
she stands trembling; with her other foot resting near the fold of her left knee,
her limbs are languid from the heavy burden of her broad hips, which are covered by the skin of a massive tiger.
She carries a stream of flowing blood upon her breast and bears a garland of human heads on her chest.

With her left hand, she holds a red lotus— its stalk raised, its petals wide open, and its two throbbing, crimson, broad utpala-like halves fashioned like a playful bow; as if drawing in the entire three worlds with a fierce goad, she protects the Earth, that very lotus being her peerless, innate kingdom of passion.

On his head are five skull-cups that mock the splendor of the light of the self-willed moon; his five limbs are transformed by the ornaments of the five mudrās according to the sequence of the five Buddhas.
If the supreme practitioner, bearing the passion-vajra upon his head and becoming one with it, recites its mantra with the *klīṃ* seed-syllable, then his feet shall be worthy of worship by the gods.
By the command of the Lord Līlāśanirāja, this supreme means was composed;
whatever merit has been acquired by the poet named Karuṇa through it,
may that [merit] cause the arising of an exceedingly stainless and pure wisdom to expand.
The world is established in great bliss, luminous and flowing according to its own will.
The Sadhana of Kurukullā, extracted from the Śrī Hevajra Tantra, is completed.
This work is by the poet named Karuṇa. Thus, there are 12 verses.
Oṃ, homage to Kurukullā!
By the mere remembrance of whom gods, asuras, and humans—
They certainly become her servants; I bow to that Kurukullā.

First, the practitioner, having performed the cleansing of the mouth and other preliminary rites, sits in a comfortable posture. Within his own heart, upon a moon disc produced from the syllable *a*, he visualizes the syllable *hrīḥ*. From its rays, he invites the goddess Kurukullā, and with special offerings emanating from the seed-syllable at his heart, he worships her.

Having performed worship, prostration, confession of misdeeds, rejoicing in merit, dedication of that merit, going for refuge to the Three Jewels, the generation of the mind of enlightenment (*bodhicitta*), and the cultivation of the four divine abodes (*brahmavihāra*),
one should contemplate emptiness, empower it with the mantra, and [visualize] a red *kuvalaya* lotus produced from the seed-syllable in the heart.
Having visualized her within a moon mandala produced from the syllable *a*,
one should contemplate the Blessed Lady, who is the complete transformation of all that, red in color, and seated upon a red moon-lotus throne.

She is clad in red garments and wears a red crown; she has four arms, with one right hand bestowing fearlessness and another holding an arrow drawn to the string; with one left hand she holds a jeweled bow and the other a red lotus;
Amitābha adorns her crown; she dwells within the interior of Mount Kurukullā; she is radiant with the sentiment of love (śṛṅgāra-rasa) and possesses fresh youth.
One should meditate upon Kurukullā until weariness arises; when weariness occurs, one should recite the mantra. In this regard, the mantra is as follows:

having fashioned a triangular maṇḍala and worshipped the Goddess there with red flowers, one should oneself wear red garments, step upon the target with the foot while he is naked, distressed, and with disheveled hair, and [strike] his heart with the bud of a red lotus.
One should recite the mantra as if piercing [the target]. In this regard, the mantra is: *oṃ kurukulle hrīḥ amukaṃ me vaśīkuru svāhā*.
Thus ends the *Kurukullā-sādhana*.
Homage to the lineage of the Kurus!

Oṃ kurukulle svāhā! One should recite one hundred thousand times the heart-mantra of Noble Tārā—which possesses unimpeded power and is renowned for the rite of subjugating the three worlds—while remaining in the previously described meditative absorption (*samādhi*).
Afterwards, whatever flowers, incense, ointments, perfumes, powders, betel, and so forth are given after being consecrated by this [mantra], that person becomes submissive.
By means of fragrant incense, [it becomes fragrant] (the phrase "it becomes fragrant" is omitted in manuscript K).

One should fumigate oneself; one will become beloved by all people. One should offer *bandhūka* flowers (*rakta-bandhūka*) into the fire while reciting the name of a person; that person becomes submissive. Having consecrated food and drink with mantras, whoever is given these becomes submissive. For the subjugation of a great person, white mustard seeds should be offered into the fire. Afterwards...

Having performed the worship and other rites of the Bhagavatī according to the proper lunar days, asterisms, and so forth, one should draw a sixteen-spoked wheel in the shape of lotus petals upon birch bark or cloth using saffron, *gorocanā*, camphor, and other substances. In the center of the wheel, one should write the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*) together with the mantra. On the petals, one should write "ku ru ku lle."

One should write only the name of the person to be accomplished, constrained by four syllables. Having encircled this with the syllable *ĀḤ* tripled, and having wrapped it with a red thread, one should place it in the center of the heart of a doll made of *madana* wood and heat it with charcoal from the *khadira* tree; this effects the drawing of the feet [subjugation] for the purpose of bringing under control either a man or a woman.
Having pierced the vulva and the two feet with a copper needle, one should apply heat;

there is no doubt that she will come under one's control. Having performed worship of the Blessed Lady, this king of mantras should be recited with great faith. In this manner, through this sequence, all accomplishments are attained.
Thus ends the application of the ritual procedure for the expansion of activity.
Gaṃ raṃ vaṃ yaṃ paṃ śaṃ caṃ ḍaṃ oṃ Kurukulle, destroy all evil ones, destroy them! Pin them down, pin them down! Break them, break them!
Crush, crush! Destroy, destroy! Drive away, drive away! Grant me peace; grant me nourishment; grant me my desire; bring all sentient beings under my control! Hrīḥ svāhā! Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ!
HŪM HE HĀ HĀḤ.
This is the ritual procedure for the bali offering to Kurukullā.
Homage to Uṣṇīṣavijayā!

According to the previously described procedure, one should visualize the Blessed Lady as white, born from the syllable Bhrūṃ on a moon disc; she has three faces, three eyes, is in the prime of youth, wears various ornaments, and possesses eight arms.

Her right and left faces are yellow and black; she holds in her four right hands a crossed-vajra, a lotus with a Buddha upon it, an arrow, and the gesture of granting boons; in her four left hands, a bow, a threatening finger, a noose, and a full vase; she is situated within the interior of a caitya-cave.

Having visualized her with Vairocana upon her crown, one should meditate on one's own seed-syllable situated in the heart. Thereafter, one should visualize the five syllables—HŪṂ, TRĀṂ, HRĪḤ, AṂ, and AḤ—in sequence upon the crest-lock, forehead, throat, navel, and feet. Then...
One should recite the mantra: Oṃ bhrūṃ svāhā.
This is the *Uṣṇīṣavijayā-sādhana*.
p.

395) According to the previously described procedure, one should visualize the Blessed Lady Sitātapatrāparājitā— born from a white syllable OṂ within a moon mandala in the heart— as having three faces, six arms, and three eyes on each face.
White in color, with faces that are blue and reddish-brown on the right and left respectively, holding a wheel, a goad, and a bow in her right hands,
and holding a white vajra, an arrow, a noose, and a threatening gesture in her left hands; possessing a wrathful gaze, she is the destroyer of all grahas,
adorned with divine ornaments and garments, and has Vairocana as her leader.

Having meditated, one should bind the mudrā: placing the index finger of the right hand fist at the heart, one should raise the left hand fist. The mantra for recitation is: *oṃ sitātapatrāparājite sarvagrahān trāsaya trāsaya hana hana [hana hana hana hana] hruṃ*.
HRAṂ HRUṂ HŪṂ [K, ḌH, G: HŪṂ HŪṂ PHAṬ PHAṬ] PHAṬ SVĀHĀ.
Thus ends the *Sādhana* of the Noble Aparājitā Sitātapatrā.

Following the previously described procedure, immediately after the meditation on emptiness, one should visualize a vajra born from the syllable *HŪṂ* situated upon a sun disk atop an eight-petalled lotus, its hub empowered by the syllable *VAṂ*.
From the transformation of that, one meditates on Vajracarcikā, who has three eyes and one face, and performs a *tāṇḍava* dance in the half-lotus posture.
Seated upon a corpse, with a slender body, fierce and terrifying with prominent fangs,
her neck adorned with a garland of human heads, decorated with bone ornaments,
wearing the five mudrās, crowned with Akṣobhya, and clothed in a tiger skin.

Having meditated upon her with loose hair, six arms, holding a vajra, sword, and wheel in her right hands, and a skull-cup, jewel, and lotus in her left hands; she is red in color, though she may possess white or other colors according to the specific ritual action; and having visualized the wisdom-circle (jñānacakra) brought forth from the syllable *caṃ* at one's own heart—
Having established [the deity] in front once more, having performed the worship and so forth, one should cause [the disciple] to enter;
then one should recite the mantra: *oṃ vajracarcike hūṃ svāhā*.
Thus concludes the *Vajracarcikāsādhana*.
Homage to Mahāpratisarā!

Following the previously described procedure, after the meditation on emptiness, upon a moon mandala produced from the syllable *A*, there is the yellow syllable *Praṃ* produced from [the syllable] *Paṃ*.

Having transformed the Blessed Lady Mahāpratisarā—who has performed various rays for the sake of others—one should instantly manifest oneself as her: yellow in color, with four faces, three eyes, and eight arms; the first face is yellow, the right white, the western blue, and the left red.
Holding a sword, a wheel, a trident, and an arrow in her right hands,
and holding an axe, a bow, a noose, and a vajra in her left hands; she stands in the *lalitākṣepa* posture upon a moon seat on a double lotus,
possesses a red halo, is adorned with all ornaments, and is clothed in variegated garments.

Having thus visualized her with a silken upper garment and a crown of various jewels, one should then contemplate the three syllables Oṃ, Āḥ, and Hūṃ— white, yellow, and blue— upon the moons of body, speech, and mind. Then, having visualized the syllable Praṃ situated upon a moon between the breasts, and seeing oneself being worshipped by various goddesses, for that long...

One should perform the visualization until weariness arises. When weariness occurs, one should recite the mantra while visualizing it like a string of pearls within the *caṇḍī* at one's own heart: *oṃ maṇidhari vajriṇi mahāpratisare hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ svāhā*.
The Sadhana of Mahāpratisarā.

First, the yogi, having become concentrated in mind, visualizes a double lotus (*viśvapadma*) transformed from the syllable *paṃ* in his heart; above that, a moon mandala transformed from the syllable *a*; and there, he places the yellow syllable *praṃ*.
Having summoned the Gurus, Buddhas, and Bodhisattvas by means of the rays of light emerging from that [visualization], and having brought them before oneself seated upon various thrones,

one should perform prostration, offering, confession of misdeeds, rejoicing in merit, going for refuge in the Three Jewels, the generation of the bodhicitta, and the dedication of merit; then, having recited, "I am of the nature of the Vajra of the Wisdom of Emptiness," and having meditated on emptiness, [one should contemplate] it within one's own mind.
Instantly, having visualized a yellow moon disc, one should meditate on Pratisarā arising from its transformation—

vividly yellow, wearing a jewel crown, with four faces that are yellow, white, yellow, and red, three eyes, and eight arms; she holds a sword, a wheel, a trident, and an arrow in her right hands, and a noose, an axe, a bow, and a vajra in her left hands.

Having visualized her seated in the *lalitākṣepa* posture upon a lotus and moon seat, adorned with various jewel ornaments, one should place the syllables OṂ ĀḤ PREṂ HŪṂ— white, red, yellow, and black respectively— upon the moon at her head, throat, heart, and secret place. Then, by the recitation of this mantra, one should identify oneself with the form of the Goddess.
Then, having exhorted Akṣobhya and the others by means of rays of light emerging from one's own heart, and having summoned them— [after this point, the manuscript ḍ, dh,
inserts a lengthy and unnecessary fragment consisting of the concluding portions of the *Saptashatika Haragriiva-sadhana*, the *Trailokyavijaya-sadhana*, and the *Vajrajvalanalarka-sadhana*].

(beginning). *Īt* repeats this portion again at the end. [See infra] The reason seems to be that some leaves of the original codex were not in order. Having received the consecration (*abhiṣeka*), one should contemplate Akṣobhya as the presiding lord (*adhipati*) upon the crown.

Then, having emanated the offering goddesses from one's own heart and performed worship, one should recite the hundred-syllable mantra and meditate for as long as fatigue does not arise. When the mind becomes weary, one should mutter the mantra: *oṃ maṇidhari vajriṇi*.
Mahāpratisare hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ svāhā.
Furthermore, the mantra is: Oṃ Vajrasattva, protect the pledge;
abide as Vajrasattva; be firm for me, be well-pleased with me, be well-nourished by me, be devoted to me.

Bestow upon me all accomplishments (*siddhi*) in all activities, and make my mind (*citta*) auspicious; *hūṃ hahaha hoḥ*. O Blessed One, Vajra of all Tathāgatas, do not abandon me; become the Vajra; O Great Samaya Being, *āḥ*. This is the hundred-syllable mantra. At the time of rising, having performed the worship and other rites...
One should ask for forgiveness.
Thus ends the sādhana of Mahāpratisarā.

Therefore, having cultivated through instruction a mind of loving-kindness toward all people who are distressed by the pains of birth, death, and disease, as well as compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity,
one should regard the entire world as being like an illusion or a dream, empty of all conceptual constructions.
Then the mantra-practitioner should visualize before him a body consisting solely of consciousness, and by means of that [consciousness], he should proceed.
Rolling upon the orb of the moon with its bright form, she makes her yellow nature manifest through her own rays, fulfilling the virtuous desires of the universe in every direction.
Having meditated upon her as seated upon a moon-disc shining within the heart of a universal lotus, possessing four faces— yellow, yellowish-white, white, and reddish—
and adorned with three eyes;
Wearing a crown adorned with jewels and variegated garments, she is encircled by a halo of red radiance;
her upper silk garment clings to the pair of breasts tossed in playful motion.
With her sprout-like arms, she bears a sword, a discus, an arrow, a trident, an axe, a noose of Śrī, a thunderbolt, and a bow.
May the Pratisarā herself become the practitioner.

With the syllables OṂ ĀḤ HŪṂ, one of sharp intellect, having seen within the heart of the mountain of the body the white, the one joined with the ritual (vidhi), the yellow, and the blue-natured [syllables] situated upon the moon—on that true moon [which is like the pair of breasts of all the Indrās]— The result of the practice is the attainment of the state of Vajradhara. One should contemplate the syllable OṂ as being of the nature of the moon, the syllable ĀḤ as being of the nature of the sun, and the syllable HŪṂ as being of the nature of fire. Having meditated thus, one should visualize the three syllables as being of the nature of the three bodies (trikāya). Then, by means of the wind, one should cause them to enter the central channel. Once they have entered, one should contemplate the syllables as being of the nature of the five wisdoms. By this, the yogin attains the state of Vajradhara. This is the supreme secret of the Buddhas. One should not reveal it to those who are not vessels for the Dharma. It is the essence of all mantras and the source of all accomplishments. Thus it is said.
He should meditate upon his own body as being completely filled by the goddesses, who have arisen from the flames produced by the friction between their pairs of breasts.
And when, even during such an expansion, one becomes weary of the process of withdrawal,
then, with a steady mind, one should recite while meditating upon the peerless King of Mantras— resplendent with a spreading network of rays— situated upon the moon over the heart.
With a pure intention, he constantly, respectfully, and skillfully [practiced] for a very long time.
In this regard, the king of mantras is as follows: Oṃ maṇidhari vajriṇi mahāpratisare hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ svāhā. [The Sadhana of Mahāpratisarā.]

400) According to the previously described procedure, [one should visualize] Mahāmāyūrī, born from a green syllable *māṃ*, seated upon a moon disc on a universal lotus; she is green in color, has three faces and six arms, possesses three eyes in each face, and has a black face on her right and a white face on her left.

In her three right hands, she holds in sequence a peacock feather, an arrow, and the varada-mudrā; likewise, in her three left hands, she holds a cluster of jewels, a bow, and a flask resting on her lap. She is adorned with various ornaments, embodies the erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra-rasa), is in the prime of youth, and sits upon a moon-throne, possessing the radiance of the moon.
One should meditate upon oneself as Amoghasiddhi, seated in the half-lotus posture and adorned with a crown.

Then, having visualized the four syllables Oṃ, Āḥ, Māṃ, and Hūṃ respectively upon the moons located at her head, throat, heart, and navel, one should perform the radiation and reabsorption [of light]. Then...
One should recite the mantra: Oṃ mahāmāyūrī vidyārājñī hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ svāhā.
Thus ends the Sādhana of the Noble Mahāmāyūrī.

According to the previously described procedure, one should meditate on oneself as Mahāsāhasrapramardanī, arising from the syllable *buṃ* upon a moon disc atop a universal lotus; she is white in color, with one face and six arms, holding a sword, an arrow, and the boon-granting gesture (*varadamudrā*) in her three right hands, and a bow, a noose, and an axe in her three left hands.
Wearing various ornaments, endowed with beauty, youth, and passion, crowned with a diadem of Vairocana, and possessing the radiance of a lotus and moon seat.
Thus concludes the sādhana of the Noble Mahāsāhasrapramardanī.
Mahāmantrānusāriṇī—black in color, with one face and four arms;
holding a vajra and displaying the gesture of granting boons (varada) in her two right hands, and holding an axe and a noose in her two left hands; her seed-syllable is *HŪṂ*.
[She is] Akṣobhya-crowned and possesses the splendor of a solar seat. Thus ends the *Ārya-mahāmantrānusāriṇī-sādhana*.

Mahāsitavatī has four arms and one face; she is red in color. With her two right hands, she holds a rosary and displays the varada mudrā. With her two left hands, she holds a vajra-aṅkuśa and a book placed at the region of the heart. Jīṃ. [ḍh, g]
She has three seed-syllables, Amitābha upon her crown, stands in the half-lotus posture, is adorned with various ornaments, and possesses a solar seat and radiance.
Thus ends the *Ārya-Mahāsītavatī-sādhana*.

Now, according to another tradition, the five great deities are specified. Among them, Mahāpratisarā is yellow, has three faces, each with three eyes, and ten arms; her right and left faces are black and white respectively, and in her five right hands, in due order—
A sword, a vajra, an arrow, a boon-granting gesture, and parasols resting upon their hearts; likewise, (p. 402) a noose.
In her five left hands, she holds a bow, a banner, a jewel-tuft, an axe, and a conch;

she wears a crown of Ratnasambhava, a black bodice, and a red upper garment; she stands in the graceful *lalitākṣepa* posture with one leg half-crossed, and is adorned with divine ornaments and garments.
Mahāmāyūrī is green, with two arms and one face; she is divine, and her right and left hands hold a peacock feather and grant the boon of charity respectively.
Mahāsāhasrapramardanī is exactly as described before.
Mahāmantrānusāriṇī has four arms and one face; she is black, and her two right hands hold a sword and display the gesture of granting boons, while her two left hands hold an axe and a noose.
Mahāsitavatī has four arms and one face; she is red.
The two right arms hold the sword and the boon-granting gesture (*varada*), and the two left arms hold the axe and the noose.
Their mantras are marked with three syllables, containing their respective seed-syllables in the middle and accompanied by their own names.
[This concludes the Mahāpañcarakṣāsādhana; this colophon is found only in ḍh and b.]

Mahāpratyaṅgirā is black, with six arms and one face; her right hands hold a sword, a goad, and a *varda*; her left hands hold a red lotus, a trident, and a noose with a threatening gesture (*tarjanī*) placed at her heart; her seed-syllable is *HŪṂ*; she is crowned by Akṣobhya, adorned with all ornaments, and endowed with beauty and youth.
Thus concludes the [4] Sadhana of Mahāpratyaṅgirā.
Dhvajāgrakeyūrā is black, three-faced, and four-armed; her right and left faces are red and dark blue respectively;
she holds a sword and a noose in her two right hands, and in her two left hands she holds a vajra-marked *khaṭvāṅga* and a wheel.

[Omitting *cakra*: Her hair is tawny and stands erect; her head is adorned with five dry skulls; she is clothed in a tiger skin; her face is made terrifying by fangs; she has a protruding belly; she stands in the *pratyālīḍha* posture; she possesses the splendor of the sun as her seat; she wears yellow garments and a bodice; her seed-syllable is *HŪṂ*; and she bears Akṣobhya upon her crown.
Thus ends the *Dhvajāgrakeyūra-sādhana*.

Aparājitā is yellow, two-armed and one-faced, adorned with various jewels, and trampling upon Gaṇapati. Her right hand is in the gesture of dealing a slap, while her left hand holds a noose and a threatening forefinger at her heart;
she has an exceedingly terrifying, fierce, and wrathful face, and she is the destroyer of all Māras.
And she has raised parasols by the retinue of deities such as Brahmā, who are wicked and fierce.
Thus ends the *Aparājitāsādhana*.
Vajragāndhārī is black, six-faced, and twelve-armed; her tawny hair stands upright, she stands in the *pratyālīḍha* posture, her faces are terrifying with bared fangs, and each face has three eyes.
In her six right hands, in successive order:
In the six left hands, he holds a vajra, a vajra-bell, a sword, a trident, an arrow, and a wheel;
in the right hands, a khaṭvāṅga, a goad, a bow, an axe, a noose, and a threatening gesture at the heart. His first face is black.
The other faces are five-colored, and they rest upon seats of double-lotuses and suns. "Oṃ hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ svāhā" is the mantra for recitation. [After this, *k* repeats the same *sādhana*.]

In this very context, there is the *Dhāriṇī*: Homage to the Three Jewels! Homage to Caṇḍavajrapāṇi, the great general of the yakṣas! Homage to the Blessed One, Mahāvajragāndhārī, whose blazing splendor is ignited by many hundreds of thousands, the fierce, terrible, and fearsome Yoginī! [Repeated in k, g].
[O you who are] the sister of Bhīṣma,
twelve-armed, with disheveled hair, wearing various forms and diverse garments, come, come, O Blessed One Mahāvajragāndhārī, [you who belong] to the Three Jewels!

By truth, seize, seize Baladeva and the others! And those others who do not abide by their pledge, I shall swiftly bring them back! Grasp, grasp, grasp! Oṃ ala ala ala ala hulu hulu mulu mulu culu culu dhama dhama rakṣa rakṣa!
Protect, protect! Fulfill, fulfill! Enter, enter! O Blessed One, Mahāvajragāndhārī, the accomplished Caṇḍavajrapāṇi commands: *hrīḥ* [ḍh: *hrīḥ haḥ hahaha oṃ g:
*hrīḥ haḥ ha he hūṃ*] *haḥ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*. The range of her activities is manifold.
Thus ends the *Vajragāndhārīsādhana*.
Homage to the Noble Pratisarā!
First of all, the practitioner, having performed the cleansing of the mouth and other preliminary rites, should sit upon a comfortable seat in a place conducive to the mind.
Having sat down, one should empower the protection through the yoga of the place and oneself with the mantra: *oṃ āḥ hūṃ rakṣa rakṣa hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*.

Then, from the syllable *a* in one’s own heart, a moon mandala arises; above that, rays of light emanating from the syllable *paṃ* illuminate the Gurus, Buddhas, and Bodhisattvas, whom one visualizes as being present before oneself.
One should worship Mahāpratisarā and the others, together with their hosts and retinues.
Having presented flowers, incense, lamps, perfumes, offerings of food, and other oblations, one should confess one's misdeeds, go for refuge to the Three Jewels,
generate the mind of awakening (bodhicitta), dedicate the roots of virtue, and ask for forgiveness.

Then one should cultivate the four divine abodes (*brahmavihāra*): compassion (*karuṇā*) which removes their suffering; loving-kindness (*maitrī*) which establishes them in happiness; sympathetic joy (*muditā*) through their stable happiness; and equanimity (*upekṣā*) by way of the nature of suchness (*tathatā*). Then, having mentally apprehended all phenomena and contemplated them as non-conceptual, [one recites]: *Oṃ, I am of the nature of the vajra of the wisdom of emptiness*. Then, with the syllable *Hūṃ*...

One should preside over the ground consisting of the universal vajra. With that very vajra, one should visualize a vajra-penthouse, a vajra-fence, and a vajra-canopy. In the center of that, one should contemplate Mount Sumeru, transformed from the syllable *suṃ*, as the palace of the city of great liberation, strewn with various flowers; above that, by means of the syllable *hūṃ*...
The double-vajra arises from the transformation of the syllable *paṃ*, as does the double-lotus, complete with a pericarp and filaments.

Above that, in the center of a moon-maṇḍala, one should radiate rays from the syllable *paṃ*; having drawn in [the deities] consisting of the five wisdoms by means of those rays and unified them with all the Tathāgatas, through the transformation of the seed-syllable into a state of liquefaction—
Mahāpratisarā, whose color and form will be described below, is fair-complexioned, has the appearance of a sixteen-year-old,

and has her head adorned with a *caitya*. She stands upon a moon-seat, treads upon a solar disc, sits in the vajra-paryaṅka posture, possesses three eyes, has eight arms, and is beautified by swinging earrings.

Adorned with necklaces and anklets, decorated with golden armlets, a girdle, and wearing all ornaments, that Blessed Lady’s first face is fair-complexioned, the right is black, the one at the back is yellow, and the left is [red].
In the first right hand he holds a red discus, in the second a vajra, in the third an arrow, and in the fourth a sword;
in the first left hand a vajra-noose, in the second a trident, in the third a bow, and in the fourth an axe.
He is adorned by the Bodhi tree and embellished with various flowers, fruits, and the like.
She is praised by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Maheśvara, Nandikeśvara, and others; she is to be honored on her right side by gods,
nāgas, yakṣas, and gandharvas, and is lauded by the deities Indra, Yama, Varuṇa, Vaiśravaṇa, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, mahoragas, and so forth.

It severs the bonds of the latent tendencies of passion, hatred, and delusion; it is the destroyer of evil-minded ones who employ supreme mantras, mudrās, poisons, kākhorddas, powders, incantations, and malevolent rites.
She is devoted to making offerings to all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and the supreme assembly of noble ones;
she is the protector of those who are dedicated to upholding, writing, reciting, reading, chanting, hearing, and maintaining the Mahāyāna. Such is she... [kh, a: omitted]

Having relied upon the Blessed Lady in her form through the yoga of radiating and reabsorbing [light], by means of diligent and uninterrupted practice, her recitation mantra is: *oṃ maṇidhari vajriṇi mahāpratisare hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ svāhā*.
Regarding that Mahāpratisarā, in the eastern direction, one should proceed in the same manner as the previously described yoga.
In the center of a universal lotus, from the syllable *hūṃ*, through the transformation of the vajra symbol,
there arises Mahāsāhasrapramardanī; she is black in color, with tawny hair standing erect, adorned with a human skull,
her face terrifying with furrowed brows and bared fangs, seated upon a radiant solar disc in a graceful, striding posture.
Treading upon the great yakṣas of the great elements, adorned with bracelets and armlets, and terrifying with necklaces and anklets, she [is placed] on her first right arm.

In the second [right] hand he holds a *varada-vajra*, in the third a hook (*aṅkuśa*), in the fourth an arrow, and in the fifth a sword; in the first left arm a noose with the threatening gesture (*tarjanī-pāśa*), in the second an axe (*paraśu*), in the third a bow, and in the fourth a sixteen-jeweled lotus. Her root face is black, and the right [face] is white.
Yellow on the back and green on the left, with three eyes, her body adorned with various jewels and ornaments,
possessing great strength and prowess, of fierce appearance, graced by the banyan tree,
she causes terror to the deities beginning with the Seven Mothers; her mind strikes fear even into the planets such as Revatī.

She who terrifies the eight nāgas beginning with Vāsuki; she who purifies wind, bile, phlegm, and the like; she who causes the dispersal of clouds of fierce, blinding darkness; she who wards off all untimely death. Her mantra for recitation is:
*oṃ amṛtavare varapravaraviśuddhe hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ*.
*svāhā*. Then, in the southern quarter of the residence of Mahāpratisarā, upon a universal lotus (*viśvapadma*) in the center of a moon mandala,
through the transformation of the seed-syllable *māṃ*, there suddenly appears Mahāmāyūrī, yellow in color, standing in the *ālīḍha* posture upon a sun mandala.

She sits in the sattva-paryaṅka posture, has three faces, three eyes, and eight arms; she wears a jewel crown and is adorned with all ornaments. In her first right hand she displays the gesture of granting boons (varada), in the second she holds a jeweled jar, in the third a wheel, and in the fourth a sword.
In her first left hand she holds alms-food over an alms-bowl, in the second a peacock feather, and in the third a bell.

In the fourth [hand] is a double-vajra (viśvavajra), and then a jewel-banner; the root face is yellow, the right face black, and the left face red; she is adorned by an *aśoka* tree; standing at her side are seven [beings];
she is the one who covers the seven poisons, the one who destroys the fierce, tawny-faced *rākṣasīs*, and [the protector] of all the *nāgas* and others.
Causing terror, she is to be saluted by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, and gandharvas;
she is to be served by the twenty-seven lunar mansions, the nine planets, and so forth.

She who liberates from the poisons of both stationary and moving beings, and who causes the delusion of gods, daityas, and asuras— this is the recitation mantra of that Blessed Lady: *oṃ amṛtavilokini garbhasaṃrakṣaṇi ākarṣaṇi hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ svāhā*.
To the west of that Pratisarā, upon a universal lotus in the center of a moon mandala,

one should visualize Mahāmantrānusāriṇī, born from the transformation of the seed-syllable *maṃ*, white in color, with twelve arms, three eyes, standing in the ālīḍha posture upon a radiant sun mandala, and wearing a jewel crown.
Adorned with all ornaments, endowed with fresh youth, and decorated with necklaces, anklets, earrings, and the Śirīṣa tree; her first two hands display the *dharmacakra-mudrā*,
the second two display the *samādhi-mudrā*, the third is in the boon-granting gesture (*varada*), the fourth is in the fear-dispelling gesture (*abhaya*), and the fifth holds a vajra.
In the sixth [hand] there is an arrow; in the third, a noose on the index finger; in the fourth, a bow; in the fifth, a mass of light rays;
and in the sixth, a vase marked with a lotus. (Note: *kamala* is read in some manuscripts, but this is absurd; here *kalaśa* is substituted, as it appears in iconographic representations.)

[She is generally seen with one of the twelve hands of Mahāmantrānusāriṇī: her principal face is white, the right black, and the left red; she is strewn with various flowers, worthy of worship by the gods headed by the eight world-protectors, praised by the hosts of gods including the Four Great Kings, and honored by the Samālā Vidyādharas. Of her—
The recitation mantra is: *oṃ vimale vipule jayavare amṛte viraje hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ svāhā*.
Then, to the north of Mahāpratisarā, upon a universal lotus, in the center of a moon mandala, is Mahāsitavatī, born from the transformation of the seed-syllable *trāṃ*, green in color.
She stands in the *ālīḍha* posture upon a solar disc, has three faces, three eyes, and six arms;
she wears a crown of Tathāgatas, is adorned with all ornaments, and is clothed in divine garments.

In her first right hand she holds the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya*), in the second a vajra, and in the third an arrow; in her first left hand a noose with the threatening gesture (*tarjanī-pāśa*), in the second a bow, and in the third a jewel-banner (*ratna-dhvaja*). Her principal face is green, the right white, and the left red. Adorned by the *campaka* tree, she is worshipped by the gods headed by Kāmadeva and others.

She who destroys Yakṣas and Yakṣiṇīs such as Stutasaha and others; she who causes the dispersal of crows, owls, vultures, hawks, pigeons, and so forth; she who bewilders Bhūtas, Pretas, Piśācas, Vetālas, Rākṣasas, and the like. Her recitation mantra is: Oṃ bhara.
*bhara sambhara sambhara indriyabalaviśodhani hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ svāhā*.

Having thus visualized the maṇḍala as it has been described, one should emit rays of light from their respective seed-syllables (*bīja*) which are pervaded by a mass of radiance; and those rays, having completely permeated the entire triple world, [dissolve] back into that very syllable.

One should cause them to enter. Having again expanded them into the hollow of space, one should draw in the wheel of gnosis (*jñānacakra*), praise it, move it about, and cause it to enter the wheel of one's own commitment (*svasamayacakra*). Then, having visualized the two as having become a single unified mass, one should draw in all the Tathāgatas with rays of light from that [union], worship them, and request empowerment (*abhiṣeka*).
The wise practitioner should visualize himself being sprinkled; preceded by worship, praise, and the tasting of nectar, he should meditate thus:
Mohavajrī Mahāpratisarā is in the two eyes; Dveṣavajrī Mahāsāhasrapramardanī is in the two ears;
Mātsaryavajrī Mahāmāyūrī is in the nose; and Rāgavajrī is in the mouth.

Mahāmantrānusāriṇī is Sparśerṣyāvajrī Mahāsitavatī. Thus, one should specifically understand that the deities are to be known as having the very nature of the aggregates (skandha), elements (dhātu), and sense-bases (āyatana) of form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, through their purification. Having become a practitioner of the pledge (samayin) in that very state, one should recite the mantra with this [verse]:

According to the prescribed rite: one should recite those very syllables of the mantra, joined with the deity and interwoven with the name of the person to be accomplished, with a peaceful mind and without interruption.
In cases of fever, poison, and likewise disease, as well as in battle;
and when one is oppressed by ḍākinīs, spirits, withered corpses, rivers, or enemies.
Therefore, one should constantly recollect the mantra that destroys all fears, [especially] when amidst thunderbolts, lightning, and clouds, or on a mountain, in a forest, or on a path.
The procedure for that very occasion is as follows:
For the sake of the welfare of all sentient beings, and for the arising of the welfare of all sentient beings,
one should request [the ritual] by any means whatsoever for the purpose of increasing the lifespan.
And I shall write down the ritual procedure for the Five Protections (Pañcarakṣā), a source of well-being,
while turning the auspicious maṇḍala for the sake of the welfare of sentient beings.
On a pure ground, auspicious and delightful, smeared with cow dung,
and covered with a canopy draped with various kinds of cloth.
Having smeared it all over especially with sandalwood paste,
one should then prepare a mandala measuring twenty-eight finger-breadths.
The rite for pacification (śāntikarma) is praised when performed with white and red powder;
one should fashion an eight-petalled lotus provided with a pericarp and filaments.
Having established five water-pots, adorned with garlands, cords, and cloths,
and covered with sprouts together with umbrellas and banners;
A book, the Dharmadhātu, and a cloth painting suspended above;
flowers, incense, perfumes, and offerings of bali and naivedya presented.
One should worship the gods in the cardinal and intermediate directions according to the prescribed rite, using white flowers, especially those combined with *dūrvā* grass and *kunda* blossoms.
Having offered a bali-oblation of jaggery-rice, white flowers, and especially milk-rice (pāyasa) to the Gandharvas, one should establish them in their former place.
One should offer an oblation to the Kumbhāṇḍas filled with sesame, black liquor, fish, meat,
and onions, and place it in the southern direction.
Having placed milk-rice, curd, milk, and especially clarified butter as a great offering for the nāgas in the western direction.
Having placed black gram, mung beans, horse gram, and Jambu-liquor in the northern direction, one should offer the bali-oblation to the yakṣas.
Beginning from the northeastern direction and extending as far as the range of the road,
there are white, red, and green garlands suspended [or yellowish-green garlands hanging down].
A white garland in the middle made of various kinds of flowers,
as well as bowls of milk and blood, and the fragrance of resin (sarjarasa).
Having given the appropriate price for each specific object according to its true value,
one may take whatever fruits or non-fruits are obtained, such as sweetmeats, sugar-balls, and fried cakes.
Having placed the offering of flour-cakes and the like— as previously described— along with special portions of sugar and milk on the south, adorned with the eight auspicious signs;
And so it is said: "The Dharma-preacher, the Ācārya, and likewise the Karmavajrī,
having performed their ablutions and being clad in clean garments, are considered pure with respect to the seat."
One should always stand facing the east and recite with the head-dress on;
for mendicants who subsist on alms-food, pure conduct is praised.
A certain teacher, having purified himself, should teach [the text];
beginning with one recitation and so forth, he should proceed up to twenty-one and beyond.
If there is deficiency or excess in the recitation of the ritual rules, perfect accomplishment will not arise;
[only] one endowed with fortitude and vigor, through exertion for the sake of compassion and the welfare of sentient beings, [attains it].
One should perform that rite of auspiciousness spoken by the former Buddha;
those who partake of white vessels and food should avoid meat.
Having made everything free from worldly motives and in accordance with all the scriptures,
the preceptor, facing north, should commence the ritual there.
One should meditate upon the previously mentioned object of focus for the deity,
engaged in praise and worship, and intent on the ringing of the bell.

Homage be to the Buddha whose range is infinite; homage be to you, O Sage, who illuminates the truth! Having established yourself in the truth, you are the liberator of all beings; may all desires become fruitful.
Homage to you, O heroic being; homage to you, O Tathāgatas;
homage to you, all deities; homage be to you, O Dharmadhātu!
Combined with *dūrvā* grass and *kunda* flowers, and interwoven with the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*),
one should likewise worship the Dharmadhātu upon the head of the deity.
Having recited the mantra once, one should worship with yoga once;
by performing the rite ten thousand times, the omniscient one increases one's lifespan.
Having been requested by anyone at all, one should cause her mandala to be turned;
likewise, the kingdom, the realm, the left side, the cattle-pen, and even the garden.
The incursions of non-human beings, diseases, epidemics, and famines perish;
by that karma, even dry pieces of wood protect themselves spontaneously.
Whatever inconceivable karmic sufferings one desires to undergo,
protection will certainly be achieved through the performance of this protective rite.
Diseases born of wind, diseases born of bile, diseases born of phlegm, and those born of the combination of all three—
may all such ailments be destroyed, and may there always be well-being;
by means of reciting and studying this, one will certainly become free from obstacles.
The Ritual Procedure for the Five Protections (Pañcarakṣāvidhāna)
Homage to Vajraśṛṅkhalā and the others!

According to the previously described procedure, one should visualize Vajraśṛṅkhalā, arisen from the gnosis of the green syllable HŪṂ upon a moon disc in the heart; she has three faces and six arms, with her right and left faces being blue and white respectively, and she possesses three eyes.

Having visualized oneself as [the goddess] who is dark green in color, with a slightly smiling face, adorned with all ornaments, and the destroyer of wicked beings— her three right hands holding a vajra, a chain, and an arrow, and her three left hands holding a threatening gesture (*tarjanī*), a noose, and a bow— one should form the mudrā with both hands separately.
Having formed the *vajramuṣṭi* separately, one should bind the little finger and the index finger in the shape of a chain.
[k, g: add "Oṃ, one should worship in the shape of a vajra-chain. "Oṃ vajraśṛṅkhale hūṃ phaṭ svāhā" is the mantra for recitation (*jāpamantra*).
The Sadhana of Vajraśṛṅkhalā.
p.

414) Following the previously described procedure, immediately after the meditation on emptiness, one arises from the green syllable *HŪṂ* situated upon a sun disk atop a universal lotus; she is green. [k, g: omit "green"]

She has three faces and eight arms; her first face has a slightly smiling expression, the right face is tawny with tawny eyes, and the left face is red, fierce with frowning brows and bared fangs. In her four right hands, she holds the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya*), a vajra, a chain (*śṛṅkhala*), and an arrow; in her four left hands...
Having visualized her holding a skull-cup filled with blood, a threatening gesture, a noose, and a bow; seated in a graceful, sidelong pose;
wearing a cloak of cat-skin; with brown hair standing upright and adorned by Amoghasiddhi; one should recite the mantra: *oṃ vajraśṛṅkhale hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*.
Thus ends the sādhana of Vajraśṛṅkhalā according to another tradition.

First of all, the practitioner, seated on a comfortable seat, should utter, "All phenomena are empty," and having thus generated the perfection of view— that all phenomena arise from such [emptiness] and so forth— he should take refuge in the Three Jewels and so on. Then...

"However many sentient beings are included within the category of sentient beings, all of them must be established by me in the knowledge of the Omniscient One. Then, in the heart, there is a multi-petaled lotus; above that, a sun mandala;
and from that, the syllable *HŪṂ* arises, which is the nature of Vajraśṛṅkhalā.
She who cuts all bonds, the slayer of wicked beings, Śyāmā,
with three faces and three eyes— the second eye being tawny— her left face frowning,
her fangs blood-red and terrifying, while her first face is slightly smiling; she has eight arms.

In the first right hand she grants the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya*), in the second a vajra, in the third a vajra-chain (*vajraśṛṅkhalā*), and in the fourth an arrow; in the left hands, [she holds] a skull-cup filled with blood in the first, and (p. 415) [a bow] in the second.

One should visualize [her] holding a threatening gesture in the third [hand], a noose in the fourth, and a bow, radiant, surrounded by clouds of Buddhas, seated in a graceful posture, with a cat skin as her upper garment: OṂ VAJRAŚṚṄKHALĀM! Enlightenment is attained in an instant; how much more so other accomplishments? OṂ VAJRAŚṚṄKHALE HŪṂ PHAṬ SVĀHĀ!
The ritual manual for the sādhana of Vajraśṛṅkhalā is completed.
Homage to Dhvajāgrakeyūrā! Having bowed to Dhvajāgrakeyūrā, who removes the fear of all miserable rebirths,
her accomplishment through the means of practice is here written down by me with faith.
First of all, the mantra-practitioner, having performed the cleansing of the mouth and other preliminary rites, seated himself on a comfortable seat in a place agreeable to the mind—
purified in mind through loving-kindness and the like, and devoted to the perfection of generosity.
One should meditate upon Tāriṇī, who brings about the destruction of Māra in battle.

Having recited the mantra *oṃ candrārkavimale svāhā*, one visualizes within one’s own heart a moon and sun transformed from the syllables *a* and *ā*, joined together; above them, by means of yellow rays of light from the syllable *dhvaṃ*, one beholds the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas in the expanse of space.

Having performed worship with mentally created flowers and other offerings, one should recite the Verse of the Three Refuges. Immediately thereafter, having uttered the mantra "Oṃ, all phenomena are pure by nature; I am pure by nature," one should meditate on emptiness for a moment. Then, Oṃ...

Having generated the ego-identity (*ahaṅkāra*) with the thought, "I am of the nature of the vajra of the knowledge of emptiness," and with the intention of rescuing sentient beings and so forth, one should— upon the union of the moon and sun which resembles a reflected image—
adorn infinite sentient beings in the form of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas by means of the yellow rays of light from the syllable *dhvaṃ*, and [place them] in their hearts.
Having entered and then returned,
one should visualize the mass of rays entering the seed-syllable; having transformed all that, [one visualizes] Saṃgrāmatāriṇī.
The goddess is yellow in color, enchanting, with four faces and eight arms; she is wrathful, standing in the *pratyālīḍha* posture, auspicious, and pot-bellied.
Her three round eyes are red, she wears deep blue garments, and her right hands hold a sword and a discus.
With her two left hands, she holds a threatening gesture (*tarjanī*) and a noose, and a white pestle marked with a black vajra.

One should meditate steadily upon oneself as the Samayasattva: embracing a trident with the left arm, first having a yellow face, with the left [face] red and the others white, with a distorted, smoke-colored face at the top, bound with upward-pointing tawny-red matted hair, adorned with five skulls, and stationed in the center of a lotus and sun disk. Having thus accomplished the Samayasattva.

Having summoned the Jñānasattva by means of the rays from the seed-syllable located in the heart of the one situated in the sun, and having worshipped him, one should draw him in, cause him to enter, bind him, and bring him under control using these syllables: *jaḥ hūṃ vaṃ hoḥ*. Then, one should entreat the Tathāgatas:
"May all the Tathāgatas consecrate me! Thereupon, the Tathāgatas, beginning with Akṣobhya, [emerge] from their own hearts.

One should visualize oneself being consecrated by hands holding golden vases filled with the five nectars spread wide. In this regard, the verse for the consecration is as follows: "The great vajra-consecration, honored by the three worlds..."
I bestow [this] which arises from the abode of the three secrets of all the Buddhas.

Oṃ sarvatathāgatābhiṣekasamayaśriye āḥ hūṃ svāhā. Then, having transformed the remaining water, Akṣobhya arises upon the crown. One who speaks the truth and is devoted to compassion should constantly recite this mantra.
Oṃ, O Blessed One, O you who possess armlets at the top of the banner, O destroyer of enemy armies, O protector of one’s own army, O lady with the ūrṇā-tuft on your face!

Kha kha khāhi khāhi! Strike, strike the enemy army with your infinite mouths and infinite arms! Hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ svāhā!—this is the heart mantra. Oṃ, O you who cause all planets and constellations to become darkened!

*Svāhā*—this is the *upahṛdaya-mantra*. The *mālā-mantra*, however, is to be found in the *dhāraṇī*. At the time of rising: "The welfare of all sentient beings has been accomplished by you; success has been granted according to [your] following."
Go to the realm of the Buddha, for the sake of returning again. Muḥ.
Having dismissed [the deity] with this mantra, one should dwell [in that state].
Thus ends the *Dhvajāgrakeyūrāsādhana*.
This work is the composition of the scholar Madhyamakaruṣidharmākaramati.
Homage to the Noble Uṣṇīṣavijayā!

First, the practitioner, having performed the cleansing of the mouth and other preliminary rites, sits upon a comfortable seat and should cultivate the four divine abodes (brahmavihāras). Immediately thereafter, he should visualize a moon disc in his own heart, transformed from the syllable *A*.

Having meditated on that, one should see a white syllable *bhrūṃ* above it; having visualized the entire world illuminated by the masses of light rays emanating from it, and having contemplated all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas before oneself, one should perform the worship, confession of misdeeds, and so forth. Then:
*oṃ śūnyatājñānavajrasvabhāvātmako ’ham*. Then once again, upon the moon in one’s own heart, [one should visualize] the syllable *paṃ*, born from which...
Having meditated upon a lotus with a thousand petals and having visualized the syllable *Bhṛṃ* shining in the center of a moon disc above it,
one should contemplate Uṣṇīṣavijayā, who is produced from its transformation; she resides within a shrine-cave, is white in color, has three faces and eight arms,
is adorned with all ornaments, and stands upon a moon on a lotus with a thousand petals.
She is seated in the vajra-paryaṅka posture; her first face is white, the right face is yellow, and the left face is blue.
Her lips are pressed against her bared fangs. In her four right hands, she holds a double-vajra (*viśvavajra*), a red lotus upon which rests a skull-cup, and so forth.
One should visualize her holding a bow, a threatening gesture, a noose, and an auspicious jar in her hands; wearing a crown of Vairocana,
clad in divine garments and upper robes, adorned with various ornaments, and surrounded by a white radiance.

To her right is Lokeśvara, and to her left is Padmadhārī; the former holds a fly-whisk in his right hand, while the latter holds a vajra upon a blue lotus in his left hand and a fly-whisk in his right. These two should be visualized as seated. Then, to the right, [is one] holding a fly-whisk in his hand; these two should be visualized as seated. Then...
In the east, south, west, and north are Acala, Ṭakkirāja, Nīladaṇḍa, and Mahābala.

All are blue in color, two-armed, one-faced, and three-eyed; they stand in the *pratyālīḍha* posture, wear tiger-skin garments, have hair standing erect, and are adorned with eight snakes. They trample upon suns atop double-petaled lotuses, hold a threatening gesture (*tarjanī*) and a noose in their left hands, and [hold a staff] in their right hands.

They should be meditated upon as holding a sword, a goad, and a vajra-staff in their hands. Above them, two sons of gods belonging to the Śuddhāvāsa realm should be visualized raining down full vases of nectar and ambrosia.
Having thus meditated upon the Blessed Lady together with her retinue, one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*): *Oṃ* at the head, *Āḥ* at the throat.
HŪṂ at the forehead, TRĀṂ at the navel, HRĪḤ at the navel, and AṂ and AḤ at the feet. Then one should form the mudrā:

having made the *sampuṭāñjali* (the hollowed-palm gesture), contract the two index fingers, and give the "well done" (*sādhukāra*) with the thumbs and the two middle fingers. After reciting the dhāraṇī once together with three OṂ syllables, one should thereafter recite it without the mudrā.

Oṃ bhrūṃ svāhā—this is the heart mantra (hṛdayamantra). Oṃ amṛtāyurdade svāhā—this is the near-heart mantra (upahṛdayamantra). Oṃ amite amitodbhave amitacakrānte amitagātre amitagāmini amitāyurdade gaganakīrtikari sarvakleśakṣayaṃkarīye svāhā—this is the garland mantra (mālāmantra).
The sādhana of the noble Uṣṇīṣavijayā is completed.
Having prostrated before Padma, the Lord of the World, who is beloved by the world through his absorption in meditation,
I shall describe the worship of Uṣṇīṣa, a means for accomplishment, for my own remembrance.
In a certain region, monastery, or delightful mountain and so forth,
the yogi, seated upon a comfortable seat, should contemplate within the mind.

There, one should worship the Buddhas dwelling in the three times with a radiance that illuminates them, using the syllable *sabhrūṃ*, which brings benefit to sentient beings and possesses shimmering light.

Having worshipped them, the teacher who knows the instructions should confess before them the sins born of actions of the body and so forth, arising from the divisions such as those committed intentionally and so on.
One should rejoice in all that is virtuous and purify that which arises from it;
one should go for refuge to the Three Jewels, including the elaborations,
in their proper order.
Having made firm the instruction until the attainment of enlightenment,
one should cultivate the thought of awakening (bodhicitta) by taking hold of sentient beings through compassion.
The emanation is without support and devoid of intrinsic nature, like the element of space;
therein, upon a lunar disc situated upon a lotus arisen from the syllable ĀḤ.
The goddess, born from that seed, having three faces and three eyes,
endowed with fresh youth, and the locus of the erotic and other aesthetic sentiments.
She is strewn with all the qualities of a Buddha, adorned with every ornament, obstructing all directions with her mass of radiance,
and resembling the autumnal sky.
She has the luster of Jāmbūnada gold, radiant with a peaceful right face,
and a most fierce face that shines like a cloud at the time of universal dissolution.
With his right hand he holds a vajra fixed to the heart of Viśva;
with the second [hand], he holds a Buddha seated upon a lotus; and with the other, he holds an arrow.
And with the fourth left hand, in due order, [he displays] the granting of boons,
the noose held with the threatening gesture (*tarjanī*), the bow, and likewise the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya*).
One should meditate on her holding a full water-pot and dwelling in a sanctuary cave;
one should contemplate the unsurpassed lotus with its seed-syllable situated at her heart.
The sky was filled on all sides with clouds of Buddhas and great arrays of Bodhisattvas, who were practiced in the impulse of his white radiance-net.
Those who possess great compassion, existing throughout the three times, should also be contemplated with effort as bestowers of consecration by means of the mantra.
The syllable Oṃ within the caitya has the form of a *trāma* and is luminous;
likewise, the collection of seed-syllables Hūṃ, Hrīḥ, Aṃ, and Aḥ follow in their proper sequence.

The yogi should meditate upon Maheśvara, who resides in the crest-lock, the forehead, and the throat, who is situated in the heart, the navel, and the feet, and who dwells in the center of the lunar disc.
Resembling the radiance of the autumn moon and shimmering with garlands of rays,
they are born from the lotus and the vajra, holding chowries in their right hands.
On her right and left sides are Padma and Vajradhara;
in front is the extremely fierce Kekara, and on the right is Ṭakkirāja.
One should place Nīladaṇḍa behind and Mahābala on the left;
their hands are formed by holding a sword, a goad, a vajra, and a staff.
These [clouds], with the roar of the ocean at the time of universal dissolution accompanied by the falling of lightning and thunderbolts,
are the destroyers of the lives of those who are afflicted by the gaze of the summer sun.
With nooses in their left hands and raised right hands,
they are to be meditated upon as surrounded by garlands of flames, seated upon a sun-maṇḍala on a double lotus.
Thus, the practitioner of mantra who knows yoga and meditates day and night shall,
before long, attain the awakening that sets the Vajrayāna in motion.
Thus ends the *Uṣṇīṣavijayā-sādhana*.
Homage to Vasudhārā!
Having meditated on the sequence up to emptiness as before, one should instantly visualize oneself in the form of Jambhala, within the center of a moon mandala in one's own heart.
One should meditate upon the Blessed Lady Vasudhārā, born from the seed-syllable *vaṃ*,
golden in color, adorned with all ornaments, having the appearance of a sixteen-year-old, granting boons with her right hand and [holding] with her left hand...
One should visualize the Blessed Lady Śrī Vasundharā holding a cluster of grain and bearing Akṣobhya in front; to the right, Vasuśrī;
to the west, Śrī Vasumukhī; and to the left, Vasumatiśrī.
These should be contemplated as having their seed-syllables beginning with the first letter of their names and possessing forms identical to those of their principal deity. Having thus meditated:
One should recite the mantra: *oṃ vasudhāriṇi svāhā*, *oṃ vasu svāhā*, *oṃ vasuśriye svāhā*, *oṃ vasumukhi svāhā*, *oṃ vasumatiśriye svāhā*.
Every day, having prepared a square mandala measuring two cubits with cow dung at the three junctions of the day, one should perform the practice.
Having worshipped with fragrant flowers, for those who recite it four thousand times, it fulfills their heart's desire within six months.
Having performed four hundred thousand oblations with whatever flowers are available, great prosperity will arise.
Thus concludes the *Vasudhārā-sādhana*.

Now, if one wishes to meditate upon Vasudhārā, then everything is exactly as before; however, the seed-syllable is the third of the sixth [vowel], adorned with a half-moon and a bindu. From that very syllable, Vasudhārā is manifested, yellow in color, holding in her left hand a vessel raining down ears of grain and various jewels.

To her right, one should visualize [the goddess] granting boons, adorned with all ornaments, surrounded by a retinue of female companions, thinking "I am indeed Vasudhārā. Having formed fists with both hands, with the middle fingers bent at the third joint—this is the mudrā of Vasudhārā. Then one should perform the recitation: *oṃ śrīvasunidhānakṣetre svāhā*.
Having unrolled the Blessed Lady from her silk scroll and performed a great worship, one should meditate upon her and go to sleep. Then the Blessed Lady becomes accomplished.
|| The Sadhana of Vasudhārā ||
According to the previously mentioned procedure, one should visualize [the goddess] as yellow in color, transformed from the syllable *vaṃ*, with two arms and one face;

she is youthful, adorned with ornaments and garments, holding in her left hand a cluster of grain and a jar raining down various jewels, while her right hand displays the gesture of granting boons; she is surrounded by numerous female companions and seated upon a moon on a double lotus.
Having instantaneously visualized [the deity] wearing a crown of Ratnasambhava with her own seed-syllable at the heart (p.
423), one should bind the mudrā: having formed fists with both hands, [raise] the middle fingers.
The third joint is broken—this is the *vasudhārā* mudrā. Then one should recite the mantra: *oṃ vasudhārā ratnanidhānakṣetre svāhā*.
[End of] the *Vasudhārā-sādhana*.
In front of a cloth painting or an image of Vasudhārā, having prepared a square mandala with sandalwood paste,
one should mentally invoke the Blessed Lady there and worship her; then, with hands smeared with sandalwood paste,
[one should offer] a garland of flowers bound to the thread of the manuscript of the Vasudhārā Dhāraṇī.

Having placed a water vessel before him and directed a mind of great loving-kindness toward all sentient beings, he should recite the Vasudhārā Dhāraṇī while focusing his heart on the attainment of his desired goal;
and as he recites, he should utter the word "svāhā" at the end of each mantra that concludes with "svāhā."

One should place white flowers, dūrvā grass, unbroken rice grains, and water into a vessel for a period of six months. At the conclusion of the recitation, one should discard that water in a clean location.
The Instruction on the Vasudhārā Dhāraṇī.

p. 424) Homage to Vajravārāhī! Having risen in the morning, the yogin, having performed the cleansing of the mouth and other such rites, [takes] the pledge-pill (*samayagulikā*)... [k, ḍh, g: ...should consume it. Then, having offered a lamp with fragrant oil, he should recite the mantra one hundred and eight times. Then, having made offerings to the maṇḍala, he should perform the worship of the deity. Then, having circumambulated the maṇḍala three times, he should enter the maṇḍala. Having entered, he should sit upon a comfortable seat and meditate on the self as the deity. Then, having visualized the seed-syllable in the heart, he should emanate the retinue of deities. Then, having offered the inner offering, he should recite the mantra of the principal deity one thousand times.
