Then, having offered the outer offering, he should perform the recitation of the mantra. Then, having offered the torma, he should request the departure of the deities. Then, having dissolved the visualization, he should conclude the practice. Thus ends the procedure for the daily practice. May there be success!

Having placed the *guḍikā* in the mouth and seated upon the Viśvavajra throne in a delightful place such as a mountain cave, one should recite the *ālikāli* three times, having made the firm resolve: "I shall become Vajravārāhī and shall transform the entire world into her form. Then, within the sun at the lotus of one's own heart, one should visualize a red syllable *vaṃ*.

Having summoned Vajravārāhī— who resides in the Akaniṣṭha realm and possesses the arms and weapons to be described later— along with the Gurus, Buddhas, and Bodhisattvas, by means of her red light rays as unbearable as the fire of universal destruction, and having established them in the sky before him and worshipped them with offerings emanated from the light rays of his own heart, [he stands] in their presence.

Having performed the confession of misdeeds, rejoicing in merit, the dedication of merit, and the taking of the three refuges and the generation of the bodhicitta, and having meditated upon the four divine abodes (brahmavihāras)— [as Ḍh adds: likewise,
all phenomena have the nature of the vajra of the wisdom of emptiness]— thereafter, Oṃ.

Realizing the meaning of the mantra, "I am of the nature of the vajra of the knowledge of emptiness," one should remain for a moment in a non-abiding form by the power of previous vows. Then, arising from that meditative absorption, one visualizes in space the bow, triangle, circle, and square, which have arisen from the syllables YAṂ, RAṂ, VAṂ, and LAṂ.

One should visualize the maṇḍalas of the four great elements—yellow, blue, red, and white—stacked one above the other. Above that, one should contemplate Mount Sumeru, arising from the syllable *suṃ*, square in shape, composed of the four jewels, and adorned with eight peaks.
Above that, [one recites]: *oṃ medinī vajrībhava vajrabandha hūṃ; oṃ vajraprākāra hūṃ vaṃ hūṃ*.
Oṃ vajrapañjara hūṃ phaṭ hūṃ | Oṃ vajravitāna hūṃ khaṃ hūṃ | Oṃ vajraśarajāla trāṃ śaṃ trāṃ | Oṃ vajrajvālānalārka (p. 425) |

With these mantras— *hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ*— having fashioned the sixfold vajra-ground and so forth, one should visualize within that a peaked pavilion (*kūṭāgāra*) endowed with all characteristics such as being square and so on; in its center is an eight-petalled lotus born from a red syllable *paṃ*, and in its pericarp, between the moon and sun produced by the transformation of the vowels and consonants, in their midst...
One should visualize a red syllable *vaṃ* within a red vajra, naturally luminous.
Through the complete transformation of all this, one should see oneself as the Blessed Lady Vajravārāhī, resembling the pomegranate flower, with two arms, holding a *khaṭvāṅga* in her right hand...
She has the nature of innate bliss (*sahajānanda*), holds a vajra and a threatening gesture (*tarjanī*) in her right hand, and carries a skull-cup (*karoṭaka*) and a *khaṭvāṅga* staff in her left;
she is single-faced, three-eyed, with loose hair, sealed with the six mudrās, naked, consisting of the five gnoses, and having the nature of innate bliss.
One should visualize her standing in the *pratyālīḍha* posture, trampling upon Bhairava and Kālarātri; her body adorned with a garland of fresh heads, drinking flowing blood.
Likewise, on the four petals starting from the east, one should visualize Ḍākinī, Lāmā, Khaṇḍarohā, and Rūpiṇī in counter-clockwise order.
One should visualize these [deities] as being black, dark green, red, and fair-complexioned; each has one face and four arms.

In their left hands they hold a skull-cup, a khaṭvāṅga staff, and a skull-cup; in their right hands they hold a ḍamaru drum and a flaying knife. They have three eyes, loose hair, and are naked, standing in the *ālīḍha* posture and adorned with the five mudrās. In the intermediate petals, there are four [more].
One should visualize skull-cups filled with the thought of awakening (bodhicitta) and other substances.

Thereafter, rays of light emanating from the seed-syllable in the heart of the Blessed Lady, together with the syllable JAḤ, invite the wisdom-circle (jñānacakra); then, by means of the syllable HŪṂ, one causes it to enter the circle of one's own commitment (samayacakra) like water merging into water; and finally, by means of the syllable VAṂ, one performs the binding.
One should perform the act of pleasing with the syllable *hoḥ*. Then, one should awaken the abodes with the syllables *bhrūṃ*, *hūṃ*, *khaṃ*, *āḥ*, *ḍāṃ*, and *ḍaṃ*.
One should [awaken] the Blessed Lady with the mantra-words purified by the six goddesses.
One should armor oneself: Oṃ vaṃ at the navel; hāṃ yāṃ at the heart; hrīṃ moṃ at the face; hreṃ hrīṃ on the head; hūṃ hūṃ at the crest-lock; phaṭ phaṭ.
One should place the weapon-mantra upon all the limbs. Then, one should offer *oṃ āḥ hūṃ* into the paths of the body, speech, and mind of the Blessed Lady.
When weary from meditation, one should recite the mantra. There, the mantra is: *oṃ vajravairocanīye hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*.
One should meditate upon the Blessed Lady at the three junctions of the day, preceded by the offering of bali. While meditating...
Dwelling [in this state], one should always dwell in the form of the Blessed Lady.
Thus ends the *Vajravārāhīsādhana*.
This work is the composition of the great scholar-adept, the venerable Advayavajrapāda.
Homage to Vajravārāhī!
She who is skilled in burning away ignorance and has destroyed the side of base talk (or weakness).
Having abandoned the mass of people struck by poison, she has effortlessly attained liberation;
enriched with the bliss of tranquility, the goddess Vajravārāhī— Kokadatta writes her collection [of hymns].

There, when half a watch of the night remains, having arisen according to the ritual procedure, one should go to some place such as a cremation ground that is agreeable to the mind and smeared with excellent sandalwood paste and other substances.
Having sat down comfortably, either on a seat of a corpse or on a seat adorned with a scattering of various flowers,
one should first cultivate loving-kindness and the other [immeasurables], and then [visualize] in one's own heart a solar disc arising from the syllable *aṃ*.

Having illuminated them with networks of light rays produced from the white *hrīḥ* syllable, one beholds in front, in their respective places, the Gurus, Yoginīs, Bodhisattvas, and Tathāgatas, headed by Vajravārāhī; then, from the seed-syllable in the heart, [one visualizes] Pracaṇḍā, Caṇḍākṣī, and so forth—
[Ḍh: adds *devībhiḥ* after this] By the goddesses, who possess blue, red, and white complexions;
whose heads bear Akṣobhya, Amitābha, and Vairocana; who sit upon lunar seats and possess three eyes and wear the five mudrās;
and whose heads are adorned with three topknots bound with garlands of vajras, lotuses, wheels, and skull-cups.

Having worshipped with offerings such as *argha* preceded by those whose sprout-like hands are busily engaged with a hand-drum (*kartri*), a skull-cup (*kapāla*), and a staff (*khaṭvāṅga*), one should place one's joined palms together at the head for the sake of realizing the knowledge of emptiness through the performance of salutation, confession of sins, and so forth.

One should request the Tathāgatas by means of the following verse: *Oṃ, may all the accomplishments of all sentient beings be fulfilled as praised by all the Tathāgatas; may all the Tathāgatas bestow their blessing! Oṃ, all phenomena are pure by nature; I am pure by nature.* Immediately thereafter—
Adhimukting all phenomena— the object of worship, the act of worship, and the worshipper— as being empty, signless, and wishless in nature, like a dream or a mental construct,
and personally realized within; and having rendered them non-apparent by means of the net of light rays from the heart-mantra.
p.

428) One should form the ego-identification (*ahaṅkāra*) thus: "Oṃ, I am of the nature of the vajra of the knowledge of emptiness. Then, one's own mind is perfected in the form of a red syllable *paṃ*; that transforms into [the seat] upon a red lotus.

[The text reads *raktapadmo* after *kusumavirājita*: Having meditated on a red lotus transformed from that, upon a solar mandala produced from the syllable *AṂ*, and within a white *HŪṂ*, there is a five-pronged vajra, reddish in color, presided over by the syllable *HRĪḤ* situated upon the sun.
Preceded by the processes of emanation and reabsorption, she is transformed from that [seed-syllable] into a maiden sixteen years of age, white as the autumnal moon, with red,
circular eyes and three eyes, her face slightly terrifying with protruding fangs,
and adorned with half-bound hair that is loose and beautified by various flowers.
She has a triple crest bound by a garland of skulls situated between two rows of black vajras;
she is adorned with a discus, earrings, a necklace, bracelets, and a girdle;
and with her radiant right hand, which displays three fluttering banners, she holds the aforementioned vajra for the sake of the personification of ignorance.

She follows with fear, holding in her left hand a lotus vessel filled with the blood of the four Māras, which has a single-pronged black spike at the bottom and five white-pronged spikes pointing upward;
she wears a long garland of fifty heads strung together with intestines dripping with blood, suspended over a red lotus.
Upon the personification of ignorance situated in the sun, she stands in the *ālīḍha* posture, naked, with the radiance of a fierce sun,
her garland of body hair quivering; equal to a reflected image, endowed with the sentiments of love (*śṛṅgāra*) and the rest,
she is intent on the welfare of the world through various emanations in the ten directions.
One should meditate on oneself as Vajravārāhī, whose heart is a vajra situated upon a sun disk, which is itself presided over by the syllable Hrīḥ situated upon a sun disk.

Then, having emanated all sentient beings into that same form by means of networks of light rays from the seed-syllable in the heart, and having caused them to enter into oneself, one should cultivate the divine pride: "I myself am the Blessed Lady Vajravārāhī."
Thereafter, having visualized a white syllable *hrīḥ* upon a red solar disc within a universal lotus at one's own navel, [one should visualize] its mantra-garland in the form of a rosary.
One should meditate on [the syllable] *SITĀ* being emitted from the opening of the mouth by means of the process of rotating a wheel,

taking up the power of the multitude of jewels that are the Buddha’s qualities, mantras, medicinal herbs, the moon and stars, scripts, treatises, arts, and so forth, and entering the cavity of the navel— its very nature being the burning away of all ignorance in oneself and others. From this...
Having visualized the Wisdom Goddess (jñānadevī) situated in the sky, impelled by the rays from the seed-syllable in the heart,
and having worshipped her in front with the previously mentioned host of goddesses preceded by the water-offering (arghya) and so forth,
one should bind the flame-gesture (jvālāmudrā) at the forehead while reciting the Phetkāra mantra.
Whirling it in a counter-clockwise direction, one should invoke her. There, through the state of single fusion (*ekalolībhāva*), one should effect the identification with the mantra.
In this regard, the mantra is: *oṃ yogaśuddhāḥ sarvadharmāḥ yogaśuddho 'ham*.
Then, having summoned the Tathāgatas, Akṣobhya and the others, who reside in the sky and are impelled by the seed-syllable in her heart, with them—

With vases containing the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) and embodying the five Tathāgatas, accompanied by the sounds of various musical instruments produced therefrom— conchs, drums, small kettledrums, lutes, flutes, and songs— and with gods and asuras intent on uttering cries of joy, raining down saffron, camphor, musk, and fragrant flowers;
Just as all the Tathāgatas were bathed immediately upon birth,
so shall I bathe you with pure, divine water.

Having consecrated oneself while reciting the verses, one should empower oneself with "Oṃ sarvatathāgatābhiṣekasamayaśriye hūṃ," and then visualize that [the goddess] has her head empowered by Akṣobhya, who is seated upon a multicolored lotus and sun disk.
Then, having worshipped oneself with the fierce goddesses such as Pracaṇḍā created by that [deity], and with the various kinds of offerings created by them,
one should partake of the nectar according to the sequence to be described, for as long as one desires.
Having meditated, one should recite the mantra—free from defects such as rapidity and the like—preceded by its radiation and reabsorption. Therein, this is the mantra:
*hrīḥ*. When desiring to rise, [one should dissolve] the garland of mantras into the syllable *hrīḥ* located at the navel.

Having internalized [the mantra], preceded by worship, having made the aspiration (praṇidhāna), and having dedicated the merit, one should recite the hundred-syllable mantra three times; then, maintaining the divine ego-identity and perceiving all phenomena as having attained that very form, one should dwell at ease.
In this regard, the hundred-syllable mantra is as follows: (Oṃ Āḥ) Oṃ Vajrasattva, maintain your pledge;

abide as Vajrasattva; be firm for me; be well-pleased with me; be well-nourished by me; be devoted to me; grant me all accomplishments; and in all activities, make my mind auspicious! Hūṃ Haha Haha Ha Ha.
"HOḤ! O Blessed One, Vajra of all Tathāgatas, do not abandon me; become a vajra, O Great Samayasattva! ĀḤ HŪṂ!

Even during the intermediate twilight, having instantly manifested the form of the Goddess before oneself, preceded by offerings and so forth, one should meditate as long as desired, recite the mantra as before, and perform everything as previously described. However, at the midnight twilight:
Having performed everything as before, at the time of sleep, one should see the Guru, the Buddhas, and the Bodhisattvas in the position of one’s head;

having worshipped them with the intention of prostrating with the eight limbs, one should sleep in the lion’s posture (*siṃhaśayyā*). Then, at the dawn twilight, being awakened by the Goddess, one should perform everything as before.
Alternatively, having sat in a comfortable posture in the corpse-cross-legged position (śavaparyaṅka) in some location,
and having taken hold of all sentient beings with compassion, one begins the confession of misdeeds and proceeds up to the generation of the bodhicitta;
then, upon one's own tongue transformed into the syllable *ĀḤ*—

Having visualized the syllable *hrīḥ*, blazing and radiant, within the form of a lotus petal for as long as desired, and having made it stable, [one should recite] with a rosary of fifty beads (*gulikā*) on a string.

The yogi should recite [the mantra] at the three junctions of the day or the four junctions. When desiring to sleep, he should sleep according to the previously mentioned rule. Thus, consisting of recitation and meditative cultivation, having duly received permission, freed from the eight worldly dharmas, faithful, and established in the commitments and vows;

The compassionate yogi, intent on propitiating the spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*), becomes proficient in the entire range of all scriptures and arts through seven hundred thousand recitations; he becomes intelligent, heroic, confident,
invincible in assemblies, and a skilled debater.
One becomes free from affliction by fevers, poisons, *garas*, *ḍākinīs*, and the like. Whatever one eats becomes nectar (*amṛta*).

When this recitation of the mantra has been perfected, a wooden stylus consecrated with this mantra is placed into the hand of whomever it is given; even if that person is dull-witted, they become a poet. By its mere scent, serpents and other such creatures do not remain in the vicinity.
He becomes capable of providing every kind of assistance to others who are afflicted by these calamities. What need is there for much speaking?

Even I, of dull intellect, having undergone no hardship regarding this treatise and with a distracted mind, have composed this *Prajñālokasādhana* by means of two hundred thousand recitations of this mantra. Furthermore, those who...
Those whose minds are steadfast and who are endowed with the qualities just mentioned will achieve success all the more easily.
Thus ends the *Prajñālokasādhana* (The Means for Attaining the Light of Wisdom).

Having brought sentient beings under control, the ritual for subjugation (*vaśyavidhi*) is taught for the purpose of introducing them to the Four Noble Truths. Then, having visualized the Blessed Lady as perfected according to the previously mentioned sequence— red in color, arising from the transformation of the red seed-syllable and its emblem— and having worshipped her:

One should perform the praise with the verses beginning with "Akṣobhyavajra. Upon three skull-cups facing downward, which have emerged from the *citta-tattva*, there is a vessel consisting of a vajra-lotus born from a red syllable *Āḥ*. Within it, the ten pledges (*samaya*) are empowered by the sixteen vowels and the thirty-four consonants beginning with *ka*. Below...

Having seen them, one performs the heating with the fire-flames by means of the wind and fire mandalas transformed from *ya* and *ra*; then, having summoned the multitudes of Tathāgatas impelled by the rays of light from the seed-syllable placed upon the pledge (*samaya*), and having caused them to enter therein, [one visualizes] upon the moon born from the first vowel (*a*), [the syllable] *hūṃ*, situated on a moon arising from the letter *kha*.

By the entry of the Vajradhara and the Moon-Vajra through the net of radiating rays from the white five-pronged vajra presided over by that [deity], one becomes free from defects such as the fear of birth and doubt; then, having meditated on the syllable *oṃ* above that,
by its rays, the Tathāgatas assume the form of nectar, and the nectar residing in various world-systems also [enters] there.

Having caused [the disciple] to enter through the entry of the *praṇava*, and having seen the nectar produced according to rule, one should consecrate it three times with the three principles (*tritattva*), taste the nectar according to the ritual, and contemplate it as long as desired; then,
seeing the person to be perfected (*sādhya*) standing before one, transformed from the syllables of his own name—

Having drawn him in with rays of light emerging from that garland of mantras and caused him to enter within, one should meditate on his mind as transformed into the syllable *A*, in the form of a slightly reddish lunar disc; then, [one should visualize] the goddess, red in color, emerging from that garland of mantras with her left hand...

Having visualized her standing before the object of practice (*sādhya*), holding a noose marked with the syllable *hrīḥ* in her right hand and a vajra-hook resembling the bud of a red lotus, one recites: *oṃ āḥ hrīḥ amukasya*.

"Draw forth the mind! Hūṃ Jaḥ!"—thus the yogin commands her. Then that goddess, having entered according to the rite, having bound [him] with the noose and prodding him with the hook, brings him back as prescribed and causes him to enter his own mind. The goddess, however, should be visualized as being contained within the garland of mantras. Then, he—with his hair disheveled, agitated, and his throat [choking]—[is brought forth].
Facing the practitioner, she says, "What shall I do? || The *Vajravārāhīsādhana* is completed.
One should visualize Vajravārāhī naked, with disheveled hair, dancing at the region of the navel while holding a flaying knife and a skull-cup;
she brings about subjugation.
This is the ritual procedure for the subjugation by Vajravārāhī.
p.
434) Oṃ, homage to the Blessed Noble Vajravārāhī!
Now, therefore, [concerning] the Blessed Ladies, the Sovereigns of Secrets...
Of all the goddesses, she is the one of great intellect— the Great Secret, the Great Illusion, the Great Sovereign—
who destroys the three worlds and creates the three worlds.
...is created again.
This mother of the Guhyakas, renowned as Mahāmāyā,
is a lore that terrifies the three worlds; may I take refuge in her.
I shall attain this Great Goddess.
By means of that very knowledge, as soon as it is realized,
the lordly practitioner [overcomes] the hosts of gods and gandharvas, along with yakṣas, asuras, and humans.
He brings under his control the Vidyādharas, Piśācas, Rākṣasas, Uragas, and Kinnaras,
as well as all spirits born of water and land.
This science produces great wonder and likewise creates illusions;
it effects enchantment, paralysis, as well as inciting enmity, eradication, and so forth.
When recited, this vidyā brings about subjugation, attraction, and the crushing of enemies, as well as manifold wonders; it grants the perfection of speech to the practitioner.
For him, neither recitation nor vows nor fasting are prescribed;
O Goddess, accomplishment comes without hardship—I speak the truth.
O Mahāmāyā, you who have accomplished all the three worlds, I shall proclaim your mantra through divine lines of syllables in this great yoga.
Oṃ! Homage to the Blessed Lady Vajravārāhī, the Noble Unconquered One, the Mistress of the Three Worlds, the Great Knowledge, who brings fear to all spirits,
the Great Vajra, seated upon the Vajra-throne.
O unconquered one, O unvanquished one, O you who bring others under control, O you who move through the clouds, O purifier of poison, O wrathful one!
O Karālinī, Santrāsanī, Māraṇī,
Suprabhedanī, Parājaye, Vijaye, Jambhanī, Stambhanī, Mohanī, Vajravārāhī, Mahāyoginī, Kāmeśvarī, Khage— namely, O Protaṅge!
Protāṅge, slay, slay the vital breaths!
Kiṅkiṇi, kiṅkiṇi! Khekheṇi, khekhiṇi! Shake, shake, O Vajrahastā! Dry up, dry up, O bearer of the khaṭvāṅga and skull-cup!
O you who consume great quantities of flesh and blood, who are clothed in human entrails,
who wear a garland of fresh human heads strung together, O Sumbha and Niṣumbha! Strike, strike away the life-breaths of all sinful beings and of all sacrificial victims!
O you who cut through flesh, O embodiment of wrath, O you with terrifying fangs, O Great Seal (Mahāmudrā), chief queen of the god Śrī Heruka, thousand-headed, thousand-armed,
seated upon a hundred-thousand-fold throne, blazing with splendor, O Flame-faced One (Jvālāmukhī)!

O you with tawny eyes, whose body is adamantine, seated upon the adamantine throne! O you who have joined your eyebrows, O Terrifying One! Mili mili! Timili timili! He he hūṃ hūṃ kha kha dhu dhu dhuru dhuru muru muru!
O Non-dual Great Yoginī, perfected by recitation! Dreṃ dhraṃ...
KHAṂ DREṂ DHAṂ DHAṂ GRAṂ GRAṂ HE HE HA HA BHĪME HASA HASA VĪRE HĀ HĀ HO HO HŪṂ HŪṂ TRAILOKYAVINĀŚANI ŚATASAHASRAKOṬITATHĀGATAPARIVĀRITE HŪṂ PHAṬ SIṂHARŪPE KHAḤ GAJARŪPE GAḤ TRAILOKYODARE.
O you whose girdle is the great ocean! Grasp, grasp! Hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ! In the non-duality of heroes!
Hūṃ hūṃ hā hā! O deluder of the great beast!

O Mistress of Yoga, you are the Ḍākinī, worthy of homage by all the worlds, the one who produces immediate conviction, HŪṂ PHAṬ! O Terrifier of spirits, Great Heroine, Supreme Siddha, Sovereign of Great Knowledge,
HŪṂ HŪṂ PHAṬ HŪṂ HŪṂ PHAṬ SVĀHĀ!
The practitioner repeats the portion of the mantra beginning with *oṃ namo bhagavati kāmeśvari khage*, adding *hūṃ phaṭ* at the end.
[The title *Jvālāmukhīsādhanaprayogaḥ* is found only in manuscript ḍh.]

This Blessed Mahāmāyā is accomplished through recitation. Her sādhana is as follows: during a lunar eclipse or a solar eclipse, while not looking at the planet, one should recite [the mantra] twenty-one times. Thereupon, she becomes accomplished. As long as one continues to recite it, one is followed by thousands of women. By reciting it once, one attracts or kills with a wrathful mind.

It performs expulsion (*uccāṭana*), inciting enmity (*vidveṣaṇa*), and immobilization (*stambhana*). By reciting the mantra once over a flower according to one's desire and casting it into the sky, one summons Brahmā and the other gods.
By reciting the mantra once over charcoal from a cremation ground and casting it into a house, a village, or a city, one causes a conflagration to appear.

If one whirls a peacock feather that has been empowered with a single recitation in the sky, it causes [the army] to subside again. If one throws sugar that has been empowered with a single recitation in the four directions, it displays a fourfold army. If one whirls the peacock feather in reverse, the withdrawal [of the army] is accomplished.
The Ritual Manual for the Sadhana of Mahāmāyājvālāmukhī-Vajravārāhī.

347) Now, the cremation grounds of Mahāmāyā are described. In the eastern direction of the mandala is the cremation ground named Sādhakānugraha; to the north is Advaitakara; and to the west is Krodhānana.
In the south is Ghorāndhakāra; in the southeast, Mahāpralaya; in the southwest, Mahāmelāpakayogabahula; in the northwest, Siṃhanādamahāphetkāra [k: phaṭ];
and in the northeast, the cremation ground named Sarojabīja. And in these, according to their respective order—

In due order,

there are the yakṣas of great supernatural power with the faces of a buffalo, a cat, a brown bear, a tiger, a horse, a vulture, a boar, and a piśāca; and all around, in the eight cremation grounds, [are those] immediately following [the aforementioned].
Jackals, vultures, owls, crows, vetālas, bhūtas, and so forth—
this is the cremation ground of the goddess Mahāmāyā.
Homage to Vajravārāhī!

Oṃ hrīḥ ghātaya sarvaduṣṭān hūṃ phaṭ svāhā! Having offered the bali, one should perform meditation: in the center of the navel is a triangular fire-maṇḍala born from the syllable raṃ; in its center...
A four-petaled lotus of red color, upon which is the syllable *hrīṃ*— blazing intensely like the fire at the end of an eon—
and from its transformation, one visualizes oneself as Vajravārāhī, red in color, [upon the petals of which...]

Having visualized the vessel as a lotus vessel filled with the five nectars, [one should visualize her] seated upon a *preta*, standing in the *ālīḍha* posture, naked, with hair standing on end, and wearing a crown of skulls.
She is endowed with the five mudrās, has four arms, and holds a vajra and a vajra-hook in her right hands,

while in her left hands she holds a skull-cup, a khaṭvāṅga, and a noose with the index finger raised; she is one-faced, three-eyed, with a face made terrifying by a frown, possessing a vajra-nose, extremely fearsome, large-bellied, and with a protruding tongue.

One should meditate. *Oṃ vajravārāhi āveśaya sarvaduṣṭān hrīṃ svāhā*—this is the secondary heart mantra (*upahṛdaya*). *Oṃ hūṃ hrīṃ hāṃ*—this is the heart mantra (*hṛdaya*). Having become composed, one should recite it one hundred thousand times. One succeeds; there is no doubt in this.

Oṃ aḥ hrīṃ hūṃ hāṃ haḥ | Having prepared a powder of human flesh with this mantra, one should offer it as incense before the cloth painting. It is accomplished in twenty-one days, and not otherwise. Oṃ hrīṃ haṃ [k, ḍh, g:
hūṃ] hāṃ [k, ḍh, g: hoṃ] haḥ haḥ haḥ hīḥ hīḥ heṃ.

At night, one should utter the *phetkāra* "heḥ phet phet phet" for the purpose of pacifying all Māras. The night offering (*niśābali*) should be presented with the five services (*pañcopacāra*). This must not be told to anyone whatsoever; the Vajrayoginīs preside over it—of this there is no doubt.
Doubt. The ritual manual of Śrī Vajravārāhī, which accomplishes all aims.
[The concluding colophon "The Sādhana of Vajravārāhī" is found only in Ḍh and B.]
A red lotus transformed from the syllable *paṃ*; above that, a black wind-maṇḍala transformed from the syllable *yaṃ*, bow-shaped and marked with a banner;
a red triangular fire-maṇḍala transformed from the syllable *raṃ* and marked with flames; and a white, circular water-maṇḍala born from the syllable *vaṃ*.
The square, green earth mandala, marked with a jar and born from the syllable *laṃ*, and Mount Sumeru, which arises from the syllable *suṃ*.

A square [mandala] with four gates, adorned with eight pinnacles; in its center is a lotus transformed from the syllable *paṃ*; above that is a double-vajra (*viśvavajra*) produced from *hūṃ*; in its hub is the union of the vowels and consonants (*ālikāli-yoga*); in its center is a vajra transformed from the syllable *vaṃ*. From the transformation of this [vajra] arises Vajravārāhī, red in color, three-eyed, with disheveled hair.
Naked, adorned with a girdle of bone fragments, with a long garland of fifty fresh human heads hanging down,
she holds a skull-cup in her left hand that contains the blood of wicked Māras, and in her right she threatens the quarters, being the wielder of the vajra that threatens all the wicked.
Possessing the great splendor of the fire at the end of an eon, she flows forth, being fond of blood.
One should visualize her standing with her feet upwards. On the petals of the lotus starting from the east:
Ḍākinī, Lāmā, Khaṇḍarohā, and Rūpiṇī.
Likewise, on the intermediate petals, four beautiful skull-cups should be visualized.
And the mantra for this is: Oṃ sarvabuddhaḍākinīye vajravarṇanīye hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ svāhā. Śrī [Oḍḍiyāna].
The sādhana of Vajravārāhī with upraised feet, emerged from the vajra-seat of Oḍiyāna, is completed.

First of all, the yogin, in a delightful place such as a cremation ground, should bring the gurus, buddhas, and bodhisattvas by means of the rays of light from the syllable *oṃ* within the moon at his own heart; having supported them before him, he should perform the worship, confession of misdeeds, and so forth.
Having made the three realms equal to space and having contemplated it thus, upon the ground transformed into a *hūṃ*-vajra, in the midst of the eight cremation grounds,
within the *dharmodaya*, upon the pericarp of a lotus, is a *vajra* consisting of the syllable *vaṃ* situated between the sun and moon disks;
from that seed-syllable arises the Blessed Lady Vajravārāhī, resembling the fire of universal destruction, with one face.
She has two arms; with her right hand she threatens all directions as the Vajra-terrorizer of all the wicked,
and with her left she holds a skull-cup (or, according to manuscripts k, ḍh, and g, she holds a skull-cup and a khaṭvāṅga staff).
She holds a khaṭvāṅga staff resting upon her staff-like arms which are adorned with a universal banner; she tramples upon Bhairava and Kālarātri,

dances in the pratyālīḍha posture, is naked, has disheveled hair, wears a girdle decorated with fragments, has a face formidable with fangs, possesses three eyes, a distorted countenance, and bears a universal vajra upon her head.
Adorned with a garland of vajras and a skull-bowl, her body graced on both sides by a wreath of severed heads, her limbs decorated with all ornaments,
born from the empowerment of all Buddhas, arisen from the Vairocana family, she is the bestower of all accomplishments.
Having performed the worship, praise, and tasting of the nectar of the goddess whose form is the throbbing withdrawal [of the world], the concentrated yogi,
constantly meditating with devotion, swiftly attains Buddhahood.
is not attained].

Having performed the meditation, the knower of yoga should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) and offer the sacrificial oblation (*bali*). Oṃ vaṃ Vajravārāhī at the navel; hāṃ yāṃ Yāminī at the heart; hrīṃ moṃ.
Hreṃ Hūṃ Hrīṃ Sañcālanī on the face; Hūṃ Hūṃ Santrāsanī on the head;
Phaṭ Phaṭ Caṇḍikā on the crest-lock; and Astra on all limbs.
Having placed [the hands] at the navel, the heart, and likewise the mouth, the head, the crest-lock, and the weapon;
having firmly pressed the middle fingers like needles and the thumbs like vajras, with the fingertips joined together— this indeed is the *madhyasūcī* [mudrā].
Having established it below the region of the forehead, one should cause it to revolve by means of a circular motion.

With his feet treading upon [the ground] and his gaze directed upward, by means of the sound of the syllable *pheṃ* from his head, he should summon the hero-yoginīs residing in the world-systems of the ten directions: *Oṃ yogaśuddhāḥ sarvadharmāḥ, yogaśuddho 'ham;
oṃ acaṇḍi hoḥ jaḥ hūṃ vaṃ hoḥ vajraḍākinyas, tvam samaya*.
At nightfall, one should offer an upward-flung *bali* with the *vajrāñjali* mudrā: *Oṃ kha kha khāhi khāhi!

May all yakṣas, rākṣasas, bhūtas, pretas, piśācas, unmādas, apasmāras, ḍākas, ḍākinīs, and so forth, accept this *bali* and protect the pledge (*samaya*). May there be the accomplishment of the pledge [for me].*
"Grant [us] just as it is; eat and drink according to your desire; do not transgress against me!
For the sake of purifying all forms of true happiness, be my helpers! Hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ svāhā!"—this is the *bali* mantra. Oṃ vajravairocanīye hūṃ.
*phaṭ phaṭ svāhā*—this is the ten-syllable heart mantra (*hṛdayamantra*). *oṃ sarvabuddhaḍākinīye vajravarṇanīye hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ svāhā*.
This is the twenty-one-syllable near-heart mantra (*upahṛdaya*). *oṃ sarvavajrakāmini sarvabhakṣyaṃ śodhaya*.
*Guhyavajriṇi hūṃ svāhā*—this is the mantra for purifying all food.
Alternatively, the oral instruction (*upadeśa*) is as follows: one who desires to stabilize one's own mind [should visualize it] upon the lotus at one's own navel.
One should meditate on a ray of light in the form of a lotus-fiber filament emerging from a minute *vaṃ* syllable situated within a lotus-bud;
one should see the triple world as luminous and having the nature of great bliss.
Thus ends the Concise Sadhana of Vajravārāhī.
Homage to Vajravārāhī!
Having realized that the world is like space and that the mind is likewise awakening,
I, being of the nature of Vajravārāhī, establish the world in awakening.

In a place agreeable to the mind, such as a cremation ground, or within one's own heart upon the moon, having beheld the Gurus, Buddhas, and Bodhisattvas in the sky by means of the rays of the syllable Oṃ, one should perform the confession of misdeeds and so forth. Thereafter, one should meditate on objectless emptiness.
Then, upon the earth and other elements which have become the Hūṃ-vajra...

In the midst of the eight cremation grounds, within the source of phenomena (dharmodaya) composed of the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu), upon the pericarp of a lotus, one should meditate on the Blessed Lady Vajravārāhī, who arises from the syllable *vaṃ* situated within the union of the sun and moon; she resembles the fire of universal destruction, has two arms and one face, and brandishes a threatening gesture with her right hand.

She brandishes a vajra for threatening the wicked in her left hand and holds a skull-cup and *khaṭvāṅga*; she tramples upon Bhairava and Kālarātri with her left leg in the *pratyālīḍha* posture and performs a dance;

she is naked, with disheveled hair, a girdle adorned with fragments [of bone], a face made terrifying by fangs, three eyes, and she holds a crossed-vajra (*viśvavajra*). Her hair is bound upward with a garland of vajras and a skull.
She whose body is beautified by a garland of severed heads, adorned with all ornaments,
consecrated by all the Buddhas, born from the family of Vairocana, the bestower of all accomplishments, and whose form consists of radiating and reabsorbing light.
Having performed worship, praise, and the tasting of nectar, one who is devoted to yoga—
By constantly meditating with devotion, one shall swiftly attain Buddhahood.
One weary of meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*) should recite the mantra: *oṃ vajravairocanīye svāhā*. Regarding this instruction:

one should meditate on a ray of light in the form of a lotus-fiber thread situated within a lunar capsule above the lotus of one's own navel. Then, one should perceive the three realms as luminosity (*prabhāsvara*), and that mind as blissful, peaceful, primordial, and unarisen.
The Concise Sādhana of Vajravārāhī is completed.
Homage to Nairātmyā! The venerable Ḍombīheruka has explained the meditation on the circle of goddesses,
having fully reflected upon the entire reality from the *Yoginītantra* of Hevajra.
Having beheld the Lord Bhaṭṭāraka, the Master and Lord of the Vajra-clan, in the sky,
the wise one should worship and pay homage to him, who is the very image of Akṣobhya.
Having meditated on one's own seed-syllable in the heart, one should fashion a cloud of offerings,
constantly through the application of the five nectars together with the eight Mothers.
The five yoginīs beginning with Gaurī are considered to be the bearers of the five nectars (pañcāmṛta).
Śabarī, Caṇḍālī, and Ḍombī are joined by embraces moist with the essence (rasa).
One should constantly confess one's misdeeds, rejoice in merit,
go for refuge to the Three Jewels, and maintain the mind set upon awakening.
First, one should meditate on loving-kindness; thereafter, one should cultivate compassion.
Again, one should meditate on sympathetic joy, and finally, one should cultivate equanimity in all respects.
Thereafter, one should recite the mantra of the Jina: *oṃ śūnyatājñānavajrasvabhāvātmako’ham*. Having contemplated oneself and others as empty, the yogi should bring to mind the vow.
With the syllable *repha*, he should visualize a sun disk in front of him, and upon that sun, a double-vajra (*viśvavajra*) born from the syllable *hūṃ*.
And with that very vajra, one should visualize the enclosure, the cage, and the binding.
In the element of space, the wise one should contemplate Prajñā in the form of the syllable *E*;
therein he should visualize the earth as square and greenish-yellow.
One should visualize the water mandala situated in the center of the earth mandala;
then one should meditate upon fire within the waters, and within that fire, the wind mandala.
Then, one should contemplate oneself situated in the center of the mandala of wind;
having become blended with the self, the wheel becomes a single form.
It is four-cornered with four gates, adorned with eight pillars,
provided with necklaces and half-necklaces, and embellished with vajra-lines.
On that wheel, one should contemplate fifteen [deities] whose vital breath has departed;
from the direction of the Yoginī, the fifteenth is considered the seat.
Upon the seat, one should place a moon, and upon the moon, a sun;
between these two, one should deposit the seed-syllable beginning with the root vowel.
The mirror-like wisdom and the wisdom of equality are proclaimed as the sun and moon; the sword arising from the letter A is said to be the wisdom of discernment.
The unity of these is their performance, their accomplishment, and their pure nature;
the body of the Yoginīs is proclaimed to consist of the five gnoses.
Just as water becomes variegated by the sun and moon and their rays, so too,
having become mixed once again, she is to be known as Nairātmyayoginī.
She is black in color, most terrible, and adorned with the five mudrās; in her right hand she holds a most fearsome *kartṛ* (flaying knife), and in her left a lotus vessel;
in her left [other] hand she holds a vajra-khaṭvāṅga, and her waist is wrapped in a tiger skin.
Ḍha and ga are at the hips.
The vowels *a*, *ā*, *i*, *ī*, and *u* are said to belong to Nairātmyā and the others; *ū*, *ṛ*, *ṝ*, and *ḷ* are declared to belong to Pukkasī and the others;

*ḹ*, *e*, *ai*, and *o* are the seed-syllables (*bīja*) of Gaurī and the others; and *au* and *aṃ* are further declared to be the seed-syllables of Adhordhvavāsinī. One should seal those [deities] with Citta, Śāśvata, Ratneśa, Amitābha, and Amoghasiddhi.
One should seal Nairātmyā and the others, who are situated within the enclosure of wisdom,
with the Tathāgatas Citta, Śāśvata, Ratneśa, and Amitāyus; likewise,
one should seal Pukkasī and the others located in the intermediate directions in their natural order.
The sealing of the four Yoginīs who always abide at the gates is performed by means of Hatred, Delusion, and Slander, as well as by the Vajra of Passion.
One should perform the sealing of body and speech, being composed in the upper and lower parts;
it is called "sealing" (mudraṇa) because one is sealed by means of a characteristic mark (lakṣaṇa).
In the east is Vajrā, in the south Gaurī, in the west Vāriyoginī,
in the north Vajraḍākinī, and in the center Nairātmyayoginī.
In the northeast, Pukkasī is renowned; likewise, Śabarī is in the southeast.
Caṇḍālī is in the direction of the Rākṣasas (the southwest), and likewise, Ḍombinī is in the northwest.
Furthermore, at the eastern gate is Gaurī; likewise, Caurikā is at the southern [gate];
Vetālī is at the western gate, and Ghasmarī is at the northern [gate].
The Bhūcarī is known to be below, and the Khecarī is remembered as being above;
all of them bestow supreme bliss, just like the Yoginī Nairātmyā.
Having meditated on one's own seed-syllable in the heart, one should then emit rays of light;
having drawn in the Perfect Buddhas by means of those rays, one should worship them with the eight Mothers.
Thereafter, one should offer this supplication to the Blessed Great Beings:
"May the Blessed Ones, all the Tathāgatas, grant me the state of empowerment."
Afterwards, the wise one is consecrated with jars filled with nectar;
while sprinkling [the disciple], he becomes Citteśa-mukuṭa (the Crowned Lord of Mind) by means of all the Perfectly Awakened Ones.
One should first meditate on her as black; in the second [moment], one should visualize her as red;
in the third, one should meditate on her as yellow, and likewise in the fourth, as green.
In the fifth [stage], the yogi should meditate on her as having a blue-colored luster; in the sixth, with a very white body; then, possessing six limbs, and finally, devoid of color.
Vajrā is in the aggregate of form, Gaurī is remembered in sensation;
Vāriyoginī is in perception, and Vajraḍākinī is in mental formations.
Abiding in the form of the aggregate of consciousness, she is the Yoginī of Selflessness;
situated within the mandala, she is the formidable one who strikes fear even into fear itself.
Earth is known as Pukkasī, and the water element is considered Śabarī;
fire should be known as Caṇḍālinī, and wind is proclaimed to be Ḍombī.
Gaurī is always renowned in the realm of form, and Caurī is proclaimed in the realm of sound;
Vetālī is in the sphere of smell, and likewise Ghasmarī is in the sphere of taste.
Bhūcarī is renowned in touch, and Khecarī arises from the *dharmadhātu*;
for through the constant purification of the insubstantial, the yogins of reality indeed attain accomplishment.
Mohavajrī is in the eyes; Dveṣavajrikā is in the ears;
Mātsaryakī is said to be in the nose; Rāgavajrikā is in the mouth;
Sparśavajrī is in touch; and Nairātmyayoginī is in the mind.
With these, through great purity, the armor is worn for the purification of the sense faculties;
the ninth noble head is held, and the divine cleaving knife is the razor.
With a skull, a defiled head, and a skull-bowl, one performs the eating atop the shoulder;
a ring is worn for the purpose of bowing to the Guru, the Ācārya, and the chosen deity.
To avoid hearing ill-spoken words from one's guru or from Vajradhara,
one should wear earrings on the ears and a necklace for reciting mantras.
Rucaka abandoned the killing of living beings and wore a girdle as a mudrā;
his body was always sealed with the thread of the five Buddhas.
The mantra: Oṃ a ā i ī u ū ṛ ṝ ḷ ḹ e ai o au aṃ aḥ svāhā. I shall describe the purification of the measures (mātrā):
Akṣobhya in the form of a wheel, Amitābha as the nature of an earring.
Ratneśa is in the necklace around the neck, and Vairocana is said to be in the hand.
Amogha resides in Mekhalā; these five are the pure Mātrikās.
They should be worn by Yoginīs for the sake of abandoning faults, and they have been constantly worn [by them].
I shall explain the internal form:
by means of the female form, one brings the world under control; by means of the wrathful form, one causes terror.
Through the union of the vowels and consonants, the external duality is practiced.
The mantra for warding off disturbances of the city: *akacaṭatapayasa svāhā*. The mantra for the bali offering to all spirits: *oṃ akāro mukhaṃ sarvadharmāṇāmādyamanutpannatvāt oṃ āḥ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*.
I shall now explain to you the *saṃvara* of Nairātmyayoginī:
the auspicious Mahāmudrā, who bestows great bliss, resides at the navel.
Because of her sharpness, she was enraged in the form of fire by the Mothers.
That wisdom, whose intrinsic nature is the primordial vowel, has been conceived by the Buddhas;
it remains pervading the three realms, yet it is not known by ordinary beings.
Abiding in the center of selflessness, the unstruck sound faces downward;
by means of the yoga of non-returning, the bodhicitta always flows forth.
Therefore, those channels within this body— the lalanā, rasanā, and avadhūtī—
have descended in the form of body, speech, and mind as the artificial seals.

The *lalanā* abides by way of the nature of wisdom (*prajñā*), while the *rasanā* abides by way of means (*upāya*; *rasanopāyena*). But the *avadhūtī*, in the central region, has the form of the support for great bliss (*mahāsukha*).
Lalanā brings about Akṣobhya, while Rasanā flows with blood;
Avadhūtī is always the foundational support for Amitanātha.
In the Sukhāvatī of the action-seal (karmamudrā), the three channels flow according to their own time, discharging body, speech, and mind— the [three] born from the vajra, the jewel, and the lotus.
The time for urination is said to be that of Vajra, who vomits while holding a jewel;
it is described as the form of Amitanātha in the state of perfect enlightenment.
Knowledge always arises, whether at the proper occasion or otherwise;
it is an innate, supreme bliss that brings happiness even to one's parents.
Just as someone might eat at night within a house illuminated by lamps,
so too would there be happiness for the seeker through bodies that are like darkness in the blinding gloom of delusion.

Having thus understood the ocean of existence to have poisonous waters, to be infested with crocodiles such as passion and the like, to be shattered by the waves of deep and clinging vines, and to possess only the great shore of true happiness—
why, O people of the thought of awakening, would you strive for a single moment solely for your own self-interest?
Those who are joined with the syllables *ṣṭha* and *ḍha* go to the further shore; having cast off the garment of the snare of delusion, they proceed to the marvelous state.
First, the wise one should perform the meditation on the generation stage; he must never forget the armor consisting solely of the purification of the mudrās and mantras, which is eternal.
Afterwards, endowed with excellence and with a mind focused one-pointedly on reality, he should practice repeatedly at every moment.
The wise one should always meditate upon the entire [deity], which destroys worldly existence through the cultivation of the generation stage.
He who moves about seated upon a tiger, adorned by various hooded serpents, and who is truly patient— by him,
out of a desire for the welfare of others, was this sovereign sādhana composed in the place known as Kaṅkageha, which abounds in enjoyments and various sweets.
May the sons of the Victorious One forgive this which has been spoken by me— the union with the limbs of secret wisdom, illuminated for the sake of the world.
The ritual manual for the practice named Amṛtaprabhā is completed.
Born into a noble family, free from madness, a holder of the commitments (samayin), and a teacher of Hevajra.
May I be compassionate and devoted to my guru in birth after birth.
May I, with hands ringing the vajra and bell, be a reciter of the profound Dharma;
may I partake of the sexual fluids of women in birth after birth.
How is Mohavajrī black? Because of the nature of Mohavajrī. The aggregate of form (rūpaskandha) is delusion (moha), for form is characterized by the Lord of Mind (cittādhipati).
Because passion is its sole cause, the mind belongs to Varuṇa in the past;
it is characterized by the signs of a passionate mind and possesses the luster of a passion-vajra.
How is Rāgavajrā dark-complexioned, since passion is considered red?
Because she is produced from the four colors, she is [manifested] in a dark complexion.
This Amoghasambhava is considered to have the form of the six Tathāgatas;
she is characterized by a dark complexion, representing the six tastes.
Envy arises from delusion, and delusion is considered to be Vairocana;
therefore, through the union of wisdom and means, envy has the characteristic of being the mind-vajra.
Since mind itself is the intellect (*manas*), how could the beings of gnosis be white? Since there would be no form taken by the intellect, it is therefore sealed with this form.
The sixfold representation is always sixfold, devoid of the forms of the Yoginīs;
whatever merit [is gained] by this clarification of the refutation of the prima facie argument—[may it be for the welfare of all].
By this [merit] attained by me, may those worlds of yours be well-ascertained through the path of mantra;
having understood it without delusion, may these beings attain Buddhahood in an instant.
The purification of the yoginīs of the Nairātmyā maṇḍala is completed.
p.

451) According to the previously described procedure, immediately after emptiness (*śūnyatā*), one should transform [the visualization]— preceded by the radiation [of light] and so forth— into a blue sword born from the seed-syllable *aṃ* within a moon-maṇḍala.

One should visualize Nairātmyā, black in color, with one face and tawny hair standing upright, wearing a crown of Akṣobhya; she stands in a dancing posture with half-lotus on the moon situated upon the heart of a corpse;
her fangs are bared and her tongue lolls out fiercely; she holds a flaying knife in her right hand and a skull-cup and *khaṭvāṅga* staff in her left.

[One should visualize her] with red, round, three eyes, adorned with the five mudrās; having seen the syllables Oṃ, Āḥ, and Hūṃ on her head, throat, and heart, and the syllable Aṃ upon the moon of the artificial fist at the moon of the heart, one should recite this mantra: Oṃ a ā i ī u ū ṛ ṝ... [kh: omits ṛ].
Ṛ Ḷ Ḹ E AI O AU AṂ AḤ SVĀHĀ. The *Kevalanairātmyāsādhana* is completed.

First, having meditated on compassion characterized by the rescue of all sentient beings, and having taken as one's object the emptiness of both the internal and external, one should contemplate the letter AṂ within the lunar disc in the intermediate space, from which arises a scissor; upon that lunar disc held in the fist, one should contemplate the letter AṂ. Then follows the radiation and reabsorption of the circle of Yoginīs.
Having visualized all that and transformed it, one should meditate upon the Blessed Lady Nairātmyā within the lunar disc at the heart of the corpse— black in color,
with two arms holding a curved knife, a skull-cup, and a khaṭvāṅga staff, having one face, and three red, round eyes.

One should visualize her with upward-pointing tawny hair. Having visualized the syllables *oṃ*, *āḥ*, and *hūṃ* at the head, throat, and heart, and having seen the syllable *aṃ* upon the moon of the artificial fist on the moon of the heart, one should recite the mantra: *oṃ a ā i ī u*.
Ū ṛ ṝ ḷ ḹ e ai o au aṃ (aḥ) svāhā — the mantra for recitation.
[End of] Nairātmyāsādhana.
The work of Sahajavilāsa.
Homage to Vajrayoginī!

Oṃ Āḥ Hūṃ! First of all, the mantra-practitioner, having sat upon some seat in any location whatsoever, should begin the meditation on Vajrayoginī. Therein, at one's own navel, is a blossomed lotus of white color.

One should meditate. There, above that, one should meditate on a sun-maṇḍala of extremely red color. Above that, one should meditate on the Dharmodayā, the color of vermilion, situated upon the syllable *hrīṃ* in its center. And there, above that, one should meditate on the Noble Lady Vajrayoginī herself, transformed from the syllable *hrīṃ* situated therein, yellow in color.
One should visualize her as having her own head severed by her own hand and held in her left hand, while her right hand holds a flaying knife;
her left arm is extended upward and her right arm is bent downward; she is naked, with her right leg extended and her left leg drawn in.
One should visualize that a stream of blood issuing from the headless torso enters its own mouth, while other streams enter the mouths of the two Yoginīs on either side.
On the left and right sides are the dark-colored Vajravarṇanī and the yellow-colored Vajravairocanī.

One should visualize the two [goddesses] with their hair loose, each holding a *kartṛ* (ritual knife) in the left and right hands, holding a *karpara* (skull-cup) in the right and left hands respectively, with the left leg extended and the right leg extended while the other [right] leg is contracted.
One should visualize a most terrifying cremation ground in the space between both sides, that is, between both yoginīs—this is the visualization.
Now the worship is described: having drawn the mandala, one should draw the source of phenomena (dharmodayā) joined to the solar abode.

Then, having placed the Bhaṭṭārikā in the center together with the syllable *hrīṃ* in the middle, one should worship her in the center of the *dharmodaya* with the mantra beginning with *oṃ sarvabuddhaḍākinīye*. Afterward, the water offering (*argha*):
with the mantra *oṃ sarvabuddhaḍākinīye hūṃ svāhā*, and then on the left side, *oṃ vajravarṇanīye*.

With the mantra *hūṃ svāhā*, one should worship on the right side; then with *oṃ vajravairocanīye hūṃ svāhā*; then again with *oḍiyāna pūrṇagiri kāmākhyā śirihaṭṭa*; and again with *dharmasambhoganirmāṇamahāsukha*. Oṃ oṃ oṃ.
*Sarvabuddhaḍākinīye vajravarṇanīye vajravairocanīye hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ phaṭ svāhā*— this is the mantra for recitation.
The *Vajrayoginīsādhana* is complete.
Oṃ, homage to Vajrayoginī!
First, in the center of the syllable *vaṃ*, upon the central pericarp of a double lotus born from the syllable *paṃ*.

Upon a solar disc transformed from a red syllable *raṃ*, by means of the transformation of the syllable *hūṃ*, there is the Blessed Lady Vajrayoginī: with loose hair, fierce radiance, naked, standing in the *pratyālīḍha* posture, two-armed, with full and elevated breasts,
red in color, with three rolling, fierce, and trembling eyes, and possessing a frown with knitted brows.
She has a tongue that dangles, fierce with fangs like bees;
she is mounted upon a formidable corpse, is in the prime of youth, and her hips are encircled by the blaze of necklaces, half-necklaces, and small bells.
She wears anklets adorned with various jewels, is endowed with the six mudrās, and holds a skull-topped staff (khaṭvāṅga) in her left hand.

To the right, one should visualize Vajradharā, who has an exceedingly terrifying form, in places such as cremation grounds. When weary from meditation, the practitioner of mantra should recite the mantra. Therein, this is the root mantra: Oṃ sarvabuddhaḍākinīye oṃ vajravarṇanīye oṃ vajravairocanīye hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ phaṭ svāhā. Oṃ vajraḍākinī hrīḥ hūṃ.
*phaṭ svāhā*—the heart mantra. *oṃ vajrayoginī hūṃ phaṭ*—the near-heart mantra.
Now, the offering mantra: *oṃ vajraḍākinī imaṃ baliṃ gṛhṇa gṛhṇa hahahaha khakhakhakha (yayayaya) āā mama*.
Grant success, hūṃ phaṭ svāhā! On the eighth and fourteenth [lunar days], the worship and other rites must be performed according to rule in places such as cremation grounds.
Thus ends the *Vajrayoginīsādhana*.
p.
455) Homage to Vajrayoginī!
One should visualize a double lotus (*viśvapadma*) in the heart through the transformation of a multicolored syllable *paṃ*; upon that—

One should visualize the source of phenomena (dharmodaya), which is a deep red color, within a solar mandala produced by the transformation of a red syllable *repha*. Above the source of phenomena is a red syllable *hrīḥ*.
Through the transformation of all the aforementioned elements beginning with the syllable *hrīḥ*, [the deity arises].

One should meditate on Vajrayoginī, golden-yellow in color, upon a solar seat in the center of a lotus; likewise, one should visualize two Ḍākinīs at her sides, holding a flaying knife (kartṛ) and a skull-cup (karoṭaka), and standing in the ālīḍha posture. In the center: *oṃ sarvabuddhaḍākinī vajrapuṣpe hūṃ svāhā*. In front: *oṃ buddhaḍākinī*.

In the north: Oṃ Vajravairocanī, yellow in color, vajrapuṣpe svāhā (or hūṃ svāhā). In the south: Oṃ Vajravarṇanī, dark green in color, vajrapuṣpe svāhā (or hūṃ svāhā). In the west: Oṃ Vajravairocanī, fair in color, vajrapuṣpe.

Svāhā! Oṃ, to the Dharmakāya Vajrapuṣpa, svāhā! Oṃ, to the Sambhogakāya Vajrapuṣpa, svāhā! Oṃ, to the Nirmāṇakāya Vajrapuṣpa, svāhā! In the center: Oṃ, to the Mahāsukha Vajrapuṣpa, svāhā! Oṃ, to the Oḍiyāna Vajrapuṣpa, svāhā! Oṃ, to the Pūrṇagiri Vajrapuṣpa, svāhā! Oṃ...
Kāmarūpa-vajrapuṣpe svāhā. In the center: Oṃ śrīhaṭṭa-vajrapuṣpe svāhā. Again, in the center:
Oṃ namaḥ sarvaguru-buddha-bodhisattva-vajrapuṣpe svāhā. Oṃ namaḥ sarvabuddha-ḍākinī. Oṃ namaḥ sarvavajra-varṇanī. Oṃ namaḥ hrīḥ sarvabuddha-vairocanī.
HŪM HŪM HŪM PHAṬ PHAṬ PHAṬ SVĀHĀ. The Vajrayoginī Sādhana is completed.
Homage to Vajrayoginī!
On the eighth day, having applied vermilion upon the surface of a perfectly polished mirror, there—

Having drawn the *dharmodaya* seal, having written the seed-syllable *vaṃ* in the corners and the central mantra, and having drawn a *nandyāvarta* on the four sides outside the *dharmodaya* in counter-clockwise order,
one should worship it with flowers and other offerings, recite the mantra as much as possible, and place vermilion (*sindūra*) in that same vessel.

One should place it. In this manner, one should perform this for six months. Then, having placed that vermilion (*sindūra*) inside a tube made from the poisonous stalk of a *lāṅgalikā* plant, one should bury it in a cremation ground, perform the offering (*bali*) and worship, and recite the mantra.
One should do this daily in due order for one month. Then, with the vermilion...

Having applied a *tilaka* in the shape of a *nandyāvarta*, one should enter the village for alms. Whomever is seen there upon whom that *tilaka* has been transferred, one should propitiate that person with effort.
Thus ends the procedure for the propitiation of Vajrayoginī according to the tradition of the venerable Siddha Śabara, by means of the *nandyāvarta*.
[The means of accomplishment] ||

First, in the center of the syllable *raṃ*, upon the hub of a multicolored lotus born from the syllable *paṃ*, and above a sun disk transformed from a red syllable *raṃ*, one visualizes oneself as the Blessed Lady Vajrayoginī,
possessing fierce rays of light, naked, standing in the pratyālīḍha posture, and having two arms.
She has full, elevated breasts, is red in color, and possesses the nature of great passion;
she has three rolling, fierce, and moving eyes, a frowning brow with knitted eyebrows, and a face made terrifying by her fangs.
She has a lolling tongue and upward-flaming red hair; she is mounted upon a corpse and possesses the fortune of fresh youth.

She is variegated by the deep, gurgling resonance of necklaces, half-necklaces, and small bells, and by the sound of jeweled anklets adorned with gems. She is endowed with the five mudrās, and in her left hand she holds a skull-cup filled with the blood of gods and asuras.
One should visualize her in charnel grounds and similar places as having an extremely terrifying form, holding a flaying knife and a raised index finger in her right hand.
When weary from visualization, one should recite the mantra. There, this is the mantra:
Oṃ sarvabuddhaḍākinīye oṃ vajravarṇanīye oṃ vajravairocanīye hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ.

*phaṭ svāhā*—the root mantra. *oṃ vajraḍākinīye hrīṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*—the heart mantra. *oṃ vajrayoginīye hūṃ phaṭ*—the near-heart mantra. The offering mantra (omitted in manuscripts *k* and *ḍh*): *oṃ vajraḍākinī idaṃ baliṃ gṛhṇa gṛhṇa hahaha*.
*Khakha khakha āā mama siddhiṃ prayaccha hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*. On the eighth, fifth, and fourteenth [lunar days], the offering of bali, worship, and so forth, should be performed in the cremation ground.
The *Vajrayoginīsādhana* is complete.
O Goddess, you who reside within the drop, who are curved and possess the luster of a half-moon,
who shine like a particle of frost, and whose splendor is equal to the vajra of the heart.
Thus, having beheld the mind as luminous and untroubled,
all desires arise day and night like a wish-fulfilling gem.
Just as space is formless and devoid of the characteristic of pervasiveness,
so too does that jewel of the mind shine forth, having the nature of Mahāmudrā.
Thus concludes the instruction on Vajrayoginī.
Oṃ śrīvajrayoginī, accomplish, accomplish all bhūtas, pretas, piśācas, and so forth; strike, strike! Burn, burn! Devour, devour! Bestow all means of attaining siddhi; fulfill all hopes, svāhā! Oṃ.
O Śrī Vajrayoginī, grant all accomplishments, grant them! Strike down all obstacles and obstructors! For the sake of my perfect enlightenment, accept this offering! HŪṂ HŪṂ HŪṂ PHAṬ PHAṬ PHAṬ SVĀHĀ.
This is the ritual procedure for the offering to Vajrayoginī.
The god named Mahāmāya— four-faced and four-armed—
with the goddess upon his lap, and four others in the cardinal directions.
Out of compassion for Mahāvajradhara himself, who possesses a terrifying form,
the sadhana of the one named Mahāmāyā is now properly explained.

In this context, the practitioner (mantrin) authorized for meditative cultivation (bhāvanā), awakened by the exhortation of the songs of the four goddesses, rises at dawn and purifies himself with rays from the syllable *HŪṂ* situated upon the sun in his own heart. Having performed the cleansing of his mouth and other preliminary rites, he effects protection for the place, himself, and the yoga with the mantra *HŪṂ PHAṬ*. Then, having entered the meditation chamber, he prepares the water offering (*arghya*) with the syllable *HŪṂ*.

Having recited [the mantra] and seated comfortably, one should visualize the Blessed One together with his retinue in the space before oneself; having worshipped him with the five types of offerings arising from the rays of the heart-mantra, one should perform the confession of sins and so forth as follows:
"I confess my own sins; I rejoice in all merits."

I dedicate all my own roots of virtue toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment for the sake of all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, noble ones, and ordinary beings; until I reach awakening, I go for refuge to the Three Jewels— the Jewel of the Buddha, the Jewel of the Dharma, and the Jewel of the Saṅgha.

The jewel of the Dharma, the jewel of the Saṅgha— oh, may I indeed attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening for the sake and welfare of all sentient beings, until they reach the ultimate goal!
[ṣṭheti] for the sake of establishing [beings] in unsurpassed *nirvāṇa* and in the wisdom of a Tathāgata. Thereafter,
having resolved that all this is merely mind (*cittamātra*) and does not exist externally, appearing in various forms just as in a dream, one should abandon all objective aspects.

One should behold that which resembles the stainless sky, free from appearances, infinite, and consisting of mere luminosity; and one should consecrate it with the thought: *Oṃ, I am of the nature of the vajra of the knowledge of emptiness*. Immediately thereafter, having visualized a crossed-vajra (*viśvavajra*) at the sun in the space before one through the syllable *Hūṃ*, [one should contemplate] its blazing rays radiating downward.

Having visualized a ground made of vajras, a horizontal vajra-fence, and a vajra-canopy above, with a terrifying cremation ground in the center, one should see within that a single-chambered gabled pavilion composed of all kinds of jewels.
It is quadrangular, with four gates, adorned with four archways,
and possesses four radiant altars graced by necklaces and other ornaments as well as celestial nymphs.

Having meditated upon an eight-petalled red lotus in the center of that, one should contemplate within its pericarp the drop of the nectar of gnosis— which is without beginning or end and resembles a pearl from the *tāra*—
as the first samādhi, known as the "Beginningless Yoga."

From the central bindu itself, one should visualize four bindus radiating out to the petals of the eight directions, which transform into seed-syllables: *hūṃ*, *svā*, *ā*, and *hāḥ*. From these, in due order, one should visualize the lords of the Vajra, Maṇi, Padma, and Karma families, along with their respective families, radiating forth; then, having reabsorbed them back into those very same syllables, one should visualize the four Yoginīs transformed from them.
On the eastern petal is Vajraḍākinī, blue in color, with faces that are blue, yellow, white, and green (p. 460),
holding a vajra, a skull-cup, a bell, and a khaṭvāṅga.

On the southern petal is Ratnaḍākinī, yellow in color, with faces that are yellow, blue, white, and green; she holds a banner with a jackal at its tip, which is pressed against her neck by a trident adorned with a stream of jewels. On the western petal is Padmaḍākinī, white in color, with faces that are white, yellow, blue, and green.
[Omitting *hariṭā*: On the northern petal is Viśvaḍākinī, green in color, with green, yellow, white, and blue faces, holding a sword, a ḍamaru drum, a noose, and a skull-cup;
all have moon-seats and radiance, and the rest of their features are like those of the Lord.
They should awaken the Lord with this vajra-song:
"O friend! The lotus has blossomed; it has been awakened by the vajra."
Alala-lalaho! He has been raised up by great bliss through dancing.
The lotus has blossomed by the sun’s rays through great bliss;
*alalalalaha*, he has been raised up in dance by means of great bliss. Friend, the lotus has opened and been awakened by the drum.
"Alala laha! With great joy, he ascended and danced."
By the sun's rays the lotus has blossomed with great joy;
Alalalalaho! With great joy he has ascended and dances.

Then, by the power of the song, the Blessed One abandons his form as a drop (*bindu*) and manifests in the shape of two seed-syllables: *oṃ* and *hūṃ*. Then, having emanated Vairocana and his family from the syllable *oṃ*, he should reabsorb them; and from the syllable *hūṃ*, he should emanate the five Jinas and their families. Then, by means of the Buddha-Ḍākinī arising from the syllable *oṃ*...
Simultaneously, the Blessed Lord Heruka arises from the syllable HŪṂ.
He is smeared with ashes, black in color, and possesses the splendor of a playful sun-disk seat.
His hair is tawny and blazing upward, and he is formidable with a crown of skulls.
He has four faces— blue, yellow, great white, and green—
and four arms, holding a skull-cup, an arrow, a khaṭvāṅga staff, and a bow.
Through the purification of the five Buddhas, he is adorned with the five mudrās:
the wheel, the earring, the necklace, the bracelet on the hand, and the girdle.
Clad in human skin, with twelve reddish eyes,
his wrath filled with garlands of flames, he is beautiful with supreme bliss.
Seated in the half-lotus posture, engaged in dance and endowed with the nine dramatic sentiments,
he accomplishes the welfare of the world through the multitudes of people manifested from his inner heart.
Śrī Buddhaḍākinī has faces that are red, yellow, white, and green; she is fond of her consort’s weapons, is red in color, and her two arms embrace his neck.
Just as the *Śabarī* empowerment of the Buddhas is sung in the *Hevajra*,
so here Heruka is fully worshipped by the Buddha-Ḍākinī.
The Buddha is "red" here because he delights sentient beings with his Buddha-body;
the phenomena are pure by nature, which is the whiteness of Vāgīśvara himself.
Thereafter, one should contemplate the syllable OṂ, red in color, at the Blessed One’s faculty of sight; the syllable HŪṂ, blue, at the faculty of hearing;
the syllable CĪ, yellow, at the faculty of smell; the syllable ĀḤ, white, at the faculty of taste;
the syllable REPHA, green, at the location of the uṣṇīṣa; and the syllable KHA, white, in the mind—thus, upon the six faculties.

The six-syllable placement (*ṣaḍakṣaranyāsa*) is the armor (*kavaca*). With *oṃ āḥ hūṃ*, one performs the consecration of body, speech, and mind respectively upon the head, throat, and heart. Having visualized the seed-syllable of one’s own deity—whose nature is that very gnosis—within the sun between the breasts, one draws in the mandala of gnosis by means of the hooks of its light rays.
Having dispelled the obstructors with the syllable *hūṃ*, offered the water of honor (*arghya*), and having drawn them in, caused them to enter, and bound them with *jaḥ hūṃ vaṃ hoḥ*— (p. 462)
Having brought [the deity] under control, one should visualize the *samaya*-maṇḍala as having become one with it.

Then, the five Yoginīs, dispatched by the Tathāgatas and impelled by the rays of light from the seed-syllable of gnosis (*jñānabīja*), arrive; they and the Yoginīs should consecrate the Blessed One with precious vases filled with the water of the five gnoses. Upon the heads of those being consecrated—
The Lord Akṣobhya arises as the lord of his own family; for the Buddha-Ḍākinīs and the others, they are respectively Śāśvata, Akṣobhya, Ratneśa, Vāgīśa, and Amoghasiddhi.
Then, by means of the rays emitted from the faces of the seeds of gnosis— [k, g: from the faces of bliss]...

One should worship the Blessed Lord and the Blessed Lady with the five types of offerings and the worship of the five strands of sensual pleasure. Then, one should praise the Blessed Lord through the mouths of the goddesses:
"Adorned with a garland of severed heads, most terrifying and formidable with protruding fangs..."
I bow down to Śrī Heruka, who is consuming great flesh.

Thus. Then, through the yoga of radiating light, the goddesses of the directions should merge into the Buddha-Ḍākinī. Then, having visualized these syllables—OṂ HŪṂ SVĀ Ā HĀ—in her head, heart, navel, secret place, and thighs respectively, by means of them radiating one another...

Having pervaded the body with that red lotus born from the syllable *hrīḥ* and a pearl pericarp born from the syllable *a*, and likewise a vajra born from the syllable *hūṃ* and a jewel born from the syllable *oṃ*, one should initiate pleasure—that is, passion—with this mantra: *yāmī*. Then, the Tathāgatas, impelled by the rays of light from the two jewels, arrive, enter through the mouth, dissolve, and fall upon the petals of the lotus. That...
One should contemplate the nectar of the five gnoses being taken up by the tip of the tongue with graceful movement.
This is the second meditative absorption, named the Sovereign King of the Glorious Mandala.

Then, impelled by the Blessed One, the Buddha-Ḍākinīs and others, through the emanations of clouds of the five bodies of the Blessed One in the five [directions], sequentially performed the welfare of sentient beings, beginning with the mirror-like gnosis (*ādarśajñāna*).
Having generated the knowledge of the utterly pure dharmadhātu, the knowledge of equality, the knowledge of discernment,
the knowledge of accomplishing activities, and the state of Mahāvajradhara, [one dissolves] one's own clouds of bodies into the root body.
"They should withdraw" means [they should cut].
This is the third meditative absorption, named Karmarājāgra.

Furthermore, if the yogi should wish to stabilize the mind for the sake of accomplishing the foremost of all meditative absorptions (*samādhi*), then, having briefly visualized the three meditative absorptions, he should contemplate— without any gap— the union of the sun and moon at the edge of the pericarp of the navel-lotus, and in their center...
Having visualized the hero as the great bliss consisting of the form of a drop (*bindu*), which is subtle, white, clear, and like a mustard seed,

one sees a line of light rays resembling a lotus fiber emerge through the center of the moon; having seen it remain after encircling the *sampuṭa* obliquely with three coils, [one observes] the three half-coils situated upon the moon.
One should visualize sixteen syllables, each individually strung together. For it is said in the *Samvarottara*:
"One should arrange the letters from *ka* to *da*, excluding *ṅa* and *ña*;
one should draw the two lines (*āli*) from *dha* to *ha*."
But by one who is impartial, the syllable *tvakāra* should be placed upon the lunar disc.

Thus it is said; here too it is stated, "with divine lines of syllables. In this way, meditating upon the Hero within the interior of the union of the sun and moon at the pericarp of the lotus in the center of the navel, and having gained conviction through the ripening of that meditation, one should perceive [the Hero] as remaining like a single flame ignited by a second subtle line of light rays. Of that—

Flooded by a stream of nectar flowing through the power [of that light], the hero and that line of rays become white. Then, having fixed his mind upon the hero, he should gaze at him until, through signs, he perceives the attainment of stability of mind. Once stability is perceived, from that line of rays, an infinite and clear light [emerges].

Having visualized [the deity] illuminating the entire universe, one should perceive everything as clearly as a myrobalan fruit in the palm of the hand and swiftly accomplish all meditative absorptions (*samādhis*).
Thus is the yoga of the drop (*binduyoga*).

Regarding the statement that "success belongs to one who has recited the *vidyā*," the recitation (*japa*) is now described. In the same manner, the yogin should contemplate for a long time the wheel of the six deities within the interior of the union of the sun and moon situated in the pericarp of the navel-lotus, and likewise...

One should recite the mantra within a triple enclosure (*sampuṭa*) formed by three lines of light rays, which are proclaimed as three rows of syllables. In this tantra, the mantras consist of three syllables. Among them, the mantra of the Blessed One is *oṃ hūṃ hūṃ*.
The mantras of Buddhaḍākinī and the others follow in order: *oṃ oṃ hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ*, *oṃ svā hūṃ*, *oṃ ā*.

HŪṂ OṂ HĀ HŪṂ. How should one recite? Having placed the seed-syllable to be recited within the interior of the *saṃpuṭa* (enclosure), and having raised the Hero (*vīra*) above its head while uttering the syllable OṂ, one should raise a line of light rays from the Hero together with the exhalation breath, and by means of that, one should make the world illuminated as consisting of the Buddha.

While reciting the seed-syllable, one should resolve that all those Buddhas have the nature of one’s own deity. Reciting the internal syllable *HŪṂ*, one should draw in by means of the breath of exhalation and dissolve this world, which consists of those Buddhas, into the Hero (*Vīra*). One should do this again and again until fatigue occurs. When [fatigue] is present...
Having rested from fatigue, one should dedicate all this merit toward unexcelled perfect enlightenment and the attainment of the desired fruit;

then, having performed worship as before, one should dissolve the mandala into the seed-syllable at one's own heart, rise up therefrom, resolve that oneself is of the nature of one's chosen deity, and perform everything [as prescribed].

Having transformed all food into the nectar of the five gnoses by means of the five seed-syllables, and having visualized and contemplated the circle of deities within one's own heart, one should offer that nectar into their tongues. While bathing,
one should perform the visualization of the rite for the consecration of the deities.

At the junctions of midday and evening twilight, however, having entered the maṇḍala-hall and emanated the foundational maṇḍala by means of the rays from the seed-syllable in one's own heart, [one should likewise emanate] the four yoginīs from that very same seed-syllable.

Having expanded [the mandala] gradually and established it in its proper place, one should perform all the rites such as the consecration (*abhiṣeka*) as before, dissolve the mandala within oneself, and then, having arisen, perform the yoga of meditative absorption (*samāhitayoga*) as previously described.
However, at the twilight of midnight, there is this distinction: having performed worship and offered the water of honor (*arghya*), one should recite "Oṃ vajramuḥ."

Having emitted the mandala of gnosis (*jñānamaṇḍala*) and internalized the pledge-mandala (*samayamaṇḍala*) within the seed-syllable of one's own gnosis, one should sleep while resolving upon the non-manifest bodhicitta. In this manner, on subsequent days as well, being roused by the exhortation of the goddesses' concert, one should perform everything as before. Thus, day after day, until one obtains the signs of accomplishment (*siddhinimitta*). Regarding that, [the procedure] for the Lord of the Mandala (*maṇḍaleśvara*)...

The mantra is accomplished through one hundred thousand recitations; the remaining mantras are accomplished through ten million recitations. The *mālāmantras* and other mantras are to be taken from other tantras. Having formed them into a circle—either on the sun at one's own heart or on the moon at the heart, as appropriate—and having visualized them with the mind as blazing like a row of lamps, one should recite them mentally as if with speech.
"Regarding the instruction 'one should recite':
by the merit acquired by me through thus proclaiming this *sādhana* of Mahāmāyā,
may I become a Buddha, a master (*vaśin*) in accomplishing the welfare of all beings."
The *Mahāmāyāsādhana* is completed.
Homage to Vajraḍāka!
Having first performed the cleansing of the mouth and other preliminary rites, one sits upon a soft seat; [visualizing] a sun-maṇḍala in one’s own heart.
Having visualized the seed-syllable *hūṃ* before oneself, one should contemplate Karuṇācalavajra with the colors, arms, and weapons to be described hereafter,
and perform the worship, confession of misdeeds, rejoicing in merit, dedication of merit, taking the three refuges, and so forth, up to the making of aspirations.

Having established it within one's own body, speech, and mind, one should meditate upon the syllable of the name. And that syllable of the name is as follows: *he* signifies that all phenomena are free from causes; *ha* signifies that all phenomena are devoid of arising and ceasing; *e* signifies that all phenomena are liberated from seeking; *ru*... [text fragment]

"Nu"—all phenomena are like an echo; "ra"—all phenomena are endowed with delight; "u"—all phenomena are subject to the nature of arising and ceasing; "ka"—all phenomena are endowed with all happiness; "a"—the syllable *a* is the gateway to all phenomena because they are unarisen from the very beginning. Having reflected thus, one should contemplate emptiness.

One should recite the mantra: *oṃ śūnyatājñānavajrasvabhāvātmako’ham*. Having dispelled obstacles with the syllable *hūṃ* and visualized a vajra-fence, one should behold the seed-syllable *hūṃ* upon a solar disc at the center of a red four-petaled lotus within the midst of the eight cremation grounds.

The four goddesses, whose essential nature consists of loving-kindness (*maitrī*), compassion (*karuṇā*), sympathetic joy (*muditā*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*), urge [the practitioner] on with the *Śrīvajragīti* in the *Abhyantarasādhana*: "Hale! [k, ḍh: *atyantabhava*]. [chāyā]...
O friend, the lotus has blossomed and been awakened by the thunderbolt;
