Alalalalaho! It has been raised up with great bliss through the dance.
The lotus has blossomed by the sun’s rays;
by great bliss, Alalalalaha has been made to ascend through dance. Friend, the lotus has blossomed and been awakened by the drum;
by great bliss, Alalalalaha has been made to ascend through dance.
By the sun’s rays, the lotus has blossomed with great bliss;
*alalalalaho*, with great bliss, he has ascended and dances.
Through the dance of Vajraḍākinī, one should cause Vajrasattva to enter.
Thus, immediately after the song, through the realization of the reality bound by illusion,

one should mentally [visualize] Karuṇācalavajra, arisen from the syllable *Hūṃ*, with four faces— blue, yellow, white, and dark— and four arms; holding a skull-cup and an arrow in the right hands, and [a bow and a noose] in the left.
Holding a skull-topped staff (*khaṭvāṅga*) and a bow, seated in a fierce posture, possessing three eyes, wearing a garland of fresh human heads,
adorned on his head with a string of skulls, decorated with ornaments of bone,
his face made terrifying by slightly bared fangs, with tawny hair standing erect— on his body [the syllable] *cī*.
The yellow syllable OṂ is at the two eyes; the white syllable HŪṂ is at the two ears; the red syllable KH is at the nose;
the white syllable ĀḤ is at the throat; and the red syllable REPHA is at the heart.
Thus characterized by the six-limbed placement (ṣaḍaṅganyāsa), embraced by a consort of his own radiance, he occupies the expanse of space.

Having visualized oneself as one who has received the Vajradhara initiation, empowered in body, speech, and mind, and whose intrinsic nature is the perfectly pure wisdom of the dharmadhātu, [one should meditate] upon Vajraḍākinī on the eastern petal;
she is blue in color, with four faces— blue, yellow, red, and dark green— and four arms, holding a khaṭvāṅga and a bell in her left hands.

On the right, Ratnaḍākinī is on the southern petal; she holds a vajra and a skull-cup in her hands, has the nature of the earth element and the mirror-like gnosis (*ādarśajñāna*), is yellow in color, has four faces—yellow, blue, red, and dark green—and four arms. In her left hand she holds a banner and a bodice...
And in the south is Jambūkaḍākinī, holding a trident and a jewel in her hands; she is of the nature of the water-element and the knowledge of equality.
On the western petal is Padmaḍākinī, white and reddish in color, with four faces—red, yellow, blue, and dark green—and four arms.
In her left hands she holds a bow and a skull-cup; in her right hands she holds an arrow and a double lotus.

On the northern petal, Viśvaḍākinī, whose nature is the wisdom of discerning the fire element (tejodhātu), is dark green in color and has four faces—dark green, yellow, red, and blue—and four arms; in her left hands... [p. 468]

In their right hands they hold skull-cups, and in their left hands they carry khaṭvāṅgas and ḍamarus; these goddesses, whose intrinsic nature is the performance of rites for the wind element, all stand in a wrathful posture, their heads adorned with garlands of skulls, wearing necklaces of strings of fresh severed heads, possessing three eyes, and having faces made terrifying by slightly bared fangs.

Having meditated on oneself as Karuṇācalavajra, surrounded by the four goddesses whose upward-pointing tawny hair is ablaze and who are garlanded with shimmering rays of light, one should visualize the mandalas of Vāyu, Mahendra, Varuṇa, and Agni at the head, heart, navel, and secret place according to the oral instruction, and perform the neuter recitation (*napuṃsakajāpa*).
The Mantra-adept: When weary, having performed the recitation of the mantra *oṃ āḥ hrīṃ hūṃ phaṭ*,

the yogi— whose nature is the Dharma established by the mantra whose essence is the self-nature of all phenomena equal to existence— should perform all activities regarding sense objects and so forth for the sake of liberation from ordinary conceptualization.
The *Mahāmāyāsādhanopāyikā* is completed.
"This work is by Kukkuripāda."
Homage to Heruka!
Seated on a comfortable seat in a meditation chamber such as a mountain and possessing a disposition of loving-kindness and compassion,
one should place within one’s own heart, upon a multicolored lotus and sun disc, the blue syllable *hrīḥ* emitting rays of light.

Having worshipped the heavy Buddhas and Bodhisattvas impelled by those rays throughout the universe, one should perform the taking of the three refuges and so forth. Then, having observed all phenomena and one’s own body as being without intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*), one should recite "Oṃ śūnyatājñāna... and so on. Thereafter, [one visualizes] a fierce blue vajra produced from the syllable *Hrīḥ*.
Having meditated on the syllable *hrīḥ* as the empowerment (*adhiṣṭhita*) upon the pericarp, one visualizes that which is transformed from all of that as blue, wearing a human skin.
His head is adorned with a garland of skulls and Akṣobhya; his tawny hair stands erect and blazing; his eyes are red and round;
he is draped with a necklace of severed heads strung together with intestines;
he wears ornaments fashioned from human bones; he has two arms and one face; his mouth is terrifying with bared fangs; and with his right hand—
Holding a *vajra* in his left hand and a full skull-cup (*pūrṇakapāla*),
with a swaying bell and banner attached to his left shoulder, adorned with a human head and a five-pronged double-vajra (*viśvavajra*),
and carrying a *khaṭvāṅga* like a sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*); his left foot is upon a double-lotus and sun disk, while his right foot is upon the thigh of that very [deity].

Having performed the placement [of the seed-syllables], one should visualize the heroic Heruka performing a dance. Then, having seen the Jñānasattva in that form, one should summon the Jñānasattva Heruka by means of rays of light from the syllable *hrīḥ* located in his heart; having offered the water for honor (*argha*) and so forth, one should cause him to enter into oneself and establish protection through the pledge-seal (*samayamudrā*) upon the heart, throat, and crown.

In this regard, the pledge-mudrā (*samayamudrā*) is as follows: having formed two vajra-fists, one should form knots with the two index fingers and, with the two thumbs and the two middle fingers, point them like needles respectively downward and upward;
the remaining fingers should be positioned in the shape of flames. Then, weary from meditation, one should recite the mantra: *oṃ heruka*.
*vajrasamaya hrīḥ sarvasattvaduṣṭasamayamudrāprabhañjaka hūṃ phaṭ*. Then one should dismiss [the deities].
Upon entering the cremation ground, having bound two *vajramuṣṭi* fists, linked them with the little fingers, formed needles with the index fingers, and held them at the forehead.

Having meditated on one's body, speech, and mind as being pervaded by all limbs through the radiations of subtle yellow vajra-rays emanating from the *mudrā*-rays, one should recite the previously mentioned mantra. One may then enter the cremation ground; there will be impenetrable protection.
The concise Heruka sādhana is completed.
Everything has the characteristic of space, and space itself is without characteristics; indeed,
the entire triple world in its entirety is like an illusion.
Just as an illusion is seen and touched from every side,
yet the existence of the entire world is not apprehended at all.

Having resolved upon this meaning with the mind, and having perceived one's own body as well as the entire collection of objects such as blue and so forth as empty through the separation of the one and the many, one perceives one's own mind— called mental consciousness— as immediately following [the object],
subtle, waveless, unimpeded, and possessing an incomparable color and shape.
Even that which is accompanied by error is for the sake of benefit, in order to bring about internal cessation;

thus, having superposed [the visualization], for the purpose of stabilizing the object of focus, one should resolve upon the form of a firefly and contemplate that as the form of a moon-maṇḍala, complete with all its digits and containing within it emptiness and compassion. Within this moon-maṇḍala...
Upon the mark of the accumulated equipment of merit, one should visualize the syllable *hrīḥ*, blue in color, which is the mark of the accumulated equipment of gnosis;
and having transformed that, one should contemplate the blue-flaming vajra, whose intrinsic nature is mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*),
which has further transformed into the form of a moon-vajra— the assembly of Jinas arising from the wrathful Śrī Karuṇācala.

One should visualize oneself as the one named Heruka, seated upon a sun disk atop a double lotus (viśvapadma) which rests on a corpse lying face down; according to the statement "having one [face] and two upper arms," he is in the half-lotus posture (ardhaparyaṅka), smeared with ashes, garlanded with a red radiance, and has tawny hair standing erect.
He wears a crown of garlands of skulls adorned with Akṣobhya and other deities; in his right hand he holds a fierce blue vajra in the *tripatākā* gesture,
while a vajra-khaṭvāṅga is slung over his left shoulder, and his left hand holds a skull-cup filled with blood.
One whose face is made terrifying by fangs and adorned with a garland of fresh human heads,
whose round red eyes roll about, and who possesses a playfully arched brow— this is what is to be described in the ultimate sense.

Because it is devoid of conceptual investigation, from the perspective of conventional reality, the form of one's chosen deity—sealed with the four mudrās, namely the Mahāmudrā, Samayamudrā, Dharmamudrā, and Karmamudrā—is like a dream, a flash of lightning, a city of the Gandharvas, a shadow, or an illusion; it becomes the bestower of all siddhis. Having visualized a vajra above a moon disc in one’s own heart...
One should visualize oneself as Śrī Heruka, endowed with five prongs, colors, arms, and postures, together with his insignia;

this is the Mahāmudrā. In the same manner, having visualized a moon and a vajra in one's own heart, and having formed the vajrāñjali at the crown of the head with the fingers spread apart, one should place the two index fingers in the shape of a *kuṇḍa* and the two thumbs [as described].

One should break [the fingers] at both sides with the two thumbs—this is the *samayamudrā*. Having placed a white vajra upon the moon-maṇḍala on the tongue, one should recite the mantra: *oṃ subhage tvamahaṃ devi hiri siri tiriṇi priye*—this is the *dharmamudrā*. Upon the moon-maṇḍala in one’s own heart...

Having visualized a crossed-vajra (*viśvavajra*) produced from the syllable *ĀḤ*, one should form the vajra-binding at the base, cover the two index fingers with the two thumbs, and break them— this is the Skull-Seal (*kapālamudrā*), the action-seal (*karmamudrā*) of the Blessed One.
*Oṃ śrīherukavajra samayamudrā hrīḥ sarvaduṣṭamudrāprabhañjaka hūṃ rulu.*
culu rulu svāhā hūṃ phaṭ.
Thus, this concise method for the practice of the Blessed One has been composed by Kalyāṇagarbha, who feared excessive prolixity. || The Sādhana of Śrī Heruka ||
p. 472) Not clear p. 473)
Having prostrated to the glorious Guru, the Lord Heruka who seizes the three worlds, [omitted in manuscript *kh*].
The procedure for its accomplishment, as taught by Śāntipāda, is now set forth in detail.
The hero has two arms and one face, his neck embraced by Nairātmyā;
he is adorned with ornaments such as wheels, possesses three eyes, and is resplendent with two legs [upon a tiger-king].

In this tantra, the yogi authorized for meditation, having risen from his bed at dawn, sees the syllable *HŪṂ* situated upon a sun disk in his own heart; having illuminated and invited Śrī Heruka with its rays,
he worships him with the fivefold offerings beginning with flowers, and [remains] before him.
Having performed the confession of misdeeds, the rejoicing in merit, and the taking of the three refuges, and having generated the mind of great awakening (mahābodhicitta),
one should cultivate loving-kindness (maitrī) characterized by the bestowal of divine happiness upon all sentient beings,
compassion (karuṇā) characterized by the removal of all suffering, and sympathetic joy (muditā) characterized by the determination to ensure that such happiness never ceases.

One should cultivate equanimity characterized by the non-mental engagement (*amanasikāra*) with respect to the afflictions (*kleśa*), secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), and the subject-object duality (*grāhya-grāhaka*). Then, having meditated upon emptiness (*śūnyatā*)— which is free from the stains of conceptual constructions regarding phenomena (*dharma*) and persons (*pudgala*), resembles the cloudless midday sky in autumn, and has the singular nature of non-dual gnosis (*advayajñāna*)— [one recites] *oṃ*.

One should perform the consecration with the thought: "I am of the nature of the vajra of the knowledge of emptiness. Then, having awakened, one should see the syllable *HŪṂ* situated upon a sun-maṇḍala in the expanse of space;

one should behold the syllable *HŪṂ* located on the central hub (*varaṭaka*) of the vajra produced from its transformation. From the rays of light emanating from that, there emerge forms of Śrī Heruka.

Having accomplished the welfare of the entire world and having dissolved it back into that very source, one visualizes Śrī Heruka, who has arisen from that transformation, seated upon a corpse on a sun-maṇḍala atop a multi-petalled lotus; he is two-armed and three-eyed, holding a vajra in his right hand and a skull-cup marked with a vajra in his left, and is in the midst of a dancing *tāṇḍava*.
Clad in a tiger skin,
he wears upon his head a crown (*cakrī*) fashioned from a human skull whose essence is Akṣobhya, and [he has an ornament] on his ear.
He has earrings made of human bone representing Amitābha on his ears, a necklace representing Ratnasaṃbhava around his neck,

a breast-ornament (*rucaka*) representing Vairocana held in his hand, and a girdle representing Amoghasiddhi at his waist; he is endowed with hair as a sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*), armlets, and anklets, possesses upward-pointing tawny hair, and is accompanied by [his consort] who has two arms and one face.
Having visualized oneself in this manner, embraced by Nairātmyā who holds a curved knife (kartrī) and a skull-cup (kapāla),

one should then resolve that Nairātmyā is in one’s ears, Vajrā in the eyes, Guptagaurī in the nose, Vāriyoginī in the tongue, Vajraḍākinī in the faculty of touch, and Nairātmyā in the mind. Then, on the head...

One should visualize a downward-facing syllable *haṃ* upon a thirty-two-petaled lotus at the throat; an upward-facing syllable *oṃ* upon a sixteen-petaled lotus at the heart; a downward-facing syllable *hūṃ* upon an eight-petaled lotus at the heart; and an upward-facing syllable *aṃ* upon a sixty-four-petaled lotus at the navel. Then:

Having summoned the wisdom-being (jñānasattva) who resembles the commitment-being (samayasattva), one should—by means of the mantra *jaḥ hūṃ vaṃ hoḥ*—attract, cause to enter, bind, and subjugate him, and then make them of one flavor like milk and water.
Immediately thereafter, one should emit rays from the syllable *hūṃ* situated in the hub of the sun-vajra at one's own heart; by those rays...
Having summoned Heruka, whose nature is that of all the Tathāgatas, and having performed worship, one should pray:

"May all the Tathāgatas confer empowerment upon me. Then, having visualized oneself being empowered by them with jeweled vases filled with the five nectars, and adorned with the crown of the Lord Akṣobhya—

One should meditate. Then, one should perform worship with the assembly of all yoginīs using their respective substances, such as the *bodhicitta*. Then: "I bow to Śrī Heruka, who is adorned with a garland of severed heads and terrifying great fangs, and who is devouring great flesh."

With this, one should perform the praise. Then, in the sky, there is a vajra transformed from the syllable *hūṃ*, and below that, a lotus vessel transformed from the syllable *āḥ*; in the center of that are the items marked with the syllable *oṃ*.
The substances for the timely expulsion of the Māras who burn the forest of evil are produced through the union of the vajra and the lotus; by means of that, the blazing of fire occurs,
and through the heating and cooking of the substances, they are liquefied, becoming the sunbeams of the mirror-like wisdom of the forms of all the Tathāgatas.

Having drawn forth the nectar of the gnosis of all the Tathāgatas from the rays of the seed-syllable of that gnosis, and having unified it with those substances, one should empower it with the three syllables OṂ ĀḤ HŪṂ; then, having fashioned a tongue made of vajra arising from a white syllable HŪṂ, one should satisfy oneself with it. Then...

Having mentally inscribed the twelve-syllable mantra garland— *oṃ trailokyākṣepa hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*— which encircles the syllable *hūṃ* at the hub of the vajra within the solar disc of the heart, blazing like a row of lamps, one should mutter it silently as if reciting it sequentially. However, during the midday and evening junctions (*saṃdhyā*), [one should perform the practice].
Having instantly fashioned oneself in the form of Śrī Heruka,
one should then perform the purification of the eyes and other faculties, the meditation on the four wheels, worship, praise, the tasting of nectar, recitation (*japa*), and so forth.
Having performed this supreme sādhana of the Hero who seizes the three worlds...
By whatever merit has been earned thereby, may every person become a wielder of the thunderbolt.
The Sadhana of Two-Armed Heruka [Ḍha, A: Vajraheruka]
p.
477) Having instantly visualized Heruka together with his consort, one should contemplate an eight-petaled lotus of red color in his heart.
Upon its eastern, southern, western, and northern petals, one should [place] the syllables *a*, *ka*, *ca*, and *ṭa* respectively.
Likewise, in the petals of the southeast, southwest, northwest, and northeast, one places *ta*, *pa*, *ya*, and *sa*;

in the central *varaṭaka* (pericarp), one places *ma*; in the east, *svā*; in the center, *oṃ*; and in the west, *hā*. All of these are situated within solar discs (*sūryamaṇḍala*) and are red in color. From their pores, rays of light in the shape of hooks (*aṅkuśa*) emerge.
Having drawn forth the *sādhya*s and caused them to fall at the feet of the practitioner, they enter into these very [mantras]; such is the tradition (*āmnāya*).
Having bowed to the feet of the excellent Guru, the Teacher who bestows all the scriptures... [k]
The gift of scripture; [Ḍha: the giver of song].
I shall declare the Siddhāmnāya; I am the King of Mantras for the agitation of the city.
One who attends correctly to reality, is devoted to the guru, delights in one's own tutelary deity,
knows the procedure for wandering at night, and is free from doubt, shall accomplish the mantra.
In the eight-petaled lotus in the heart, there are two sets of four consonants joined with the vowels;
in the center of the pericarp is the syllable *praṇava* (oṃ), conjoined with the letter of worship, and red in color.
The minister, meditating on the citizens of the mountain city— who are the color of young grass and resemble the sun—
as being bowed down before him within himself, [performs] twenty-five [breaths].
One should recite it ten thousand times.
Having thus performed the preliminary service, one should bring the circle of the excellent Gaṇas to the state of submissiveness;
and having received their command, for the sake of swift accomplishment, one should seek the supreme Siddhi from them.
Having walked a few steps and having completed the auspicious *trika* of Māmakī,
one should place that [hand] on the sole of the foot and sleep until rising.
Having recited the *Pūrvaśiras* mantra ten thousand times, one should drink it; then, having risen,
even with a single effort, one shall go to the entire expanse of the sky.
In whatever place one should reside, one should again recite the *vivara-yoga* ten thousand times;
having thus performed the excellent yoga, one becomes equal to Hevajra and worthy of worship in the world.
The instruction on the agitation of the city:
by the words *a ka ca ṭa ta pa ya śa*, the *ālikāli* (vowels and consonants) are expressed according to the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).
By the recitation of the *ālikāli*, the mantrin shall agitate the three worlds.

By means of one hundred thousand recitations. But what of "only once"? Regarding this, the *ālikāli* is spoken of as follows: namely, *a ā i ī ṛ ṝ u ū ḷ ḹ a ā e ai ar ār o au al āl ha hā ya yā ra rā va vā la lā*. This is the recitation of the *ālis* according to the sequence of emanation (*sṛṣṭi-krama*), performed with the inhalation of the breath.
During the exhalation of breath, the *kāli* is: ka kā, kha khā, ga gā, gha ghā, ṅa ṅā; ca cā, cha chā, ja jā, jha jhā, ña ñā;
ṭa ṭā, ṭha ṭhā, ḍa ḍā, ḍha ḍhā, ṇa ṇā; pa pā, pha phā, ba bā, bha bhā, ma mā;
ta tā, tha thā, da dā, dha dhā, na nā; sa sā, hya [or dya], hyā; ṣa.

*Ṣā śa śā kṣa kṣā*. Having placed the syllable *oṃ* at the beginning, and having added *vauṣaṭ* at the end for agitation (*kṣobhaṇa*) and attraction (*ākṛṣṭi*), such is the mantra for the agitation of the city (*purakṣobhamantra*). Thus it is recorded in the *Kālacakra*. The Ritual for the Agitation of the City (*purakṣobhavidhi*).
Having prostrated to the Lord Hevajra, the sole synthesis of all phenomena,
I shall here set forth the ritual for external worship according to tradition.

Then, at dawn or at the appropriate time, the practitioner of the Śrī Hevajra yoga, having performed the sweeping and other preparations on the ground, should empower the site by placing his hand upon it while reciting: *oṃ rakṣa rakṣa hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*.
There, with a pill made of the five nectars, fragrant substances, and so forth, he should...
Having first cultivated conviction (*adhimokṣa*) regarding each respective stage,

and having smeared the mandala of the *pīṭha*, *upapīṭha*, *kṣetra*, *upakṣetra*, *chanda*, *upacchanda*, *melāpaka*, *upamelāpaka*, *pīla*, and *upapīla*, one consecrates it with the mantra: *oṃ vajrarekhe hūṃ*.
Having projected there the Blessed One together with his maṇḍala— in the condensed form of all the heroes and heroines— drawn by the rays from the vajra at one's heart,

and having worshipped him with the eight Mothers preceded by the offering of water for honor (*arghya*) and water for the feet (*pādya*), one should offer to him flowers and other items consecrated by that [mantra] born from the syllable *hūṃ*. Therein...

[One should worship] the Blessed One with the three-syllable heart-mantra and sub-heart-mantra, and the Blessed Lady with her own two mantras: Oṃ gaurī hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā | Oṃ caurī hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā | Oṃ vetālī hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā | Oṃ ghasmarī hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā | Oṃ pukkaśī hūṃ...

*hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā | oṃ śabarī hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā | oṃ caṇḍālī hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā | oṃ ḍombī hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā |* With these mantras, one should worship Gaurī and the others in their respective places; then, having performed all the outer and other offerings, one should offer flowers with the mantras for the offering of flowers that exclude the three syllables (*oṃ āḥ hūṃ*).
Oṃ aṣṭānanāya hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā | Oṃ piṅgalordhvakeśavatsale hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā | Oṃ caturviṃśatinetrāya hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ || (p. 480)
phaṭ svāhā | oṃ to the sixteen-armed one, hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā | oṃ to the one whose body is like a black cloud,
hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā | oṃ to the wearer of a garland of skulls, hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā | oṃ to the one with a bloated and cruel mind, hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā | oṃ...

"Arddhadaṃṣṭriṇe hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā. Having praised him with these mantras and having performed other acts such as praise and aspiration as appropriate, one should stabilize [the practice] with the hundred-syllable mantra. The mantra is: *oṃ vajrasattva samayamanupālaya vajrasattvatvenopatiṣṭha*.
"Be firm for me; be well-nourished for me; be easily satisfied for me; be devoted to me; grant me all accomplishments;
and in all activities, make my mind auspicious! HŪṂ HAHAHAHA HOḤ!
O Blessed One, Vajra of all Tathāgatas, do not abandon me! Become vajra-like, O Great Samaya-being! ĀḤ! Then—
The welfare of all sentient beings has been accomplished for you, and success has been granted according to your needs.
Go now to the realm of the Buddhas, O friends, so that you may return again.

Having thus dismissed the wheel and internalized it within oneself, one should perform the removal of the lines and so forth. The worship of Nairātmyā is also performed in the same manner: having smeared the mandala and projected the mandala-wheel, one should offer to the Mistress with the three-syllable mantra of one's own heart and the garland-mantra, and to the others with their respective seed-mantras interspersed with *praṇava* and *svāhā*.
Having offered flowers and other articles in their proper places, one should perform the praise with the flower-offering mantras devoid of the three syllables. The remainder is as before.
Whatever merit has been acquired by me through this summary for the sake of remembering the procedure for external worship—
By that merit, may this world become a supreme vessel for the worship of the virtuous.
The Compendium of Rituals for Worship is completed.
Having paid homage to Vajraḍāka, the Jina whose nature is Mahāmāyā,
the sequence of his sādhana is here indicated in accordance with the oral tradition.
Faithful, through the application of loving-kindness and compassion, having set his mind upon perfect enlightenment,
endowed with generosity, ethical discipline, and so forth, and possessing an even disposition toward the eight worldly dharmas.
One who knows the accomplishments (*siddhi*) of mantra, tantra, and so forth, and is capable of the practice of yoga,
should sit comfortably in a certain place, having placed the syllable *HŪṂ* upon the sun within his heart.
Having worshipped with offerings arising from that radiance before one's intellect,
and having performed the offering of water for the feet (*arghya*) and other rites, one should then meditate upon emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
One should recite mentally: "Oṃ, I am of the nature of the vajra of the knowledge of emptiness.
Then, one should meditate upon five white drops, which cause emanation and reabsorption, situated within a solar disc upon a red four-petalled lotus in the sky.
In the four directions, they are born from the moon-drops (bindu), dancing and eager for union,
their very nature being the great love, compassion, and so forth practiced previously.
One should contemplate that even the four ḍākinīs urge [him], saying:
"Hale!
O friend, the lotus has blossomed; it has been awakened by the vajra."
Alala-lalaho! One is raised by means of great bliss through dancing.
The lotus has blossomed with great joy through the rays of the sun; friend, the lotus has opened, awakened by the thunderbolt.
Alalalalaho! One has ascended through great bliss by means of dance;
the lotus has blossomed by the rays of the sun through great bliss.
Then, there arises the intention to uplift sentient beings from the sufferings of cyclic existence.
Having perceived the reality of the world as it truly is, like an illusion, he—
Arising from the central bindu, blue in color and originating from the seed-syllable HŪṂ, he consists of compassion,
is beautiful with supreme bliss, and is the nature of the five gnoses and the three bodies.
He has four faces and four arms, and his body is smeared with ashes;
his primary face is dark blue like the body, while the face on the right is yellow.
Behind him is one with a white and red luster, and to the left is one brilliant like emerald;
he has three eyes and is adorned with the five mudrās, such as the human skin and so forth.
With tawny hair standing erect, unshakeable, and fierce with a crown of skulls,
he holds a skull-cup in his right hand and a khaṭvāṅga staff and a bow in his left.
The welfare of the world was accomplished by Buddhas of variegated splendor, flashing forth from ten million rays of light.
One should meditate upon Heruka dancing, embraced by his own consort Buddha-Ḍākinī during the festival of passion, his face being gazed upon by the four goddesses.
The symbols and so forth of the ḍākinīs in the four directions are described:
there, on the eastern petal is Vajraḍākinī, blue in color,
with four faces that are blue, yellow, white, red, and green.
She holds the earth, a mirror, wisdom, and so forth, as well as a pure vajra and a skull-cup in her right hands; in her left hands, she carries a bell and a khaṭvāṅga staff.
To the south is the glorious Ratnaḍākinī, who embodies the element of the water of the knowledge of equality; she holds a jewel-splendor and a trident in her hands.
On the left, Śrīvajrasattva-Ḍākinī has her neck pressed down;
she has four faces of yellow, blue, white, red, and greenish-yellow luster.
On the western petal, however, is Padmaḍākinī, white and reddish;
she possesses the nature of energy (*tejas*) and discernment (*pratyavekṣā*), and is in the bloom of youth.
Her faces resemble white, reddish, molten gold, blue, and green;
she holds a universal lotus and an arrow in her right hands, and a skull-cup and a bow in the others.
In the north, however, Viśvaḍākinī has green, yellow, white, red, and white faces; she is purified by the performance of the rites and by the wind and other elements.
In the right hands they hold a khaṭvāṅga and a ḍamaruka, and in the left, a noose and a skull-cup;
all the goddesses have three eyes, four faces, and four arms.
Attached to the sentiments of love and the rest, radiant with their defining characteristics and manifestations,
they dance while seated upon fierce postures, adorned with Lord-like splendor through their finger-rings and other ornaments.
One should perform the placement of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅgavinyāsa*), the invocation (*āvāhana*) and so forth of the Lord,
the consecration (*abhiṣeka*) by the Victors (*jināḥ*), the worship (*pūjā*), and the offering of praise, devotion, and so on.
One should place the eyes, ears, and nose on the forehead and throat, and the heart;
thus, one should utter "Oṃ Āḥ Kha Ci Ra," with the syllable "Hūṃ" following the letter "Ra."
Having summoned the wisdom maṇḍala through the union of the vajra-clapping gestures,
and having entered after first offering the guest-water (argha) and other honors, one should personally effect their unification.
Together with the wheel of commitments (*samayacakra*), for the sake of attaining the distinguished fruit,
through the entry of the vital essence (*rasa*), it is like the transformation of copper and other metals into silver.
Having exhorted the Protectors situated in the directions by means of the heart-flame residing in his own heart,
[he causes] the oceans of nectar-filled jars to arise from the vidyās produced by their radiance.
From the consecration by the Lord, from his crown, and from Akṣobhya, there arise again the divine consorts:
Śāśvata, Ratneśa, Amitābha, and Amoghasiddhi.
With goddesses released from meditative absorption, their hands busily engaged in excellent worship,
one should worship oneself as Heruka joined with the Yoginīs and offer praise.
I bow to Śrī Heruka, who is adorned with a garland of skulls and is exceedingly terrifying with his prominent fangs, and who is devouring great flesh.

Thus is the praise. Having meditated upon the seed-syllables OṂ, HŪṂ, SVĀ, Ā, and HĀ, respectively, in his head, heart, navel, secret place, and the pair of thighs, [one should contemplate her] as consisting of the five families.
Having visualized the self-arisen Śrī Buddhadaṅkī, who is red, eager for passion, with a secret lotus marked by the syllable Hrīḥ that is red, and a pericarp marked by Bhrūṃ that is yellow;
Being urged by song at the command of the four goddesses,
[he is addressed] with "Oṃ jātamaṇi hūṃ" and with "vajra-vicitra-karaṇa," and so forth.
Thinking with a mind of passion, "I shall delight the Jinas," one should begin;
having summoned [them] with the sounds of *sphāṭ* from the expanding vajra and lotus, they are made to enter through the mouth.

The host of Jinas, having swiftly emerged from the vajra due to the penetration of bliss, reaches the true mind within the lotus; then, by means of the tongue, one should [consume it] according to the ritual rule.
Within the four-petaled red lotus of the heart, which has the nature of the four elements,
it is joined with and well-encircled by the moon situated upon a bindu resting on the sun.

Having emitted the sound through the seven-and-a-half lines— each consisting of a complete series of syllables and resembling a lotus fiber— he should cause it to enter the aperture of the moon above; thus there shall be the following and the preceding.
Uttering the three-syllable mantra adorned with the illusion of *māyā* while the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) throb, one should likewise perform the entry and exit of the *nāda*.

When the wind exits upward, the sound of three syllables issues forth; when it enters, [the sound] "pravi" issues forth; when it remains, it stays within the subtle black drop (*asitabindu*) while the wind abides. Thus, with vowels and consonants joined together, the seven-and-a-half-lined [mantra] consists of entry, stay, and exit. Extremely slowly, the *parā* [speech] has arrived elsewhere.
One should contemplate with the mind. *Oṃ āḥ hūṃ* is the mantra to be recited, consisting of three syllables.
Desiring to rise, one should perform acts of worship and the like; and having seen the world suffering, one should dedicate the merit toward the vision of the reality of the world as it is.
By whatever merit has been accumulated through the meditation on Vajraḍāka,
may I become Vajraḍāka for the sake of attaining the state of the Lord of the World.
Having risen, one should perform activities such as collecting alms and explaining what has been heard,
assuming the form of Heruka for oneself and others, like a master of illusion.
The food, consecrated by the syllable *hūṃ*, resides within a skull-cup born from the syllable *āḥ*;
it is ignited and purified by the wheel of downward-moving wind and fire.
Visualizing the syllable Oṃ above as inconceivable, consecrated with mantras, and transformed into nectar,
one should satisfy [the deities] by drawing it forth through the tube of the tongue, which is a portion of the vajra.
Oṃ āḥ hūṃ, "I consume the secret food"—this is the mantra for tasting the nectar (*amṛta*). Prior to the time of bathing, one should perform the rite of consecration (*abhiṣeka*);
one should meditate in this manner briefly during all four junctions of the day (*saṃdhyā*).
Having performed the sādhana of Vajraḍāka, I have obtained merit;
by that, may the noble ones be adorned, and may I too be graced with such ornamentation.
The *Herukasādhanopāyikā* according to the *Mahāmāyātantra* is completed.
Śrīherukamahāvajra, kaṭṭa kaṭṭa, cause to enter cause to enter, bind bind, satisfy satisfy, the heart of all vajra-ḍākinīs,
hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ! Oṃ, all Buddha-ḍākinīs, accept this bali-offering!

Oṃ phaṭ | Oṃ vajraḍākinī, accept this bali, hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ ratnaḍākinī, accept this bali, hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ padmaḍākinī, accept this bali, hrīḥ phaṭ | Oṃ viśvaḍākinī, accept this bali, hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ sarvaḍākinī, accept this bali, hūṃ.
Hrīḥ hūṃ haiḥ | Oṃ, all you yoginīs, accept this bali offering, hūṃ hahaha hrīḥ!
Thus concludes the ritual procedure for the bali offering according to the Mahāmāyā Tantra.
Homage to Vajraḍāka!
The detailed exposition is generally difficult for the comprehension of children and women.
Having condensed even that which is already condensed, one should extract that seven-syllable mantra.
Between that worship and the mantra for the realization of emptiness,
one should accomplish Vajraḍāka as the intermediate limb within the limbs.
One should visualize upon the mandala of the four elements— yaṃ, raṃ, vaṃ, and laṃ— the Mount Meru arising from the syllable *suṃ*, possessing eight peaks made of the seven precious gems.
Oṃ, O Earth, become vajra; vajra-binding, hūṃ! Oṃ, vajra-fence, hūṃ vaṃ hūṃ!
Oṃ, vajra-canopy, hūṃ paṃ hūṃ! Oṃ, vajra-net of arrows, trāṃ śaṃ trāṃ! Oṃ, vajra-flame, fire, and sun, hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ!##-
Having established the sixfold foundation beginning with the vajra-ground,
one should draw a six-spoked wheel situated upon a universal lotus and encircled by a garland of universal vajras.
One should meditate right here on the Great Bliss Vajraḍāka, arising from *hūṃ*,
with six arms, three faces, and three eyes, endowed with all the auspicious marks.
The Lord, who arises from Āli and Kāli and is endowed with eighty consonants,
is absorbed in union with the vajra and bell, and wears fresh human skin.
In his left hands he holds a skull-cup, a khaṭvāṅga staff, and a trident; in his right hand he holds a garland of skulls; he wears a crown and possesses matted locks adorned with a double vajra.
He has the crescent moon as his crest-ornament, his body is adorned with the six mudrās,
his faces are blue, yellow, and green, and he is clothed in a tiger-skin garment.
[He is] with Bhairava and Kālarātri standing in the *ālīḍha* posture upon the sun; [k, g: *pratyālī*; k, g:
*sūryabhai*].
Just as it is for the Lord, so too are the arms and other features of Vajravārāhī.
The Goddess, having encircled [the disciple's] knees and being overwhelmed with supreme bliss, should perform the rites of attracting knowledge and so forth with these syllables: JAḤ HŪM VAṂ HOḤ.
The six yoginīs are arranged in the six spokes by turning counter-clockwise:
the first goddess is Herukī, and the second is Vajrabhairavī.
The third is Ghoracaṇḍī, the fourth is Vajrabhāskarī,
the fifth is Vajraraudrī, and the sixth should be Vajraḍākinī.
The goddesses are blue, yellow, red, green, smoky-colored, and white;
they have disheveled hair, are extremely fierce, possess three eyes, and are naked.
Holding a drum and a bell in her two hands other than the one [already mentioned],
and wearing human skins, they stand upon the sun over a corpse.
Wearing crowns of garlands of skulls and established in the ālīḍha posture,
all these auspicious goddesses arise from the six syllables in their respective order.
They are empowered by these five elements: *loṃ*, *māṃ*, *pāṃ*, *tāṃ*, and *khaṃ*;
and the aggregates, such as form and the rest, are likewise empowered by the syllables *oṃ*, *aṃ*, *hrīṃ*, *hūṃ*, *hoḥ*, and *hrīḥ*.

One should purify the sense bases with the syllables *bhrūṃ*, *hūṃ*, *khaṃ*, *āḥ*, *ho*, and *haṃ*. One should apply [the mantras]: *oṃ haḥ namaḥ*, *hrīḥ svāhā*, *hūṃ vauṣaṭ*, *hūṃ hūṃ hoḥ phaṭ phaṭ* to the chest, head, shoulders, eyes, and so forth. *Oṃ vaṃ hāṃ yāṃ hrīṃ moṃ jaṃ hrīṃ*.
HŪM HŪM PHAṬ PHAṬ— one should place [the mantra] at the navel, heart, mouth, head, crest-lock, and elsewhere;
one should bestow the syllables OṂ ĀḤ HŪM upon the moons of body, speech, and mind.
One should consecrate [the deity] with skull-cups filled with the liquid of the five nectars, held in the hands of the hosts of goddesses residing within the wheels of the six universal monarchs.
Having performed worship, praise, and the tasting of the nectar,
the practitioner of mantra should cultivate meditative absorption and recite the seven-syllable mantra with a mind free from doubt.
Oṃ hrīḥ ha ha hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ!
When one becomes weary from meditation and recitation, then one should recollect purity.
Śrī Heruka is the factor of enlightenment that is mindfulness (smṛti-saṃbodhyaṅga).
Herukī is the factor of enlightenment of equanimity; Vajrabhairavī is the factor of enlightenment of investigation of phenomena; Ghoracaṇḍī is the factor of enlightenment of vigor;
Vajrabhāskarī is the factor of enlightenment of joy; and Vajraraudrī is the factor of enlightenment of pliancy and concentration.

The factor of awakening of equanimity is Vajraḍākinī; this is the cultivation of the seven factors of awakening. The necklace, the bracelet, the jewel earring, the ashes, and the thread—these six are indeed the perfections (pāramitās) joined in the form of mudrās.
The *Saptākṣarasādhana* extracted by Durjayacandra is completed.
Homage to Saṃvara!
He is blue, with three faces and six arms, embracing his consort who is of the same color as himself.
Having bowed to Hūṃ-jaṃ, the lord of the six goddesses, I shall write this sādhana.

The yogi, having risen at dawn and placed the *samayagulikā* in his mouth, should sit upon a *viśvavajra* in a delightful place such as a mountain cave or a valley, and visualize a blue syllable *HŪṂ* situated upon a sun disk in his heart. From that *HŪṂ*,
he should emanate five-colored rays of light that pervade the expanse of space and encompass the triple world (*traidhātuka*), and with those...
Having drawn forth, by means of light rays, the Blessed One residing in the Akaniṣṭha realm— possessing the colors, arms, and weapons to be described hereafter—
as well as all the gurus, Buddhas, and Bodhisattvas of the Yoginīs, who appear like sesame seeds, and having established them in the space before one,
one should again dissolve those light rays back into one's own seed-syllable. Then, emanating from that seed-syllable...

One should worship and pay homage to the Blessed One, as well as the yoginīs, gurus, buddhas, and bodhisattvas, with the specific offerings of the outer, secret, and essential realities (*tattva*), according to the prescribed ritual. Then, in their presence, one should perform the confession of misdeeds,

the vow of non-repetition, the rejoicing in merit, the going for refuge in the three jewels, the generation of the mind of awakening (*bodhicitta*), the offering of one's own person, and the dedication of merit.

One should meditate on the sounds. Then, bringing to mind the meaning of the mantra which encapsulates the essence of the reality of all things—reciting "Oṃ, all phenomena have the nature of the vajra of the wisdom of emptiness; Oṃ, I have the nature of the vajra of the wisdom of emptiness"—one should contemplate.
One should remain for a moment in the luminous samādhi that is unborn and unceasing, in a form that is non-abiding. Then,

through the power of the impetus of previous vows, arising from the luminosity and perceiving the universe as being like a dream or an illusion, one should emerge into the world and contemplate one's own nature as Śrī Heruka, [visualizing] yaṃ raṃ laṃ vaṃ.

One should visualize, one above the other, the mandalas of the four great elements— blue, red, white, and yellow— which have transformed into the shapes of a bow, a triangle, a circle, and a square. Above those, [one should visualize] Mount Sumeru, arising from the syllable *suṃ*.
A square [mandala] made of the seven precious gems, adorned with eight peaks; above that: *oṃ medinī vajrībhava vajrabandha hūṃ*;
*oṃ vajrapākāra hūṃ vaṃ hūṃ*; *oṃ vajrapañjara hūṃ paṃ hūṃ*; *oṃ vajravitāna hūṃ khaṃ hūṃ*; *oṃ vajraśarajāla trāṃ śaṃ trāṃ*; *oṃ vajrajvālānalārka*.

With these mantras—*hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ*—one should fashion the sixfold foundation of vajras and so forth; within that, one should visualize a peaked pavilion (*kūṭāgāra*) beginning with a square base, and within that, one should meditate on a six-spoked wheel resting upon a universal lotus (*viśvapadma*), encircled by rows of vajras, lotuses, and wheels. Within that...
One should meditate on the syllable *hūṃ*, born from *raṃ*, situated upon the pericarp of a lotus; this is the solar disk produced from the transformation of the vowels and consonants.

Within the union of the moon and sun disks, one should visualize the blue syllable *hūṃ* in the form of Vajrasattva. Having transformed all of this, one should meditate on the Blessed Lord Vajraḍāka, born from *hūṃ*, in the state of great bliss embraced by Vārāhī.

According to the instruction, [one should visualize] the Lord, who consists of the five wisdoms such as the mirror-like wisdom and so forth, who has six arms, three faces—the central, right, and left being blue, yellow, and green respectively—and three eyes;
who is endowed with the thirty-two major marks and eighty minor signs; and who [embraces his consort] with two arms in the posture of embrace.
Holding a vajra and bell with his other two upper arms, wearing a human skin,
his left hand grasping a khaṭvāṅga staff and a skull-cup, and his right hand holding a trident;
blazing with ornaments of a garland of skulls, adorned with the six mudrās, and his waist clothed in a tiger-skin garment.

The Lord’s matted locks are adorned with a universal vajra and a crescent moon; he stands in the *ālīḍha* posture, treading upon the heads of Bhairava and Kālarātri situated in the center of a sun disc atop a universal lotus.
Furthermore, regarding the color, arms, and other attributes of Vajravārāhī, however, she is without the human skin, which is instead held in her two hands.
The Goddess, bearing a bow and arrows, having encircled both knees of the Blessed One... (p. 492) [text unclear]
p. 493) Not clear p. 494)
One should worship [it]. There is a wind-maṇḍala transformed from the syllable *yaṃ*; above that, a fire-maṇḍala transformed from the syllable *raṃ*;
above that, a lotus vessel born from the red syllable *āḥ*. In its center are the syllables *vuṃ*, *āṃ*, *jiṃ*, *khaṃ*, and *hūṃ*;
through their transformation, there is the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) and the five lamps (*pañcapradīpa*), marked with their respective seed-syllables. Its lid is the syllable *oṃ*.
Above that is a moon born from the syllable *A*; therein is a vajra produced from the syllable *HŪṂ*, marked with its seed-syllable. By means of the wind, the fire blazes;

through that heating, all the Tathāgatas become purified. The *OṂ*, the moon, and the vajra melt and fall into that skull-cup (*karoṭaka*). Then, having uttered *OṂ ĀḤ HŪṂ*, one draws in the nectar of all the deities right there.

One should cause it to enter. Having empowered it with this very [mantra], one should taste that nectar with the vajra-tube—a white vajra the size of a barley grain produced on the tip of the tongue—and offer it from mouth to mouth to the Blessed Lady and to the host of deities. Then, one becomes weary from meditation.
Bearing the *sambara* hand-gesture (*kāramudrā*), one should recite the mantra. There, the mantra is: *oṃ hrīḥ ha ha hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ*.
When weary from recitation, one should bring to mind purity. Śrī Heruka is the factor of awakening of mindfulness (*smṛtisambodhyaṅga*);
Śrī Herukī is the factor of awakening of the investigation of phenomena (*dharmapravicayasambodhyaṅga*); Vajrabhairavī is the factor of awakening of vigor (*vīryasambodhyaṅga*).
The factor of awakening of joy is Ghoracaṇḍī; the factor of awakening of pliancy is Vajrabhāskarī;
the factor of awakening of concentration is Vajra-raudrī; and the factor of awakening of equanimity is Vajraḍākinī.
[These correspond to] the necklace, the bracelet, the jewel earring, the ashes, and the sacred thread.

Through the purification of the six perfections, one should meditate upon the Blessed One at the three junctions of the day, preceded by the offering of a bali-oblation and the factors of enlightenment. Regarding that bali: the yogi, standing in the *ālīḍha* posture, should take his place in a high location.
Facing south, naked, with hair disheveled at midnight,
with his feet treading [upon the ground] and his gaze directed upward, he should [utter] the sound of the syllable *phaṭ* from his head.

Having formed the *vajrāñjali* with the fingers spread upward, and then having performed the *jvālāmudrā*, one should attract the *vīrayoginī* by circling [the hands] repeatedly, reciting: *oṃ āḥ vajra-aralli hoḥ jaḥ hūṃ vaṃ hoḥ vajraḍākinyas samayas tvaṃ dṛśya hoḥ*. Thus three times.
Having recited four or five times, one should address them: "Then, Oṃ kha kha khāhi khāhi!
All you yakṣas, rākṣasas, bhūtas, pretas, piśācas, unmādas, apasmāras, ḍākinīs, and so forth, accept this bali-offering;
grant me all accomplishments (siddhi); eat as much as you wish, according to your desire."

"Drink! Smell! Do not bypass me for the sake of the perfection of a hundredfold bliss in every way; be my companions! HŪM HŪM HŪM PHAṬ SVĀHĀ. With this, one should offer the *bali* offering. One should circulate each respective *bali* according to the oral instruction.

Having assumed the form of Śrī Cakrasaṃvara, the yogi who has restrained the senses, having resolved that the world is like an illusion, should dwell at ease. Having rendered non-duality into non-duality by means of non-duality, this is the sādhana of the seven syllables.
By this pure, attained, and auspicious [merit], may the world become Cakrasaṃvara.
The Sādhana of the Seven Syllables is completed.
This work is by the venerable scholar-ascetic, the illustrious Advayavajra.
Homage to Śrī Cakrasaṃvara!
Having prostrated at the lotus feet of the true guru, [this work] is compiled according to the oral tradition.
By relying upon the Saṃvara Tantra, I have clearly explained the procedure for external worship.
In this regard, a yogin desiring to worship the Śrī Cakrasaṃvara maṇḍala,
having risen at dawn or at an appropriate time, should remain with the yoga of the deity unobscured and likewise possess a very firm identification (*ahaṅkāra*) with that deity; however,
one whose yoga of the deity has been forgotten should possess identification with the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) and so forth.
Having first uttered the mantra of natural purity (*svabhāvaśuddha*), one should resolve upon emptiness (*śūnyatā*). Then,

through the process of emanation and reabsorption accompanied by the exiting and entering [of breath], one should visualize a moon disk transformed from the vowels and consonants, and within that, the syllable *HŪṂ*, the color of mercury.
Through the transformation of that moon-seed (the syllable *caṃ*), preceded by the radiation of light and so forth,

one who possesses the yoga of Śrī Saṃvara should place his hand— joined with a pill of the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) and perfumes in a clean place, or, in their absence, with a pledge-pill (*samayapiṇḍī*) mixed with any other substance— while reciting *śumbhaniśumbha*.

Having recited these and other such words, one should smear a square maṇḍala and consecrate it with "Oṃ vajrarekhe hūṃ. Then, placing a hand in its center, one should recite the twenty-four syllables beginning with "pūjā," which are the nature of the ten stages, including the *pīṭhas* and *upapīṭhas*.

One should recite [the mantra] preceded by the resolve (*adhimokṣa*) for each respective stage. Then, in that mandala, one should instantly visualize a *viśvacakra* moon upon Mount Sumeru situated on the four great elements, and place the syllable *HŪṂ*—which has emerged from one's own heart—thereon.
Having summoned the deities of the three wheels located in the ten directions by means of the light rays from that seed-syllable, they enter into that *HŪṂ* according to the oral instruction.

One should visualize that [transformation] as the Blessed One together with his retinue, perfected in all aspects. Then, having offered worship with the goddesses of the lute and others who have emerged from the seed-syllable in the heart, the seven jewels and so forth also emerge.
Having presented it according to the ritual procedure, one should offer a flower in the center of the maṇḍala with the three-syllable mantra using a purified hand. Again, in that very place,
one should offer to the Blessed Lord and the Blessed Lady with their heart and near-heart mantras, and then to the Ḍākinīs and the others.

With the mantras of these very deities, ending with Yamamathanī, one should offer flowers upon the mandala in their respective places— counter-clockwise in the cardinal directions and clockwise in the intermediate directions. Then, for those [deities] placed upon the hands, one should offer flowers at their respective locations with their respective mantras, beginning with *oṃ haḥ*.

Then, having cast the flower held in the palm of his left hand into the maṇḍala while reciting the eight-word mantra, and having performed the añjali-gesture at his head, he should cause the visualization, the mantra, and the wheel to enter into himself. Then, by means of the eight words beginning with the heart... [g: ...]

Having praised with mantras ending in *padānta*, preceded by hymns and accompanied by hymns recited according to the ritual procedure, and having performed confession of sins (*pāpadeśanā*) and so forth, as well as meditation, mantra-recitation (*japa*), and the making of vows (*praṇidhāna*) according to one's capacity, and having uttered the hundred-syllable mantra, [one should reflect that] all phenomena are purified through yoga— *oṃ upāya*.
Having gratified [the deity] with the *kamalāvarta* mudrā accompanied by the mantra "I am purified by yoga," and while withdrawing the mudrā preceded by the act of embracing,
one should dismiss [the deity] while reciting "Oṃ vajra muḥ" while touching the ground with the ring finger;
then, having caused that maṇḍala-circle to enter into oneself, one should perform the sprinkling of the lines of the maṇḍala and other rites.
By whatever merit I have acquired through the collection of the ritual for external worship,
may the entire world become devoted to the worship of the Buddha.
The Compendium of the Ritual for Outer Worship is completed.
The work of Śāśvatavajra.
Homage to Śrī Cakrasaṃvara!
Having prostrated to Vajravārāhī, the leader of the circle of yoginīs,
I shall now set forth the ritual for hand-worship, as it is handed down in the traditional scriptures.
There, in the circle of the assembly (*gaṇamaṇḍala*) and so forth,
one who possesses the yoga of Śrī Cakrasaṃvara [should visualize] the elements of earth, water, fire, air, and space located in his own left hand as [the goddesses] Pātanī,
Māraṇī, and Ākarṣaṇī.
Upon the tips of the thumbs, index fingers, middle fingers, ring fingers, and little fingers of the right hand,

one should visualize, in sequence, the natures of Vajrasattva, Vairocana, Amitābha, Akṣobhya, Ratnasambhava, and Amoghasiddhi, in white, yellow, red, black, and green colors respectively: OṂ HAḤ NAMO HI.

One should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) of the syllables *hrīḥ svāhā hūṃ vauṣaṭ he hūṃ hūṃ hoḥ phaṭ haṃ*. Having visualized a five-petaled red lotus instantly manifested in the palm of the hand, one should place [the syllables] in order, moving counter-clockwise on its eastern petals: *Yāminī*, *Mohanī*, *Saṃcālinī*, *Santrāsinī*, and *Ākarṣiṇī*.

One should visualize the seed-syllables *hreṃ*, *hrīṃ*, *hūṃ*, *hūṃ*, *phaṭ* [k: omits], *phaṭ*. And upon the pericarp, one should clearly visualize the reflection of the seed-syllable *oṃ vaṃ*, which is red in color and has the nature of Vajravārāhī, as well as the three wheels [or two, according to k and g] on the back of the hand below. Then, those [syllables] residing in that hand...
Having smeared the seed-syllables with the liquid substance,
one should resolve that the palm of the hand has the nature of the three wheels presided over by all the heroes and yoginīs; then,
that liquid and other substances—
One should offer [the oblation] with either the three-syllable mantra or the eight-word mantra. Then, having performed the worship,
one should recite the hundred-syllable mantra for the purpose of fulfilling any deficiencies or excesses in the ritual procedure, and for the purpose of consecrating the wheel and other elements.

Having requested [the deity] and having placed that substance upon another substance or elsewhere, one should— while reciting the syllables *HŪṂ ĀḤ OṂ*— anoint the heart, tongue, and head with the substance held in the hand, specifically grasped by the ring finger of the left hand; then, one should visualize that the host of deities has entered into oneself.

Having thus written this hand-offering (hastapūjā) related to the Saṃvara Tantra by Śāśvatavajra, according to the oral tradition of the excellent gurus, for the sake of the recollection even of those of dull intellect.
Then, with the ring finger of the left hand purified by the previously mentioned procedure,

while uttering the twenty-four syllables beginning with the *pīṭhas* and *upapīṭhas*, one should draw two triangular wheels using the *madana* (intoxicant) purified according to the rite, and in their center—

A circular maṇḍala. Therein, having visualized the common receptacle-maṇḍala— either drawn by the rays of light emanating from the seed-syllable of one’s own heart or otherwise— one offers to it food, drink, and so forth, prepared in the form of the five nectars and the like, using either the three-syllable mantra or the eight-word mantra, [the offerings] being placed within a lotus vessel.

Having taken the nectar-like *madana* with the ring and index fingers, one should satisfy the Blessed Lord and the Blessed Goddess with their respective heart and sub-heart mantras, and likewise satisfy [the goddesses] from Ḍākinī up to Yamamathanī with their own individual mantras. Then, having performed the worship:

Having recited the hundred-syllable mantra to fulfill any deficiencies or excesses in the ritual procedure, and having requested the empowerment of the *gaṇacakra*, one should recite: "Oṃ, all phenomena are pure through yoga; I am pure through yoga.
Having satisfied [the deities] with the *kamalāvarta* mudrā, one should perform the withdrawal of the heart-mudrā preceded by the gesture of embracing.
Touching the ground with the ring finger, one should dismiss that wheel with "Oṃ vajra muḥ" and cause it to enter into oneself. Then, that intoxication which has gone into the earth— (p.
Having grasped it with the left ring finger, while anointing the heart, tongue, and head preceded by the utterance of the syllables *HŪṂ ĀḤ OṂ*,
one should visualize that the circle of deities residing in that hand has likewise entered into oneself.
This hand-offering, which brings benefit to yogins, is declared as the worship of the Lord of Cakrasaṃvara, who dwells within the threefold maṇḍala.
By the merit I have obtained through performing this auspicious rite of hand-worship (*hastapūjā*),
may all people become devoted to the practice of hand-worship.
The ritual procedure for the worship of the hands is complete.
The work of Śāśvatavajra.
Homage to the illustrious Buddhakapāla!

First of all, the mantra-practitioner, having gone to a location of the earth that is pleasing to the mind, should prepare it by smearing it with the nectar of twelve-fold *argha*. Having first meditated upon his own self-consecration (*svādhiṣṭhāna*), he should emanate the primary elements and their derivatives from his own heart.
Having meditated upon the syllable *hūṃ* as fire, one should visualize the solar disc. With the syllable *oṃ*, one visualizes the lunar disc;

when these two merge into one, the supreme solar disc is perceived. Above that, the wise practitioner should contemplate the syllable *hūṃ* and emanate clouds of light rays. By means of those light rays, he should summon the gurus, Buddhas, and Bodhisattvas.

Having placed [the deity] in front, one should worship him; afterwards, one should ask for forgiveness. Having recited the mantra beginning with *svabhāvaśuddhā*, one should visualize a waveless eight-petaled lotus surmounted by the sun. One should place two syllables upon the sun. Having contemplated oneself as Heruka embraced by Prajñā through the yoga of instantaneous appearance (*jhaṭityākāra*) via the syllable *HŪṂ*.

Thus he is seen together with twenty-five yoginīs. Heruka, the Lord, should unite with all the yoginīs. Having seen them all melted together and established within the solar mandala, [he beholds] the Goddess.
Addressing the four yoginīs regarding the internal practice:
"How is the world, which has fallen into despair regarding its duty (*kṛtya*)— even though it is constant (*nitya*)— invited?"
Likewise, if you do not remember the news, everyone rises up in despair.
O dear one, even after accomplishing your own purpose, do not make the mind twofold;
all living beings have fallen into the fear of worldly existence—arise, O friend yoginī!
If you remember your former state, do not fall into despondency over this task;
for when you have set, all living beings will become destitute—therefore, exert yourself!
"Do not harbor false pride, my dear; arise, O you whose nature is emptiness!
Delight in the assembly of yoginīs, or else let this worldly existence fall away.
[Having invited the world, which is eternally free from sorrow, who indeed would not be delighted?]
Likewise, if you do not speak, all the sorrowful ones will rise up.
Even having performed the task yourself, O dear one, do not act with such harshness; O mind, having fallen into the ocean of worldly existence, let all people rise up through the power of yoga.
Remember your former state; do not harbor grief for your current condition. When that [former state] has been attained, all people will be free from the fever of envy.
O Mica and Māna, do not even think [of staying]; rise up, for the nature of the world is such.
O Yoginī, find Kāma; otherwise, your very state will perish.
With such a song, the four yoginīs, together with the yoginī of the [respective] face, color, and insignia as before, urge him on.
Then:
"That great hero, the agent of the terrible dissolution, has arisen."

Blue in color and of great stature, adorned with bone ornaments, standing in the dance posture of half-lotus (*ardhaparyaṅka*), decorated with a garland of severed heads, bearing Akṣobhya upon his crown, he has one face and four arms.

In the left hand he holds a *khaṭvāṅga* and a skull-cup, and in the right a flaying knife and a hand-drum; embraced by his consort, the goddess Citrasenā—who is intoxicated, naked, with disheveled hair, free from all fear, and green—she kisses him again and again. Having thus meditated upon himself, one should emanate [the mandala].

The Yoginīs of great supernatural power reside in the cardinal and intermediate directions. In the first inner enclosure: in the east is the goddess Sumālinī, blue; in the north, Kapālinī, yellow; in the west, Bhīmā, dark green; and in the south, Durjayā, white. In the second enclosure: in the east is Śubhamekhalā; in the north, Rūpiṇī; and in the west...
Vidyā is in the south, Kauberī in the northeast, Kāminī in the northwest, Mahodadhi in the southwest,

Kāriṇī in the southeast, and Māriṇī in the third enclosure (tṛtīyapuṭa) in the east; Bhīmadarśanā is in the north, Ajayā in the west, Śubhā in the south, Ostārakī in the northeast, and Surakṣiṇī in the northwest.
Vikālarātrī is in the southwest, Mahāyaśā in the southeast, and Sundarī in the northeast. Due to the purity of body, speech, and mind, they possess the characteristics of three layers.

I shall now state the names of the four female gatekeepers: Sundarā at the eastern gate, Subhagā in the north, Priyadarśanā in the west, and Nairātmyā in the south. All these goddesses are blue in color and have two arms.

They have one face, are adorned with bone ornaments, have tawny hair standing upright, and are devoid of skull-garlands; they hold a skull-cup in the left hand and a flaying knife in the right, standing in the dance posture upon a half-lotus seat. Twenty-five sun-disc seats for these goddesses are to be visualized. One should, however, meditate upon the mandala-circle as follows:
It is square, with four gates, adorned with four archways,
embellished by eight pillars, and provided with a pedestal and a frieze.
p.
503) One should visualize eight cremation grounds on the outside. When weary, one should recite the mantra: *oṃ mahāvajro herukavajro dharatu dharatu*.
[He] adds: *ghuru ghuru mahājñānaspheṭane śīghraṃ sādhaya stambhaya kīlaya hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*.
The generation stage (*utpattikrama*) has been explained; the perfected stage (*utpanna*) is within the domain of the Guru.
The restraint of the primary elements and their derivatives has been prescribed for the yoginīs.
The non-dual gnosis of yoga is Heruka embraced by Prajñā;
for the sake of bringing the afflictions under control, the mudrās have been prescribed.
He is steadfast, disciplined, wise, and free from all that is unwholesome.
One who is self-controlled and devoted to the guru will achieve accomplishment in just six months through the yoga of Buddhakapāla; of this there is no doubt for the practitioner.
The Sadhana of the Glorious Blessed One Buddhakapāla.
Having made this vow: "May I become a Buddha in order to remove all suffering without remainder and bestow every happiness throughout the three worlds," may I attain the welfare of the triple world.
The other form, that of the departure, is to be further augmented.
Yoga should be known as threefold, and the basis (adhiṣṭhāna) is likewise conceived;
the yoga of the perfected mental image has been formulated by the Buddhas.
Alternatively, through the yoga of instantaneous union, one becomes Vajraḍāka oneself,
having meditated upon him without a seed-syllable, like a being produced by miraculous birth.
(p. 504) unclear (p.
plīṃ [k: ṣṇīṃ, g: ṣphīṃ]—this is the heart-mantra of the Lord Buddha, ptīṃ.
This is the heart-mantra of Mañjuśrī: *hrīḥ*.
This is the heart-mantra of Noble Avalokiteśvara: *dhīḥ*. This is the heart-mantra of Vajrabhīṣma.
Among these four heart-mantras, one should recite whichever heart-mantra one desires while performing the yoga of one's respective deity.

Having performed this, eloquence, proficiency in sacred learning, retention of what has been heard, unparalleled brilliance, victory in every debate, and the attainment of the five superknowledges (pañcābhijñā) are accomplished with little effort.
Within the moon-maṇḍala in the heart, the body of the entirety of speech resides in the midst of the heart-syllables.
For those who meditate upon any one of these syllables, the knowledge of the higher cognitions (abhijñā), such as the vision of distant objects, is accomplished.
This is the instruction for the accomplishment of the heart-mantra (hṛdayamantra).
According to the previously stated procedure—
within the sun born from the letter *ra* of the *khadhātu*, [one should visualize] the syllable *HŪṂ*, blazing and radiant,
as extremely fierce like the fire at the end of an aeon, black in color, and of great splendor.
From that was born the Great Fierce One known as Vajrahūṃkāra,
who lets out a great and terrible laugh and casts the triple world into turmoil.
With both hands forming the mudrā through the application of the bell and vajra,
he stands in the pratyālīḍha posture, treading upon Bhairava and Mīra.
Having placed the three syllables Oṃ Āḥ Hūṃ at the heart, throat, and head,
one should seal [them] with the Mind-Vajra according to the ritual of consecration.
The mantra: Oṃ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā. The Vajrahūṃkāra-sādhana.
According to the previously mentioned procedure, immediately after emptiness (*śūnyatā*), upon a white lotus and sun disc,
one should visualize Mahābala, born from the syllable *HŪṂ*, with one face, four arms, and a body entirely red, his hair bound upward by a tawny serpent, and with his two right arms—
He holds a white staff and a white chowrie in his two right hands, and with his two left hands he makes the gesture of salutation and the threatening gesture with a noose;
he is clothed in a tiger skin, adorned with snakes, stands in the pratyālīḍha posture, and has a face made terrifying by fangs.
Having meditated upon [the deity] who is garlanded with the radiance of the solar disc and crowned by Amitābha, one should recite the mantra: *oṃ mahābala svāhā*.
Thus ends the *Mahābala-sādhana*.
p. 508) According to the previously mentioned procedure, upon a sun disk atop a universal lotus, one should visualize the noble Hayagrīva, arisen from the gnosis of the syllable *haṃ* in red,
red in color, with three faces and eight arms, possessing three eyes on each face, and having a blue face on the right and a white face on the left.

Adorned with snake ornaments, his first face displays a graceful gait and a gaze of wrathful vision; it is smiling with a lolling tongue. His right face has its lips bitten by fangs, and his left face is clothed in a tiger skin.
One should meditate on him with four right hands raised, holding a vajra, a staff, the karaṇa-mudrā, and an arrow;
and four left hands raised, with the index fingers touching his own breasts, holding a lotus and a bow; he has Akṣobhya as his crown ornament. Thus one should meditate.
The samādhi named Paramāśvavajra (or Jñānavajra). The mantra recitation is: Oṃ haṃ Hayagrīva svāhā.
|| The Hayagrīva Sādhana ||

Homage to Hayagrīva. Here, having understood the Buddhist doctrine that all intrinsic natures abide as unarisen from the very beginning, one [should visualize] the eight-sided summit of Mount Sumeru...
In its center is a cushion (*masūraka*) measuring one thousand *yojanas*, composed of the seven precious gems;
having sat upon it,
preceded by the going for refuge to the Three Jewels and so forth, he should empower his body, speech, and mind.
Having emanated a solar disc pervading space by that very [method],
and having meditated upon the syllable *haṃ* within it as having a blazing and radiant form, then [one should recite] *namaḥ*.

By means of the syllables *oṃ āḥ hūṃ* of the vajras of the universal body, speech, and mind, one invites all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas residing in the world-systems extending to the infinite limits of the ten directions; having caused them to enter in the form of gnosis (*jñāna*), one then, by means of the second *haṃ*, [places them] upon the neck of the horse.
Having summoned, led forth, and caused [the deity] to enter, by means of the third *hūṃ* syllable, one should think: "I am indeed of the nature of Hayagrīva-Vajra;

I am red in color, extremely terrifying, three-eyed, with tawny beard, fierce, pot-bellied, formidable with fangs, adorned with a garland of skulls and lips and teeth, wearing a crown of matted hair, and having Amitābha upon my head."

The second face is blue, horse-headed, terrifying and fearsome, emitting the sound "hī hī," reaching from the peak of the universe down to the summit of existence (*bhavāgra*), adorned with eight *nāgas*, and having the form of a short, dwarf-like being.

Clad in a tiger skin, adorned with all ornaments, and threatening all the gods and asuras, he holds a vajra-staff. [The manuscript *k* breaks at this point, and the present *sādhana* concludes here with the final portion of the *Vajrajvālānalārka-sādhana*, omitting the remainder.]

[The intermediate section that appears again at the end of the manuscript: One should meditate upon rays of various colors preceded by their emanation and reabsorption. By the power of this Blessed One, the means for attaining accomplishments (*siddhi*)—such as the wish-fulfilling gem (*cintāmaṇi*), the auspicious jar (*bhadraghaṭa*), the wish-granting tree (*kalpataru*), and the elixir of immortality (*rasāyana*)—[are attained]. [k, g]

It is stated in the *Saptaśatika-kalpa* that [the deities] become manifest facing one's direction. Furthermore, through three hundred thousand recitations of the Blessed One’s mantra, the sovereignty of both [cakravartin] kings becomes manifest,
surrounded and honored by many apsarases.
Experiencing intense bliss in the abode of the Vidyādharas,
the Lord of Devas remains there; Brahmā becomes his bearer of the parasol and his minister.
Vaimacitrī is the commander-in-chief, Hari is the doorkeeper, all the gods are in attendance,
and Nagnācārya Śaṅkara displays all the qualities; he remains there until the Blessed Maitreya attains perfect enlightenment.
And it is prophesied that he will attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
The Hayagrīva sādhana as taught in the *Saptaśatika-kalpa* is completed.

In the same way, upon the sun, one should visualize the supreme horse, born from the syllable *hūṃ* colored blue, with four faces, eight arms, and four legs; his first face is wrathful-erotic (*krodha-śṛṅgāra*) and three-eyed, the right face is fierce (*raudra*), and the left is the face of Brahmā; on his head, his lips are playfully upturned.
With his lower lip gracefully raised upward, he has the face of a green horse; with one right hand, which holds a triple-bannered flag and a double-vajra,
he performs the gesture of rising,
and with one left hand, holding a shield, he grasps a double-lotus.
Again, with his right hand in the *tripatākā* gesture, he performs the mudrā of rising; again, with his left hand, he holds a *śakti*;
again, with both right hands, he holds a sword (*khaḍga*) and an arrow (*bāṇa*).
And with his two remaining left hands, he holds a staff and a bow; standing in the *pratyālīḍha* posture, he tramples upon Indrāṇī and Śrī with one of his right feet.

One should meditate upon oneself as trampling Rati and Prīti with the second right foot, Indra and Madhukara with the first left foot, and Jayakara and Vasanta with the second left foot. The mudrā is the Viśvavajra-tripatākā, the "Arising Supreme Horse" mudrā. The mantra is: Oṃ śumbha niśumbha.
HŪṂ.
Thus concludes the *Paramāśva-sādhana*.

According to the previously described procedure, one should visualize the Lord Trailokyavijaya, born from the blue syllable *HŪṂ*, upon the sun; he is blue in color, four-faced, and eight-armed; his first face expresses wrathful passion (*krodha-śṛṅgāra*), the right face is fierce (*raudra*), the left is loathsome (*bībhatsa*), and the back face displays the heroic sentiment (*vīra-rasa*); with two hands joined at the heart holding a bell and a vajra.
He wears the Vajra-Hūṃkāra mudrā with his three right hands holding a khaṭvāṅga, a goad, and an arrow;
with his three left hands he holds a bow, a noose, and a vajra.
Standing in the pratyālīḍha posture, his left foot tramples upon the head of Maheśvara, while his right foot presses down upon the pair of breasts of Gaurī.

Having visualized oneself as wearing various garments and ornaments, such as garlands of flowers and strings of jewels, one should form the mudrā. In this case, having joined the two fists back-to-back, one should connect the two little fingers in the shape of a chain. The mantra is:
Oṃ śumbha niśumbha hūṃ! Seize, seize! Cause to seize, cause to seize!
Hūṃ! Bring it here, hoḥ! O Blessed One, King of Vidyās, hūṃ phaṭ!
The Sadhana for Trailokyavijaya (Victor over the Three Worlds)

In the same way, immediately following emptiness, upon the sun, there is the blue syllable *HŪṂ*, which transforms into the Vajra-flame-blazing-sun, blue in color, with a radiance filled with garlands of flames, four-faced, and eight-armed.
His four faces are endowed with the sentiments of the erotic, the heroic, the loathsome, and the pathetic; he holds a vajra, a sword, a discus, and an arrow in his four right hands,
and in his four left hands he holds a bell, a bow, a noose, and a khaṭvāṅga staff adorned with a variegated banner.
One should meditate upon [the deity] who has a mass of hair like the crest of a blazing fire,
who wears bracelets, a girdle, anklets, a necklace, and earrings made of most terrifying great serpents,
and who stands having seized his consort with Viṣṇu in the *ālīḍha* posture. Then, one should form the mudrā.
Having formed the *talavajrabandha* mudrā with the two thumbs raised in the center of the blazing fingers, one should recite the mantra:
*oṃ vajrajvālānalārka hūṃ*.
The *Vajrajvālānalārka-sādhana* is complete.
Homage to Bhūtaḍāmara! Having bowed to the illustrious Bhūtaḍāmara, who is skilled in destroying the pride of Śukra, Brahmā, Kubera, and the others, his sādhana is here written down.
This work, purified by the concise tradition and composed for those who delight in brevity,
has been written by me with a heart solely intent on the wonder of attaining the accomplishments (*siddhi*) of the *yakṣas*, *rākṣasas*, and other beings.

First of all, the mantra-practitioner should visualize within the moon at his own heart the seed-syllable *raṃ*, its body filled with rays of light that cause the universe to blossom. Then, [he should visualize] that which has been drawn forth in front by the hook-like forms emanating from that [seed-syllable].

Having thoroughly worshipped Ḍāmara with the sevenfold supreme offerings, one should meditate upon emptiness. Then— within the center of the bindu, which is the abode of the syllable HŪṂ, resembling a conch and like the half-moon of the night-maker (the moon), pure and radiant as a jasmine flower.
Having fully transformed everything that is radiant, one should perceive it as a lotus with eight petals as tender as the universe.

Then, in the center of that, having visualized a blue-flaming vajra born from the transformation of the syllable *hūṃ*— which itself rests upon the Lord of Herbs (the Moon) born from the transformation of the syllable *a*, and which contains the syllable *hūṃ* within its core— one should behold it as transformed: instantly appearing as a formidable blue [form], whose very nature is to terrify all spirits.
To the one who performs benefit for the world, whose sole weapon is the pervasive red [flower],
born from Hari, Hara, and Saraja, the fierce and peerless hero among warriors, possessing formidable fangs and a slightly quivering mass of wrath.
His hair is tied upward, blue and tawny;
his body is covered by a blue garment.
He holds a vajra in his right hand and, in his left, a noose with the threatening gesture (tarjanī).
He wears a crown of five skulls, holds a trident and a skull-cup in his left hands, and holds a *ḍamaru* drum and a flaying knife in his right hands;

he has a crown of tawny matted hair, three eyes, and is clad in a tiger-skin garment; white in color, he is unconquered by the lords of the great elements and stands in the *pratyālīḍha* posture, treading upon [the enemy].
The glorious Bhūtaḍāmara, with the mudrā bound by both hands.
In this regard, the mudrā is as follows:
having encircled the two ring fingers, one should bend the two index fingers.
One should press the little finger and the middle finger with the thumb.

It is adorned with eight nāgas: there, Karkoṭaka is blue as a head-wrap; Takṣaka is red as a neck-ornament; Nanda and Upananda are yellow as earrings; Ananta alone is white as a sacred thread (brahmasūtra);
Vāsuki is white as a waist-band; Kulika, the color of a pigeon, is on the upper arms as armlets; and likewise on the other two arms.

One who is solely intent on the welfare of the world should meditate upon Śaṅkhapāla as white, the two *nūpura* ornaments as Padma and Mahāpadma which are red, and likewise the pair of eyes as Rakṣa; one should contemplate the Bhūta Śrībhūtaḍāmara as exceedingly wrathful.
For the sake of constant protection, one should touch the heart, throat, ūrṇā, and head with the mudrā.
When weary from meditation, one should recite the mantra with the voice of Vajra or the voice of Krodha.
The mantra: *HŪṂ VAJRA PHAṬ*.
I have indeed been entreated by a virtuous and noble person;
something has been clearly written for me by someone or other.
May whatever merit has been obtained from this by Vairocana bring peace, removing the defilements of the worlds of the three realms.
The *Śrībhūtaḍāmara-saṃkṣiptasādhana* is completed.
Having prostrated with devotion to the *Ḍāmara*, the Greatly Accomplished One who is the Vajra of Hatred,
I shall describe his very *sādhana* in accordance with the tantra.
