The practitioner, having received initiation in the *Bhūtaḍāmara-tantra* and being authorized by his gurus,

should perform the accomplishment while staying in such places as the confluence of rivers, a cremation ground, under a solitary tree, in a temple, or in the abode of the glorious Vajradhara. First of all, he should visualize a moon mandala in both hands with the syllable *A*.

One should meditate upon it. In its center is the syllable *hūṃ*, surrounded by a garland of flames. Then one should recite the mantra for the destruction of all sins: *oṃ siddhivajra hūṃ*. Having visualized a moon disk in the heart, and having visualized a red *repha* accompanied by a bindu and surrounded by a garland of flames, one should recite this mantra: *oṃ hana*.

"Destroy! Annihilate the evil! HŪṂ PHAṬ! The mudrā for this is as follows: having interlaced the fingers with one another, extend both index fingers; by forming the index fingers like needles, it is the mudrā for the destruction of evil. Immediately thereafter, one should contemplate emptiness. Again, one should visualize the moon of bodhicitta, resembling jasmine and crystal. Then...

One should visualize an eight-petaled lotus arising from the syllable *hūṃ*. Above that, by means of the syllable *raṃ*, one should contemplate a sun mandala, and in its center, the syllable *hūṃ* surrounded by a garland of flames. Through this mantra of wrathful possession, one should effect the descent of the spirit: *oṃ krodhāveśa hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ aḥ*. Its mudrā is as follows:

Having formed the mutual fist, one should encircle the two index fingers; this is the mudrā for the descent of wrath (*krodhāveśa*). Having again bound this very mudrā, one should recite this mantra: *oṃ vajrāveśaya veśaya pātaya hūṃ*. Thereafter, one should visualize the body of one’s own deity.
Blazing with garlands of flames, radiant, and possessing a luster equal to the fire at the end of an eon.
With a massive body like crushed collyrium, he let out a loud, echoing laugh.
One should meditate upon the Lord, the sovereign of the three worlds, who is intensely wrathful,
standing firmly in the *pratyālīḍha* posture, possessing the brilliance of ten million suns,
with eyes blazing like the fire at the end of an aeon, and round like the sun at twilight.
With hair standing erect and great blazing flames, wearing a crown of garlands of skulls,
his face terrifying with fangs, and clothed in garments of dark, clear luster.
Adorned with eight serpents and resplendent with four arms,
brandishing a vajra in his right hand and threatening Hari, Hara, and Pitāmaha with his left.
[The *sādhās* that follow] with the left hand.
He stands with the binding of the mudrā, treading upon the feet of Aparājitā;
having encircled the two ring fingers, one should bend the two index fingers.
One should press the little finger and the middle finger with the thumb;
this is the supreme and most excellent mudrā, the ultimate means for accomplishing the three worlds.
Then, having formed [the previous mudrā], one should extend the two middle fingers; this is the *śiromudrā*. The mantra is: *oṃ hana vajra hūṃ*.
Into this very same mudrā, one should insert the two middle fingers and form the index fingers into a needle; this is the *śikhāmudrā*.
The mantra is: *oṃ daha vajra hūṃ*. In this very same mudrā, the two thumbs are placed on the sides.
The Eye Mudrā consists of placing the right thumb on the right eye and the left thumb on the left eye. The mantra is:
*oṃ dīptavajra hūṃ*. Having formed two fists with the hands, one should interlace the two little fingers.

Extending the index finger constitutes the heart mudrā; the mantra is *oṃ vajraropa hūṃ*. Curling the index finger of this very same mudrā constitutes the armor mudrā; the mantra is *oṃ dṛḍhavajra hūṃ kavacaḥ*. Extending both index fingers of this very same mudrā constitutes the weapon mudrā; the mantra is *oṃ hana daha paca*... [k, ḍh].

"O Pañcakrodhavajra, slay all the wicked! HŪṂ PHAṬ! Having thus performed the placement of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅgavinyāsa*), one should invoke the Blessed One. Forming the *āvāhana-mudrā* by interlacing the fingers, bending the two index fingers, and moving them slightly: the mantra is OṂ VAJRADHARA-MAHĀKRODHA.

"Observe the pledge; come quickly! Hrīḥ Jaḥ Hūṃ Phaṭ Svāhā! With this, one should invoke all the deities. Having thus invoked them and performed a special hymn of praise, one should offer the *argha* (water for honor) and *pādya* (water for the feet) with this mudrā-mantra. Forming the *añjali* (palms joined) with the hands turned upward and placing the two thumbs on the sides is the *argha*-mudrā. The mantra is:
Oṃ, may all deities be gracious; O Blessed One, Great Wrathful One, accept this argha of your own vajra! Oṃ hūṃ aḥ. Then one should offer the pādya with this mudrā-mantra:
one should curl all the fingers and join the tips of the thumbs and index fingers like a pair of tongs.
Having taken a flower and purified it, one should cast it to the left side of the Blessed One. The mantra is: *oṃ pravarasaṃskāraṃ (or *satkāraṃ) pratīccha svāhā*. Then one should offer a seat.
Having turned the left hand palm upward, with the thumb raised, one should [offer it] with the fist of the right hand.

One should grasp the left thumb with the raised right thumb, treading upon Aparājita; this is the Bhūtāsana mudrā of Vajradhara. The mantra is: *Oṃ jaya jaya krodhāvipatti krodharāja iti bhūtāsanaṃ darśaya rakṣa pratigṛhṇa svāhā*. Next follows the Devatāsana.
Having formed the *sampuṭāñjali* (the hollowed palms joined together) with all the fingers slightly spread apart, this is the lotus mudrā (*padmamudrā*). The mantra is: Oṃ.

"Oṃ, all deities seated upon the lotus-born one, svāhā! Then, having performed the expulsion of obstacles with this mudrā-mantra—one should form fists with both hands and extend the two thumbs; this is the Ākṣepa-mudrā. The mantra is: Oṃ, destroy all evil ones! Burn them! Cook them!

"Reduce the wicked to ashes! Hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ! (This is the expulsion. One should again perform the binding of the directions with this mudrā-mantra: having formed two separate fists, extend the left index finger and place it at the base of the right arm, pressing down on the nail of the little finger with the right thumb.

One should extend the remaining fingers while enraged; this is the *digbandha* (binding of the directions) mudrā. The mantra is: *oṃ vajrakrodha mahācaṇḍa bandha bandha daśa diśān hūṃ phaṭ*. Then, having bound the root mudrā of the Blessed One, one should display the *samaya* (pledge) upon beholding the *vajrākṣara* (diamond syllable) with this mantra: *hūṃ vajra phaṭ*.

Forming a mutual fist, one should encircle the two little fingers and extend the index fingers in the shape of a hook; this is the *siddhākarṣaṇamudrā*. The mantra is: *oṃ vajraroṣa mahākrodha siddhyākarṣaya hūṃ jaḥ*. Then, brandishing the vajra, one should say this:
O Great King, in the accomplishment of the attainment of wrath and the realization of the goal,
may all the gods grant me swift and unsurpassed success.
One should worship with the eight secret offerings: Oṃ vajralāsye hūṃ;
Oṃ vajramālye hūṃ; Oṃ vajragīte hūṃ; Oṃ vajranṛtye hūṃ; Oṃ vajrapuṣpe hūṃ;
Oṃ vajradhūpe hūṃ; Oṃ vajrāloke hūṃ. Then, having performed the worship, [one should place] the Blessed One within one's own body.

One should cause [the deity] to enter by binding the Vajrāveśa mudrā and reciting this mantra: OṂ PRAVISA HŪṂ HŪṂ HŪṂ AḤ. Then, having bound the root mudrā, one should recite this mantra: OṂ VAJRA PHAṬ. [The] Jñānasattva...

One should meditate on the *samayasattva* as non-different [from oneself]. Tired of meditation, one should recite the mantra without weariness. When weariness arises, having performed worship and offered water for the feet (*argha-pādya*), one should praise [the deity] with this mantra:
O great wrathful one who grants the accomplishment of all and bestows the attainment of bliss,
having granted the great accomplishment to the mantra-practitioner, go forth to the unsurpassed siddhi!

Now follows the mudrā: having formed the *sampuṭa-añjali* (the hollowed palms joined together) with the head slightly bowed, this is the *pūrṇa-mudrā*. The mantra is: *oṃ siddhivajra āpūraya āpūraya sarvasattvānām āśām amukasiddhiṃ me prayaccha hūṃ*. Merely by the recitation of this, [the accomplishment is attained].

All mudrās become firm. Having formed the lotus mudrā (*padmamudrā*) and raised the left thumb, one should dismiss [the deities] with this mantra: *oṃ sara sara visara visara gaccha gaccha śrīvajradharaḥ samājñāpayati svāhā*. While dismissing them, having formed the armor mudrā (*kavacamudrā*), [one should touch] the heart, the *ūrṇā* (between the eyebrows), the throat, and the head.
Having performed protection by means of the two armpits—[g: the protection of the two]—one should dwell with the pride of that [deity].
Thus ends the *Sādhana* of *Bhūtaḍāmara*.
520 not clear p. 521)
(Not clear, p.
522) Placing the right thumb on the right eye and the left thumb on the left eye is the *netramudrā*. Oṃ dīptavajra.

HŪṂ! Forming a mutual fist and wrapping both little fingers together, extend the index fingers; this is the heart mudrā. The mantra is: OṂ VAJRAROṢA HŪṂ. From this same mudrā, curl the two index fingers; this is the armor mudrā. The mantra is: OṂ DṚḌHAVAJRA HŪṂ. Extending both index fingers is the weapon mudrā.
The mantra is: Oṃ hana daha paca krodhavajra sarvaduṣṭān māraya hūṃ phaṭ. Then one should invoke the Vajrakrodha.
Having interlaced the fingers with each other, the two index fingers are bent. Oṃ.
O Vajrakrodha, maintain the samaya; come quickly! Hrīḥ Hrīḥ Jaḥ Hūṃ Phaṭ Svāhā!

Then, having formed the añjali with palms upturned, one should place the two thumbs on the sides. Oṃ, may all the deities be gracious; O Blessed One, Great Vajrakrodha, accept this argha! Hūṃ Aḥ! Then, one should offer the seat.

Having turned the left hand palm upward, one should grasp the left thumb with the fist of the right hand, the thumb of which is raised. *Oṃ jaya jaya mahākrodhādhipati krodharāja idaṃ bhūtāsanaṃ darśaya rakṣa pratigṛhṇa svāhā*.

Having formed the *sampuṭāñjali* (the hollowed-palms gesture) and separated all the fingers, the *padmamudrā* (lotus gesture) is performed; this is the *āsana-mudrā* (seat gesture). The mantra is: *oṃ padmodbhavaniṣaṇāḥ sarvadevatāḥ svāhā*. Then one should perform the *ākṣepa* (casting gesture): having made fists with both hands, [extend] the thumbs...

Having extended the left fist and placed it at the heart, and having positioned the right fist as if in the gesture of striking, one should recite the mantra: *oṃ nāśaya sarvaduṣṭān daha paca duṣṭān bhasmīkuru hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ*. Then, one should perform the binding of the directions (*digbandha*) with this mantra: having formed two separate fists facing each other.
Extending the left index finger separately, one should place it at the base of the right upper arm, pressing the nail of the little finger with the right thumb.
Extending the remaining fingers, one should whirl them in the ten directions: *oṃ vajrakrodha mahācaṇḍa bandha daśadiśaṃ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ*. Then, brandishing the vajra, one should recite this:
"O Great King, Accomplishment of Wrath, in the accomplishment of what is doubted regarding success!"
May all the gods grant supreme accomplishment swiftly.
One should worship with the sixteen Lāsyā offerings.
Having bound the root mudrā of the King of Wrath, one should recite *hūṃ vajra phaṭ* and bestow the visible commitment (*dṛśyasamaya*). Then, of the Blessed One...
Having performed the worship and bound the mudrā of the wrathful possession, one should cause Vajrakrodha to enter one’s own body:
*oṃ praviśya vajrakrodha hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ āḥ jvālāmālākulabhīṣaṇavajra āḥ*. Having internalized him within one's own body...

Having performed the armor-rite (*kavaca*) and all else for the sake of fulfillment, one should form the *sampuṭāñjali* mudrā and recite the fulfillment mantra: *oṃ siddhivajra āpūraya āpūraya hūṃ phaṭ*. By this, everything that is deficient or excessive becomes completely full. Then, one should generate the pride (*ahaṅkāra*), thinking: "I am Vajrakrodha."

With the mantra *dhā aṃ hāṃ*, one should attract all accomplishments (*sarvasiddhi*). Having formed the mutual fist with this mudrā-mantra, one should encircle the two little fingers, extend the index fingers, form them into coils, and move them slightly.
One should visualize the letters—[the seed-syllables] *ka*, *ḍha*, and *ga*—as having upward-pointing crests, situated within the lunar mandala.

Like a row of blue lotuses, [recite]: *oṃ vajra hūṃ phaṭ*. Then, one should visualize from all the pores of the skin the form of a wrathful deity, radiating and performing the act of withdrawal. When weary from meditation, one should begin the recitation; with that as the mental object, one should recite with a single-pointed mind focused on the syllables. When weary, [one should again visualize] the form of the wrathful deity.

Having internalized it within one's own heart (p. 524) and formed the *sampuṭa-añjali* mudrā [according to versions k, ḍh, and g: having made it], one should pray for all accomplishments (*sarvasiddhi*).
O Siddhivajra, fulfill the hopes of all sentient beings; grant me all accomplishments, HŪṂ JAḤ. [Ḍh:
adds "one should worship as previously described" after this. Then, one should move the two thumbs with the lotus mudrā;
this is the mudrā for dismissing all the deities. The mantra is: OṂ SARA SARA VISARA VISARA GACCHA. [G: omits this.]

"Go, go! Go to all the deities! Śrīvajradhara commands you! Svāhā! Then, having armored one's own body, one should dwell at ease with a mind characterized by the pride of the wrathful deity, according to this sequence. One should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times; it will be swiftly accomplished. Now, the practitioner who has been consecrated, authorized, and has performed the preliminary service—
Desiring to accomplish the practice of Vajradhara, one should recite [the mantra] one thousand times at the three junctions of the day for one month.

Then, on the full moon day, having performed worship according to one's means, being well-composed and having bound the wrathful mudrā, one should recite throughout the entire night. Then, at dawn, the earth trembles and the mudrā blazes; by the mere act of its blazing, [the goal is attained].
"One becomes like Vajradhara; one possesses a divine form that is free from old age and death," so said the Blessed One, Vajradhara.
This *Sādhanopāyikā* of the *Bhūtaḍāmara*, which is concise, complete, clear, sequential, and coherent, was composed by Trailokyavajra for the sake of delivering all sentient beings.
The *Caritā* is completed.
Homage to Bhūtaḍāmara!
Having prostrated before the Wrathful One who consists of wisdom and skillful means and arises from the bodhicitta, I shall explain the propitiation known as the Bhūtadāmara.

In that regard, one who establishes the existence [of the deity]— having entered the maṇḍala, been consecrated in all the samayas, and received permission— should, in some place conducive to the mind such as a mountain cave, worship the Blessed One whose form is depicted on a cloth or similar medium with external and internal offerings of incense and so forth, and then perform the confession of sins and other rites.
The Triple Gem is my refuge; I confess all my misdeeds; I rejoice in the merit of the world; I direct my mind toward the enlightenment of a Buddha.

Thus: having meditated on a moon-maṇḍala in both hands with the syllable *A*, and upon it the blazing syllable *HŪṂ*, and forming the hollowed-añjali gesture, one should say this: *OṂ SIDDHAVAJRA HŪṂ*. With the syllable *HRĪḤ*, one should visualize an eight-petaled lotus at the throat;
and upon the petal of the tongue, with the syllable *HŪṂ*, one should consecrate the "Auspicious Vajra" (*śubhavajra*), [thinking] "the tongue is the vajra, etc. This is the protection of the place.

One should perform [the ritual] according to this procedure. Herein is the procedure: while uttering the syllable *hūṃ*, one should instantaneously manifest oneself as the King of Wrath (*Krodharāja*), and [visualize] the stakes (*kīlaka*)—which have been produced from the syllable *hūṃ* and are adorned with red flower garlands and so forth bound with red thread—as being of the nature of the *ayoni*.
Visualizing [the obstacles] as resembling monsoon clouds, shaped like spikes below the navel region, and having the form of upward-rising wrath,

one should drive away the obstacles below with a sharp stake while reciting the mantra: *Oṃ gha gha ghātaya ghātaya sarvaduṣṭān kīlaya kīlaya sarvapāpān phaṭ hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ vajradhara ājñāpayati sarvaduṣṭakāyavākcittam*.
*Kīlaya hūṃ phaṭ*!
And before that [deity], there is a solar disc born from the syllable *Āḥ*, blazing with rays of light.
One should visualize stakes with blazing rays in all directions.

And with those [mantras], having visualized within one's own heart a sun represented by the syllable *aṃ* inside a cage bound together in succession, and upon that the syllable *raṃ* like the fire of cosmic destruction (*kalpāgni*), one should interlace the thumbs and extend the two index fingers;
then, beginning from the forehead, one should strike [the cage] away by means of the "striking of evil" (*pāpāsphoṭa*). *Oṃ hana vidhvaṃsaya nāśaya*.

Having incinerated [the sins] with "pāpān hūṃ phaṭ," and having shattered the sins consisting of external and internal conceptual constructions, one should contemplate oneself as being like the sky, liberated from the grasped and the grasper. Then:
"The mind, shaken free of conceptual construction, is self-cognized and luminous."
The syllable *hūṃ*, which produces bliss in the heart, is interlaced with two *ho* syllables.
One should bring the mind, which is pervaded by the element of intoxication and manifested as mere consciousness,
into unity with one's own mind by means of intense accumulations of rays.

One should visualize [the moon] joined with a half-moon like a reflection. Then, having placed the vowels beginning with *a* upon the solar disc, one should emit the short vowels as the nature of method (*upāya*) and the long vowels as the nature of wisdom (*prajñā*), performing the miraculous transformations of the Buddhas. One should then contemplate them as entering back into their own vowel-rays and remaining established through the application of the digits (*kalā*). [Likewise, one should contemplate] the consonants beginning with *ka*.

Afterwards, by that same method, one should likewise contemplate the factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipakṣa), excluding the letters ṅa, ṇa, na, ma, and va. Then, having emanated and caused the entry of Buddhas of five colors, one should visualize a white lotus resting within many wombs (*garbha*).
Upon that, one should recite "HŪṂ" and meditate on oneself as the Glorious Wrathful King (*Śrī-krodharāja*), drawn forth by flames.

The Possession by Wrath: Then one should form the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*) with the thought, "I am Krodhavajra. Having again emanated and re-absorbed that family (*kula*), and having produced the firm conviction, "I am Śrī Bhūtaḍāmara," [one recites]: *Oṃ vajrāveśaya pātaya hūṃ*. And the possession by wrath (*krodhāveśa*) is the entry of the Vajra when joined with the mantra. Then, [one visualizes] oneself...
Having resolved upon the Vajra Wrath, one should bind the Samaya-mudrā and say: "I am the Samaya; abide as the Samayasattva within me."
Having encircled the two ring fingers, one should bend the two index fingers;
then, with the thumb, one should press down upon the little finger and the middle finger.

Its mantra is: *oṃ vajra phaṭ*. Having established it at the heart, the *ūrṇā* (between the eyebrows), the throat, and the head, one should preside over [the rite]. Then, one should perform the placement of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅgavinyāsa*) with their respective mudrās and mantras. Forming a mutual fist, one should extend the middle fingers; this is the *śiromudrā*. The mantra is: *oṃ hanavajra hūṃ śiraḥ*. Of this very [mudrā]...
Having inserted the two middle fingers, this is the *śikhā-mudrā*. The mantra is: *Oṃ dahavajra hūṃ śikhā*.
With this same mudrā, placing the two thumbs on the sides—the right thumb on the right side and the left on the left—this is the *netra-mudrā*.
The mantra is: *Dīptavajra hūṃ netra*. Having formed two fists with the hands, one should encircle them with the two little fingers.
Extending the index finger constitutes the heart-mudrā. Having meditated on the Wrathful Vajra, empowered by the syllable *HŪṂ*, at the heart, the heart-mantra is:
*OṂ VAJRAROṢA HŪṂ*. Making the index finger of this very same mudrā into a coil constitutes the armor-mudrā.
The mantra is: *OṂ DṚḌHAVAJRA HŪṂ KAVACA*. Of this very same mudrā, [the two index fingers...]
Extending the weapon-gesture (*astramudrā*), the mantra is: *oṃ hana daha paca koṭivajra duṣṭān māraya māraya hūṃ phaṭ*.
This is the weapon-mantra. Having recited it three times while uttering *hūṃ aḥ*, one should visualize the Blue Wrathful King upon a sun-maṇḍala in front;
then, speaking the words "I am Vajra," and turning around, one should contemplate, "I am the Wrath of Wrath. Then...
One should invoke the Blessed One together with all the deities. Having interlaced the fingers one with another, one should slightly move the two index fingers, which are bent, using the two thumbs.

One should beckon with the two index fingers: *Oṃ vajramahākrodha, protect the samaya; O Blessed One, come quickly together with all the deities! Hrīḥ jaḥ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā!* The *Sādhana* of *Bhūtaḍāmara* is completed.
Homage to Yamāntaka!

First of all, the practitioner, seated on a comfortable seat, should visualize a red solar disc arising from the syllable *ṅkā* (or *ḍh*) at his own heart; having placed upon it a red syllable *hūṃ*, he should [visualize] in front of him...
Having focused one's mind on Raktayamāri of the form to be described,
as well as the gurus, buddhas, and bodhisattvas, and having worshipped them with flowers and other offerings, paid homage,
and performed the taking of the three refuges and so forth, one should meditate on emptiness: *oṃ*.

"I am of the nature of the vajra of the knowledge of emptiness. Immediately thereafter, one should visualize a white staff marked with a moist red severed head and presided over by the syllable *HŪṂ*. Having transformed all of this, one should contemplate oneself as Yamāntaka, red in color and standing in the pratyālīḍha posture.

[While the state is established: one-faced and two-armed, holding in the left hand a skull-cup filled with blood, and in the right hand a white staff topped with a severed head; adorned with ornaments of snakes, terrifying in appearance, with tawny hair standing erect, wearing a dripping tiger-skin garment, together with his own consort.

One should meditate upon oneself being embraced by her, who is adorned with various ornaments and stands in the *ālīḍha* posture. Afterwards, within the heart of the Blessed One, there is a sun-maṇḍala presided over by the syllable *HŪṂ*; that [maṇḍala] transforms into— (p.
Having visualized the motionless white staff marked with a moist skull,
one should visualize within it a red syllable *HŪṂ* situated upon a red solar disc. Then,
the secret vajra is transformed from the syllable *HŪṂ*, and the eight-petalled lotus of the Blessed Lady’s secret place is formed by the red syllable *ĀḤ*.

Thereafter, one should recite the mantra: *oṃ sarvatathāgatānurāgeṇa vajrasvabhāvātmako ’ham*. Thereafter, one should visualize below the navel a blazing red syllable *hrīḥ* upon a red eight-petaled lotus. As for the Wisdom Consort, she is overwhelmed by intoxication, her silken garment slipping away.

One should meditate upon Raktayamāri, who has two arms and one face, abiding in the *sampuṭa* (union) yoga with the Blessed One; thus constituted, he stands upon a multi-petalled lotus atop a buffalo, following the preliminary rites of the commitment (*samaya*) and so forth.
One should meditate on this during the two, three, or four junctions of the day. *Vuṃ āṃ jiṃ khaṃ hūṃ* is the mantra for the empowerment of the commitment.

Oṃ hrīḥ ṣṭrīḥ vikṛtānana hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ svāhā. This is the root mantra (mūlamantra). Oṃ Yamāntaka hūṃ. This is the heart mantra (hṛdayamantra). [The Ārya-raktayamāri-sādhana] (The Sadhana of Noble Red Yamāri) [Note: K provides the name of the author in the following words:]
"This is the work of the Siddhācārya Virūpākṣapāda"—this [colophon] is omitted in all other manuscripts:
ḍ, dh, dh, viś., g, k, b, ḍh, and kh.

In the same way, having preceded this with the confession of sins and so forth, one should contemplate emptiness; then, upon a sun disk arisen from a red syllable *HŪṂ*, there is a red syllable *HŪṂ*, which transforms into a white staff marked by a fresh yellow severed head and presided over by the syllable *HŪṂ*.
One should meditate. Through the transformation of that [syllable], one should visualize oneself as Yamāntaka, with one face and two arms, standing in the pratyālīḍha posture.
His left hand holds a skull-cup filled with blood, and his right hand holds a white staff topped with a fresh yellow severed head.
He is adorned with ornaments of snakes, has tawny hair standing erect, and wears a garment of tiger skin.

One should meditate upon her wearing a crown of Akṣobhya, embraced by her own Prajñā, standing upon a sun disk atop a multi-petaled lotus on a buffalo; and one should meditate upon the Bhagavatī as having two arms and one face,
adorned with various ornaments, standing in the ālīḍha posture, and intoxicated with passion.

Having thus meditated on her, who wears a tiger skin as a garment and stands in the *pratyālīḍha* posture in union (*sampuṭayoga*) with the Blessed One, one should visualize in the heart, upon a solar disc, a white staff marked by a skull transformed from the syllable *HŪṂ*,
with the syllable *HŪṂ* situated in its center upon the sun; then, one should visualize the Blessed One’s vajra, which is transformed from the syllable *HŪṂ*.

Having visualized a lotus transformed from the syllable *ĀḤ* belonging to the Bhagavatī, one should consecrate it with the thought: *Oṃ, by means of the passion of all Tathāgatas, I am of the vajra-nature*. Thereafter, one should contemplate a blazing red syllable *Hrīḥ* upon a deep-red eight-petalled lotus below the navel. Then, *Vuṃ*...

One should meditate during two, three, or four sessions of the day, preceded by the consumption of the *samaya* substances, using the mantra syllables: *āṃ jiṃ khaṃ hūṃ*. The mantra recitation is as follows: *oṃ hrīḥ ṣṭrīḥ vikṛtānana hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*. *oṃ yamāntaka hūṃ*.
The *Ārya-raktayamāri-sādhana* is completed.

531) Oṃ hrīḥ ṣṭrīḥ vikṛtānana hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ svāhā | Oṃ Yamāntakṛt hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ | First, the mantra-practitioner, seated upon a comfortable seat, [visualizes himself as] red-colored—

One should meditate. Having drawn forth with its rays the red Yamāri who stands before one, and having worshipped and paid homage to the Guru, Buddhas, and Bodhisattvas with flowers and other offerings, one should perform the confession of misdeeds and so forth. In that regard, one should visualize oneself and the triple world as...

Relying on emptiness, which is like an illusion, a dream, or a magical display, one should contemplate it. One should empower the mind with the thought: *Oṃ, I am of the nature of the vajra of the wisdom of emptiness.* Then, there is a white staff marked by a moist, red severed head; in its center is a sun-maṇḍala transformed from the syllable *rakta* (red).
In the center of that, one should visualize oneself as Yamāntaka, having transformed all of that into the form of the syllable *HŪṂ* which is red in color; he stands in the *pratyālīḍha* posture,
with fangs bared and a lolling tongue, a distorted face, and adorned with eight fierce serpents.

One should meditate on [the deity] whose hair is flaming, tawny, and erect; who wears a dripping tiger-skin garment; and who is embraced by Prajñā, who is red in color, adorned with various ornaments, and stands in the *ālīḍha* posture. Afterwards, one should visualize the sun arisen from the transformation of the original seed-syllable in the heart of the Blessed One, and upon that, the syllable *HŪṂ*, which is transformed from that [sun].

One should meditate on the motionless white staff marked with a fresh severed head. Within its fist, one should contemplate a red syllable *HŪṂ* situated upon a solar disc. Afterwards, one should visualize the Blessed Lady as the transformation of the secret-vajra *HŪṂ*, holding a staff marked with a fresh severed head.
At the secret place is an eight-petaled lotus with a red syllable ĀḤ. Thereafter, one should recite the mantra: OṂ SARVATATHĀGATĀNURĀGEṆA.
"I am of the nature of the vajra-svabhāva. Thereafter, one should visualize below the navel a blazing red syllable Hrīḥ upon a red eight-petaled lotus. The Blessed One has one face and two arms;
in his left hand he holds a skull-cup filled with blood, and in his right he holds a white staff topped with a severed head, standing upon a buffalo.

One should meditate upon [the consort] seated on a universal lotus, intoxicated with passion, her silken garment slipping away, possessing two arms and one face, and abiding in the *sampuṭa-yoga* (union) with the Blessed One. One should meditate upon Yamāri in this manner. Having visualized him at the three junctions of the day or the four junctions, one should offer the *bali* oblation: *vuṃ āṃ jiṃ khaṃ hūṃ*.
The mantra for the empowerment of the pledge: Oṃ kha kha khāhi khāhi!
May all yakṣas, rākṣasas, bhūtas, pretas, piśācas, unmādas, kumbhāṇḍas, apasmāras, ḍākas, ḍākinīs, and so forth, accept this bali offering, protect the pledge, and grant all siddhis.
"Grant [this]! Just so, enjoy as you wish, drink, do not transgress, for the sake of all success;
be my helpers! HŪṂ HŪṂ PHAṬ PHAṬ SVĀHĀ"—this is the mantra for the bali offering to all spirits (*sārvabhautika*).
One should visualize [the deity] with red, black, yellow, and white colors according to the corresponding ritual action (*karma*). Then, one should recollect the recitation (*jāpa*): OṂ HRĪḤ ṢṬRĪḤ.

Vikṛtānana hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ, perform peace for Devadatta, namaḥ svāhā! For nourishment, vauṣaṭ; for attraction, jaḥ vuṃ; for delusion, hoḥ; for subjugation, laṃ; for paralyzing, hūṃ phaṭ; for inciting, hūṃ; for suppression, [use] the two others for eradication. Thus are paralyzing and the other rites.
One should interlace the ritual applications of karma.

For pacification (*śāntika*), protection is achieved by means of *rocanā* (bezoar). Having drawn two wheels upon a white cloth, or on a cloth washed with *bhūrja* bark or bamboo bark, or on a piece of cloth...

Having written [the mantra] interspersed with salutations (*namaskāra*), placed it in a pair of earthen bowls free from black roots and the like, immersed it in the midst of ghee and honey, wrapped it with a white thread, and worshipped it with white flowers at the three junctions of the day (p.
Having visualized oneself in the form of Yamāntaka, white in color and facing east, and having seen the person to be protected (sādhya) seated upon a moon disc in front,
one should meditate on [Yamāntaka] consecrating him with white vases filled with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta),
and then recite the mantra: *oṃ hrīḥ ṣṭrīḥ vikṛtānana devadattasya śāntiṃ kuru namaḥ svāhā*.

The ritual for pacification (*śāntika*): For men, in a rite of pacification or nourishment (*pauṣṭika*), one should draw two wheels with saffron, place them together with the syllable *vauṣaṭ* in the midst of ghee and honey, set them within a pair of earthen bowls (*śarāva*), and wrap them with a yellow thread.
Having worshipped at the three junctions of the day with yellow flowers, one should visualize oneself facing north,

assuming the form of Yamāntaka which is yellow in color, situated in the center of a yellow fourfold maṇḍala, and being consecrated by yellow golden vases filled with yellow-colored nectar; then [recite] the mantra.
One should recite: *oṃ hrīḥ ṣṭrīḥ vikṛtānana hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ devadattasya puṣṭiṃ kuru vauṣaṭ svāhā*.
This is the rite for nourishment (*pauṣṭika*).

Having drawn two wheels on birch bark or a cloth fragment with lac and red sandalwood mixed with the blood from the ring finger, having encircled them with the name accompanied by the syllable *hoḥ*, and having placed them within a well-baked pair of red earthen bowls,
one should immerse them in ghee and honey, worship them with red flowers, and [sit] facing west.

Having meditated on oneself in the form of Raktayamāri, and having visualized the person to be subdued (*sādhya*) situated in the center of a red moon-maṇḍala, one should recite the mantra: *oṃ hrīḥ ṣṭrīḥ vikṛtānana hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ* for the sake of Devadatta. [While reciting, one should visualize that rays of light issuing from one’s own body consecrate the person, who then becomes overwhelmed and falls at one’s feet. (Note: The portion "kṛte" is omitted in manuscript *k*.)
"Subjugate Yajñadatta! Hoḥ! Svāhā!
If he does not come under control, then [one should heat] that very wheel with fire, [using fuel] devoid of ghee and honey.

One should heat [the object] over smokeless embers while reciting the mantra: *oṃ hrīḥ ṣṭrīḥ vikṛtānana hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ devadattasya kṛte yajñadattaṃ vaśaṃ kuru hoḥ*. One should thus chant the mantra.
The ritual for subjugation (*vaśyavidhi*):
On a cloth from a cremation ground or on a cloth from a menstruating woman, having drawn two wheels with lac-dye mixed [with other substances],
and having performed the *vidarbha* (interlacing) by means of the syllables *jaḥ* and *hrīḥ* together with the letters of the person's name, one should place it within the cavity of a female skull.

Having worshipped with red flowers and meditated upon oneself in the form of Yamāntaka, resembling the sun at twilight, red in color, and holding a hook and a noose, one should imagine that his heart is pierced by the hook and his throat bound by the noose as he approaches. If he does not come, then:

One should heat [the object] over *khadira* wood fires while reciting the mantra. Thus, the various ritual applications (*karmaprasara*) are to be understood from the tantra. The *Sādhana* of Raktayamāri is completed.

He has assumed a body for the purpose of granting fearlessness to the three worlds; his disposition is gentle by nature, yet he displays a red form and a terrifying physique to accomplish the welfare of all beings.
Having prostrated before the enemy of the illustrious Raktakāla, who causes wonder by subduing the army of Māra,
this *sādhana* of his own is clearly written here in an abbreviated form.
In the beginning of the mantra practice, seated comfortably, one visualizes within one's own heart a red solar mandala,
which is red in form, colored by the mantra, peerless, and blazing in the form of the syllable *HŪṂ*.
Having visualized the Buddhas and Gurus, together with the glorious Raktayamāntaka and others, drawn forth by the dense mass of red light rays emanated from that [syllable], from the syllable *HŪṂ*:
Having performed the ritual of worship in various forms with diverse flowers, fragrant incense, and perfumes, one should confess before him whatever impurity exists within oneself.
Afterwards, having duly performed the remaining rites, one should [contemplate] that emptiness.
One should meditate with the verse beginning "Oṃ, void... and so forth; thereafter, [one meditates on] the red [syllable], born from the form of the letter Ra.
Having gazed for a long time at this entire staff— emanated from the syllable *hūṃ*, possessing the luster of the moon, marked with a moist severed head, and adorned with the syllable *hūṃ*—
the practitioner should contemplate his own body as the glorious Raktayamāntaka.
Standing in the pratyālīḍha posture, extremely distorted, with red limbs, and most wonderful.
Then, one should visualize [the deity] as wrathful, with a single face, endowed with two arms; on the left side he holds a skull-cup filled with blood,
and it is marked by a severed head on the right.
[He holds] a staff whose beauty has begun to be fashioned by a multitude of serpents with white bodies,
whose tawny hair stands erect, and who wears a tiger skin draped around his neck.
With his neck embraced by her who sits impetuously in his own lap,
her garment slipping from her hips, her single lotus-face joined with his pair of arms,
and her hands pressed together in a firm embrace while she stands with one leg extended in the *ālīḍha* posture;
Afterwards, in the heart of the Lord, one should visualize the fierce-rayed sun, born from the syllable HŪṂ in that form.

The adept [should visualize] a staff that is exceedingly white, joined with a moist head, and flashing with flames; and in its center, the excellent *hūṃ* syllable, intensely red, situated within a radiant orb of light.
One should visualize the secret distinction of the Blessed One, namely the vajra born from *hūṃ*,
and the eight-petalled lotus of the Blessed Lady’s secret place, produced from the transformation of the true seed-syllable.

The practitioner, with focused mind, should again recite the incomparable mantra "Oṃ sarve. Then, upon the surface of the navel, he should visualize the syllable Hrīḥ, perfectly blazing and crimson in color, within an eight-petaled lotus; above that, he should contemplate a white, elongated line directed toward the sky.
The glorious Lord Yamāri, intensely red and peerless.
One should meditate upon all this with a mind solely intent on protecting the world—
the unsurpassed one seated upon the lotus of the back of a buffalo.
The yogi, endowed with the aforementioned commitments and preceded by those very commitments,
should meditate on everything at the three junctions of the day with a mind free from doubt.
For him who meditates thus, this most excellent Teacher of the World will certainly grant success—

he whose mind is fixed solely on the rescue of suffering people submerged in the ocean of misery, who illuminates the world, who is compassionate toward the deluded, and who has begun his work of compassion.
From that time forth, the minister shall also be daily honored by the lords of the gods and asuras, exceedingly inviolable,
happy, and certainly protected from wicked, fierce spirits and the like.

Through the composition of this dark-colored *sādhana* of the glorious Raktayamāntaka, whatever merit has been acquired by me from drinking the words of the incomparable true guru according to the oral tradition—
may that, through Vairocanarakṣita, arise for the sake of the complete attainment of all goals of the world.
[The Buddhas,] whose bodies are submerged in the mire of existence and who are the enemies of the darkness of the afflictions—
[namely, the defects such as passion and so forth].
Oṃ ā& ji& kha& vu& hū&: the mantra for the empowerment of the samaya. Oṃ hrīḥ ṣṭrīḥ vikṛtānana hū& hū& phaṭ phaṭ svāhā. Oṃ.
Yamāntaka hūṃ phaṭ! The *Svādhiṣṭhāna-raktayamāri-sādhana* is completed.

Homage to Raktayamāri! Having bowed to him who stands in the *pratyālīḍha* posture, whose upward-pointing crest of hair and manes cause the stars to tremble, who wears a garland of skulls and a terrifying serpent, who is formidable with his raised staff-like right hand, and who is embraced by Prajñā.
For the sake of those who hold the view that the self is identical with Raktayamāri, we shall explain its sādhana.
Having stayed in cremation grounds, forests, mountain caves, or in delightful mansions, the mantra-practitioner should then,
within his own mind, visualize a red syllable *HŪṂ*— arisen from the form of the sky and surmounting the sun— emitting infinite, surging rays of light.
One should worship that infinite multitude of Buddhas, made manifest by their rays of light within the midst of the bodhisattva conduct in the sky,
with abundant flowers arising from the lake of one's own mental focus.
And by means of the seven types of consciousness.

538) That which is about to be described is the subduer of enemies, who eclipses the splendor of the exceedingly crimson new moon, the full moon, and the twilight; [k:
...the worshipper of the moon... k and g: repeat the concluding portion of the previous *sādhana*]
Having worshipped [the deities] from those submerged in the ocean of suffering up to the conclusion following the present *sādhana*, he—
possessing a mind of loving-kindness, compassion, and sympathetic joy— becomes equanimous, having indeed withdrawn all that was aroused.
In the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu).
Then, having realized that everything is empty, resembling the stainless and vast sky of autumn, one should perform the recitation of the mantra:
*Oṃ, all phenomena are pure by nature; I am pure by nature.*
Furthermore, in order to suppress the view of a real self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) that takes the form of one's own body, the mantra-practitioner should then meditate on the mantra in this way:
Oṃ, I am of the nature of the vajra of the wisdom of emptiness. Then, having relied on the power of my former vows to protect the world,
from that [emptiness] arises the form of a lotus, and upon it, the orb of the sun.
A white syllable *hūṃ*, its stem extremely dense, as if adorned with a garland of fresh flowers dripping with blood from its swaying head.
Then, having indeed transformed [the offering] with all these [mantras], one should meditate upon oneself in the form of a hero,
with a fierce face and terrifying, jagged fangs,
or as one who strikes fear into the three worlds with three eyes.
It produces hundreds of thunderclaps through its loud, mocking laughter, made terrifying by the crests of existence.
I then pay homage to that Durdamana, who holds in his right hand a white staff marked with a *hūṃ* syllable born from the syllable *hūṃ*, and in his other hand a skull-cup filled with blood.

One should meditate upon Him who is reddish with radiance, whose thick upward-pointing tail is as firm as the binding of the pure hero-scarf of the lord of serpents, and whose tawny mane of formidable manes is quivering.

His tongue is lolling, his mouth is filled with the syllable HŪṂ, and from its thick and fierce base, a terrible poison spreads forth.
Having thus meditated in one's mind upon Raktayamāri, who is complete with himself, clad in a single tiger skin,
with his waist bound by a fierce, prominent serpent, and adorned with lordly serpents,
[one should visualize him] born from the *hūṃ* syllable of the vajra with fierce rays.
One should meditate upon [the deity] holding a blazing staff, with feet accompanied by mantras, and marked with the syllable HŪM.
Thereafter, she was embraced by her own Wisdom (Prajñā), who had been beheld by Madana, and who possessed two excellent arms— one red and one black— shining with the syllable *Hūṃ*;
she, of upright intellect, was herself embraced by him with the impetuous flash of the secret lotus born from the red syllable *Āḥ*, and he was single-faced.
"Clearly" refers to the final limit; it is the form embraced by the wisdom of the rays streaming forth from one who is possessed, through the yoga of the *sampuṭa* (enclosure) shape.
Here, however, one should visualize below the navel an eight-petaled lotus.
The syllable Hrīḥ is situated upon her white lotus, which spreads with a reddish hue.
Having thus visualized his own form as that of a deity with a terrifying face and tawny beard,
he should recite the mantra which is like a lamp of great passion.
Oṃ! Through the passion of all the Tathāgatas, I am of the vajra-nature.
[I invoke] the fashioned Yakṣa Mahākāla, the red-bodied Yamāntaka.
By meditating with constant yoga, one enjoys the fruit before long.
The five Sugatas with flickering forms, radiating and withdrawing intense rays of light;
adorned with a king of serpents and outstretched hands, their hands further embellished by terrifying staffs.
With a mane possessing the luster of a mass of golden lightning, his crest formed by a circle of pure skulls,
he has two arms and one face, with palms joined together in reverence, accompanied by Sahajā who possesses a radiance identical to his own.

One should contemplate this enemy, the Destroyer, by means of these substances of the Samaya: the five nectars together with the five meats, beginning with excrement and urine, which are the supreme illuminators.
If poetry, happiness, wisdom, fortitude, sovereignty over the earth, or even anything else is desired, all that arises from the *raktayamāri-samādhi*; there is no doubt that it exists here.

Thus, the yogi, joined with the practice of Raktayamāri, may go anywhere— even to a remote, vast mountain, a cremation ground, or a terrifying place— where he is then difficult to conquer by predatory creatures,
spirits, hosts of rākṣasas, or even by gods and asuras.
His hand is adorned with a vajra whose tip is matted with blazing, flickering flames, just as [the Buddha's hand was].

Weary from meditation, that mantra-practitioner should recite the King of Mantras— which, like the sun, destroys the dense darkness of accumulated dullness— emanating from the seed-syllable of the mind:
*oṃ hrīḥ ṣṭrīḥ vikṛtānana hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ svāhā*.

For the sake of the well-being of sentient beings, the yogi, having suddenly taken the form of the Blessed One as his object of focus and beheld it, should then offer the bali to the guardians of the directions while bound by the vajra-mudrā.
Oṃ, *hrīḥ* to Indra; *ṣṭrīḥ* to Yama; *vi* to Varuṇa; *kṛ* to Kubera;
*ta* to Īśāna; *ā* to Agni; *naiṛtye* to Nairṛti; *vāyavye* to Vāyu; *na* to Candra; *hūṃ* to Arka; *phaṭ* to Brahmāṇī; *phaṭ* to Vasundharā.
Vemacitrine svāhā! To all beings, hā hā hī hī hūṃ hūṃ heṃ heṃ svāhā!—this is the *bali* mantra.
Having quickly recited this here, may the stainless merit that I have acquired by means of this practice be attained by those who have fallen [into lower realms].

Possessing the true Dharma, it serves as a substitute for a bridge for those wishing to cross to the far shore of the ocean of existence— the source of extreme suffering for the three worlds of living beings.
The *Āryayamārisādhana* is completed.
This work is by the feet of the alms-gathering monk Guṇākaragupta.
Homage to Kṛṣṇayamāri!
Those whose minds are not wicked do not easily resort to the path of the disciples because of their entirely gentle disposition.
Thus, I, being devoted, perpetually bow down to him by whom the form of Yamāri was clearly manifested.
At the request of another, this practice is performed by me;
for a compassionate person does not regard his own strength even when performing what is difficult to do.

Having become the glorious enemy of Yama, one who is thus engaged in yoga, thinking "I shall make this entire world of such a nature," beholds the primordial seed-syllable within the sun in his own heart;
having performed worship to the Jinas, being possessed of vast compassion, [he is surrounded] on all sides by their splendors.
Seated before them, one should perform the going for refuge in the Three Jewels with all one's being.
The Three Jewels are my refuge; I confess all my misdeeds;
I rejoice in the merit of the world; and I set my mind upon the enlightenment of a Buddha.
Because it is devoid of the characteristic of emptiness and because the causeless is defective,
there is no aspiration anywhere, since it is not an object of reasoning.
Oṃ, I am of the nature of the vajra of the wisdom of emptiness.
Within the hollow of the source of phenomena (dharmodayā), there is a caitya situated in the center of a universal lotus and vajra;
within its interior, upon a lunar disc, the yogi should meditate on the syllable HŪṂ as a vajra.
Oṃ, I am of the nature of the Vajra. From that, he emanated Vajradhara together with his consort, having blue and reddish faces, with a white central face.
Having correctly and thoroughly visualized [him] seated upon the vajra-throne, marked with the signs of a vajra, a sword, a lotus, and excellent jewels;
Having clearly visualized oneself as the three-syllable mantra encased within two *hoḥ* syllables,
with spheres of light rays emerging and filling all directions;
The knower of the ritual should enter through his mouth; then he should proceed swiftly into that lotus.
Through the union with its rays, the parents dissolve; then, here, this song of the deities of the directions [arises].
O Vajracitta, Lord of the World, protect me within the realm of sentient beings through your desire for great purpose and delightful pleasure!
O Great Bond, progenitor of beings, desire me if you so wish!
O Mañjunātha, you are life itself; O Vajrakāya, you possess a wheel of limbs dear to many beings,
and you perceive for the sake of the Buddhas the ultimate meaning of awakening and the welfare of others.
O Mañjunātha, if you desire my life, then love me with passion according to the convention of passion.
O Vajravāc, you who are compassionate for the welfare of all and always engaged in performing deeds for the sake of the world;
O Samantabhadra, desire me in the practice of sexual union, if you wish for my life, O Mañjunātha!
O Vajra-body, supreme of commitments, for the sake of great benefit, ornament of the lineage of perfect enlightenment, you who are compassionate with equanimity;
desire me, O treasury of qualities, who am like a mine of many jewels, if you wish for my life, O Lord Mañjuśrī!
Having accepted the Vedic injunction, one partakes of the essential body of the meaning of one's own mantra.
Endowed with the heart that begins with *bhā* (bhāvanā), one is united with the self that is the source of auspiciousness.

There, having visualized the forms of one's own deities and having caused them to enter by means of the gathered rays [of light] according to the ritual rule, one shall become Yamāri, most terrifying.
Resembling the neck of a mature peacock, with his left side white and the other red,
he is seated upon a lotus of the universe in the posture of the wrathful paryaṅka.
Possessing the great bliss of the elixir from tasting the innate Vidyādharī,
his hair is tawny and blazing upward, and his eyebrows, beard, and eyes are tawny.
Clad in the attire of a multitude of lordly serpents, with teeth as white as lotus stalks,
he holds a mallet and a sword in his right hands, while grasping a lotus and a jewel in his left.

Oṃ, I am of the nature of the vajra-dharmadhātu. One should meditate upon *kṣiṃ*, *jaṃ*, *khaṃ*, *gaṃ*, as well as *kṣaṃ*, *saṃ*, *raṃ* within the eyes and other sense organs. Likewise, one should place *jaḥ*, *hūṃ*, *vaṃ*, *hoḥ*, as well as *khaṃ* and *raṃ*, upon external objects such as forms (*rūpa*) and so forth. And among the elements, one should likewise place *loṃ*, *māṃ*, *pāṃ*, *tāṃ*. Now, *vuṃ*, *āṃ*, *jiṃ*...

One should purify the five aggregates with the syllables *khaṃ* and *hūṃ*. Having meditated upon the Lords born from the syllables *hūṃ*, *āḥ*, and *oṃ*—located respectively in the heart, the speech, and the crown of the head, and situated in the centers of the vajra, lotus, and wheel—one should recite this mantra:
*oṃ sarvatathāgatacittavajrasvabhāvātmako ’ham*; *oṃ sarvatathāgatavāgvajrasvabhāvātmako ’ham*.

Oṃ, I am of the nature of the vajra-body of all Tathāgatas. Then, having visualized the Buddhas situated within the expanse of the sky, by means of those [emanations] arising from the mantra at the heart—
By means of the water from the lotuses released from the tips of the hands of all the goddesses, which had arisen from the rays emitted by him.
With all his limbs sprinkled [with nectar], and with the Lotus-Crested One presiding over his crown through his majestic power,
the yogi should then continuously manifest the five families within the various parts of his body.

At the crown of the head, as well as in the middle of the breasts, the navel, the secret place, and down to the feet, there are the seed-syllables of the Goddess known as Oṃ, Hūṃ, Svā, Ā, and Hāḥ. With the vajra produced from the syllable Hūṃ, by means of the secret lotus fashioned from it, and through the bliss of passion with the Goddess, one [should worship] all the Buddhas residing within the interior of the entire expanse of space with the mantra: *Oṃ sarvatathāgatānurāgeṇa*.

"I am of the nature of the vajra-svabhāva. Having placed the Buddhas within lotuses by means of the vajra-lotus-mudrās, one should worship the Buddhas according to their own nature with forms and other qualities arising from their radiance. *Oṃ sarvatathāgatapūjāvajrasvabhāvātmako 'ham*.

Having perceived all things, both the stable and the moving, as being devoid of the relationship between the signified and the signifier, one should praise the Buddhas with these [verses] endowed with the perfection of truly existent qualities.
Akṣobhya, great wisdom-vajra, vajra-realm, great Buddha,
triple-maṇḍala, supreme among the three vajras, Vajra of Sound— homage be to you!
Vairocana, great purity, vajra-peace, great delight;
O supreme among the supremely luminous by nature, Vajra of Hatred, homage be to you!
O King of Jewels, most profound, stainless as the vajra of space and the sky,
pure by nature and untainted— homage be to you, Vajra of Desire!
O Vajrāmita, great passion, free from conceptual construction, holder of the space-vajra;
you who have attained the perfection of passion, O Bhāṣavajra, homage be to you!
O you who are born from the unfailing vajra, who fulfill all hopes,
who are born from the nature of purity— Vajrasattva, homage be to you!
Having meditated upon the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) situated within a skull inside a wheel of wind and fire,
accompanied by the syllable *praṇava* (oṃ), one should [use] that very [substance] recited with the three-syllabled mantra together with the word *sārcis*.
One should satisfy both oneself and others, and then recite the mantra with vibrating energy;
having performed worship, one should withdraw [the visualization] at the end and dismiss it into the nature of one's own yoga.
By this auspicious moon-disk thus composed through its arrangement,
may the world, endowed with blessings, attain the supreme and eternal state of the Jina.
The Sadhana of Śrīmad-Yamāri.
The work of the venerable Maṅgalasena.
Homage to Yamāntaka!
Having produced the seed-syllable *hūṃ* up to the point of purification, one visualizes Yamāntaka— arisen from the syllable *hūṃ* situated upon a sun disk—
as wrathful, with hair standing erect, black in color, six-faced, six-armed, and six-legged, mounted upon a buffalo.

One should visualize [the deity] standing in the *pratyālīḍha* posture, adorned with human skulls and headless trunks, possessing an extremely terrifying form, and clothed in a tiger skin; holding a sword, a mallet, and a vajra in the right hands, and a bell, a vajra-noose, and a club in the left hands; and with Akṣobhya upon his crown. Then, one should bind the *samaya-mudrā*.

Having formed the *sampuṭa-añjali* mudrā, one should spread the two thumbs and bend the third joints of the pair of middle fingers. One should recite the mantra: *oṃ hrīḥ ṣṭrīḥ vikṛtānana hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ svāhā*. *The Sādhana of Kṛṣṇayamāri.*

(p. 547) First of all, the practitioner, seated upon a comfortable seat, should visualize within his own heart a solar disc arisen from the syllable *raṃ* of a red appearance, and above that, the blue syllable *hūṃ*.

Having arranged [the deities], relying upon the Gurus, Buddhas, and Bodhisattvas— such as Yamāntaka and others who arise from the rays of light of the syllable *hūṃ*— and having honored them with flowers and other offerings and paid homage,
one should perform the going for refuge and so forth, and then meditate on emptiness: *oṃ*.

"I am of the nature of the vajra of the knowledge of emptiness. Immediately thereafter, one should visualize a sun mandala arising from the syllable *rakta* (red), upon which is the syllable *hūṃ*. From the transformation of that [syllable], one should visualize a blue staff marked with a vajra, presided over by the syllable *hūṃ*, preceded by the entry of all Tathāgatas impelled by the rays of light from the syllable *hūṃ*. Having transformed all of this, [one becomes] Yamāri.
One should contemplate oneself as Yamāri, standing in the *pratyālīḍha* posture, with one face, two arms, and blue in color;
holding in the right hand a raised blue staff marked with a vajra, and in the left hand a noose with the threatening gesture (*tarjanī*) at the heart.
One should meditate on such a Yamāri, whose form radiates and reabsorbs [light], standing upon a sun disk atop a multi-petaled lotus, mounted upon a buffalo.

Then, within the sun-maṇḍala at the heart of the Blessed One, there is Nīladaṇḍa, transformed from the syllable *HŪṂ* and empowered by the syllable *HŪṂ*. Having illuminated the world with rays of light emanating from the syllable *HŪṂ*, one should cause them to re-enter that very same place. In this manner, one should perform the radiation and withdrawal [of light] as desired, following the ritual procedures for the pledge (*samaya*) and so forth. Thus...
One should meditate twice, thrice, or four times a day and recite the mantra: *oṃ hrīḥ ṣṭrīḥ vikṛtānana hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ svāhā*. The *Sādhana* of Kṛṣṇayamāri is completed.
By him, out of compassion, even that which was internally like frost was displayed as fierce toward those people who were to be disciplined by force.
May my prostration be to that Yamāntaka, who is the dancer in the drama of the methods for benefiting the entire world.
At the outset, that excellent practitioner, seated comfortably upon a cushion in a meditation chamber fragrant with delightful perfumes,
should— with a concentrated mind— meditate within his own heart upon the orb of the fierce-rayed sun, originating from a red form.
Above that, having worshipped Yamāntaka and the others, who are produced from hundreds of rays of light from the syllable *HŪṂ*— blue in color and possessing rays of light situated above it—
one should prostrate with devotion using various kinds of mentally created flowers, incense, lamps, and so forth.
[I worship].
One should perform the confession of previously committed sins and so forth; thereafter, one should contemplate the entire world as empty.
Then, with the mantra-word "Oṃ Śūnyatājñānavajrasvabhāvātmako ’ham," one should respectfully cultivate the meditation on the nature of the self.
A blue staff marked with a vajra in the form of a blue *hūṃ* syllable, arising from a fierce red shape;
it holds a *hūṃ* syllable upon the staff, radiating a mass of shimmering light rays,
which enters the eyes of all the Tathāgatas thus impelled.
Having seen all this and subsequently transformed it, one should quickly contemplate oneself in the form of Yamāri.
With a blue body, one face, and two arms, he is wrathful; in his right hand, he holds a blue staff marked with a vajra.
In his left hand at his heart, he holds a noose with the index finger;
his lotus-face is made tawny by a mass of eyebrows and beard;
and the region of his private parts is covered by a garment of tiger-skin.
With a serpent-like tongue flickering within the interior of his mouth.
Seated upon a solar throne atop a lotus with six petals, she is expert in treading upon the fierce Mahiṣa;
she has a protruding belly, a face with formidable fangs, a dwarfish stature,
and three eyes that rival the orb of the sun.
He whose ornaments are formed by eight furious serpents, who wears a thick, tawny garland of jackals strung together with a row of skulls,
who has a long necklace made of freshly dripping human heads, and who has conquered the army of Māra with the savor of his loud, boisterous laughter.
Thereafter, having reflected,
one should visualize a blue staff joined with the syllable *hūṃ* situated upon a sun disk located in the heart of the Blessed One;
then, illuminating the entire universe with rays of light from the *hūṃ* situated therein, one should once again effect its entry [into that staff] without delay.
Having thus performed the emanation and withdrawal at will in due order,
and having again contemplated all this together with the four junctures (*saṃdhyā*) according to the rule, one who is weary—
One should perform the recitation of the mantra exactly as prescribed.
By this merit, which has arisen from my composition of this brief sādhana of the Blessed One Yamāri, may the glory of loving-kindness be born here.
By that [merit], may the entire universe become the form of the Blessed One, the Enemy of Yama; and may I too, before long, become the Enemy of Yama.
In this regard, the king of mantras is: Oṃ hrīḥ ṣṭrīḥ vikṛtānana hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ svāhā.
[The Sadhana of Kṛṣṇayamāri.]

Having prostrated with my head before the glorious Lord Yamāri— who is inwardly composed of compassion yet outwardly possesses a fierce form for the sake of sentient beings— I shall write his sādhana for the sake of those who desire it.
First, however, the practitioner, with a joyful mind, seated on a comfortable seat and having made his vow,
should worship the Protectors with various collections of offerings arising from the syllable HŪṂ placed upon the heart.
Then, having performed the confession of sins and so forth before them, and having contemplated the void,
one should first visualize the wind-maṇḍala, which has the appearance of smoke, arises from it, and resembles a bow.
Furthermore, the red mandala known as fire, which originates from the seed-syllable *raṃ* and is triangular in shape.
The Varuṇa-maṇḍala, born from the syllable *vaṃ*, is like a water-pot, white, and facing downwards.
The form of Mount Mahendra, arising from the syllable *laṃ*, is perfectly level, beautifully yellow,
and square in shape; then,
from the syllables *hūṃ* and *suṃ*, there arises King Sumeru with its eight peaks, in due order.
[Previously omitted: k, ḍh, k, b] ||

Having reflected upon the previously mentioned mandalas of wind and so forth in successive order from above downwards, one should then [visualize] the vajra-ground arisen from the syllable *hūṃ*, together with its enclosure and fivefold lattice, in the central portion.
[One should visualize] Mañjuvajra, born from the syllable *dhīḥ* situated within the orb of the moon perfected by the syllable *a*;
a youth and hero, with his left hand holding a book at his heart and his right hand raised, brandishing a beautiful sword.
Having meditated upon him— whose limbs are yellowish-red, who wears five white silken garments, who sits in the adamantine posture, and who is exceedingly peaceful— one should then,
with the mind fixed on his heart, [visualize] from the orb of the rising sun born from the syllable *dhīḥ* situated there.
With red rays of light emanating from all sides, they pervade the triple world and remain perfectly established.
Having summoned and brought forth the wrathful deities, the Vidyās, the Jinas, and the Bodhisattvas, [one should place them] within the solar disc.
Having been suddenly absorbed into that [sun], having become one with it, it arises once again in the sun—
extremely radiant with shimmering rays and red in color.
And there it is even more extensively spread out.
From the syllable *hūṃ* arises a black, formidable vajra containing the syllable *hūṃ* within it, emitting a manifold web of light rays;
then, having emanated from that the Jinas and other Bodhisattvas, and by means of them once again—
Those abiding in the six realms of existence.
Having established all sentient beings in awakening, having disciplined them, and having led them all into the vajra,
one should immediately transform that into a vajra and meditate upon Yamāri as two-armed and one-faced.
In his left hand he holds a vajra-noose with the index finger extended, and in his right hand he brandishes a vajra-staff;
he stands in the ālīḍha posture, treading upon Yama, who is lying face up as if falling.
The chief queen.
Dwarf-like, with a face distorted by fangs, possessing a massive belly and a long, hanging tongue;
with tawny-brown beard and hair standing erect, with brown eyebrows and a pair of intensely red eyes.
He is black, wrathful, with a frown upon his forehead, and his limbs are adorned by eight hissing nāgas.
He wears the skin of a tiger as a garment, has a skull as his crest-ornament, is dark blue in color, and bears a garland of severed heads hanging from his neck.
Terrible, blazing with the radiance of the fire at the end of an eon, and instilling fear even in the fearsome;
fierce, yet bowed down by hosts of Buddhas and by assemblies of supramundane deities.
Terrifying all the gods, asuras, and others on every side with his loud, boisterous laughter,
he put to flight the entire hosts of fierce māras throughout the three worlds without exception.

Thus, always devoted to meditation, that mantra-practitioner, reciting the mantra day and night without hesitation and remaining in charnel grounds and other such places through the yoga of reality, being pure and established in the commitment (samaya), will certainly attain accomplishment.
By whatever merit I have gained from composing this *Sādhanamālā*,
may all people in the world become heroic Yamāris, swiftly acting to destroy the mass of fierce sufferings of the universe.
Samlāna, k, b: saṃsāra.
The *Sādhana* of Kṛṣṇayamāri is completed.

First of all, the mantra-practitioner, endowed with compassion, seated in a comfortable posture, should visualize the Blessed One Yamāntaka as depicted on a cloth painting or similar support before him, and having beheld the gurus, Buddhas, and Bodhisattvas, he should worship them with various offerings.

Having prostrated, one should perform the confession of sins and so forth. Immediately thereafter, having resolved upon intrinsic purity through the mantra beginning with *svabhāvaśuddhāḥ*, and having meditated upon the selflessness of all phenomena (*sarvadharmanairātmya*), one should recite one’s own mantra:
*oṃ śūnyatājñānavajrasvabhāvātmako ’ham*. Then, in one’s own heart, upon a moon-maṇḍala arisen from the syllable *a*, [one should visualize...]
Having visualized a blue syllable *HŪṂ* situated upon a sun disk, and having seen that *HŪṂ*, one should crush the obstructors with its rays; then,

having emanated wrathful deities in the form of Yamāntaka who are intent on accomplishing the welfare of sentient beings, one should instantly contemplate oneself as Yamāntaka through the transformation of that [syllable]— black, with three faces and six arms, or in some cases, six faces.
He has six legs, a face made terrifying by fangs, and blood-red eyes; his three right arms hold a discus, a sword, and a club,
while his three left arms hold a vetālī, an axe, and a noose.

Holding a sword, a mallet, and a vajra in his right hands, and in his left hands a bell, a vajra-noose, and a pestle; sometimes his tawny hair is tied upward and his crown is adorned with a garland of severed heads; he has ornaments fashioned from eight lordly nāgas and bears a crown of Akṣobhya, seated upon a solar disc atop a multi-colored lotus.

Having visualized [the deity] standing in the *pratyālīḍha* posture within a reddish-hued mandala, one should behold the syllable *HŪṂ* in the moon-mandala between the breasts. One should then behold the three syllables *OṂ ĀḤ HŪṂ*, white, red, and black respectively, within the mandalas of body, speech, and mind. Immediately thereafter—
Having worshipped oneself with the goddesses emerged from the seed-syllable at one's own heart,
and having offered praise, one should recite the mantra: Oṃ hrīḥ ṣṭrīḥ vikṛtānana hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ svāhā.
The Sadhana of Kṛṣṇayamāri.
p. 555) 279. [This sādhana is given twice in the ḍ, dh, dh, k, ḍh, and g manuscripts.
Oṃ, homage to Yamāntaka!
Having bowed to the Lord Yamāntaka— the hero adorned with a garland of skulls and fierce ornaments such as serpents— his sādhana is here written down.
Seated comfortably on a pleasant seat, having placed the syllable *hūṃ* in blue at his heart,
he should worship the Lord before him with devotion through the specific rites of recitation and worship.
Having performed the confession of sins and so forth in its presence,
one should instantly perceive the entire world as being devoid of intrinsic nature from every perspective.
Arising from the seed-syllable in the heart and from the [central] emblem, he has his lotus-feet in the *pratyālīḍha* posture;
his face is terrifying with a frown, and his beard and hair are tawny.
With three faces and lolling tongues, terrifying with formidable fangs;
red-eyed, with a large belly, and possessing the luster of a fresh blue cloud.
He stands within the orb of the sun, his head adorned with bones,
clad in a tiger-skin garment, short of stature, and the remover of all pride.
It filled all the quarters of space with the great splendor of the sun's radiance,
resembling the fierce fire at the end of an eon with its rows of blazing flames.
He bears a discus, sword, mace, radiant staff,
axe, and noose in his six divine hands, which are arranged on the right and left.
One should meditate, free from fear, upon the enemy of Yama, the crusher of Māra— wrathful, terrible, and exceedingly fierce, with his throat filled with the syllable *hūṃ*.
A knower of mantras who always recites twenty-five thousand mantras with an undistracted mind attains his desired accomplishment.
And this mantra is accomplished for practitioners through the rite of preliminary service;
its color has not been stated here according to the specific ritual action, because it would be too extensive.
And that reality (tattva) should be contemplated according to the teacher’s instruction for the sake of attaining one's desired goal;
it should be known with effort by the steadfast. One should consume all five kinds of meat as an offering of oblations, and this should be performed at the four junctions of the day.
[It is] to be performed.
Thus is the mantra for recitation: Oṃ hrīḥ ṣṭrīḥ vikṛtānana hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā.
The *Yamāntakasādhana* is complete.
Homage to Yamāntaka.

First, the practitioner, having performed the purification of the mouth and other preliminary rites, should visualize a black syllable *yaṃ* upon a moon disc arising from the syllable *aḥ* in his own heart.
Having summoned the gurus, Buddhas, and others with its rays and worshipped them, he should perform the confession of misdeeds and so forth.

[One should meditate]. Then, the yogin, whose nature consists of the syllable *yaṃ*, having brought emptiness (*śūnyatā*) face-to-face and having empowered it, should recollect his vow. Thereafter, having visualized a sun disk arising from the syllable *raṃ* and a vajra-mallet born from the syllable *hūṃ*, marked with its own seed-syllable, he should visualize the vajra-ground produced by that.
One should visualize a vajra-fence and a vajra-canopy; in their center,
one should perceive a moon-maṇḍala consisting of the thirty-two vowels and consonants, which gives rise to the thirty-two marks of a Great Man and has the nature of wisdom (prajñā).

Above that, another [mandala] is produced, doubled by the eighty secondary marks (*anuvyañjana*) of purity, and further doubled by the consonants *ḍa*, *ḍha*, *da*, *dha*, *ya* [and *ra*, *la*, *va*], along with the letters beginning with *ka*.

One should meditate upon the lunar disc as the form of skillful means (*upāya*), radiating infinite rays of light. Then, within the sun produced from the perfection of both [the moon and the disc], one should visualize [the deity] born from the blue syllable *HŪṂ*:
dark blue like a fresh rain-cloud, pot-bellied, with intensely tawny eyebrows, beard, and hair standing erect, and possessing formidable fangs.
Seated upon a pot-bellied buffalo as large as a *kharva*, wearing a tiger skin and an upper garment of the skin of the lord of beasts, he is extremely terrifying;

his body vibrates with the five wrathful deities created from the rays of light of his own form, he has made the king of serpents into an ornament, and he wears a garland of half-human heads from which blood is dripping.

He has six arms; with the right hands he holds a mallet, a sword, and a vajra, and with the three left hands he holds a threatening gesture (*tarjanī*), a noose, and a pestle. He has six faces: the first is blue, the upper one is also blue, and the faces on the right and left are respectively white, yellow, red, and black in sequence.
All his faces have red, circular eyes with three pupils;

he performs a dance with two feet in the *pratyālīḍha* posture, while with the other two he assumes the *sattvaparyaṅka* posture; he stands in the midst of a blazing sun, trampling upon the obstructing spirits (*vighnas*).

[She wears] a most terrifying garland of skulls, well-joined with eight cranial bowls. Following that, those born from the seed-syllables KṢIṂ, JAṂ, KHAṂ, LAṂ, SKAṂ, and SAṂ— namely Kṣitigarbha, Vajrapāṇi, Khagarbha, Lokeśvara, Viṣkambhin, and Samantabhadra— are [placed] in the eyes and ears.

In the nose, tongue, breasts, and navel, [one should visualize the deities] holding a wheel, a thunderbolt, a jewel, a lotus, and a hundred-pointed arrow in their right hands, while the left hand displays the *tarjanī* (threatening) mudrā;
they are white, black, yellow, red, dark green, and white respectively, and are seated upon moons. Thereafter, [visualize them] on the head, throat, and heart.
Abiding in body, speech, and mind, seated upon moon discs, and arisen from Oṃ Āḥ Hūṃ,
they are white, red, and black in color; holding a wheel and a lotus with their right and left hands respectively, they should be visualized performing the tarjanī mudrā.

Then, having summoned the Jñānasattva by means of rays from the seed-syllable in the heart and visualized him as being of one flavor (*samarasatā*), one should meditate for a long time on oneself as having Akṣobhya upon the crown of the head. When weariness arises, one should recite the mantra. In this regard, it is as follows:
The mantra is: *oṃ hrīḥ ṣṭrīḥ vikṛtānana hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ svāhā*. Then, having dismissed [the deity], one should rise.
Thus ends the sādhana of Yamāntaka.

First of all, the practitioner, seated on a comfortable seat, should visualize a solar disc arisen from the syllable *rakta* (red) at his own heart; having placed upon it the blue syllable *hūṃ*, and having invoked Vighnāri by means of the rays of light from the *hūṃ*,
he should pay homage to and worship the Gurus, Buddhas, and Bodhisattvas with flowers and other offerings.

Having performed the going for refuge and so forth, one should meditate on emptiness with the mantra: *oṃ śūnyatājñānavajrasvabhāvātmako ’ham*. Immediately thereafter, one should visualize a red syllable *hūṃ* upon a sun-maṇḍala born from the letter *ra*, which transforms into a vajra presided over by the syllable *hūṃ*.

Having first caused all the Tathāgatas to enter by means of the rays of light impelled by the syllable *HŪṂ*, one should transform all this into the ritual action and contemplate oneself as Vighnāntaka, standing in the *pratyālīḍha* posture,
with one face, two arms, blue in color, and holding a noose with the threatening finger in the left hand.
With a raised vajra in his right hand, he is terrifying, with tawny hair standing erect; then, in the heart of the Blessed One,
upon a solar disc, is a vajra transformed from the syllable *hūṃ* and empowered by the syllable *hūṃ*.
One should meditate upon the Enemy of Obstacles (Vighnāri) in such a state, his form radiating and withdrawing [light], standing upon a sun disk atop a lotus with a thousand petals.
One should meditate on him twice, thrice, or four times daily, preceded by the ritual procedures beginning with the commitment (samaya). Oṃ āḥ Vighnāntakṛt hūṃ.
This is the *Sādhana* of Vighnāntaka.
Homage to Yamāntaka!
Oṃ, to Indra Hrīḥ, to Yama Ṣṭrīḥ, to Varuṇa Vi, to Kubera Kṛ,
to Īśāna Ta, to Agni Ā, to Nairṛti Na, to Vāyu Na, to Candra Hūṃ, to Arka Hūṃ, to Brahmā.
[To the Brahman] phaṭ! To Vasudhārā phaṭ! To Vaimacitriṇī svāhā! To all beings hā! hī hī hūṃ hūṃ heṃ heṃ svāhā! This is the mantra for the bali offering. Whatever is eaten, all that—
It should be offered to Yamāri.
This is the bali mantra of Yamāntaka.
p.

560) According to the previously mentioned procedure, upon a lunar disc, one should visualize [the deity] transformed from the yellow syllable *maiṃ*, seated upon a universal lotus (*viśvakamala*), with three faces, three eyes, and four arms; his right and left faces are black and white respectively, and he is golden-yellow in complexion.

Visualizing oneself in the form of Maitreya— seated in the sattvaparyaṅka posture, with two hands holding the gesture of exposition (vyākhyānamudrā), the right and left hands holding a flower and a cluster of blossoming *nāgakeśara* flowers respectively, and adorned with various ornaments— one should perform the mudrā. With both hands, [place them] separately at the breasts.
Having formed a fist, one should join the two index fingers, raised between the thumbs, in the shape of a flower. Then follows the mantra for recitation: Oṃ maiṃ Maitreya svāhā.
[The Maitreya-sādhana (this sādhana is given twice in Kh)]
Homage to Jambhala!

Having contemplated as before up to the limit of emptiness, one should meditate on the Blessed Lord Jambhala, born from the syllable JAṂ upon a moon disc atop an eight-petaled double lotus; he is golden-colored, pot-bellied, and adorned with all ornaments.

He holds a mongoose and a citron with his left and right hands, wears a crown of Ratnasambhava, and bears a garland of blue lotuses. On the petals in the east and other directions are Māṇibhadra, Pūrṇabhadra, Dhanada, and Vaiśravaṇa;
on the petals in the southeast and other directions—
Likewise, according to the stated sequence, [one should place] Kelimālī, Vicitrakuṇḍalī, Mukhendracara, and Indrāṇī.

And within those very [circles], one should visualize these yakṣiṇīs: Vasudhārā, Citrakālidattā, Asudattā, Āryā, Subhadrā, Guptā, Devī, and Sarasvatī. However, Vasudhārā is accompanied by Jambhala; all the yakṣiṇīs are like Vasudhārā, while the yakṣas are like Jambhala—having meditated thus.

One should recite the mantra. Among them, the mantras of the yakṣas are: Oṃ jambhalajalendrāya svāhā | Oṃ māṇibhadrāya svāhā | Oṃ pūrṇabhadrāya svāhā | Oṃ dhanadāya svāhā | Oṃ vaiśravaṇāya svāhā | Oṃ kelimāline svāhā | Oṃ vicitrakuṇḍaline svāhā | Oṃ...

Svāhā to Mukhendrā! Oṃ, svāhā to Carendrā! Now, the mantras of the yakṣiṇīs: Oṃ, svāhā to Vasudhāriṇī! Oṃ, svāhā to Candrakālī! Oṃ, svāhā to Dattā! Oṃ, svāhā to Sudattā! Oṃ, svāhā to Āryā! Oṃ, svāhā to Subhadrā!

Svāhā! Oṃ, to Guptā, svāhā! Oṃ, to Devī, svāhā! Oṃ, to Sarasvatī, svāhā! For those who meditate thus, recite [the mantra], and offer eight hundred handfuls of water at the three junctions of the day, she bestows sovereignty over the three worlds. Furthermore, for those who recite it in the midst of water at dawn before the cry of a crow has sounded—

There arises an abundance of inexhaustible wealth. Then, having drawn Vasudhārā together with the Yakṣiṇīs on one leaf and the Blessed Jambhala surrounded by Yakṣas on a second leaf, and having placed them within a casket, one should perform worship;
she will grant even the eight great siddhis.
Thus ends the sādhana of Jambhala.
p. 562) unclear p. 563)
[Not clear, p.
564] Immediately after the meditation on emptiness, [one visualizes] Jambhala, born from a yellow *jaṃ* syllable within a sun disk, having three faces and six arms.
