He wears a crown with a coiled lock of hair surmounted by Akṣobhya; he holds a citron, a goad, and an arrow in his three right hands;
with one of his first left arms he is embraced by Prajñā standing at his left side, and with his other two left arms...

Having visualized oneself as holding a water-jar, a mongoose, and a bow, and having superimposed that same form before oneself through meditation, one should meditate on Mahāvajradhara upon its head and, consecrating it with that substance, cause one hundred and eight handfuls of "Vajra-water" to fall. The mantra is: *oṃ jambhalajalendrāya svāhā*.
The Jambhala Sādhana according to another tradition.
According to the previously mentioned procedure, one should visualize within the moon at the heart the seed-syllable of the second [letter], which is the third [consonant], yellow in color,
presided over by the deity Śūnya, adorned with a crescent moon upon its head; from that very seed-syllable, the venerable Jambhala is produced.

Yellow in color, with two arms, holding a *bījapūraka* fruit in the right hand and a *nakulī* flower from which a rain of jewels falls in the left; wearing a crown adorned with the five Buddhas; treading upon two great treasures—a conch-shell and a skull-cup—both shaped like lotuses; and wearing a garland of blue lotuses.

One should visualize oneself in the form of Jambhala, adorned with all ornaments. One should contemplate oneself entering one's own house while raining down various jewels and other treasures. Then, one should form the mudrā: having formed fists with both hands, the middle joints of the middle fingers are bent.

The mudrā of Jambhala: Oṃ jambhalajalendrāya svāhā. With this mantra, one hundred and eight handfuls of water should be offered to the Blessed Lord. Afterwards, having performed worship, [recite] the mantra.
One should recite [the mantra]. Thereafter, one becomes a lord of great wealth; of this there is no doubt. The concise *Sādhana* of Śrī Jambhala is completed.

According to the previously mentioned procedure, having worshipped the Buddhas and others with rays of light emanating from the yellow syllable *jaṃ* on a moon disc upon a universal lotus in the heart— [that which has arisen]— and after the confession of sins and so forth,
one should manifest emptiness; then, in that very state, [one visualizes] that which arises from *jaṃ* upon a moon disc on a universal lotus.

The *bījapūraka* (citron) contains the seed; by means of its rays, having accomplished the welfare of various kinds of sentient beings, through that transformation, there appears Jambhala, golden in color, wearing a crown of the five Buddha-jewels, adorned with divine garments and ornaments,
two-armed and one-faced, holding a *bījapūraka* in his right hand, and in his left hand holding a mongoose from whose mouth various jewels are emerging.

Having visualized oneself as holding a garland of blue lotuses, with two yakṣas stationed on both sides raining down clusters of jewels, and with a jar containing clusters of jewels placed beneath one's feet, and being surrounded by many garlands of light rays—one should recite the mantra: *oṃ jambhalajalendrāya svāhā*. Having formed a fist with both hands...
By breaking the middle third of the joint with the mudrā, one should place it on the heart, throat, head, and the ūrṇā-hair-tuft.
Having thus meditated instantaneously even in the morning, one should offer one hundred and eight handfuls of water with this: *oṃ jambhalajalendradhanaṃ dehi svāhā*.
The Concise Sadhana of Jambhala
Homage to the glorious Jambhala, the bestower of all prosperity!
First of all, the practitioner of mantra should contemplate all objects and his own body as empty.
Immediately after that, there appears a slightly reddish lunar disc consisting of wisdom and means; this very same yakṣa-cart takes the form of an eight-petalled lotus.
In its center, from the syllable *vaṃ*, arises Vasudhārā, yellow in color, holding a cluster of grain in her hand, bestowing boons, adorned with all ornaments, and surrounded by eight yakṣiṇīs.

Namely: Bhadrā, Subhadrā, Guptā, Suguptā, Devī, Sarasvatī, and Āryā Candrakāntā— surrounded by these, the Great Goddess [visualizes] herself within the center of her bhaga by means of the syllable *jaṃ*, wearing the crowns of the five Buddhas, holding a citron in her right hand and a mongoose in her left, and likewise [visualizing] the five Tathāgatas.

With two feet, one should visualize the two great treasures, Śaṅkhamuṇḍa and Padmamuṇḍa, raining down jewels and other riches, situated in the region of one’s own home. One should visualize the yellow-colored Lord Śrī Jambhala, wearing a garland of blue lotuses, embraced by Vasudhārā, and emerging from the emission of the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*).

One should visualize the entire expanse of space pervaded by a mass of jewels. At the moment of emission, one should visualize Pūrṇabhadra of blue color in the eastern direction, Vaiśravaṇa of yellow color in the southern direction,
and Dhanada of red color in the western direction, in the northern direction.
One should visualize Maṇibhadra of yellow color in the southeast, Vicitrakuṇḍalin of red color in the southwest,

Kelimālin of blue color in the northwest, Pīta-carendra in the northeast, and Pītamukhendra in the [remaining] direction; all of these are situated in the midst of the vulvas of the eight yakṣiṇīs, raining down jewels, and should be meditated upon as resembling Jambhala.
At the eastern gate are Dhanada and Mahādhanada, naked,
with pendulous testicles, raining down jewels; at the southern gate are Padma and Mahāpadma.
At the western gate are Padmaka and Mahākelin (or Keli and Mālin according to some versions), and at the northern gate are Pūrṇa and Supūrṇa; these too have pendulous testicles.
One should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the mantra syllables and so forth of Lord Jambhala in their natural order: *Oṃ* at the crest-lock (*śikhā*), *Jaṃ* at the mouth.
*Bha-la* on the two arms, *ja* at the heart, *leṃ* at the navel, *drā-ya* on the two thighs, *svā-hā* on the two knees;
and likewise, *Māṇibhadra* on the head, *Vaiśravaṇa* on the two eyes, *Indra* situated on the face, *Pūrṇabhadra* between the breasts, and *Dhanada* at the navel.

The Yakṣa Keli­mālin is on the two thighs; Vicitra­kuṇḍalin is on the two feet; and Carendraka is on all the limbs. Lord Jambala is to be meditated upon as one's very own self. Now follows the placement of the syllables (akṣara-nyāsa): Oṃ at the head; Jlūṃ [K, G: hu] on the forehead; Blūṃ [Kh: ttlūṃ] on the two ears; and Saḥ on the back of the head.

One should perform the placement (*vinyāsa*). Now the hand-placement (*hastanyāsa*) is described: with the syllables of the deities—*oṃ maṇibandhe jluṃ* at the wrist, *bluṃ* in the middle of the hand, *saḥ* on the tips of all the fingers, and *sarvāṅgulīmūle* at the roots of all the fingers—and with the mantra *oṃ jambhalajalendrāya svāhā*.
The consecration (pratiṣṭhā) should be performed. On the index finger is Māṇibhadra; on the middle finger, Pūrṇabhadra;
on the ring finger, Dhanada; on the little finger, Vaiśravaṇa; likewise on the side of the hand, Mukhendra; at the wrist, Kelimālin; and on the thumb, Vicitrakuṇḍalin.
The lord of Cares (Carendraka) is on the ring finger and thumb; Jambhala-jalendraka is in the middle of the hand.

Regarding the five nectars beginning with Vajrodaka, in their absence, one may drink even Vajrodaka from a handful mixed with water; having drunk thus, one hundred and eight handfuls should be offered at the three junctions of the day. Before long, he becomes like Jambhala himself.

(568) Abounding in wealth and gold, he makes the earth full of riches. Having uttered "Oṃ jluṃ bluṃ saḥ," handfuls and other offerings should be given. If [the rite] is not successful, one should meditate on oneself as the illustrious Vajrahūṃkāra and [visualize] an image of Jambhala.

Having drawn [the figure] with poison, *rājikā* seeds, nimba leaves, *dhustūra* seeds, and charcoal from a cremation ground, one should meditate upon it. Likewise, one should dry it in the sun and subsequently heat it in the fire of a cremation ground. Even if one is angry, one will certainly achieve success.
The *Śrījambhalasādhana* is completed.
The Sādhana of Śrī Jambhala is completed.
Having meditated on the syllable *jaṃ* in yellow at the tip of the ring finger, and having meditated on Jambhala in the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) made of clay or other materials,

one should recite the syllable *jaṃ* one hundred and eight times while imagining that a stream of water from the ring finger’s base is being poured by the other hand, falling directly onto the breast and the crown of the head.
The Instruction on Jambhala of the Continuous Stream (Dhārājambhalopadeśa)

Having visualized the five Tathāgatas, produced from the five seed-syllables beginning with *vaṃ* situated upon a moon in his right hand, and having melted them together with the moon, one should manifest the well-known Jambhala arising from the syllable *jaṃ* before oneself; then, with the aforementioned liquid mixed with water, one should [sprinkle it] upon his head one hundred and eight times using the "widely opened half-fist" gesture with the index fingers extended.
One should pour out a handful [of water], whereby all prosperity comes to be.
This is the instruction of Jambhala.
The Jina Vairocana is renowned, as well as Ratnasambhava;
Amitābha, Amoghasiddhi, and Akṣobhya are also proclaimed.
The colors of these [deities] are white, yellow, red, green, and dark blue;
their mudrās are the Bodhyaṅgī, Varada, Dhyāna, Abhaya, and Bhūsparśa.
Having meditated upon the Tathāgatas arising from the five syllables— *vuṃ*, *āṃ*, *jiṃ*, *khaṃ*, *hūṃ*— located within the moon-disk held in the right hand,
one should visualize them in the form of five liquified essences.
Having meditated upon Jambhala, who has arisen from the syllable *jaṃ*, one should reverently take a handful of water,
recite his mantra, and offer it one hundred and eight times with milk.
The Ritual for Offering a Handful of Water to Jambhala.

Having invoked with "Oṃ Aḥ," one should [visualize] Jambhalanātha within one's own heart, by means of the previously mentioned *ākāra* mantra, arising from a *hūṃ* syllable— equal in color to an indragopa insect— situated in the center of a moon disc transformed from the letter *a*, which is itself in the center of a nine-spoked vajra formed by the *hūṃ* syllable.
Entering [the womb], he has the form of a withered child (or the form of Jambhala),
with unpierced ears, black in color, with tawny hair standing erect, short in stature, knitting his brows, and possessing fangs.

He wears a crown of Ratnasambhava and is adorned with ornaments of eight nāgas; he holds a nakulī in his left hand from which jewels and other things overflow, and in his right hand he holds a skull-cup filled with blood; the top of his head is golden in color, and he is adorned with various ornaments.

Having visualized oneself as Ucchuṣma, who bestows the wealth of those who have fallen [into misfortune], who supports [the world] with his feet, who emits showers of jewels and the like, and who is filled with a shimmering garland of radiating rays— one should contemplate the syllable *oṃ* produced from the right hand as a cart (*śakaṭa*), and the syllable *vaṃ* produced therefrom as a *bhadraghaṭa* (auspicious jar), as if it were speaking.

Holding the syllable *jaṃ* in the middle of his hand, he holds the syllable *bha* on the index finger, the syllable *la* on the middle finger, the syllable *ja* on the ring finger, and [the syllable *kha*] on the little finger. (p. 570)
The syllable *leṃ* is placed on the thumb, *drā* at the wrist, and then the syllable *ya*;

thus, "Oṃ svāhā" is the sequence for the visualization of the mantra-assignment (*mantranyāsa*). Having consecrated the mouth, one should offer water. "Oṃ jluṃ bluṃ svāhā" is the mantra for offering a handful of water. "Oṃ aindrāṇi mukhabhramari svāhā."

From the hand to the mouth, from the mouth to the hand—one should cause it to enter his mouth. By means of this practice, for the sake of cutting through the suffering of poverty of all sentient beings, one should meditate upon Jambhala; thus, one becomes Jambhala himself.
The Sadhana of Ucchuṣma-Jambhala.
What state of mind could there be for those whose hearts are struck by the suffering of poverty, even at the sight of the Sugata’s creation?
And so, as if out of anger, Jambhala assumed a withered form that inspired fear.
Having bowed to that Lord Jambhala, the swift fulfiller of all hopes,
who is a great hero in the form of a child, I shall clearly explain his sādhana.

Oṃ Aḥ! Having invoked [the deity], one should then meditate within one's own heart, in the center of a full moon that has been reborn, upon a nine-spoked vajra that radiates stainless light, born from the black syllable *HŪṂ*.
From the syllable *JAṂ*, which is like sapphire, a web of light rays fills the sky, appearing in the form of all the Ucchuṣmas, within the hub of that excellent vajra.
Then one should meditate upon the wrathful form as having two arms and a single face.
His infant body has the luster of a cloud; his face is knit with a frown, and his eyes are fixed upon a state of wrath.
He is large-limbed, black in color, naked, and terrifying with his formidable fangs.
His ears are pierced with earrings, his body is adorned by eight wrathful serpents,
he is short in stature, with tawny hair standing erect, possessing the brilliance of a flickering fire,
and the luster of a garland of diamonds.
With his body swallowed by Ghorā, holding a mace, and with a downward-facing mouth vomiting blood, he stands upon the earth treading with his two feet upon Kubera out of rage;
he is languid from drinking from a skull-bowl filled with blood, his hair stands on end with joy, and he presses down upon her whose mouth emits jewels.
[He should hold] the *nakulī* [flower] with his left hand.
[He is] the one who removes all the darkness of suffering through the luster of his jewels,
who is worshipped by Viṣṇu, Brahmā, Hara, Indra, the Daityas, sages, and the lords of the worlds,
and who is cherished by Lakṣmī and honored by celestial nymphs and yakṣa maidens.
The auspicious gift was given for the purpose of debate, not with the intention of sowing seeds in another's mind, nor for the sake of King Dhanada.

Having poured a handful of water into the mouth with the mantra *oṃ jluṃ svāhā*, one should draw that water back out from the mouth, place it in the hand, and recite comfortably: *oṃ aindrāṇi mukhabhramari svāhā*.
Again, with this very same mantra, one should offer one hundred and eight handfuls of water.
For six months, one who is faithful should give to Jambhala and also recite [the mantra].
Having offered water brought from him and having worshipped him thus, one should dismiss him.
Thus, through practice for six months with an undistracted mind, one who is devoted in heart should meditate; and at dawn, during the crowing of the crows,
he who offers cool water of perfect purity shall become equal to Ucchuṣma, and he shall always remove the suffering of all poverty with his very glance, free from obstacles.
Like a lord of wealth, he is the master of the worlds, uniquely skilled in the enlightened activities of a Buddha.
The *Sādhana* of Ucchuṣma-Jambhala is completed.
I bow at the feet of that Jambhala, who possesses a mass of pure qualities, whose form is inconceivable,
and before whom the lords of gods and asuras prostrate themselves.
Even the mere remembrances of him extinguish the forest fire of poverty with rains of jewels, gold, and fine garments.
Having performed purification, with his body scented and wearing clean garments, the practitioner, seated on a comfortable seat,
should cultivate loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, equanimity, emptiness, and so forth— all according to the ritual procedure— with a completely purified mind.

First, having invoked the pair of syllables *oṃ* and *aḥ*, which are white and red in color, into the center of the moon within one's own heart; and [having likewise invoked] the abode of the clearly manifest *hūṃ* syllable, which arises from the dark-blue *hūṃ* syllable, into the nine-spoked vajra situated in the courtyard of the sky.
From the seed-syllable *hūṃ*, which resembles fresh saffron, one should [visualize] the Lord Ucchuṣma by means of the powerful, previously mentioned supreme mantra—
he who possesses the luster of a blooming blue lotus, with tawny hair standing erect, and a crown variegated with jewels and gold.
He whose beautiful ear-lobes are pierced by the form of a virtuous impression, whose fine fangs are the spreading crescent of the new moon,
whose crest-jewel is the Lord of Gems, and who is adorned by eight supreme serpent-kings.
With his left hand holding a snake that bears a crest-jewel upon its head.
With his other hand placed upon a skull-bowl completely filled with blood, he sits in a posture having pressed down with the sole of his foot.
His attire is variegated with the gold and jewels of the golden mountain;
his terrifying face is gnawed by the scattering rays of gems.
Seeing the Giver of Wealth (Dhanada) entering with his left side turned toward him, the yogin should instantly become the very form of Jambhala,
resplendent with a vast canopy of shimmering rays; then, with a peaceful mind, he should first place the seed-syllable *Oṃ* upon the lotus of his right hand.
Having visualized the interior of a *bhadraghaṭa* (auspicious jar) born from the syllable *vaṃ*,
one should place the seed-syllable *ja* in the center of this hand, and the syllable *mbha* upon the index finger.
The letter *la* is situated on the seat of the middle fingers; the seed-syllable *ja* is placed upon the ring fingers;
and the syllable *leṃ*, having the form of a drop (*drākṛti*), rests upon the little fingers.
Having meditated upon the root of the hand and performed the *svāhā*-offering with an unwavering state of mind, one should,
according to the instruction, place water into his mouth without hesitation or transgression.
In this manner, being cultivated in due order, [the practitioner] will certainly attain honor, intelligence, wealth, sons, wife, and sovereignty.
The illustrious Jambhala grants every desired object here and dispels all suffering in the other world.

Whatever merit I have gained by performing this, by that may all people quickly become like a wish-fulfilling gem, a vessel of the auspicious jar, and may I myself become the remover of all suffering.
In this existence.
Oṃ aindāṇi mukhabhramari svāhā—this is the *culuka* mantra. Oṃ jluṃ svāhā—this is the water mantra. Oṃ jambhalajalendrāya svāhā.
The *Sādhana* of Ucchuṣma-Jambhala, composed by the scholar and elder Kumārākaragupta, is completed.
Homage to Jambhala!
Having visualized, as before, up to the point of emptiness, one should recite the invocation mantra *oṃ aḥ* (or *āḥ*, or *aṃ*) and contemplate the lunar mandala born from the syllable *a*. Upon that—
One should meditate on a nine-spoked vajra born from a black syllable *hūṃ*; in its center, one should contemplate a syllable *jaṃ* resembling an *indragopa* insect, and from that, the syllable *ā*.

Through the complete transformation of all these, one should visualize the Lord Jambhala as Ucchuṣma, having the form of a child, with unpierced ears, drooping ears, tawny hair standing erect, and a dwarfed stature.
Short and stout, blue in color, with a large belly, frowning brows, and a face made terrifying by fangs;
with Ratnasambhava situated upon his crown, he is encircled by the eight nāgas: Ananta, Takṣaka, Karkoṭaka, Mahāpadma, Kulika, Śaṅkhapāla, Vāsuki, and Padma.
Adorned with ornaments, he has two arms; with his left hand he holds a mongoose disgorging various substances such as jewels,
and with his right hand he holds a skull-cup filled with blood in the gesture of drinking.

[He has] blood-red eyebrows and eyes, and a vajra-seat situated upon the moon; with his right foot he tramples the downward-facing, fallen Dhanada, who is adorned with various ornaments and a jewel-crown.
He is filled with a shimmering garland of vajra-rays. Immediately thereafter, one's own two right feet are the syllable Oṃ in the form of a cart.
In the middle of the hand, one should visualize the syllable *vaṃ* as if holding a *bhadraghaṭa* (auspicious jar); the syllable *jaṃ* on the index finger, *bhaṃ* on the middle finger,
*laṃ* on the ring finger, *jaṃ* on the little finger,
*leṃ* on the thumb, *drāṃ* at the wrist, and the syllable *yaṃ* in that same place, along with *svāhā* near it.
And by performing this meditation, one becomes Śrī Jambhala in person;
and being so, one is capable of dispelling the poverty of sentient beings.
In this regard, the procedure for the gift of water is as follows: having cast a handful of water into one's mouth with the mantra *oṃ jluṃ svāhā*,
and having drawn it back out and placed it in the hand, one offers that water to Jambhala situated below with the mantra *oṃ aindrāṇi mukhabhramari svāhā*.
One should give it. This same procedure applies even when using one hundred and eight handfuls (culuka) of water. Regarding the merit of giving this water:
"Success is declared to be achieved within six months; there is no doubt that this must be done.
What is there that cannot be accomplished by mantras when they are applied according to the prescribed rule?"
Thus ends the sequence for the transformation of water through the meditation on Ucchuṣma-Jambhala.
Homage to the illustrious Ucchuṣma-Jambhala!
May that youth among sages bestow the riches that consist of the emptiness of the Lord of Sages.
He whose feet are kissed by the jewels adorning the crest of the friend of Tryambaka (Śiva), and who is supreme through his abundant splendor.
He is the leader of the jewel-city of non-dual, unsurpassed qualities;
desiring to swiftly lead the world to his own perfection, let him be served.
Therein, first of all, with the intention that "having propitiated the glorious Jambhala through the sequence of attaining the ground,

I shall now establish the ultimate welfare— beginning with the worldly prosperity— of those beings who are his own," one should visualize a bright letter *A*, devoid of a nasal vowel (*anusvāra*) and situated in an empty space.

From that, a moon disc with shimmering rays arises; in its center is the syllable *HŪṂ*, blue in the middle and slightly yellow on the outside, with a mass of shimmering yellow rays and an upward-pointing head. From that arises a vajra, with four prongs below and five above, thus possessing nine prongs in total.
Through the purity of the ninefold scriptural tradition (*pravacana*), others, however,
perform the ritual of syllables like the syllable *HŪṂ*, having unified the upper, lower, and middle as a single needle-point, forming a nine-needled array.
One should visualize [the deity] situated within the moon inside the fist, joined with the syllable *hūṃ*. Then, rays of light radiate from the *hūṃ* and the vajra,
performing the welfare of sentient beings in the ten directions while preceded by the recitation of the mantra *oṃ aḥ*.

Having brought forth the form of Jambhala by the method of leading from another lamp, one should visualize his solitary form before oneself; then, with rays of light, perform the fivefold offering and the confession of misdeeds, up to the stage of equanimity. Immediately thereafter, having dissolved the entire body into the rays of the *hūṃ*-vajra, [one should abide] in the state of being devoid of all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
Within the moon, vajra, and seed-syllable rays whose intrinsic nature is emptiness, one should draw forth [the deities] by means of the radiating *oṃ* and *aḥ*,
and cause them to enter the Blessed One. Immediately after their entry, one should visualize oneself as being instantaneously produced from the moon and the other [elements].

The Blessed One Ucchuṣma has the form of a five-year-old boy, is short of stature, stands upon a double lotus on a moon disc, is adorned with snake ornaments, wears a jewel crown, and from his mouth emits jewels; he stands upon the sleeping Kubera, whose body is yellow and who is emitting jewels from his mouth.
With his right foot treading upon the throbbing forehead and his left foot treading upon both feet, his form is in the *pratyālīḍha* stance; he is naked, with an erect phallus,
a protruding belly, and [his gaze fixed] on the heart.

His gaze is directed toward the skull-cup filled with blood held in his right hand; with his left hand resting upon his left shank, he holds a downward-facing mongoose from which streams of jewels are gushing forth;
his two ears are adorned with unperforated *ḍholla* earrings, and his face is formidable with fangs like a half-moon.
He has three red, circular eyes, a frowning forehead,
and hair standing erect like a flame; his head is marked by the blue Akṣobhya in the earth-touching mudrā,
his hair is bound by Ananta, dark as a tamāla tree, and his ears are adorned with the red Takṣaka.

He whose necklace is made of great lotuses as white as lotus-stalks, whose sacred thread is made of karkoṭaka serpents dark as dūrvā grass, whose girdle is made of the white Vāsuki, whose anklets are made of lotuses as beautiful as kunda flowers,
whose bracelets are made of yellow Śaṅkhapāla, and whose armlets are made of Kulika serpents variegated like smoke— he is blue in color.
Having meditated on [the deity] slightly yellowish on the outside all around, with a shimmering mass of rays,

one should place *oṃ* upon the vajras at the forehead, face, right and left arms, and heart; and within the nine lunar discs situated in the hollows of the right and left calves and the right and left feet.
One should visualize the syllables "Jambhalajalendrāya svāhā" as yellow and emitting yellow rays.

Thereafter, at the moment the breath exits through the nostrils, rays from the syllable Oṃ and other syllables radiate from the heart, and rays from the HŪṂ-vajra flash forth in the four directions; by their mere touch—
p.

578) At the moment when the wind of the mind and mental factors of all sentient beings enters the forms of the Blessed Ones, one should invoke with the syllable *hūṃ* by means of stabilizing the entering mind.

One should cause various jewels located throughout all world-systems to enter into the mouths of the Nākulī and Dhanada [deities]. Then, upon the exhalation of the breath, one should meditate on the Nāgas and others vomiting forth the swallowed jewels before them; in this manner, one should repeatedly perform the radiation and reabsorption, and so forth. Thereafter, when fatigue occurs, one should recite: "Homage to the Three Jewels! Homage to Māṇibhadra!"

One should recite the mantra *mahāyakṣasenāpataye oṃ jambhalajalendrāya svāhā* or the ten-syllable placement mantra (*daśākṣaranyāsa*). At the time of offering water, one should visualize the right hand turned palm-upward, with rays of light from the syllable *vaṃ* in its center transforming the hand into a "blessed jar" (*bhadraghaṭa*), and the base of the hand joined with rays of light from the syllable *oṃ* in the form of a bracelet.
For the Yakṣa; *ḍh*, *b*: *karuṇā*. In the center, *jaṃ*;
on the tips of the index, middle, ring, little, and thumb fingers, the syllables *bha-la-ja-la-in-dra* [ḍh, *b*: Jambhala; ḍh, *b*:
*indrāya*] are placed in sequence; between the syllables *oṃ* and *vaṃ*, the syllable *ya*.

On the left and right sides, there is the syllable *svāhā*. One should meditate upon these—beginning with the syllable *oṃ*—as being situated in the cavities of their respective locations, resting upon the moon, yellow in color, and emitting yellow rays.
Having placed his hand, which holds water and flowers within it, near his mouth, he recites: *oṃ aindrāṇi mukhabhamari svāhā*.

One should consecrate [the water] seven times with the mantra. Then, as the water is being offered by the outstretched hand, it is made yellow by the rays of the syllable *jaṃ* entering through the mouth and by the rays of the *vajra-hūṃkāra* residing in the heart; emerging from the mouth of the *vajra*, it instantly becomes present before this Blessed One who stands facing him, held in the hand.
One should offer [the oblation] one hundred and eight times into the cavity of the image’s mouth with the mantra *oṃ jluṃ svāhā*, and seven times with the mantra beginning with *namo ratnatrayāya*.

Having recited "Namo ratnatrayāya" and so forth just once, one should offer a bali-oblation to the Blessed One with roasted rice grains mixed with molasses and other such items. Having thus performed the practice according to one's ability—either at the three junctions of the day or at a single junction—one should perform praise and the dedication of merit. That which is thus consecrated...
One should dismiss the Blessed One with "Oṃ Vajramuḥ. Furthermore, on the full moon day of Kārttika, Phālguna, Vaiśākha, or Āṣāḍha,
or on any other auspicious day, one should take a piece of stone and instantly manifest the form of the Blessed One.

Having performed worship, one who has undertaken the religious observances (vratadhara) should have an image fashioned by a single artisan in a single day through the process of chiseling; and having visualized oneself here in sequence as the form of the Blessed One, complete with the ritual placement of syllables (akṣaranyāsa).

The instruction is that one should propitiate [the deity] by means of water offerings and so forth. At that time, however, one should not dismiss [the deity], for one should honor the Blessed One who remains eternally present in the form of the image.
Thus concludes the Sādhana of Ucchuṣma-Jambhala composed by Paṇḍita Abhayākaragupta.

May the glorious Lord of Waters, who has shaken off the entire web of conceptual constructions, whose self is permeated by compassion and loving-kindness, and who constantly bestows wealth, protect you.
To you, the Blessed One, who are yourself free from fear yet terrified by the fear of worldly existence.

First of all, the mantra-practitioner, having performed the going for refuge to the Three Jewels and so forth, should recite: *oṃ svabhāvaśuddhāḥ sarvadharmāḥ svabhāvaśuddho 'ham* ("Oṃ! All phenomena are pure by nature; I am pure by nature"). Furthermore, [he should contemplate] the entire triple world...

One should contemplate [all things] as being like an illusion. Afterwards, upon a double-lotus (viśvapadma) transformed from the syllable *paṃ*, there is a moon-maṇḍala transformed from the syllable *aṃ*. Above that is the syllable *jaṃ*, resembling blazing gold and radiating light in all directions with a multitude of various kinds of wealth. By means of that, one should visualize oneself transformed into the form of Jambhala, with the color of shining gold.
Having visualized oneself as Jambhala— dwarfish, adorned with all ornaments, wearing a jewel crown, and holding a mongoose and a citron in his right and left hands respectively—
one should then contemplate the syllable *jaṃ* above the citron held in the right hand, and above that, streams [of nectar].
Or one should cast [the water] into rivers and the like, or offer water to another person who has that same form as Jambhala. The mantra is: *oṃ jaṃ svāhā*.
By such offerings of water, the Lord of Wealth (Jambhala) becomes pleased in heart.
Therefore, one who is intent on effort should achieve fame, for it bestows inexhaustible means of livelihood.
The *Śrījambhalasādhana* is completed.
The work of Sujana Bhadra.
Instantly, preceded by emptiness,
[he arises] from the transformation of a red syllable *HŪṂ* as a blue and red face on the right and left, born from a red vajra.
His face and entire body are white; he holds a red vajra and sword in his right hands, and in his left, nine emerald lotuses; with his two primary arms, he embraces his consort of his own nature;
he is seated upon a moon-disc on a double-petalled universal lotus, possesses moon-like radiance, sits in the vajra-paryaṅka posture, and is presided over by Akṣobhya.

Having visualized oneself as Vajrasattva in essence— the form of great bliss, established from the beginningless cycle of existence, consisting of the waters of all the Tathāgatas, overwhelmed by compassion that effects the welfare of immeasurable worlds, shimmering with hosts of infinite lords of sages who are like reflections, and possessing a crown of radiant rubies that is devoid of intrinsic nature— [End of sentence/verse]
Having caused a host of Tathāgatas, drawn in by rays of light issuing from the syllable *HŪṂ* situated in the moon of his heart, to enter his own seed-syllable,

that very [syllable] takes the form of lunar fluid emerging through the door of the secret jewel; it becomes stable within the lotus of Wisdom (*prajñā*), and through its transformation, it arises as the Lord, born from a citron fruit produced from the yellow syllable *JAṂ*.
The noble Jambhala holds a citron and a sword in his right hands, and a mongoose and a jewel in his left;
he embraces his own consort with two arms, wears a crown of Vajrasattva, is pot-bellied, has the form of a short dwarf,
and has his primary face placed within the opening of the secret vajra-jewel.

Visualizing the host of Tathāgatas drawn forth by the rays from the seed-syllable at the heart, one should satisfy Jambhala with a stream of moon-melted [nectar] issuing from the seed-syllable and the vajra. When offering water,
one should rely upon the Blessed One and offer it with a conch-like vessel filled with the liquid of the five nectars, empowered by the mantra *vuṃ āṃ jiṃ khaṃ hūṃ*.
One should cause [the deity] to swell by reciting the mantra while pouring a hundred mouthfuls of water. There, this is the mantra: Oṃ Āḥ Jaṃ, give me wealth, Hūṃ.
[The Jambhala Sādhana.]
Meditated upon within the interior of a moon disc, arising from the first of all vowels,
he has a radiance like molten gold in the center of the forehead.
It bestows abundant prosperity, destroys those who are hostile,
brings all mantras under one's control, and increases good fortune and health.
The syllable *jluṃ* (or *hlūṃ*) is indeed all-pervasive and bestows the fruit of all desires;
having thus meditated upon the vajra in the hand, one should offer water according to one's wish.
He too shall surely become Jambhala, devoted to the welfare of all sentient beings.
|| The Ritual Procedure for Subjugating Jambhala ||
Seated upon a moon-maṇḍala seat cultivated by the syllable *ka*, facing forward,
together with the fluids of Śāśvata and the others arising from the five seed-syllables beginning with *vuṃ*.
One should offer water mixed together while withdrawing the index finger;
having visualized Jambhava in front and Jambhala upon his head.
Thus concludes the instruction on the gift of water to Jambhala.
Homage to the illustrious Vajramahākāla. [Repeated for ḍ, dh, dh, k, g, and ḍh, kh.]
Then the Blessed One brought forth the sādhanā of Vajramahākāla from his own body, speech, and mind:
"He is perfected from the reality of the syllable HŪṂ; he has two arms and one face, is black in color, possesses great flames, and holds a flaying knife and a skull-cup."
Wearing a garland of severed heads as a necklace, terrifying and formidable with his fangs,
he had a dwarfish form and great splendor, with blood flowing from his mouth.
He who is always hostile toward the teacher, who is angry even with the Three Jewels,
and who destroys many sentient beings, is devoured by Mahākāla.
One should cause him to cut off the flesh of his limbs and drink from a stream of his blood; or else,
having settled upon his head, one should cut it away even down to the size of a sesame seed.
One should offer a bali-oblation to Mahākāla consisting of a piece of meat, wine, flowers, incense, and ointment, using indeed the nectar of the five meats.

The mantra: Oṃ! To Mahākāla, who assists in the teaching, who is saluted by the host of Mothers dwelling in the cremation ground of Sadyomukti; this is the final time; if you remember your vow, then devour, devour, devour this wicked one named so-and-so, who harms the Three Jewels! KHA KHA KHĀHI!

Eat! Kill! Kill! Seize! Seize! Bind! Bind! Strike! Strike! Burn! Burn! Cook! Cook! Slay, slay in a single day! Hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ! [Seize] the offering of all yakṣas, rākṣasas, bhūtas, pretas, piśācas, and those possessed by madness!

"Seize, seize my success! Grant peace! Grant protection! [This is] the *bali* offering. Having fashioned a figure of *kuśa* grass with this mantra, and having made an image of the enemy using poison, *rājikā* (black mustard), and the three filths (*tripaṭṭaka*), one should fill its body with thorns and heat it over a fire of *khadira* wood; he will be seized by fever and released at that very moment. Or else:

With a paste made from *viṣarājikā* and *citraka*, one should draw a *dharmodaya* on a fragment of a skull and surround it with eight *oṃ* syllables. In the center, one should interlace the name of the person to be targeted (*sādhya*). One should then heat it over a fire; [the target] will be seized by fever. If one washes it with milk, liberation occurs.

Now the procedure for meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*) is described: having drawn a triangular mandala and worshipped it with the five offerings (*pañcopacāra*), the preceptor, assuming a black attire and applying a sectarian mark (*tilaka*), becomes one with [the deity] while maintaining the previously mentioned visualization; thus, the preceptor himself becomes Śrī Mahākāla, and subsequently, through his own rays, [he becomes] Kālī.

Accompanied by the five yoginīs— Karālī, Varālī, Kaṅkālī, Mahākālī, and [the fifth]— who assume forms of great sport and carry knives and skull-cups, he goes with the speed of the wind, hacking at flesh, drinking blood,
cutting open entrails, tearing out the navel, and reducing [the body] to the size of a sesame seed.
The instrument [is] blazing with anger.
Thus ends the *Mahākālasādhana*.
p.

585) Following the previously described procedure, immediately after the meditation on emptiness (*śūnyatā*), upon a universal lotus and sun disk, there is the syllable *HŪṂ* of black color; from its complete transformation arises the venerable Lord Mahākāla.

He has two arms, one face, and is black in color; he has three eyes and great radiance, holding a curved knife and a skull-cup in his right and left hands respectively; his tawny hair stands upright and is adorned with a garland of severed heads, and above it he wears five skull-cups.

Having instantly visualized oneself as having a short stature, with a face dripping with blood, terrifying and formidable with fangs, adorned with serpents as ornaments and a sacrificial thread (*yajñopavīta*), one should recite the mantra.
There, this is the mantra: *oṃ mahākāla hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*. [With] the juice of poison and blood...
Having offered incense of white mustard seeds to Mahākāla,
one should present the bali offering consisting of meat, jambu-fruit, liquor, flowers, incense, and ointment.
One should offer a bali-oblation to Mahākāla with the nectar of the five meats.

With this mantra—namely: *Oṃ mahākālāya śāsanopakāriṇe | eṣo'paścimakālo'yam ratnatrayāpakāriṇam | yadi pratijñāṃ smarasi tadā imaṃ duṣṭaṃ kha kha khāhi khāhi māra māra gṛhṇa gṛhṇa bandha bandha hana hana daha daha paca paca dinaikena*— [Recite this: "Oṃ, to Mahākāla, the benefactor of the teaching! This is the final time; [act against] the one who harms the Three Jewels! If you remember your vow, then devour, devour this wicked one! Kill, kill! Seize, seize! Bind, bind! Strike, strike! Burn, burn! Cook, cook! In a single day!"

"Kill! Hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ! Regarding this, the ritual procedure is as follows: having fashioned an image of the target using the three pungent substances (trikaṭuka), filling its limbs with thorns, and smearing it according to rule with poison and black mustard seeds, one should heat it over a fire.
By means of the target's name, that person becomes invisible and perishes at that very moment. Now—
He who is always hostile toward the teacher and is enraged even at the Three Jewels; [as noted in k, g, ḍh, b: he who has destroyed the Three Jewels].
The destroyer of many beings is devoured by Mahākāla.
They cut off the flesh of his limbs and likewise drink his blood.
Having placed it upon the head, one should shave off only a portion the size of a sesame seed.
Thus, and so forth, the mantra should be recited in detail.
The *Śrīmahākālasādhana* is completed. [This *sādhana* is repeated after this in K and G.]
Homage to Mahākāla!

Having fashioned Mahākāla from nimba wood, with hands encircled by a knife and a skull-cup, hair standing erect, a crown of skulls, his body adorned with serpent ornaments, a red face, and a mouth formidable with fangs.

Having visualized [the deity] standing upon a corpse-seat, with his waist covered by a tiger-skin, encircled by a garland of severed heads, wearing a necklace of human heads, and rising up—on the eighth day of the dark fortnight, one should begin the practice with a knife in the midst of a terrible darkness. This [deity], whose form is facing south, should be established; then, facing east, one should recite the mantra.
Having offered ten thousand oblations with the substance of the pledge (*samayadravya*), one should offer *guggulu* incense.
Having arranged a profusion of various flowers, one should recite: *Oṃ maṇimaṇḍitatriśūlahasta ehyehi mahākāla sarvaśatruniryātaye jvareṇa gṛhṇāpaya gṛhṇāpaya*.

p. 587) *Hūṃ phaṭ*. One should recite [the mantra] while fasting. Having caused a fever, one should recite the mantra for one's own benefit. An offering (*bali*) should be presented as before: *Oṃ mahākāla hana hana vajreṇa svāhā*. One should recite it one hundred thousand times (*lakṣam ekaṃ*). *Oṃ mahākāla*...

"HANA HANA VAJREṆA MAMA KĀRYAṂ KURU SVĀHĀ. One should recite this two hundred thousand times. "OṂ MAHĀKĀLA HANA HANA VAJREṆA ETAT PREṢAYĀMI KARISYATHA SVĀHĀ. One should recite this three hundred thousand times. "OṂ MAHĀKĀLA HĀHĀ HAHĀ RAKṢA RAKṢA BALIṂ GṚHṆA KĀRYAṂ KURU JAḤ. Having performed the supreme *sādhana* of Vajrayoginī, [one should recite as follows].
One should accomplish Mahākāla.
[The Sadhana of Mahākāla]
His eye has the dense luster of blue lotuses, tamāla leaves, and collyrium; it is as red as the flames of the western rays spreading boundlessly like the newly risen sun,
wandering within the interior of his mouth which is brilliant and formidable with the tips of his fangs.
Bhīṣmaśrīrasana, Tanūttama, Mahākāla, and Jagatpiṅgala.

One should meditate upon true loving-kindness, compassion, and likewise sympathetic joy; thereafter, one should practice equanimity. Then, by the command of the glorious Guru, one should perform the confession of all defilements and so forth. Having contemplated emptiness—which consists of the wisdom of the infinite Sugatas and possesses all aspects— [The practitioner should then recite: oṃ svabhāvaśuddhāḥ sarvadharmāḥ svabhāvaśuddho 'ham | Then, visualizing oneself as the deity: oṃ śūnyatājñānavajrasvabhāvātmako 'ham | Next, from the syllable *bhrūṃ* arises a vajra seat, from which a lotus and moon disc arise. Upon that, from the syllable *aḥ*, there appears a skull-cup, within which are the five meats and five nectars. From the syllable *haṃ* comes fire, from *yaṃ* wind, and from *raṃ* water. One should contemplate [the deity] possessing a clearly blue syllable *hūṃ*, like that of the Sambhogakāya.
That seed-syllable is the Blessed One, who fills the sky with a garland of flames from his fierce rays,
whose excellent form possesses the shadow of a mass of billowing darkness, and who is most terrifying.

590) Having then fashioned another triangular pit (*kuṇḍa*),
he— his hair disheveled and his body facing west— [should place] eight thorns within it.
The wrathful one, Prakhannamuṇḍa, is present; let the mantra-practitioner certainly offer oblations into the fire in accordance with the expansion of that rite,
and the accomplishment of his heart’s desire will surely come to pass, just as it has been spoken by the Buddhas.
Having prostrated at the feet of the master Līlāvajra and placed his command upon my head like a garland, I have completed this *sādhana* of the Protector of the City of the Jinas;
by whatever merit has been gained through this work by the compassionate poet, may it [be for the benefit of all].
The entire world was submerged in the surging waves of the great river of the overflowing nectar of compassion of Viśvāntara.
Oṃ mahākālāya hūṃ phaṭ.
Thus ends the Vajramahākālasādhana.
This work is the composition of the poet named Karuṇa.
Homage to the illustrious Mahākāla! He is mounted upon the son of Gaṅgā (Ganeśa), standing in the pratyālīḍha posture;
he is short-statured, with a protruding belly and a stout body, possessing a luster like that of crushed collyrium.
With blazing tawny hair standing erect, adorned by eight wrathful serpents,
with a fierce tongue protruding from fangs, and a garland of skulls upon his head.
Adorned with a garland of fresh human heads and the five mudrās,
wearing a tiger-skin garment, he is terrifying, three-eyed, and has a distorted face.
Having one face and a terrifying mouth, six arms, and a wrathful form,
he is born from the sound of the syllable *HŪṂ* and dwells in the midst of the eight cremation grounds.
In his right hands, he holds a vajra-marked curved knife, a rosary, and likewise a ḍamaru drum; in his left hands, he holds a skull-cup, a trident, and likewise a vajra-noose.
Greatly fierce with the radiance of emptiness, causing even fear to be afraid;
a great wrath crowned with garlands of flames, the destroyer of all the wicked.
I bow down to that which is served by spirits, ghosts, and piśācas, by the lords of the planets and the protectors of the Jinas, and by yakṣas, rākṣasas, and kumbhāṇḍas.

The wise one should accomplish [the rite] according to the prescribed method for the sake of destroying those enemies who harm the Three Jewels and possess malicious intentions— those who are destroyers of Māra.
Thus ends the *Sādhana* of Six-Armed Mahākāla. [G adds "This is the composition" after the colophon, though it does not mention the author.]
Homage to Śrī Mahākāla!
He is blue in color, mounted upon a corpse, standing in the pratyālīḍha posture, and possesses four arms;
he holds a curved knife, a skull-cup, a sword, and a radiant khaṭvāṅga staff.
In the *Senābhañjana-tantras*, for the purpose of agitating the weapons of battle,
the wise one should accomplish Mahākāla according to the prescribed ritual procedure.
Thus concludes the Sadhana of Four-Armed Mahākāla.
Homage to the illustrious Mahākāla!
He stands in the center of a sun-disk upon a universal lotus, in the pratyālīḍha posture, with two arms.
Dark-complexioned, most fierce, and adorned with ornaments of serpents.
He holds a knife, a skull-cup, and a trident, adorned with a long garland of severed heads;
he possesses great splendor, drips with blood, has a lolling tongue, and is terrifying.
Thus concludes the sādhana of Mahākāla.
This is the work of Sumatibhadra.
Oṃ, homage to the illustrious Gaṇapati!

Oṃ āḥ gaḥ, bring about peace for me! Hrīṃ bhrūṃ hūṃ svāhā—this is the heart mantra. Oṃ, O Rāga, grant success, grant success! Make all my aims favorable, make them favorable! Hūṃ ja ja svāhā—this is the near-heart mantra. Oṃ āḥ gaḥ.

HŪṂ SVĀHĀ | OṂ VARADAKARĀYA SVĀHĀ | OṂ VAKTRAIKADAṂṢTRE VIGHNEŚA HŪṂ PHAṬ SVĀHĀ | OṂ GAṆAPATYAI SVĀHĀ | OṂ ŚĀNTIṄKARI BHRŪṂ HĀRIṆEŚAḌĀKINI HŪṂ PHAṬ SVĀHĀ | OṂ JAḤ MESI HŪṂ KURU VAṂ OṂ ANYE HOḤ JA JA SVĀHĀ ||

Then follows the visualization of Gaṇapati: one should meditate upon the Blessed Lord Gaṇapati as red in color, wearing a crown of matted locks, adorned with all ornaments, possessing twelve arms, a protruding belly, and a single face.
Performing the *tāṇḍava* dance in the half-lotus posture, three-eyed and single-tusked, with an axe, arrow, and noose in his right hands—
this concludes the *sādhana* of Gaṇapati.
Oṃ, homage to Tārā!
Seated in the center of the lunar disc within the pericarp of a universal lotus,
she is fair-complexioned, with two arms and one face, and is established in the *lalitāsana* posture.

One should meditate upon the Mother Tārā, the Universal Mother, the Compassionate One, adorned by the Victors, holding blue lotuses marked with the hand-symbols, endowed with garments and ornaments, and decorated with golden jewelry.
Lakṣmī bestows victory and triumph; she is the giver of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
On the right, she is yellowish-red, three-eyed, with four arms and one face;
her right hands hold the gesture of fearlessness and a rosary, while she carries the bowl of the Victor and an *aśoka* branch.
She is blue, has one face, four arms, and is terrifying;
she is adorned with a flaying knife, a skull-cup, a sword, and a lotus stalk.
Thus concludes the *Saddharmāvatāriṇī*, the sādhanā of the illustrious Tārā.
O Goddess, you alone are Girijā; you alone are the skillful Padmāvatī; you are Tāriṇī, the mother of the gods.
Pervading the three worlds, you are the single form of the universe; homage be to you from our mind, body, and speech!
You are praised in the three vehicles as the "ten perfections" (daśapāramitā), and for those of the extensive vehicle, as the "emptiness of the jar" (*kalaśūnyatā*).
O Mother, filled with the nectar of the fluid of wisdom (*prajñā*), who are ever-active in its application—homage be to you from our mind, body, and speech!
Not so.

O you whose essence is innate bliss and joy, the Mother of the Universe who does not revolve apart from the three wheels, possessing the luster of lightning, accessible through gnosis yet devoid of a [physical] heart— homage be to you with our mind, body, and speech!
O Goddess, what need is there for much talk from me in this matter?
Whatever is desired at whatever time, you are the giver of all fruits; salutations be unto you!
Praise to Tārā
Oṃ, homage to the venerable Śrīpīṭhatārā!
She who carries with her left hands a bell, a khaṭvāṅga staff, a red lotus, and a beautiful jewel... [she] bears [these].
May Sandhyā protect us here— she who begins with Vaktrākā, who is adorned with a shimmering sword and a *ḍamaru* drum,

well-clothed, three-eyed, the mistress of ritual action (*karmeśā*), possessing a body like Varuṇa and accompanied by the moon, joyful, of two-fold lineage, with a radiant continuity like the luster of *dūrvā* grass and gold, and the Tārā of the sacred seat (*pīṭha*).
Yellow, green, red, white, crimson, and dark-blue, holding leaves, with a face like the reflection of the dawn,
foremost in passion, grey-haired, delighting in an excellent seat, her right hands adorned with a hand-drum and a skull-cup.
With a small flag and a bell, the left hand becomes practiced;
these [ornaments], originating from the wrist and the forearm, become beneficial in eight ways in succession.

With the upper half of her body red on the left and the beautiful right half green, she flows; with a wheel and a curved knife in her right hands, and a banner and a blood-filled skull-cup in her left hands, she rests upon the moon.
The other twelve, beginning with Śiṣyā, are located in the other enclosure.

May the deity who arises from the first letter of her own name, who has a single head upon her body and dispels the fear of worldly existence, protect you— she who, at the time of the sun, stands in the *sālīḍha* posture, possesses matted hair, is the sovereign of that place, and bears in her right and left hands the Kāmboja and other [weapons], as well as a skull-cup, a banner, and a ritual vessel.
May those who possess faith, whose pure majesty consists of mindfulness and meditation,
who effect the destruction of the aggregates, the afflictions, the gods, the sons of Māra, and the hungry ghosts, grant the arising of all colors in every direction.
Thus concludes the sādhana of Pīṭhatārā.
Oṃ tāre tuttāre ture hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ tāṃ khāṃ hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ ānanda oṃ paramānanda oṃ viramānanda oṃ sahajānanda hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ tāre tuttāre ture ||
To the sovereign of the entire seat, grant me the accomplishment of the entire seat! *ture hūṃ phaṭ*. In the center:
*oṃ surateśvari hūṃ phaṭ*, *oṃ suratasundari hūṃ phaṭ*, *oṃ suratacandri hūṃ phaṭ*, *oṃ suratamālini hūṃ phaṭ*, *oṃ suratakāmini hūṃ phaṭ*.

Oṃ suratabhakṣaṇi hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ suratakāmini hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ suratogre hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ suratottame hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ śikhā hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ bhīme hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ śikhaṇḍī hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ karālī hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ jaṭilī hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ raudrī hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ jaṭī hūṃ phaṭ |
Phaṭ! Oṃ Caṇḍī hūṃ phaṭ! Oṃ Māṇḍī hūṃ phaṭ! Oṃ Vikaṭotkaṭā hūṃ phaṭ!
Oṃ Kiriṭī hūṃ phaṭ! Oṃ Nartakī hūṃ phaṭ! (12) Oṃ Kambojī hūṃ phaṭ! Oṃ Pukkaśī hūṃ phaṭ!
Oṃ Caṇḍovī hūṃ phaṭ! Oṃ Homohī hūṃ phaṭ! (4) Thus is the Flower-Placement (puṣpanyāsa).

Oṃ! Homage to the Blessed One, Sovereign Lady of the Vajra Seat, dwelling in the center of the moon within the lotus of the celestial chariot-wheel; Sovereign Lady of the Great Family, whose nature is the five families, four-faced, twelve-eyed, eight-armed, holding a vajra, wheel, bell, sword, jewel, axe, khaṭvāṅga, ḍamaru, and utpala.
Seated in the half-lotus dance posture, surrounded by twenty-four yoginīs, possessing a form of compassionate wrath, affectionate toward devotees,
dwelling in the divine garden, and bestower of all desires.

Accomplishing all aims, enter, enter! Pervade, pervade! Strike, strike all obstacles! Cook, cook all Māras! Burn, burn all bhūtas, vetālas, kumbhāṇḍas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, piśācas, apsarases, evil grahas, cruel ones, and so forth!
Shatter, shatter my desires! Fulfill them, O Goddess Tārā, Sovereign of all the grounds, whose radiant form consists of the moon, sun, and fire,
who possesses the singular nature of suchness— *tuttāre*, to you, *ture*, *hūṃ phaṭ*!
The Garland Mantra of the Bhagavatī.
Oṃ, homage to the glorious Mahākāla!

Following the cultivation of loving-kindness and the other [immeasurables], and immediately after emptiness, one should meditate on oneself as the Blessed Lord Mahākāla with sixteen arms, arising from the syllable HŪṂ upon a sun disk produced from the syllable REPHA.

He has eight faces, twenty-four eyes, four legs, and sixteen arms; with his right hands he holds a flaying knife, a vajra, an elephant hide, a mallet, a trident, a sword, and the staff of Yama; and with his left hands he holds a skull-cup filled with blood, an elephant hide, a bell, a goad, a white fly-whisk, a *ḍamaru* drum, and a human head.
With his remaining two arms, he embraces Prajñā; he is short and black, his mouth filled with the sounds "hā hā," "hī hī," "he he," and "ho ho";
he is extremely fierce, embodies the three bodies (trikāya), and wears a crown of the five Buddhas.

Adorned with a garland of human skulls, she causes fear to worldly existence. To the east is Mahāmāyā Maheśvarī, trampling upon a lion, standing in the *pratyālīḍha* posture, and possessing four arms; in her left hands, she holds a skull-cup and a second [hand] holds a *ḍamaruka* drum.

She plays [a musical instrument] with her right hand and holds a mallet in the second; she is black in color, with loose hair, three eyes, and protruding fangs. To the south is Yamadūtī, blue in color, with four arms; with her two right hands she holds a lotus-stalk and a knife, and with her two left hands she holds a skull-cup filled with blood and a fly-whisk.

Standing in the *pratyālīḍha* posture, treading upon Yama’s buffalo, naked, with disheveled hair—Kāladūtī is in the west. She holds a skull-cup and a human head in her left hands, and a mallet and a trident in her right; she is mounted on a horse, stands in the *pratyālīḍha* posture, is red in color, has disheveled hair, and possesses three eyes. All these deities...
With protruding fangs and adorned with serpent ornaments, there are four goddesses in the four corners:
in the southeast corner is Kālikā, black in color, with two arms, holding a flaying knife and a skull-cup, standing in the pratyālīḍha posture, mounted upon a corpse;
in the southwest corner is Carcikā, red in color.

Holding a curved knife and a skull-cup in her hands, everything is as before; in the northwest corner (Vāyavya), Caṇḍeśvarī is yellow in color, mounted upon a corpse, holding a fierce deer in her hand, and standing in the *prayālīḍha* posture.
In the northeast corner (Īśāna), Kuliśeśvarī is white in color, holding a vajra-staff in her hand.

Mounted upon a corpse and standing in the *pratyālīḍha* posture, all the goddesses are naked, with protruding fangs, three eyes, and loose hair. Surrounded by these eight yoginīs is the corpse of the blissful Sadvajra, established in the samādhi of emptiness, who stands in the *pratyālīḍha* posture treading upon Vajrabhairava.
Having meditated upon the Blessed One in such a manner, one should recite the mantra. In this regard, the mantra is as follows: Oṃ ṣoḍaśabhujāya hūṃ hūṃ kili kili.
To the fierce, terrible, fanged, and formidable Bhairava, the bestower of all accomplishments: *hili hili kili kili he svāhā*. One should recite this mantra.
By the constant recitation of this king of mantras, one attains Buddhahood in this very life.

By reciting [the mantra] ten thousand times, one gains the memory of past lives (*jātismaratva*), and the eight great accomplishments (*mahāsiddhi*) are attained. Now, if one wishes to offer a sacrificial oblation (*bali*), one should visualize the Blessed One together with his retinue before oneself and offer the oblation eight times with the *balimantra*. In this regard, the *balimantra* is as follows:
*Oṃ namo mahākālāya mahādaṃṣṭrotkaṭabhairavāya*.

To the Lord of Great Wrath, whose hair is tawny and upright, who has sixteen arms and twenty-four eyes: Oṃ turu turu kha kha khāhi khāhi! Accept, accept this offering! Haha hihi huhū hehai hohau haṃhaḥ!
O Mahāvajrabuddha, establish me within your body; remain, remain!

Ṭaṭa ṭaṭa maṭa maṭa kaṭa kaṭa! Cause [them] to sound, cause [them] to sound! Roar, roar! To the Lord of Terrific Great Anger, destroy, destroy all enemies! O Tamer of wicked beings, protect, protect me! Grant, grant [me everything]! Destroy, destroy all! Hūṃ hai! Kili kili! Bhaḥ! Hūṃ hūṃ! And all yakṣas and piśācas!

O Rākṣasas and Kinnaras, bring about complete peace, bring about peace! Haṃ haḥ! Destroy, destroy! To Mahākāla, who has the form of Time, the most terrifying one—subdue, subdue, tame, tame! O destroyer of all wicked beings, deliver, deliver the terrified ones to the Lord of Nāgas! Tāraya tāraya!
Destroy, destroy! Deliver, deliver! Haḥ haḥ! Kaṭaḥ kaṭaḥ! Khaṭaḥ khaṭaḥ! Phaṭaḥ phaṭaḥ! Cut, cut!
Strike, strike! Burn, burn! Cook, cook! Churn, churn! Destroy, destroy! Ghaṭa ghaṭa! Move, move! Trāṃ! O Wrath! Svāhā! This is the *balimantra*.
